design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analysis of randomised and quasi-randomised trials of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT: gum, patch, tablet or lozenge, inhalator, nasal spray, oral spray, combinations, or a choice of products) against placebo or no NRT, in people who smoked cigarettes and were motivated to quit. Primary outcome: abstinence from smoking at 6 months or longer (strictest definition available per trial, biochemically confirmed where available; people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). 136 studies included; 133 comparisons (131 trials) with 64,640 participants in the main pool. Search July 2017. Adverse events were collected from included and some excluded trials but pooled only for chest pain or palpitations. This version is the NRT-versus-control half of a review that was split in 2017 (the comparisons between forms and doses went to a companion review, Theodoulou et al. 2023).
can_establish: The average relative effect of offering NRT, against placebo or no NRT with the same behavioural support, on abstinence 6 months or more after the start of a quit attempt in people motivated to quit who agreed to take part in randomised trials, overall and by product, support level and setting, as of a July 2017 search.
cannot_establish: Effects in people who are not trying to quit, in people who smoke fewer than about 10 to 15 cigarettes a day (the authors say there is little evidence), in adolescents (two small trials) or in everyday use outside trials; head-to-head differences between products (the product comparisons are indirect subgroups of trials against control); how often side effects occur (adverse events were not pooled except chest pain or palpitations) or whether rare serious harms are raised; whether the pooled size is smaller than estimated because of unpublished trials or manufacturer funding (the authors say it may be); effects beyond the 6 to 24 months of follow-up.

sample.recruitment: Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group Specialised Register (CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and hand-searched conference abstracts), searched 6 July 2017; 1,059 records screened in the latest search. Trials were run in North America (62), Europe (56), Australasia (2), Japan (2), South America (2), Iran (2), several regions (2) and one each in India, Syria, Taiwan and Thailand (Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 1st paragraph). Participants were typically adults who smoked at least 15 cigarettes a day, average age 40 to 50, with similar numbers of men and women, recruited mostly as community volunteers answering advertisements and treated in clinical settings, and from primary care (21 trials), hospitals (13), smoking clinics and settings meant to resemble over-the-counter sale (4 trials). Median trial size 257 (under 50 to over 8,000).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomised or quasi-randomised trials of NRT against placebo or no NRT in people who smoked and were motivated to quit, with a cessation outcome at 6 months or longer (shorter follow-up allowed only for pregnancy trials, and then not in the main analysis). Excluded: trials without a cessation outcome, with follow-up under 6 months, of smoking reduction rather than quitting, trials in which every arm received NRT or NRT was compared with bupropion (moved to other reviews; 34 earlier trials removed), and trials whose control group had access to free NRT.
sample.demographics: Mostly adults; two trials in adolescents (Moolchan 2005; Scherphof 2014); six trials only in pregnant women and four only in women; two trials in African-American participants; single trials in people with alcohol dependence, in methadone-maintained smokers, in people with a history of drug use, in cardiac disease, in hospital patients with cardiac or pulmonary illness and in people with serious mental illness. Average cigarettes a day above 20 in most trials.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. People lost to follow-up or dropping out were counted as still smoking, which the authors say gives conservative absolute quit rates; attrition in NRT groups was generally similar to or lower than in control groups (Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 1st paragraph). Per-trial attrition sits in the risk-of-bias tables of the Characteristics of included studies, which were searched but not read trial by trial.
sample.selection_effects: A single register was searched, and manufacturers were last written to when the review was first prepared. Trials needed at least 6 months of follow-up and a cessation outcome. Participants were people motivated to quit who accepted randomisation to a possible placebo, typically heavier smokers, and most were treated in clinical or clinic-like settings; in about 60% of trials a drug company funded or supplied the study product (editors' count from the study notes, see key findings). Six trials rest on abstracts, conference presentations or registry entries only. The authors report some funnel-plot asymmetry and say unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing.

exposure.measurement: Allocation to an NRT product or product combination in the trial; adherence was not synthesised (compliance is described trial by trial in the Characteristics tables, which were not read in full).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported, not recommendations. Gum trials mostly used the 2 mg strength (a few the 4 mg strength for more dependent participants), usually for 2 to 3 months (range 3 weeks to 12 months). Patch trials usually used up to 15 mg over 16 hours or 21 mg over 24 hours for at least 3 weeks to 3 months, with one trial offering a 52.5 mg patch among options. Lozenges, sublingual tablets, nasal and oral sprays and inhalators were each tested in 1 to 8 trials. Seven trials tested a patch plus a short-acting form and seven offered a choice of products.
exposure.polysubstance: Single trials enrolled people with alcohol dependence (Hughes 2003), methadone-maintained smokers (Stein 2013) and people with a history of drug use (Heydari 2013); other substance use was not analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinence was measured at 6 months or more after the start of treatment (a 6-week window around the 6- or 12-month visit was allowed); 117 trials (87%) biochemically validated self-reported abstinence at longest follow-up, mostly by expired-air carbon monoxide with cut-offs from under 4 to 11 parts per million.

comparison.controls: Placebo product in most trials; 43 trials had no matched placebo (24 gum, 9 patch, 6 choice-of-product, 3 combination and 1 lozenge trial) and two more had both a placebo and a no-placebo control, which were combined.
comparison.matching: Randomisation (adequate allocation concealment reported in 39 trials, 29%); all trials gave both arms the same behavioural support, though the amount of support differed between trials.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomised, so baseline differences are by chance within each trial. Results by baseline dependence, motivation, prior quit attempts, sex or other participant traits were not pooled (subgroup results are uncommon in trial reports); the authors cite two earlier meta-analyses of sex differences that covered a subset of trials.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Whether control participants used NRT or other cessation aids outside the trial was not systematically extracted; one trial was excluded because its control group had access to and used free NRT at high levels.

outcomes.instruments: Abstinence at 6 months or longer (12-month data used where available): sustained abstinence in 89 trials (66%), point prevalence only in 39 (29%), unclear in 6; biochemical validation in 117 trials.
outcomes.validity_norms: Carbon monoxide cut-offs varied from under 4 to 11 ppm; four trials counted people smoking 2 or 3 cigarettes a week as abstinent (dropping them changed nothing); 21 trials did not validate all self-reports (dropping the 17 that never attempted validation changed nothing).
outcomes.operationalization: Quit = the strictest abstinence definition each trial reported, with anyone lost to follow-up counted as smoking. Adverse events were tabulated by study (Appendix 3) and were not pooled except for chest pain or palpitations.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Subgroup analyses by product, abstinence definition, support intensity and setting are described as checks on consistency rather than as hypothesis tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The review authors did not blind themselves to trial results or arms (stated). Within trials, 44 (33%) were judged low risk and 23 (17%) high risk of performance and detection bias, mostly because there was no blinding; the authors did not assess whether blinding held.

analysis.effect_sizes: Fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI, abstinence at 6 months or longer. All forms pooled: RR 1.55 (1.49 to 1.61), 133 comparisons, 64,640 participants, I2 39%. Gum 1.49 (1.40 to 1.60), 56, 22,581, I2 40%. Patch 1.64 (1.53 to 1.75), 51, 25,754, I2 24%. Tablets or lozenges 1.52 (1.32 to 1.74), 8, 4,439, I2 71%. Inhalator 1.90 (1.36 to 2.67), 4, 976, I2 0%. Nasal spray 2.02 (1.49 to 2.73), 4, 887, I2 0%. Oral spray 2.48 (1.24 to 4.94), 1 trial, 479. Choice of product 1.37 (1.25 to 1.52), 7, 8,288, I2 42%. Combinations: patch plus inhalator 1.07 (0.57 to 1.99), 1 trial; patch plus lozenge 1.83 (1.01 to 3.31), 1 trial; patch plus gum 1.15 (0.64 to 2.06), 2 trials; patch plus gum plus lozenge 15.00 (2.00 to 112.54), 1 trial. By setting: community volunteers treated in a medical setting 1.62 (1.53 to 1.72), smoking clinics 1.70 (1.48 to 1.96), primary care 1.50 (1.33 to 1.69), hospitals 1.39 (1.24 to 1.55), over-the-counter-like settings 1.40 (1.26 to 1.55), antenatal clinics 1.22 (0.92 to 1.62). Sensitivity (analyses not shown in the review): excluding high-risk trials 1.61 (1.52 to 1.69); only the 12 low-risk trials 1.53 (1.37 to 1.71); validated abstinence only 1.62 (1.55 to 1.70); placebo-controlled only 1.61 (1.53 to 1.70). Chest pain or palpitations: odds ratio 1.88 (1.37 to 2.57), 15 trials, 11,074 participants. Absolute figures (Summary of findings table): 105 per 1,000 without NRT against 162 (156 to 168) with NRT; 40 against 62 (60 to 64) with limited support; 150 against 232 (224 to 242) with intensive support. No tau-squared or prediction interval (fixed-effect model).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Subgroup analyses by abstinence definition (gum, patch), intensity of behavioural support (gum, patch) and setting, plus a meta-regression of setting by product type; no meta-regression on participant characteristics.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol first published in Issue 2, 1996. The History table records later changes of scope or method: effect measure changed from odds ratio to risk ratio (2007), adverse-events table added (2012), and in 2017 the review was split, moving comparisons between NRT types and with bupropion elsewhere. This version has no section comparing the review with its protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The Methods name no selective-reporting domain among the risk-of-bias items (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, other), so selective outcome reporting was not assessed per trial. Adverse events were recorded where reported and not synthesised because reporting varied. The sensitivity analyses are reported in a sentence each, without a table. The review does not say whether registered primary outcomes were compared with published ones.
analysis.power: The main pool is large (64,640 participants). Individual trials were often small: in 73% of trials the interval for the RR included 1, and 12 trials had lower quit rates with NRT (all intervals crossed 1). Product subgroups with the highest estimates rest on few trials: inhalator 4 trials (976 participants), nasal spray 4 (887), oral spray 1 (479), and the 15.00 estimate is one trial in which one control participant quit.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across randomised trials of people motivated to quit, offering any form of NRT was followed by more people abstinent at 6 months or longer than placebo or no NRT: 162 against 105 per 1,000 overall (about 6 more in 100), about 2 more in 100 with limited behavioural support and about 8 more in 100 with intensive support (editors' arithmetic from the Summary of findings table). The relative effect (RR about 1.5 to 1.6) was similar across gum, patch and lozenge or tablet, with wider and higher estimates for inhalator, nasal and oral spray from few trials, and similar across support levels and most settings, though not significant in four antenatal-clinic trials (RR 1.22, 0.92 to 1.62). Restricting to low-risk or placebo-controlled trials gave similar estimates. Side effects were mainly local irritation at the site of use; chest pain or palpitations were reported by 2.5% with NRT against 1.4% with control (OR 1.88). Serious adverse events were not pooled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and authors' conclusions state high-quality evidence that all licensed forms help, that NRT raises quitting by 50% to 60% regardless of setting, that further research is very unlikely to change the estimate, that the form of delivery is unrelated to effectiveness, and that serious adverse events were extremely rare. The plain language summary adds that there is no evidence NRT raises the risk of heart attacks. Gaps: (1) regardless of setting sits beside a non-significant estimate in antenatal clinics; (2) unrelated to effectiveness rests on indirect subgroup comparisons whose estimates run from 1.49 (gum) to 2.48 (oral spray, one trial), so it is a statement of no demonstrated difference, not of equivalence, and the companion review (Theodoulou 2023) is the direct evidence; (3) relative gains of 50% to 60% are given without absolute numbers in the abstract (the Summary of findings gives them); (4) high quality is the authors' GRADE judgement even though only 12 of 136 trials were low risk of bias, the funnel plot is asymmetric, about 60% of trials involved a manufacturer and the authors themselves say the true effect may be smaller; (5) the safety statements go beyond the data: adverse events were deliberately not pooled, serious events were not counted across trials, the review has no heart-attack outcome, and the text calls events at 2.5% and 1.4% extremely rare; (6) the abstract's wording about quitting applies to people motivated to quit in trials, while observational studies of everyday use that the review discusses give mixed results (the authors attribute this to confounding by choice of treatment).

timeline.event: First version of this Cochrane review (Silagy et al.); the number of included trials has more than doubled since, and the authors state the pooled estimate has stayed stable.
Update changes the effect measure from odds ratio to risk ratio and modifies some comparisons.
Update adds a table of adverse events by study.
Review split: this version covers NRT against control; comparisons between forms, doses and schedules move to a companion review.
This version (Hartmann-Boyce et al.), search July 2017; marked stable, with no further updates planned.
Companion Cochrane review of different forms, doses and durations of NRT (Theodoulou et al.), read for the same claims.
Cochrane living review of electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation, which uses NRT as a comparator; read separately.

replication.where_it_stands: The main finding that NRT, offered with the same support as control, raises abstinence at 6 months or more is consistent across 20 years of trials and is not an artefact of any single trial; the size, however, comes from trials in people motivated to quit, often with clinic support, and about 60% involved a manufacturer. A 2023 companion review (Theodoulou et al.) compares forms head to head and finds combinations better than single forms and fast-acting forms similar to patches. Observational work on everyday use is mixed and confounded by who chooses NRT. Primary trials inside this pool (for example Anthenelli 2016, Jorenby 1999, Shiffman 2009) must not be counted as independent support beside this review.

funding.funder: National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) infrastructure funding for the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group; NIHR School for Primary Care Research (support for the Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, University of Oxford, the group's editorial base); one author (JHB) funded in part by the NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre. No industry funding of the review is declared.
funding.declared_conflicts: One author (CB) was involved in a trial of pre-cessation NRT (Bullen 2010), which this review lists among trials contributing adverse-event data only; the other authors declare none known. Funding of the included trials, from their notes in the Characteristics of included studies (editors' count; the review did not analyse by funder): of the 136 included entries, about 80 name a drug company as funder, co-funder or supplier of study product (for example Pharmacia, Kabi, Elan, Marion Merrell Dow, Ciba-Geigy, Glaxo, Novartis, Pfizer, McNeil, Lundbeck, Leo; some of these supplied product only, such as Ahluwalia 2006, Oncken 2007 and Piper 2009), about 40 name only government, charity or university funders, and about 15 report no funding source. The authors cite a meta-analysis (Etter 2007) in which gum and patch trials with pharmaceutical funding had slightly higher effect sizes, and say the magnitude of NRT's effect may be smaller than their estimates suggest.
funding.affiliations_note: Author affiliations were not part of the page text read for this card.

what_would_settle_it: A comparison of effect sizes between trials funded by manufacturers and trials funded independently (a funder-stratified meta-analysis, which this review did not run); registered trials with all outcomes and adverse events reported by arm; pragmatic trials of NRT given without clinic support, in people not planning to quit and in people smoking fewer than 10 cigarettes a day, with follow-up beyond 12 months and with serious adverse events counted in a prespecified way.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People who smoked and were motivated to quit; licensed NRT forms; placebo or no-NRT control; abstinence at 6 months or more plus adverse events; randomised and quasi-randomised trials.
A Cochrane protocol was published in 1996 and the History table lists later changes, including the 2017 split, but this version does not compare the review with its protocol or justify each change.
Randomised and quasi-randomised trials, with a sensitivity analysis for quasi-randomisation; restriction to trials is the standard design for an efficacy question, with no separate justification.

Register built from CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and hand-searched conference abstracts, strategy in Appendix 1, no date or language limits, searched July 2017 (within a year of publication). Not stated: searching reference lists of included trials; manufacturers were last contacted when the review was first prepared; trial registries are mentioned only in the Discussion.
Two authors screened independently in the last two updates; earlier updates used one screener, so older selections were not duplicated.
Two authors extracted independently, disagreements settled by discussion or a third person; translators used for non-English reports.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Characteristics of excluded studies lists each study with its reason.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Each trial has a table of country, recruitment, participants, interventions, outcomes, validation, funding notes and risk-of-bias judgements.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data and other bias, in a table per trial; the Methods name no selective-reporting domain, so selection of the reported result was not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: The Notes field of each trial gives funders and suppliers or says not reported (about 15 trials).

Fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios with I2 reported (39% overall; 71% in the lozenge subgroup, traced to one trial); placebo-controlled and no-placebo trials pooled but checked in a placebo-only sensitivity analysis; loss to follow-up counted as smoking. Judged met on balance, a close call: no random-effects check despite moderate heterogeneity.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk trials, keeping only the 12 low-risk trials, excluding unvalidated trials and keeping placebo-controlled trials only, all consistent (reported without tables).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The GRADE footnote and the Limitations section state that most trials were unclear or high risk and that the estimate was unchanged in the sensitivity analyses.
I2 reported by subgroup; the high value in the lozenge subgroup attributed to one trial; subgroups by abstinence definition, support and setting.
A funnel plot (Figure 4, an image) was inspected and its asymmetry discussed with the pharmaceutical-funding finding of Etter 2007; no statistical test.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Sources of support and declarations of interest are given; no industry funding of the review.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical item is judged no. Three critical items are only partly met (2, 4 and 9), which AMSTAR 2 does not count as flaws, so the mechanical rating is high confidence. AMSTAR 2 rates how the review was done, not how good the trials are: most of the 136 trials were unclear (88) or high (36) risk of bias, six rest on abstracts or registry entries, selective reporting was not assessed, the funnel plot is asymmetric and about 60% of trials involved a manufacturer. The authors' own sensitivity analyses (low-risk trials only, validated abstinence only, placebo-controlled only) give RR 1.53 to 1.62 against 1.55, which is why the efficacy estimate is usable. May be cited for: the pooled efficacy of NRT against control and its absolute size under limited and intensive support; product-level estimates as indirect subgroup results; the descriptive list of local side effects; the funnel-plot and industry caveats. May not be cited for: which form works best (use the companion review), everyday-use effectiveness, how often side effects occur, or whether NRT is safe.

key_findings.finding: Any form of NRT against placebo or no NRT, abstinence at 6 months or longer: pooled RR 1.55 (95% CI 1.49 to 1.61), 133 comparisons from 131 trials, 64,640 participants, fixed-effect, I2 39%. The authors rate the evidence high certainty (GRADE).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1
key_findings.note: The Results say 131 trials (133 comparisons); the abstract and Table 1 say 133 studies (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Absolute figures in the Summary of findings table: without NRT 105 per 1,000 abstinent, with NRT 162 per 1,000 (156 to 168); with limited behavioural support 40 against 62 per 1,000 (60 to 64); with intensive support 150 against 232 per 1,000 (224 to 242). Editors' arithmetic: about 6, 2 and 8 more people in 100 abstinent.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings, Table 1

key_findings.finding: RR by product (comparisons; participants): gum 1.49 (1.40 to 1.60; 56; 22,581; I2 40%); patch 1.64 (1.53 to 1.75; 51; 25,754; I2 24%); tablets or lozenges 1.52 (1.32 to 1.74; 8; 4,439; I2 71%); inhalator 1.90 (1.36 to 2.67; 4; 976); intranasal spray 2.02 (1.49 to 2.73; 4; 887); oral spray 2.48 (1.24 to 4.94; 1 trial; 479); choice of product 1.37 (1.25 to 1.52; 7; 8,288); patch plus inhalator 1.07 (0.57 to 1.99; 1); patch plus lozenge 1.83 (1.01 to 3.31; 1); patch plus gum 1.15 (0.64 to 2.06; 2); patch plus gum plus lozenge 15.00 (2.00 to 112.54; 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, table after the 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1
key_findings.note: The 15.00 estimate is one trial in which one control participant quit. Subgroup estimates are indirect comparisons of trials against control, not head-to-head.

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity and single trials: the lozenge or tablet subgroup had I2 71%, driven by one new trial with RR 1.08 (Fraser 2014). Twelve trials had lower quit rates with NRT than control (all intervals crossed 1) and in a further 73% of trials the interval included 1. One large patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease (Joseph 1996) found quit rates of 14% with active patch and 11% with placebo at 6 months, and 10% and 12% at 48 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Quit rates in control groups rose with behavioural support: gum trials 3.5% (low-intensity support), 9% (high-intensity individual) and 11.7% (group-based); patch trials 9.0%, 9.5% and 17.0%. Relative effects were reported as similar across support levels. By setting, control quit rates were 8.4% (over-the-counter-like), 6.9% (primary care), 14.3% (smoking clinics), 9.3% (antenatal), 12.5% (community volunteers in a medical setting) and 12.3% (hospitals).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to intensity of behavioural support; Sensitivity to treatment settings, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Data and analyses give gum RR 1.66 (1.46 to 1.88) with low-intensity support, 1.32 (1.18 to 1.49) with high-intensity individual support and 1.57 (1.40 to 1.76) with group support; the text says no significant difference between groups.

key_findings.finding: RR by setting: community volunteers treated in a medical setting 1.62 (1.53 to 1.72; 65 trials; 24,597); smoking clinics 1.70 (1.48 to 1.96; 12; 3,300); primary care 1.50 (1.33 to 1.69; 24; 11,974); hospitals 1.39 (1.24 to 1.55; 13; 7,037); over-the-counter-like settings 1.40 (1.26 to 1.55; 9; 13,163); antenatal clinics 1.22 (0.92 to 1.62; 4; 1,675), the only setting without a statistically significant effect.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to treatment settings, 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 4

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses (not shown in the review): excluding high-risk trials RR 1.61 (1.52 to 1.69); only the 12 low-risk trials 1.53 (1.37 to 1.71); excluding trials without biochemical validation 1.62 (1.55 to 1.70); placebo-controlled trials only 1.61 (1.53 to 1.70).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to risk of bias and study methods

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: 12 trials low risk in all domains, 36 high risk in at least one domain, the rest unclear. Allocation procedures adequately reported in 39 trials (29%); 44 trials (33%) low and 23 (17%) high risk of performance or detection bias; 43 trials had no matched placebo; six trials rest on abstracts, conference presentations or registry entries; 117 trials (87%) validated abstinence biochemically; follow-up was only 6 months in 15 gum, 19 patch, 4 combination and 1 lozenge trial.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Adverse events were not pooled, because the nature, timing and duration of symptoms were reported too variably; main events are tabulated by trial in Appendix 3. Local effects reported: gum, hiccoughs, gastrointestinal disturbance, jaw pain and orodental problems; patch, skin sensitivity and irritation (up to 54% in one cited source), usually mild; inhalator and nasal or oral spray, irritation at the site of use (throat irritation, coughing, oral burning; nasal irritation and runny nose; hiccoughs); sublingual tablets, hiccoughs, burning in the mouth, sore throat, cough, dry lips and mouth ulcers. Adolescents reported similar events to adults.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Appendix 3

key_findings.finding: Chest pain or palpitations: odds ratio 1.88 (1.37 to 2.57), 15 included and excluded trials, 11,074 participants, with 2.5% of NRT groups and 1.4% of control groups affected. An earlier meta-analysis (Mills 2010) found OR 2.06 (1.51 to 2.82) in 12 studies. The authors describe the events as extremely rare and report no evidence of an excess of serious cardiac problems.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 6
key_findings.note: The text calls events at 2.5% and 1.4% extremely rare.

key_findings.finding: Cardiac disease and pregnancy: in one patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease serious adverse events were not more common with the patch, and cardiovascular events such as worse angina (about 16% of participants) did not differ by arm (Joseph 1996). A cited network meta-analysis (Mills 2014) found more cardiovascular events with NRT overall (RR 2.29, 1.39 to 3.82), driven by lower-level events such as tachycardia, and no significant excess of serious cardiac events (printed RR 1.95, 0.26 to 4.30). Six trials in pregnant women did not detect significant increases in serious adverse events.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Figures from Mills 2014 are quoted from another review and were not checked.

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy (six trials): abstinence at end of pregnancy RR 1.32 (1.04 to 1.69; 2,129 participants); at longest postpartum follow-up RR 1.29 (0.90 to 1.86; four trials, 1,675 participants). The review refers readers to a separate Cochrane review for pregnancy.
key_findings.locator: Data and analyses, Comparison 5; Discussion › Trials in special populations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adolescents: two small trials (Moolchan 2005; Scherphof 2014) did not detect an effect on quitting at 6 months or longer, and a separate Cochrane review of young people also found none, with wide intervals. The authors state there is little evidence about NRT in people smoking fewer than 10 to 15 cigarettes a day.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Trials in special populations, 1st paragraph; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing; a funnel plot shows some asymmetry; a cited meta-analysis (Etter 2007) found nicotine gum and patch trials with pharmaceutical funding had slightly higher effect sizes on average; the authors conclude that the magnitude of effectiveness may be smaller than their estimates. They did not repeat their letter to manufacturers after the first version.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence base, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1 footnote 2
key_findings.note: Summary of findings footnotes give the authors' reason for not downgrading the high rating: most studies were at unclear or high risk of bias but restricting to low-risk trials did not alter the effect, and given the large number of trials the asymmetry does not suggest that adding smaller trials with lower risk ratios would change the results significantly.

key_findings.finding: Funding of the included trials (editors' count from the Notes field of the Characteristics of included studies, by company-name matching and reading; the review itself did not analyse by funder): of 136 included entries, about 80 name a drug company as funder, co-funder or supplier of study product, about 40 name only government, charity or university funders, and about 15 report no source.
key_findings.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Notes of each study (editors' count)
key_findings.note: Approximate. Some entries are two halves of one trial (Shiffman 2002; Shiffman 2009), and some company links are product supply only.

key_findings.finding: Everyday use outside trials: the review discusses observational studies finding no difference or lower quit rates among people who used over-the-counter NRT (California surveys, 2002; a UK prospective cohort, OR 0.69, 0.49 to 0.94, against no pharmacotherapy or service) and others finding higher quit rates among people who used NRT (two multi-country cohorts, in one only for patches); it attributes these differences to residual confounding, because people chose their own treatment.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Intensity of additional support and treatment setting, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Follow-up: trials needed at least 6 months, most reported at least 12 months from the start of treatment, and the relative effect was not smaller in trials with longer follow-up. The authors cite work suggesting the relative effect falls once treatment stops but does not change beyond a year (12 trials), with later relapse shrinking the absolute difference.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Limitations of the evidence base, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Methods in brief: Specialised Register searched 6 July 2017 (CENTRAL issue 11 2016, MEDLINE to May 2017, Embase to week 24 2017, PsycINFO to May 2017; no language restriction); duplicate screening and extraction; Cochrane risk-of-bias tool; fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios; GRADE for the main outcome only.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search methods for identification of studies; Data collection and analysis

reporting_issues.issue: The number of trials in the main pool is given three ways. The abstract and Table 1 say 133 studies; the Results say Analysis 1.1 included 131 trials (133 comparisons); and the trial counts by product in Description of studies (56 gum, 51 patch, 8 tablet or lozenge, 7 choice, 4 spray, 4 inhalator, 2 patch and gum, 1 oral spray, 1 patch and inhalator, 1 patch and lozenge, 1 patch, gum and lozenge) add up to 136, the number of included studies. The text explains that some trials contribute to more than one subgroup and that two studies were split into four comparisons.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote 133 comparisons (131 trials) rather than 133 trials; the product-level counts cannot be added.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's worked absolute effects do not reconcile with the risk ratio or with each other: an increase of 2% to 3% on a 3% to 5% baseline is given an NNTB of 56 (2 to 3 per 100 would give about 33 to 50), and a further 8% on a 15% baseline is given an NNTB of 11 (editors' arithmetic: 100 divided by 8 is about 12.5; a baseline of 15% with RR 1.55 gives about 8 more per 100).
reporting_issues.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the Summary of findings table (105 against 162 per 1,000; 40 against 62; 150 against 232) for absolute numbers, not the Discussion's NNTBs.

reporting_issues.issue: Events at 2.5% (NRT) and 1.4% (control) are called extremely rare, and the abstract calls serious adverse events extremely rare although serious events were not counted across trials.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd paragraph; Abstract
reporting_issues.consequence: The reassuring wording is stronger than the data; the claim states the percentages instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusions say NRT raises quitting regardless of setting, yet the antenatal-clinic subgroup (four trials, 1,675 participants) has RR 1.22 (0.92 to 1.62), which the text itself notes is the one setting without a significant effect; and they state the form of delivery is unrelated to effectiveness while product subgroup estimates run from 1.49 to 2.48 with wide intervals and few trials for the higher ones.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice; Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to treatment settings
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat regardless of setting and unrelated to the form as no demonstrated difference in these indirect comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The Mills 2014 serious cardiac events estimate is printed as RR 1.95 (95% CI 0.26 to 4.30). A ratio estimate that sits well above the centre of its interval on the log scale (about 1.06) may reflect a typing error in the upper limit or a skewed credible interval from a network meta-analysis; it could not be checked here.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is not used in any claim.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentages are calculated on different denominators: 117 trials is given as 87% (which fits 134 trials), 44 trials as 33% (fits 133) and 89 trials as 66% (fits about 134).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 3rd to 6th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote counts rather than percentages.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6353172 (abstract, plain language summary, Summary of findings table, background, methods, results, discussion, authors' conclusions, feedback, what's new and history, acknowledgements, Appendix 3, the Data and analyses tables, the excluded and ongoing studies lists, sources of support and declarations of interest read; the Notes field of every entry in Characteristics of included studies was extracted programmatically to count funders and read in a printed list, but the risk-of-bias tables of individual trials were not read trial by trial; Figures 1 to 4, including the flow diagram, risk-of-bias graph, forest plot and funnel plot, are images and were not extracted)

design_detail: Single-author review updating the author's 1990 critical review: which of ten self-reported symptoms are valid effects of stopping cigarettes, and their time course. A documented search (MEDLINE, PsycInfo, EMBASE, SSCI, the CDC tobacco database, an SRNT e-mail list and authors of conference abstracts) of studies from 1990 to 2004 found more than 3,500 citations; 792 abstracts and 290 articles were read and 120 are cited (p. 316). Synthesis by counting studies and by the author's judgment, relying mainly on 15 comprehensive prospective studies (Table 1, p. 317); no meta-analysis and no formal appraisal tool. The author states that data collection and interpretation rested solely on his subjective judgments (abstract, p. 315; p. 316), so the card treats it as a narrative review with a documented search.
can_establish: Which abstinence symptoms the author judged valid, possible or unsupported, and the time courses reported in the prospective studies he selected, as a map of the evidence to 2004 with pointers to the primary studies.
cannot_establish: How often each symptom occurs, how strong it is or how long it lasts in any defined group (no pooled estimates, rates or effect sizes: the review counts studies); whether the selection of results is complete or unbiased (one reviewer who chose results on his own judgment); and anything about craving, hunger, weight or performance, which were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). The 15 core studies (Table 1, p. 317) are prospective studies of 11 to 178 people each: placebo or no-treatment arms of cessation trials (9), self-quitters (2) and people not trying to quit who abstained for the study (4, one with inpatients); follow-ups from day 1 to day 365.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: published or in-press prospective studies of cigarettes, more than 18 hours of abstinence, new information since the 1990 review, ten symptoms (anger/irritability/frustration, anxiety, depression, difficulty concentrating, drowsiness, fatigue, impatience, insomnia, physical symptoms, restlessness). For anger, anxiety, concentration, insomnia, impatience and restlessness only post-1990 studies were reviewed; for depression, drowsiness, fatigue and physical symptoms all studies. Excluded: abstracts, craving, hunger and weight, performance, delirium, drug use, medication levels, pain, neonatal withdrawal, physiological correlates, psychiatric disorders and treatments (pp. 316-317).
sample.demographics: Not reported at review level; Table 1 gives only sample size, the kind of participant (for example male or female smokers not trying to quit, women with weight concerns) and follow-up days.
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level; the author notes that only 5 of the 15 core studies had low attrition (p. 318).
sample.selection_effects: One reviewer, who chose which results to include on his subjective opinion of rigor, consistency and size of effect (p. 316); published studies only, which the author notes may bring publication bias. Of the 15 core studies only 2 had control groups, 2 generalizable samples, 3 more than 90 participants, 3 several pre-quit values and 5 low attrition (p. 318). Five of the 15 are by the author or his co-authors (Hatsukami et al., 1984 and 1988; Hughes & Hatsukami, 1986; Hughes et al., 1991; Hughes, 1992; editors' count from the reference list).

exposure.measurement: Stopping cigarettes: cessation within trials (placebo or no-treatment arms), self-initiated quitting, or abstinence arranged for a study; how abstinence was verified in each study is not described in the review.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cigarettes only; more than 18 hours of abstinence; amounts smoked before stopping not summarized.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed in the review.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: From 1 day to a year after stopping (follow-up days in Table 1); 11 of the 15 core studies had several assessments in the first week (p. 318).

comparison.controls: Mostly each person's own pre-quit ratings; only 2 of the 15 core studies had a separate control group (one a non-smoker group, Ward et al., 2001). One core study (Gritz et al., 1991) had no pre-quit values (Table 1).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Pre-quit mood was usually not reported, so whether it changes the course of low mood after quitting is unknown; a history of major depression may predict low mood after quitting (p. 319).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: Withdrawal scales of several kinds, Profile of Mood States subscales, Beck Depression Inventory and CES-D; sleep EEG for sleep fragmentation; accident statistics on the UK No-Smoking Day as one objective index of drowsiness. No study used objective measures of anger, depression or fatigue, and no abstinence study with objective anxiety measures was found (pp. 318-320).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed beyond the author's remarks that people may be poor at reporting alertness (p. 320) and that one later study suggests retrospective reports overestimate how long withdrawal lasts (Shiffman et al., 2006; p. 322).
outcomes.operationalization: A symptom counts as a valid abstinence effect if abstinence reliably changes it across studies; each is typed as a withdrawal effect (biphasic, transient), an offset effect (one-way change) or indefinite; prospective designs with pre-abstinence values were required (p. 317).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; self-report outcomes in the primary studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: None; counts of studies and time courses as cited. Anger: peak in the first week, duration 2 weeks (7 studies), 3 weeks (1) or 4 weeks or more (2). Anxiety: rises in the first 1 to 3 days and lasts about 2 weeks in most; one well-validated study found a fall (West & Hajek, 1997). Low mood: rose in 6 core studies and not in 2 (a third, Hillemann et al., 1992, found a fall), peaking at 1, 2 or 3 weeks and still raised at 30 days in two. Difficulty concentrating: peak in the first few days, duration from a week or less to 4 weeks or more. Alertness: fell in 2, rose in 2 and did not change in 3 core studies. Fatigue: no change in 3 of 4 studies. Impatience: rose for 3 to 4 weeks or more in 3 studies. Sleep fragmentation: consistently increased in sleep-EEG and clinical studies lasting 5 to 14 days. Restlessness: peak on days 1 to 3, duration 2 to 4 weeks (1 week in one study). Whole syndrome: total scores at or near pre-quit levels after about 2 weeks and by 3 to 4 weeks; in two studies 38% and 61% of people did not follow this average course (pp. 318-322).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol; a single-author review.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results were selected on the author's judgment and are cited by direction without sizes. Some sentences cite more studies than they count (reporting issue 1).
analysis.power: Not applicable; core studies had 11 to 178 participants and only 3 had more than 90.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Within the selected prospective studies, anger, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, impatience, restlessness and waking at night rose after stopping in most studies, peaking in the first week and mostly back at or near pre-quit levels within 2 to 4 weeks; low mood was mixed; drowsiness contradictory; fatigue, headaches, sweating, a racing heart, tremor and rash were not found; constipation, cough, dizziness, dreaming and mouth ulcers were reported in one or two studies each. Time courses varied between studies and, in two studies, between people.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract lists seven symptoms that “are valid withdrawal symptoms that peak within the first week and last 2–4 weeks” (p. 315). Gaps: (1) depression is among them in the abstract and Table 2, although the text calls the evidence surprisingly mixed and less reliable than for other symptoms (p. 319); (2) the 2-to-4-week course is an average, while in two studies 38% and 61% of people followed other courses (p. 322); (3) the abstract does not mention that one study suggests recall makes withdrawal seem longer (p. 322); (4) firm conclusions rest on one reviewer's subjective synthesis, which the abstract does state.

timeline.event: Hughes, Higgins & Hatsukami, critical review of the effects of tobacco abstinence, which this review updates.
Shiffman, West & Gilbert, SRNT recommendations: the only earlier review naming valid and invalid symptoms; it did not count anxiety as valid (as described, p. 324).
Shiffman et al., natural history of nicotine withdrawal: retrospective reports may overestimate its duration (as described, p. 322).
This review.

replication.where_it_stands: A standard narrative summary of tobacco abstinence symptoms to 2004, offered for the DSM-IV and ICD-10 criteria. Claims may rest on it for the list of symptoms and the shape of the time course, citing it as second-hand, and must say that it gives no sizes or frequencies.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse Senior Scientist Award DA000490 (Acknowledgments, p. 324).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, University of Vermont; the review was circulated before submission to four named experts (p. 324). Five of the 15 core studies are by the author or his co-authors.

what_would_settle_it: A registered systematic review with individual-participant data from prospective studies with pre-quit baselines and biochemically verified abstinence, reporting for each symptom the share of people affected, the size of the change and its duration, with momentary ratings rather than recall.

domains.note: Several databases, an e-mail list and conference authors were searched, with stated criteria and counts (pp. 316-317), but one reviewer chose which results to include on his own judgment, and only published studies were used.
Fifteen more rigorous studies are singled out and described (Table 1; p. 318), but without a formal tool; one of them lacks the pre-quit values the methods require (reporting issue 2).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Five of the 15 core studies are by the author or his co-authors, and the review updates his own 1990 review.
Mechanisms (for example dreaming as a by-product of waking) are labelled as hypotheses, and gaps in the evidence are named.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against each symptom being an effect of stopping
domains.note: Negative studies are reported for low mood, anxiety, alertness, fatigue and physical symptoms, but the critiques that question nicotine withdrawal altogether (Atrens, 2001; Frenk & Dar, 2000; p. 315) are named without being answered, and the study suggesting that recall exaggerates duration gets one sentence.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The search is broader and better documented than in most narrative reviews, but selection and synthesis were one person's judgment, five core studies are his group's, and no study was formally appraised. Cite it for the list of symptoms the evidence supported and for the shape of the time course, second-hand, and cite the primary studies for any size or duration.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: more than 3,500 citations, 792 abstracts read, 290 articles read and 120 cited; inclusion required published prospective studies of cigarettes with more than 18 hours of abstinence; results were chosen on the author's subjective opinion of rigor, consistency and size.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Method › Study selection and synthesis, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Data extraction and synthesis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fifteen comprehensive prospective studies (11 to 178 participants; 872 in all by the editors' sum) carry the conclusions: all but one had pre-quit values; 11 were published after 1990, 11 studied people trying to stop and 11 had several assessments in the first week; 9 used control arms of trials; only 2 had control groups, 2 generalizable samples, 3 more than 90 participants, 3 several pre-quit values and 5 low attrition. No meta-analysis was done because of methodological heterogeneity.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of abstinence effects, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 317) and 3rd paragraph (p. 318); Table 1

key_findings.finding: Anger peaks in the first week and lasts 2 weeks (7 studies), 3 weeks (1) or 4 weeks or more (2); anxiety rises in the first 1 to 3 days and in most studies lasts about 2 weeks, but one study of well-validated abstainers found a fall (West & Hajek, 1997).
key_findings.locator: Results › Anger/irritability/frustration, 2nd paragraph; Anxiety, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Low mood: the evidence is called surprisingly mixed; 6 core studies found a rise, two did not and one found a fall; in positive trials it peaked at 1, 2 or 3 weeks and in two it was still raised at 30 days; a history of major depression may predict it; the author still classes it as a withdrawal symptom with lower reliability.
key_findings.locator: Results › Depression, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Difficulty concentrating peaks in the first few days and lasts from a week or less to 4 weeks or more; restlessness peaks on days 1 to 3 and lasts 2 to 4 weeks (1 week in one study); impatience rose for 3 to 4 weeks or more in all 3 newer studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Difficulty concentrating, 2nd paragraph (p. 319); Impatience, 2nd paragraph (p. 320); Restlessness, 2nd paragraph (p. 322)

key_findings.finding: Drowsiness: of the core studies, 2 found less alertness, 2 more and 3 no change; one of two No-Smoking Day studies found more accidents and one sleep study found shorter sleep latency. Fatigue: 3 of 4 studies found no effect, so it is not counted as an abstinence effect.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drowsiness/decreased alertness or arousal, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Fatigue

key_findings.finding: Sleep: in sleep-EEG and clinical studies, stopping consistently increased sleep fragmentation (waking at night, stage shifts), mostly with a withdrawal pattern, in studies lasting 5 to 14 days; increased recall of vivid dreams was reported; REM latency did not shorten. The author proposes describing the insomnia as increased awakenings or intense dreams.
key_findings.locator: Results › Insomnia, all paragraphs (pp. 320-321); Discussion › Valid symptoms of tobacco abstinence, 4th paragraph (p. 324)

key_findings.finding: Physical symptoms: all studies were negative for headaches, sweating, a racing heart, tremor and skin rash; dizziness showed a transient pattern in two studies but not in a third; constipation, mouth ulcers and cough were each reported in one study (constipation and ulcers not found in another); composite physical scores rose in some studies and not others.
key_findings.locator: Results › Physical symptoms, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Time course of the whole syndrome: total withdrawal scores are back at or very near pre-quit levels after about 2 weeks and by 3 to 4 weeks, so the author states it lasts 2 to 4 weeks; onset could not be determined. In two studies 38% and 61% of people did not follow this average course (symptoms rose again around 3 weeks or did not fall), with different relapse risks; one study suggests retrospective reports overestimate duration; prolonged withdrawal of 6 months or more does not appear to occur, except possibly for craving and hunger.
key_findings.locator: Results › Time course, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Summary classification (Table 2): valid withdrawal symptoms anger, anxiety, depression, difficulty concentrating, impatience, insomnia, restlessness; possibly valid constipation, cough, dizziness, increased dreaming, mouth ulcers; reviewed but not validated drowsiness, fatigue, physical symptoms; craving, hunger, slower heart rate, EEG changes and impaired performance not reviewed but probably valid.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Valid symptoms of tobacco abstinence, 1st paragraph; Table 2

reporting_issues.issue: The fatigue paragraph says that three of the four more comprehensive studies conducted since the 1990 review found no effect, but cites four studies for that, one of them from 1986 (Hughes & Hatsukami).
reporting_issues.consequence: The vote count for fatigue cannot be reconstructed from the text; the conclusion (no abstinence effect) may still hold but its basis is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods require pre-abstinence values for a valid abstinence effect (p. 317), yet Gritz et al. (1991), listed in Table 1 with no pre-abstinence values, is among the core studies cited for anger and impatience.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the core studies does not meet the review's own design requirement; the anger and impatience conclusions lean partly on it.

reporting_issues.issue: The text counts 3 core studies with several pre-quit values and 5 with low attrition (p. 318), but the Table 1 comments mark several pre-quit values in 2 studies and low attrition in 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study features cannot be checked from Table 1; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3's notes give the ICD-10 footnote as 'c' while the table header uses 'b'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting; no effect on content.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent; AI reader 120, first reader)
verification.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Hughes_2007_AbstinenceSymptomsTimeCourse..pdf, pp. 315-327 (all pages read in a text extraction; p. 318 checked on the rendered page, where the text layer prints '=' as '5'); final published version

design_detail: Laboratory chemical screening of seven commercial oral products for 43 compounds, funded and designed by the maker of two of them (see funding): two variants of the maker's tobacco-free pouch brand (ZYN dry and moist), one Swedish snus (General) made by the same company, two moist snuffs (a reference product and a US pouched product), and two nicotine replacement products (a lozenge and a gum). One batch of each product, triplicate analyses, results per gram of wet weight. Most analyses were done at an external accredited laboratory, some in the company's own laboratory. The schema has no design for a laboratory analysis of products; 'in-vitro' is the nearest. No people, no nicotine uptake and no health outcome were measured.
can_establish: What the maker-funded screening found above its quantification limits, per gram of product, in these seven products; that for the two ZYN variants none of ten nitrosamines and none of seven polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons was above the limits used, while a few other constituents (formaldehyde, chromium, ammonia and, in one variant, nickel) were; and how the number and level of quantified constituents compared across the pouch, snus, moist snuff and replacement products in the same programme.
cannot_establish: Anything about tobacco-free nicotine pouches as a category (two variants of one brand, one batch each); that nitrosamines are absent (the limit for the four tobacco-specific ones was 0.01 microgram per gram, which the AI reader works out as roughly 4 to 8 ng in a ZYN pouch, roughly ten times or more above the limit in the independent German analysis); what people take in or whether any product is harmless or less harmful than another (no uptake, biomarker or health outcome was measured, and the Discussion's 'low toxicity' is an inference from content); that snus or moist snuff in general resemble the single products tested; or what an independent laboratory would find in the same products.

sample.recruitment: Products, not people. The two ZYN products and the snus came from the maker's own distribution centre in Stockholm; the replacement products from online pharmacies in Sweden; the moist snuff reference product from a university tobacco laboratory in North Carolina; the pouched moist snuff from a wholesaler in Kentucky (Material and methods › Sample handling and analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Compounds chosen by the maker: 36 on the US Food and Drug Administration's list of harmful and potentially harmful constituents, four for the maker's own snus standard and two more nitrosamines to cover the four tobacco-specific ones (Material and methods › Selected compounds, 1st paragraph). Agrochemicals covered by the standard were left out as beyond scope (2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (products).
sample.attrition: None described. Where one or two of three replicates were below the quantification limit they were set to half the limit for the mean and standard deviation; polonium-210 was a single measurement.
sample.selection_effects: One batch of each product, chosen by the funder, with its own pouch and snus samples supplied from its distribution centre rather than bought at retail; one flavour per pouch variant; one product per comparison category. The date of analysis is not stated (analyses were done within 3 weeks of obtaining each product; the references were accessed in March to June 2021). The authors say no chemical data on ZYN had been published.

exposure.measurement: Mostly an external laboratory accredited to ISO 17025 (Eurofins, Lidköping): metals by ICP-MS; nitrosamines (NNN, NNK, NAT, NAB, NDMA) by HPLC with tandem mass spectrometry; polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons by GC-MS or HPLC with fluorescence; aldehydes, nitrite, ammonia, aflatoxins, ochratoxin A, coumarin, ethyl carbamate, total nicotine and pH by standard or in-house methods. Done in the maker's own laboratory: uranium-235 and -238, five more nitrosamines (NDELA, NMOR, NPIP, NPYR, NSAR), anabasine and nornicotine, and the calculation of unprotonated nicotine from pH. Polonium-210 at a Canadian laboratory. For the replacement products the methods were validated but not accredited. Triplicate analyses of the whole product including the pouch (Material and methods › Sample handling and analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 2). Quantification limits for the four tobacco-specific nitrosamines 0.01 microgram per gram; NDMA 0.20 ng per gram; other nitrosamines 10 to 25 ng per gram; benzo[a]pyrene 1 ng per gram; other polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons 30 ng per gram (Tables 3 and 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Measured product content, not a dose: total nicotine in mg per gram wet weight (Table 6): ZYN dry 7.63, ZYN moist 12.00, replacement lozenge 3.20, replacement gum 1.30, snus 8.13, loose moist snuff 9.97, pouched moist snuff 8.47; unprotonated nicotine 4.87, 7.87, 2.57, 1.28, 7.11, 3.23 and 3.65; pH 8.3, 8.3, 8.6, 9.9, 8.9, 7.7 and 7.9; product mass 0.4, 0.8, 0.6, 1.2, 1.0 (loose not given) and 1.3 g (Table 1). Content per pouch is not printed; multiplying gives about 3 mg for ZYN dry and 10 mg for ZYN moist against 8 mg for the snus pouch (AI reader's arithmetic). Oral use; no use was studied.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (products). Forty-three compounds screened; those below the limit of quantification are not reported as zero.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (products).

comparison.controls: Within the study: one Swedish snus, two moist snuffs and two nicotine replacement products, analysed by the same programme. No cigarette was analysed; no other pouch brand was analysed.
comparison.matching: Per gram of wet weight, so products of different mass (0.4 to 1.3 g) are not compared per unit of use; moisture ranges from 3% to 53%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a product analysis; what was not measured: other pouch brands, other batches, product ageing, nicotine uptake, flavour compounds, and agrochemicals.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Concentrations above the quantification limit, mean and standard deviation of triplicates, in Tables 3 to 6; counts of compounds quantified per product.
outcomes.validity_norms: Methods are described in Table 2 with validation and accreditation status in the text; recoveries, blanks and uncertainty are not given in the main text. No thresholds or safety limits are applied.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is not measured; 'low toxicity' is inferred from the number and level of quantified constituents (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive; no tests).

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes. Nitrosamines: none of ten above the limits in either ZYN variant or either replacement product; snus NNN 0.44, NNK 0.19, NAT 0.31 and NAB 0.02 microgram per gram and NDMA 0.24 ng per gram; loose moist snuff NNN 3.63, NNK 2.27; pouched moist snuff NNN 2.53, NNK 0.92 microgram per gram, so five to 12 times the snus levels (Table 3). Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons: none in ZYN, replacement products or snus; six of seven in loose moist snuff and five in pouched, benzo[a]pyrene 113 and 74 ng per gram (Table 4). Other constituents (microgram per gram unless stated): ZYN dry formaldehyde 10.3, chromium 0.160, ammonia 62, nickel 0.067; ZYN moist formaldehyde 1.5, chromium 0.099, ammonia 66; replacement lozenge nickel 0.086; replacement gum cadmium 0.043, chromium 0.850, lead 0.067, nickel 0.243, acetaldehyde 4.7, ammonia 4.5, uranium-235 0.14 and uranium-238 2.76 Bq per kg; snus arsenic 0.062, cadmium 0.270, chromium 0.523, lead 0.177, nickel 0.817, selenium 0.088, acetaldehyde 10.0, ammonia 847, formaldehyde 1.6, anabasine 28.5, nornicotine 162, ochratoxin A 0.86 ng per gram and polonium-210 5.4 Bq per kg (Tables 5 and 6). Compounds quantified, nicotine included: replacement lozenge 2, ZYN moist 4, ZYN dry 5, replacement gum 9, snus 19, pouched moist snuff 26, loose moist snuff 27 (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (a laboratory screening).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 43 compounds are in Tables 3 to 6. The maker chose the compounds, the products and the comparison categories; agrochemicals were left out. Data are said to be available on request; recoveries, blanks and uncertainty were not in the text read.
analysis.power: Not applicable (no tests). One batch per product, triplicate analyses.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one batch each of two ZYN variants, none of ten nitrosamines and none of seven polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons was above the quantification limits (0.01 microgram per gram for the four tobacco-specific nitrosamines; 30 ng per gram for most polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons); formaldehyde, chromium and ammonia were quantified in both and nickel in the dry variant; four or five compounds in all, against two or nine in the replacement products and 19 in the snus and 26 or 27 in the moist snuffs. Moist snuff held five to 12 times the nitrosamines of the snus. Nothing was measured in people.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract: tobacco-free pouches 'may serve as a low-risk alternative' to cigarettes and to snus and moist snuff; the two ZYN products 'contained no nitrosamines or' polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; the number of quantified constituents was similar for ZYN and replacement products and found at low levels. Discussion: few constituents at low levels 'suggesting that the products have a low toxicity'; the results 'confirm' a manufacturer's earlier study; clinical data suggest 'a lower abuse liability' than cigarettes. Gaps: (1) the low-risk and low-toxicity statements are inferences; neither risk nor toxicity was measured, and the paper itself says a full risk assessment needs more data; (2) 'no nitrosamines' means none above limits of about 4 to 8 ng per ZYN pouch for the tobacco-specific ones, and an independent German laboratory with a limit roughly ten times or more lower found traces in 26 of 44 other pouch products (see sc_mallock_2024); the two do not conflict, but the abstract's wording does not carry the limit; (3) the results are for two variants of one maker's brand, yet the title and abstract speak of 'novel nicotine pouch products'; (4) the Background's 'convincingly shown' lower harm of snus than smoking cites one review, which was itself supported by the same company (see sc_lee_2013); (5) the Discussion's inferences on uptake and abuse liability rest on other studies whose funders are not stated here and were not read. In the authors' favour, they state that the data are limited to constituent content and that long-term epidemiological data are needed.

timeline.event: Azzopardi et al.: a similar screening of 26 compounds in a pouch brand, a Swedish-type snus, a moist snuff and replacement products, which this paper says it confirms; the German paper in this batch describes the study as by a manufacturer and its quantification limit as much less sensitive than its own (as described; not read).

Independent German laboratory analysis of 46 pouch products from 20 producers: nicotine 1.79 to 47.5 mg per pouch; tobacco-specific nitrosamines detected at trace levels in 26 of 44 nicotine pouches with a limit of quantification roughly ten times or more lower than this paper's (AI reader's arithmetic); funded by a federal risk-assessment institute; no company funding declared.

Scoping review of pouch studies that splits findings by industry and non-industry funding. It does not cite this paper or the German analysis above, but reports other content analyses (70 US tobacco-free products, 50 pouches, 31 pouches sold in Germany).

Systematic review of snus and pouches that cites this paper as showing similar numbers of constituents in pouches and replacement products, noting only that the pouches came from one manufacturer; it does not say that manufacturer funded the study.

replication.where_it_stands: A single maker-funded laboratory comparison of two ZYN variants with a snus, two moist snuffs and two replacement products. It has not been re-run on the same products by an independent laboratory, and the independent German analysis of other products used a more sensitive nitrosamine method and found traces. Read as what these seven products held, per gram, at the stated limits.

funding.funder: Swedish Match AB, which markets the ZYN and General products described (as printed).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors are employees of or otherwise funded by Swedish Match AB (as printed). The funding statement says the funder designed the study, interpreted the data and wrote the manuscript, and that analyses and data collection were mainly (the wording adds 'if possible') done at external laboratories.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors are in Regulatory & Scientific Affairs, Swedish Match AB, Stockholm. The company's own laboratory did part of the analysis (Table 2). The Background cites one review for the statement that long-term studies have 'convincingly shown' lower harm from snus than from smoking, which is a review supported by the same company (see sc_lee_2013). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the measurements: most were made at an accredited external laboratory and are tabulated in full, and the claim sets this paper beside the independent German analysis.

what_would_settle_it: Independent, replicated analysis (several batches and brands, blanks and spiked controls, sensitive nitrosamine methods with limits per pouch reported) of pouches beside snus, moist snuff and nicotine replacement products in one laboratory, repeated over time; with measurements in people who use each product (nicotine uptake and urine or blood markers of nicotine, nitrosamines and metals) beside people who smoke and people who use no nicotine; and, for health, cohorts followed for years.

domains.domain: Products tested and how they were chosen
domains.note: Two variants of one maker's pouch brand, one snus, two moist snuffs and two replacement products, one batch each, the maker's own samples supplied from its distribution centre; chosen by the funder.

domains.domain: Independence of design, analysis and interpretation
domains.note: The funder designed the study, interpreted the data and wrote the manuscript; all four authors are its employees or funded by it; part of the analysis was done in its own laboratory.

Mostly an accredited external laboratory, triplicate analyses and limits printed for every compound; replacement-product methods not accredited; polonium a single measurement; recoveries and blanks not in the main text; nitrosamine limit roughly ten times or more above that of the independent German analysis (AI reader's arithmetic).
The same laboratories and methods for all seven products allow a like-for-like comparison, but there is one product per category, per gram of wet weight, and no cigarette.

'No nitrosamines' is a finding of 'below a quantification limit'; low toxicity and low risk are inferred from content; the text says 38 of 43 compounds were below the limit in both ZYN variants (true for the dry variant; 39 for the moist) and that ZYN dry formaldehyde was about five times snus (Table 6 gives 6.4 times).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for a laboratory analysis of commercial products (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to this design; the overall judgment cannot be less severe than the worst domain. The measurements come largely from an accredited external laboratory and are tabulated in full, so they can be read as what these seven products held per gram at the stated limits; the choice of products, the design and the interpretation sit with the maker. Citable for that content and for the comparison of those products; not for tobacco-free pouches as a category, for the absence of nitrosamines below the stated limits, or for any statement about uptake, toxicity or health.

key_findings.finding: Design and sources: seven oral products screened for 43 compounds, one batch each, triplicate analyses on the whole product, results per gram of wet weight; the two ZYN variants and the snus came from the maker's distribution centre. Most analyses at an external laboratory accredited to ISO 17025, some in the maker's laboratory; replacement-product methods validated but not accredited.

key_findings.finding: Nitrosamines: none of ten above the quantification limit in either ZYN variant or either replacement product (limits 0.01 microgram per gram for NNN, NNK, NAT and NAB). Snus held NNN 0.44 and NNK 0.19 microgram per gram; loose moist snuff 3.63 and 2.27; pouched moist snuff 2.53 and 0.92, five to 12 times the snus.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results, 3rd, 4th, 7th and 8th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Below the limit does not mean absent; limit equals roughly 4 to 8 ng per ZYN pouch (AI reader's arithmetic from Table 1 masses).

key_findings.finding: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons: none above the limits in ZYN, replacement products or snus; six of seven in loose moist snuff and five in pouched moist snuff, benzo[a]pyrene 113 and 74 ng per gram.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other constituents in ZYN: formaldehyde (10.3 microgram per gram in the dry variant, 1.5 in the moist), chromium (0.160 and 0.099), ammonia (62 and 66) and, in the dry variant only, nickel (0.067). Snus held formaldehyde 1.6, chromium 0.523, nickel 0.817, ammonia 847; the replacement gum held chromium 0.850, nickel 0.243, cadmium, lead, acetaldehyde, ammonia and uranium isotopes, and the lozenge only nickel (0.086).
key_findings.locator: Tables 5 and 6; Results, 3rd to 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: ZYN dry formaldehyde was the highest of all seven products.

key_findings.finding: Counts of compounds quantified, nicotine included, of 43: replacement lozenge 2, ZYN moist 4, ZYN dry 5, replacement gum 9, snus 19, pouched moist snuff 26, loose moist snuff 27. Snus held five nitrosamines, six metals, acetaldehyde, ammonia, anabasine, formaldehyde, nornicotine, ochratoxin A and polonium-210.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Nicotine: total nicotine per gram was 7.63 (ZYN dry), 12.00 (ZYN moist), 3.20 (lozenge), 1.30 (gum), 8.13 (snus), 9.97 (loose moist snuff) and 8.47 mg (pouched moist snuff); unprotonated nicotine and pH are in Table 6 and Table 1. The authors say unprotonated nicotine does not capture how much is extracted in use, and that nicotine uptake needs clinical studies.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Tables 1 and 6; Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' reading: few constituents at low levels in ZYN 'suggesting that the products have a low toxicity'; consistent with in vitro studies they cite; the data are limited to constituent content, and long-term epidemiological data are needed for a full risk assessment. They say their results confirm a manufacturer's similar study in which no tobacco-specific nitrosamines or benzo[a]pyrene could be quantified in a pouch or replacement products.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th, 8th and 9th paragraphs; Conclusions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Framing: the Background states that long-term studies have 'convincingly shown' snus to carry substantially fewer adverse effects than smoking (citing one review), describes the 'Swedish Experience' and the US Food and Drug Administration's 2019 modified-risk order for eight snus products including General, and says tobacco-free pouches 'should, at least in theory' not expose people to nitrosamines.
key_findings.locator: Background, 1st to 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Context and hypothesis, not a result of this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the two ZYN products 'contained no nitrosamines or' polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and the Conclusions say none were 'found'. The finding is none above quantification limits of 0.01 microgram per gram for NNN, NNK, NAT and NAB (about 4 to 8 ng per pouch given the masses in Table 1), 10 to 25 ng per gram for other nitrosamines and 30 ng per gram for most polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Conclusions; Tables 3 and 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence below a limit; an independent laboratory with a much lower limit found traces in many other pouch products (see sc_mallock_2024).

reporting_issues.issue: Results say 38 of the 43 compounds were below the limit in 'the two types' of ZYN; that holds for the dry variant (five quantified) but the moist variant had four quantified (39 below). The abstract lists nickel among both products' findings; it was quantified only in the dry variant. The text says ZYN dry formaldehyde was about five times snus; Table 6 gives 10.3 against 1.6 microgram per gram, 6.4 times.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Table 6
reporting_issues.consequence: Small; use the table values.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract speak of 'novel nicotine pouch products' and the Discussion infers 'low toxicity', but two variants of one brand were tested, one batch each, and no toxicity, uptake or health outcome was measured.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Title; Abstract; Discussion, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The results describe these samples; they cannot stand for pouches in general or for risk.

reporting_issues.issue: The funding statement says the analyses and collection of data were mainly 'if possible' carried out at external laboratories; Table 2 shows that analyses of five nitrosamines, two uranium isotopes, anabasine, nornicotine and unprotonated nicotine were done in the company's own laboratory.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Funding; Material and methods › Sample handling and analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Which constituents were measured in-house is recoverable only from Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion supports 'lower abuse liability' and in vitro findings with other studies (its references 17 to 19, 21 to 23 and 25 to 29) without stating who funded them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Those studies were not read; their funders are unknown here.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9985244 (HTML): abstract, all sections of the main text, Tables 1 to 6, funding, competing-interest and affiliation statements; the reference list and the cited studies (Azzopardi 2021, Lee 2013, the in vitro and clinical papers) were not read

design_detail: Umbrella review plus top-up systematic review, commissioned by the Australian Department of Health, of the health effects of e-cigarettes in humans (nicotine and non-nicotine; tetrahydrocannabinol products, animal, in-vitro and biomarker studies excluded when possible). The umbrella part starts from the 2018 National Academies report and eight major independent reviews (2017 to 2021); the top-up part searched six databases in July 2020 for studies from July 2017 to July 2020 not in the National Academies report. 400 publications were synthesised narratively by health outcome, with conclusions worded on the National Academies evidence scale and the certainty of each outcome rated with GRADE.
