Registration: PROSPERO CRD42020200673 (top-up systematic review). Pooled estimates quoted come from the authors' earlier reviews, not new meta-analyses.
can_establish: What a government-commissioned, two-reviewer synthesis of studies up to mid-2020 (and of major reviews up to 2021) concluded about each type of health outcome of e-cigarette use, how strong it rated the evidence, and which outcomes had no usable studies.
cannot_establish: Anything after mid-2020 (the two PATH cohort papers on heart and lung disease read for this batch came later), pooled effect sizes (the main text reports no pooled estimate of its own; the Methods say meta-analyses were done when possible and refer to the supplement), the relative harm of vaping against smoking (the authors state that comparisons with smoking cannot reliably show the direct health impact of e-cigarettes, and the review excludes biomarker studies), or the content of the 400 studies (the evidence tables are in a supplement that was not read).

sample.recruitment: Top-up search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library and PsycINFO in July 2020 for peer-reviewed human studies published July 2017 to July 2020, plus forward and backward citation searching, one grey-literature item, and 37 studies from the authors' two earlier reviews of smoking uptake and cessation; umbrella part: grey-literature search for major reviews to 31 December 2021 (later reviews to November 2022 considered in the discussion only) (Methods; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Peer-reviewed original research on health effects of e-cigarettes. Excluded when possible: e-cigarettes delivering THC, animal, in vitro and biomarker studies. 86 publications excluded because the design precluded causal inference; three otherwise eligible studies excluded for low quality scores. Cessation analyses limited to randomized trials with biochemically verified cessation and at least four months' follow-up. Design order of preference: randomized trials, prospective cohorts, case-control, non-randomized intervention studies; other designs when these were unavailable.
sample.demographics: Not summarised in the text; evidence tables are in the supplement (parts 3 and 4, not read). Nicotine content was generally not reported, and the authors assumed reported effects concerned nicotine-containing products unless stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The review answers the questions its design can: acute and device-related outcomes, dependence, smoking uptake and cessation. Excluding biomarker and cross-sectional-only evidence for causal questions removes the exposure data that other reviews rely on (for example the PATH biomarker comparison). The search ends in July 2020, so the longitudinal cohort papers on heart and lung disease published later are not in it. 126 of the 400 publications (about 31%, editors' count from Box 2) are surveillance reports, case series and case reports on burns, injuries and poisoning, which can show that a harm occurs but not how often.

exposure.measurement: E-cigarette use as defined by each included study; most did not report e-cigarette type or e-liquid contents, and the authors note products labelled nicotine-free often contain nicotine.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesised; the review notes long-term evidence is unavailable and that the products studied do not necessarily reflect current devices (for example nicotine-salt pods).
exposure.polysubstance: Outcomes are reported separately for people who smoke and people who do not; dual use is described as the most common pattern in many countries, with unknown direct health impact (Discussion, 7th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Varies by study. The authors state that people neither smoking nor using e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group, and that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to estimate effects of e-cigarettes, because statistical adjustment is unlikely to fully remove confounding by smoking (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; the authors name residual confounding between e-cigarette use and smoking as a major problem.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Outcomes grouped by organ system or event (clinical disease endpoints, subclinical outcomes, other); conclusions worded on the National Academies scale (conclusive, substantial, moderate, limited, insufficient, no available evidence) and the certainty of each integrated body of evidence rated with GRADE (supplement part 2, not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Methodological quality of top-up studies assessed independently by two authors with Joanna Briggs Institute checklists; the included major reviews are not formally appraised, though the authors rate the 2022 Cochrane review as less independent because four of its authors were investigators in included trials.
outcomes.operationalization: 'No available evidence' means no included studies on the outcome; 'insufficient' means studies exist but cannot support a conclusion.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No new pooled estimates are reported in the main text. Counts per outcome (Box 2/3): dependence 52, cardiovascular disease 21 (1 meta-analysis, 11 randomized trials, 1 cohort, 7 non-randomized intervention studies, 1 case report), cancer 1, respiratory disease 58 (10 randomized trials, 6 cohorts, 8 non-randomized intervention studies, 18 surveillance reports, 7 case series, 9 case reports), burns and injuries 67, poisoning 59, less serious adverse events 47, smoking uptake 28, cessation 11; smaller categories: oral health 4, developmental and reproductive 3, mental health 3, environmental hazards 25, neurological 13, ocular 1, olfactory 1, endocrine 2, allergy 4, sleep, wound healing and haematological 0. Editors' check: the row totals in Box 2 add to 400, and the selection arithmetic works (227 + 10 + 1 - 86 + 37 = 189 top-up studies; 112 + 189 + 99 = 400).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42020200673, posted 31 August 2020 according to the Methods, which is after the July 2020 search; the abstract calls the registration prospective. Only the top-up systematic review is registered; deviations are not discussed; search strategy and GRADE method are in the supplement (not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The main text reports conclusions by outcome rather than study-level data; which individual studies drove each conclusion cannot be checked without the supplement.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As of studies to mid-2020 (and major reviews to 2021), the review rated the evidence as conclusive for poisoning, burns and injuries, seizures and e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (largely THC products), substantial for dependence in people who do not smoke, moderate for acute rises in heart rate, blood pressure and arterial stiffness in people who smoke and for mild adverse events, limited (people who do not smoke) or insufficient (people who smoke) for acute changes in spirometry, insufficient (people who smoke) or no available evidence (people who do not smoke) for asthma, bronchitis and COPD, and 'no available evidence' for heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death and cancer. It rated certainty for clinical and subclinical outcomes low or very low.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that e-cigarettes 'can be harmful to health', particularly for non-smokers, children, adolescents and young adults, that effects on many important outcomes are uncertain, and that they may benefit smokers who use them to quit completely and promptly. The Discussion goes further in places: it says there is evidence of adverse effects on lung function (Box 3 rates this limited or insufficient), cites human and animal studies on nicotine and adolescent brain development (the review excluded animal studies and rates development outcomes 'no available evidence'), applies the precautionary principle, and says the evidence supports policy to reduce use in the general population. The Results describe the cessation trials as showing e-cigarettes 'as efficacious as' nicotine replacement while Box 4 says 'more efficacious than'.

timeline.event: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report: the starting point of this umbrella review; 112 of its 400 publications come from it, so the two are not independent (card sc_nasem_2018).

McNeill et al., Nicotine vaping in England: identified by the authors after their umbrella search and described as lacking direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and as finding more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes, mainly on comparisons with smoking and biomarkers (card sc_mcneill_2022).

Mendelsohn et al. published a critique whose title names the report on which this article is based (reference 13 here, 'Electronic cigarettes and health outcomes: systematic review of global evidence'); it was not read for this card, so what it criticises is not recorded here.

Cochrane review of e-cigarettes for smoking cessation (Hartmann-Boyce et al., 2022 update): discussed by the authors, who rate it less independent because four of its authors were investigators in included trials and note it rated trial risk of bias lower than they did; not read here.

replication.where_it_stands: A government-commissioned synthesis whose conclusions on chronic disease ('no available evidence', 'insufficient') describe the state of the literature in 2020 to 2021, before the PATH cohort papers on heart and lung disease. It agrees broadly with the major reviews it builds on, which share much of its evidence. A published critique is listed in the library and has not been read.

funding.funder: Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), as part of an independent program examining the health impacts of e-cigarettes; Banks holds an NHMRC Principal Research Fellowship (1136128). The work was commissioned by the Department of Health and its report also informed the 2021 RACGP smoking-cessation guideline update and a 2022 NHMRC statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: 'No relevant disclosures.' The report on which the article is based was reviewed by members of the NHMRC Electronic Cigarettes Working Committee and staff of the Department of Health, and subject to an independent methodological review under NHMRC processes.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors are at the National Centre for Epidemiology and Population Health, Australian National University. No tobacco, e-cigarette or pharmaceutical funding is declared. The commissioning body is a government health department; its staff and an NHMRC committee reviewed the underlying report, which the article says also went through an independent methodological review.

what_would_settle_it: An update of the same review with a search beyond 2020 that includes the longitudinal cohort studies of heart and lung disease and any trials with clinical endpoints, appraised with a risk-of-bias tool for non-randomized studies of exposures, with published evidence tables and a list of excluded studies, and with a pre-specified decision on how to treat comparisons with smoking.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (humans), exposure (e-cigarette use, with and without nicotine) and outcomes (health outcomes grouped by system) are stated, with an order of preferred designs; no comparator is part of the eligibility criteria. Comparison groups (people who do or do not smoke; people who neither smoke nor use e-cigarettes) are set outcome by outcome in the synthesis.
PROSPERO record for the top-up review, dated 31 August 2020, after the July 2020 search; the paper calls it prospective; deviations and a synthesis plan are not described in the main text.

A stated order of preference (randomized trials, prospective cohorts, case-control, non-randomized intervention) and the reason (suitability for causal inference), with other designs used where these were unavailable.

Six databases, citation searching and a grey-literature search for major reviews; terms are in the supplement (not read); no registry search is described; the main search ended in July 2020, about two and a half years before publication.
Two authors screened all titles, abstracts and articles independently; disagreements by consensus or a third author.
One author extracted with a piloted template and a second checked the data (not fully independent duplicate extraction).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The text gives reasons in aggregate (86 excluded for design, three for low quality, three cited) and a selection figure (Box 1, an image); a list of excluded studies may be in the supplement (not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Counts by outcome and design in Box 2; study-level descriptions are in the supplement (parts 3 and 4, not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Joanna Briggs Institute checklists by two authors independently, with low-quality studies excluded; individual ratings and the handling of confounding are not shown in the main text.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding and competing interests of each study were noted at extraction and used in the risk-of-bias assessment; whether they are reported per study is in the supplement (not read).

The Methods say meta-analyses were conducted when possible (supplement, part 2), but the main text presents no pooled estimate of its own; the pooled figures it quotes (smoking uptake) come from the authors' earlier review (reference 18) and published meta-analyses. Whether this item applies can be judged only from the supplement (not read).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: As item 11: depends on whether pooled analyses exist in the supplement.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Risk of bias and competing interests fed the GRADE ratings, certainty is stated as low or very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes, and the Discussion says risk-of-bias concerns were outweighed by other domains.
Inconsistency is named as a reason for low certainty, but no heterogeneity is quantified or explained in the main text; the GRADE reasons are in the supplement (part 5, not read).
Publication bias is not discussed in the main text; whether a quantitative synthesis exists in the supplement (see item 11) is not known.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funders and the absence of competing interests are stated; the commissioner's staff and a committee reviewed the underlying report.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 7, 10, 11, 12 and 15 can be judged only from the supplement or the full report, which were not read. If one of the critical items 7, 11 or 15 proved to be 'no', AMSTAR 2 would give low confidence; if two did, critically low. On the items that can be judged from the main text, no critical item is 'no' (2, 4 and 9 are partly met), and the confirmed weaknesses are non-critical (1: no comparator in the eligibility criteria; 14: heterogeneity not explained in the main text); data extraction was by one author with a second author checking (item 6, scored 'yes' as in sc_hartmann_boyce_2023, though AMSTAR 2 strictly asks for two extractors or good agreement on a sample). More than one non-critical weakness and no confirmed critical flaw gives moderate confidence at best. This is a judgment about the review's method, not about its policy conclusions. It may be cited for what the literature to 2020 and 2021 contained on each outcome and for the National Academies-scale wording of its conclusions (for example 'no available evidence' for clinical heart disease and cancer, 'insufficient' for asthma, bronchitis and COPD); not for the size of any risk, for evidence after mid-2020, for relative harm against smoking (which it does not assess: its authors say comparisons with smoking cannot reliably show the direct health impact, and it excludes biomarker studies), or as independent confirmation of the National Academies report, from which 112 of its 400 studies come.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413 (all main-text sections, Boxes 2 to 4 as text, acknowledgements, competing interests, reference list; Box 1 is an image and was not extracted; Supporting Information (search terms, GRADE method, evidence tables, certainty reasons) not read; the full report to the Department of Health not read)

key_findings.finding: Method: umbrella review starting from the 2018 National Academies report and a grey-literature search for major independent reviews to 31 December 2021 (eight included), plus a top-up systematic review of six databases searched in July 2020 for studies from July 2017 to July 2020, with two authors screening independently and Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal by two authors; PROSPERO CRD42020200673.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Umbrella review; Methods › Top-up review; Methods › Eligibility screening and Risk of bias assessment; Abstract › Registration

key_findings.finding: Selection: 6558 potentially eligible records; 227 eligible, plus ten from citation searching and one from grey literature; 86 excluded because the design precluded causal inference; 37 added from two earlier reviews by the authors, giving 189 top-up studies; with 112 from the National Academies report and 99 from other reviews, 400 publications in the synthesis. THC products, animal, in vitro and biomarker studies were excluded when possible.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Inclusion and exclusion criteria

key_findings.finding: Counts of studies by outcome (Box 2): cardiovascular disease 21 (1 meta-analysis, 11 randomized trials, 1 cohort, 7 non-randomized intervention studies, 1 case report); cancer 1 (a cohort); respiratory disease 58 (10 randomized trials, 6 cohorts, 8 non-randomized intervention studies, 18 surveillance reports, 7 case series, 9 case reports).
key_findings.locator: Box 2, rows 'Cardiovascular disease', 'Cancer', 'Respiratory disease'

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular conclusions (Box 3): clinical outcomes (heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death) and subclinical atherosclerosis outcomes: no available evidence; blood pressure, heart rate, arterial stiffness and related measures in non-smokers: insufficient evidence; in smokers: moderate evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes acutely raise heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure and arterial stiffness, limited evidence of raised endothelial dysfunction and limited evidence that long-term use after switching from smoking lowers blood pressure.
key_findings.locator: Box 3, row 'Cardiovascular disease (21)'

key_findings.finding: Respiratory conclusions (Box 3): lung injury (EVALI) conclusive, largely with THC products, but in the largest study 14% of cases were in people reporting only nicotine products and 2% non-nicotine products; asthma, bronchitis and COPD: insufficient evidence in smokers, no available evidence in non-smokers; fewer exacerbations or less progression after switching: insufficient; acute spirometry changes: limited (non-smokers) or insufficient (smokers); airway resistance after use: limited.
key_findings.locator: Box 3, row 'Respiratory disease (58)'; Results › Health outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cancer (Box 3): invasive cancer risk and pre-cancer outcomes: no available evidence (one included study).
key_findings.locator: Box 3, row 'Cancer (1)'

key_findings.finding: Certainty: rated low or very low for clinical and subclinical outcomes, because of small samples, study design and a paucity of evidence that caused serious concerns about inconsistency, imprecision and indirectness. The authors conclude the direct impact of e-cigarettes on clinical disease outcomes is largely unknown.
key_findings.locator: Results › Health outcomes, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other conclusions: conclusive evidence for poisoning, nicotine toxicity, burns and injuries, seizures and (largely THC-related) lung injury; substantial evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes cause dependence in non-smokers and limited evidence in smokers (including limited evidence that abuse liability is lower than for cigarettes); moderate evidence for throat irritation, cough, dizziness, headache and nausea.
key_findings.locator: Results › Health outcomes, 1st paragraph; Box 3, rows 'Dependence and abuse liability (52)', 'Poisoning', 'Less serious adverse events (47)'

key_findings.finding: On relative harm: the authors state that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to estimate effects of e-cigarettes, that people who neither smoke nor use e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group, that adjustment is unlikely to fully remove confounding between e-cigarette use and smoking, that statements such as 'safer than smoking' may be useful for the minority of smokers who quit completely but do not apply to non-smokers, and that comparisons with smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors describe an English review (McNeill et al., 2022, found after their search) as noting the lack of direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and that most serious adverse events were infrequent, and as focusing on comparisons with smoking and biomarkers, where it generally found more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes. They rate the 2022 Cochrane cessation review as less independent because four of its authors were investigators in included trials.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Dual use is the most frequent pattern of e-cigarette use in many countries; its direct health impact is unknown, and e-cigarettes may facilitate continued smoking. Smokers who quit completely and promptly by switching may benefit. E-cigarettes are not registered therapeutic goods in Australia.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Authors' stated limits: products are new, diverse and changing; long-term evidence is unavailable; most publications lack e-cigarette type and e-liquid constituents, and products labelled nicotine-free often contain nicotine; confounding between e-cigarette use and smoking is a major problem. Risk of bias also considered competing interests such as tobacco or pharmaceutical funding.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st to 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding: Australian Department of Health and NHMRC; competing interests 'No relevant disclosures'; the report was reviewed by the NHMRC Electronic Cigarettes Working Committee and Department staff and by an independent methodological review.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgements, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Competing interests

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe the eleven cessation trials as showing freebase nicotine e-cigarettes with clinical support 'as efficacious' as nicotine replacement or usual care, while Box 4 says 'more efficacious' than nicotine replacement or no intervention (both labelled limited evidence).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Smoking behaviour, 2nd paragraph; Box 4, row 'Smoking and nicotine cessation (11)'
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the cessation conclusion is worded two ways in the same paper; claims on cessation should rely on the Cochrane card instead.

reporting_issues.issue: Box 3 rates 'Development of children or adolescents' as 'no available evidence', and acute spirometry effects as limited (non-smokers) or insufficient (smokers), but the Discussion says there is evidence for adverse effects on lung function and cites human and animal studies for adverse effects of nicotine on adolescent brain development.
reporting_issues.locator: Box 3; Discussion, 1st and 5th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Box 3 for the rated conclusions; the Discussion sentences rely on sources outside the review's inclusion criteria.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods date the PROSPERO posting 31 August 2020, after the July 2020 search, while the abstract labels the registration prospective.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods › Top-up review; Abstract › Registration
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether registration preceded screening and extraction cannot be checked from the text; item 2 is rated partial.

reporting_issues.issue: Pooled figures for smoking uptake (about three times the likelihood of starting to smoke) and the claim that the relationship was deemed likely causal come from the authors' own earlier meta-analysis (reference 18), summarised without new data.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Smoking behaviour, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Not independent evidence; cite the earlier paper if the figure is needed.

design_detail: Research letter: prospective cohort analysis of the PATH Study (US national probability cohort, Waves 1 to 5, 2013 to 2019). Cox regression of first self-reported cardiovascular diagnosis over up to four years of follow-up in adults without cardiovascular disease at baseline, by a four-category, wave-updated measure of current cigarette and e-cigarette use (neither, e-cigarette only, cigarettes only, both). Two outcomes: any cardiovascular disease, and heart attack, heart failure or stroke.
can_establish: How the rate of newly self-reported heart disease or stroke over up to four years compared, after adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, family history, marijuana and smoking history, between US adults who currently used e-cigarettes only, cigarettes only, both, or neither.
cannot_establish: Whether e-cigarettes cause or prevent cardiovascular disease (self-reported, non-adjudicated outcomes; the e-cigarette-only group had more pack-years than the reference group and few events), what happens over more than four years, whether switching from smoking lowers risk in the same person (no within-person analysis), or anything about disease types reported separately (heart attack, heart failure and stroke were pooled).

sample.recruitment: PATH Study: nationally representative cohort of non-institutionalized US adults aged 18 or older, oversampling people who use tobacco, young adults and African-American individuals; five waves between 2013 and 2019. Initial sample 32,320; excluded: lost to follow-up at Wave 2 (5,873), previously diagnosed with cardiovascular disease (2,172), missing baseline exposure (55), baseline cardiovascular disease (99) or Wave 2 outcome data (94), leaving 24,027 (Text, 2nd and 7th paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults without a previous cardiovascular diagnosis and with exposure and Wave 2 outcome data. Follow-up counted from Wave 1 until a diagnosis, loss to follow-up, or Wave 5, to a maximum of four years.
sample.demographics: 50% under age 35, 51% women. People who used e-cigarettes only or both were younger than the reference group (62% and 54% under 35, against 51%) and had more cigarette pack-years (mean 11.0 and 15.7, against 4.2; standard deviations 46.7, 32.2 and 21.8). The pack-years of the cigarette-only group are not printed.
sample.attrition: 5,873 people (18% of the initial 32,320) lost at Wave 2 were excluded before analysis; later loss to follow-up is censored and its extent is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Excluding people lost after Wave 1 and people with existing cardiovascular disease removes some of the sickest; the reference group includes former cigarette smokers, and the e-cigarette-only group is mostly people who had smoked (their mean pack-years are about 2.6 times the reference group's). Only 41 incident events (any disease) and 15 (heart attack, heart failure or stroke) occurred in the e-cigarette-only group.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at each wave. Smoking = more than 100 lifetime cigarettes and current smoking; e-cigarette use = any current use. Four categories: no current e-cigarette use or smoking, e-cigarette only, cigarettes only, both. The category was updated at each wave (time-varying).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency, amount, device and nicotine content of e-cigarette use were not used; 'any current use' counts occasional and daily use alike. Follow-up up to four years from Wave 1.
exposure.polysubstance: Adjusted for ever use of marijuana and for time-varying current use of other combustible tobacco (hookah, pipe, cigars, cigarillos) and smokeless tobacco (snus, other).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Primary reference: people with no current e-cigarette use or smoking, which includes former cigarette smokers (acknowledged limitation). Second comparator: people who currently smoked cigarettes only.
comparison.matching: None; Cox models adjusted for baseline age (seven bands), sex, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, family history of heart attack or bypass surgery, ever marijuana use, pack-years and pack-years squared, and time-varying other tobacco use (Text, 6th paragraph; Table 1 footnote).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Time since quitting smoking, intensity of past smoking, diet, physical activity, alcohol, income, mental health, and whether people started e-cigarettes because of early symptoms (the exposure is updated at each wave, but how the timing of diagnosis relative to a change of product was handled is not described).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Marijuana: ever use only. Alcohol and other drugs not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported diagnosis in the past 12 months, asked at Waves 2 to 5: heart attack or bypass surgery, heart failure, other heart condition, or stroke. Two outcomes: any of these (composite), and heart attack, heart failure or stroke only.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite an earlier PATH paper supporting validity and reliability of self-reported heart attack, heart failure and stroke (reference 5, not read); no validation is cited for 'other heart condition', which is part of the main composite. Outcomes were not adjudicated.
outcomes.operationalization: Incident disease = first self-reported diagnosis in Waves 2 to 5 among people free of disease at baseline.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; three contrasts for each of two outcomes.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cases: any disease 1,487 (764 neither, 41 e-cigarette only, 569 cigarettes only, 113 both); heart attack, heart failure or stroke 519 (222, 15, 242, 40); the group totals reconcile with the printed cohort size 24,027. Age-adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years (95% CI), any disease: 8.0 (7.3-8.7), 9.7 (6.4-13.0), 14.8 (13.2-16.3), 17.1 (13.6-20.7); heart attack, heart failure or stroke: 2.5 (2.1-2.9), 4.0 (1.8-6.2), 6.9 (5.8-8.0), 7.1 (4.6-9.6). Multivariable hazard ratios against neither, any disease: e-cigarette only 1.00 (0.69-1.45), cigarettes only 1.53 (1.30-1.79), both 1.54 (1.21-1.96); heart attack, heart failure or stroke: 1.35 (0.75-2.42), 2.20 (1.73-2.81), 2.08 (1.40-3.09). Against cigarettes only: e-cigarette only 0.66 (0.46-0.94) and 0.61 (0.34-1.09); both 1.01 (0.81-1.26) and 0.94 (0.65-1.36). Models adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity only gave 1.16 (0.82-1.66) and 1.55 (0.87-2.76) for e-cigarette only against neither. Editors' check: ratios of the printed hazard ratios against neither (for example 1.00/1.53, 1.35/2.20, 1.54/1.53, 2.08/2.20) reproduce the printed contrasts with cigarettes only to within 0.01.
analysis.covariates: See comparison.matching. Multiple imputation for missing covariates; Wave 2 longitudinal weights for national estimates.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned; analytic code is stated to be available on request.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only two composite outcomes are shown; heart attack, heart failure, stroke and 'other heart condition' are not reported separately, and no sensitivity analyses (for example excluding former smokers, lagging the exposure, or restricting to never smokers who vape) are reported.
analysis.power: Low for the e-cigarette-only group: 41 and 15 events. The interval for heart attack, heart failure or stroke against neither (0.75 to 2.42) is compatible with anything from a quarter lower to more than double the risk. The authors state that analyses were limited by the small number of events.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over up to four years, adults who currently used e-cigarettes only did not have a detectably different rate of newly reported heart disease or stroke than adults who used neither (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.69-1.45; 1.35, 0.75-2.42 for heart attack, heart failure or stroke), and had a lower rate than adults who only smoked for the broad outcome (0.66, 0.46-0.94) but not detectably for the narrower one (0.61, 0.34-1.09). People who both smoked and used e-cigarettes had about 1.5 times the rate of people who used neither (1.54, 1.21-1.96) and a rate not detectably different from people who only smoked (1.01, 0.81-1.26).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors write that no significant difference was found for exclusive e-cigarette use against non-use, that dual use was associated with higher risk than non-use and no different from smoking, and conclude that combining smoking with e-cigarette use 'does not reduce CVD events' and that quitting both products 'is required to ensure a mitigation of risk' (Text, 8th paragraph). The first conclusion reads a non-significant comparison (interval 0.81 to 1.26) as no reduction; the second is not tested (nobody who quit both was analysed, and the e-cigarette-only group did not differ from the reference group). The letter also states the limits (self-reported outcomes, short follow-up, reference group including former smokers, few events).

timeline.event: Farsalinos et al. (National Health Interview Surveys 2016 and 2017) and Osei et al.: two large cross-sectional studies, cited by the authors, reported no significant association between exclusive e-cigarette use and cardiovascular disease. Not read here.

This research letter: the first longitudinal PATH analysis of incident cardiovascular disease by e-cigarette use named by the authors; same PATH waves and several of the same authors as the respiratory-outcome analysis (card sc_xie_2020).

replication.where_it_stands: A single short research letter. Its finding for exclusive e-cigarette use against non-use agrees in direction with the two cross-sectional surveys the authors cite, but the interval is wide, follow-up is four years and the outcomes are self-reported. No second cohort with incident cardiovascular events was read for this batch.

funding.funder: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH) and the US Food and Drug Administration's Center for Tobacco Products (grants P50HL120163, U54HL120163 and 1K01HL154130-01); a Public Policy Award from the American Lung Association. The authors state the content is solely their responsibility.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Stokes reported receiving grants from Johnson & Johnson outside of the submitted work. No other conflicts were reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Boston University (School of Public Health; School of Medicine), University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, Johns Hopkins (Ciccarone Center) and the University of Louisville. The data come from the PATH Study, which is itself a federally funded study.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people who vape, with product use measured by frequency, device and nicotine content (and checked with biomarkers), cardiovascular events adjudicated from medical records, follow-up of many years, separate results for people who never smoked and for former smokers by time since quitting, and enough events in people who vape for an interval that excludes a meaningful increase or decrease.

domains.note: Adjusted for many risk factors, but the e-cigarette-only group had about 2.6 times the reference group's pack-years (11.0 vs 4.2) and the reference group includes former smokers; time since quitting, smoking intensity and lifestyle are not in the models; people with early symptoms may switch products. Residual smoking history probably biases the e-cigarette group towards more disease, not less, but its size is unknown.
Self-reported current use only; no frequency, device or nicotine content; time-varying exposure with no description of timing relative to diagnosis.
18% of the initial sample lost at Wave 2 excluded; people with existing disease excluded; later losses censored.
Switching and quitting between waves is part of the exposure definition; its handling is not described.
Multiple imputation for covariates; loss to follow-up not quantified beyond Wave 2.
Self-reported and not adjudicated; 'other heart condition' is in the main composite without cited validation; misclassification probably non-differential but not shown.
Research letter with two composites and no components or sensitivity analyses; no plan; code on request.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, and residual confounding by smoking history, in a group that is mostly former smokers with more pack-years than the reference group, is a serious concern for the contrast with non-use. The cohort is large and national, with a few thousand events, but the e-cigarette-only group contributes only 41 and 15 events. It may be cited for the rates and hazard ratios as reported, for the wide interval around the null for exclusive e-cigarette use against non-use, and for dual use being no different from smoking alone in this cohort; not for a causal effect of e-cigarettes on the heart, for the claim that quitting both is required, or for any follow-up beyond four years.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9362726 (author manuscript of a research letter: all text, Table 1 and its footnotes, funding, conflict-of-interest statement and references; no supplement or online methods are mentioned)

key_findings.finding: Initial PATH sample 32,320 adults; excluded 5,873 lost at Wave 2, 2,172 previously diagnosed with cardiovascular disease, 55 missing baseline exposure, 99 with baseline disease and 94 missing Wave 2 outcome data; 24,027 analysed (50% under age 35, 51% women).
key_findings.locator: Text (the letter has no section headings), 2nd and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Group sizes: neither 14,832; e-cigarette only 822; cigarettes only 6,515; both 1,858. People who used e-cigarettes only or both were younger (62% and 54% under 35 vs 51%) and had more pack-years (11.0 and 15.7 vs 4.2 in the reference group).
key_findings.locator: Text, 7th paragraph; Table 1, column headings

key_findings.finding: Exposure and outcome definitions: smoker = more than 100 lifetime cigarettes and current smoking; e-cigarette = any current use; categories updated at each wave. Outcome = self-reported past-12-month diagnosis of heart attack or bypass surgery, heart failure, other heart condition or stroke (Waves 2 to 5), and a narrower outcome of heart attack, heart failure or stroke. Follow-up at most four years.
key_findings.locator: Text, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Table 1 footnote †

key_findings.finding: Incident cases: any disease 1,487 (764 neither; 41 e-cigarette only; 569 cigarettes only; 113 both); heart attack, heart failure or stroke 519 (222; 15; 242; 40). Age-adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years: 8.0, 9.7, 14.8, 17.1 for any disease; 2.5, 4.0, 6.9, 7.1 for the narrower outcome.
key_findings.locator: Text, 7th paragraph; Table 1, rows 'No. of incident cases' and 'Incidence rate'

key_findings.finding: Multivariable hazard ratios against neither, any disease: e-cigarette only 1.00 (95% CI 0.69-1.45), cigarettes only 1.53 (1.30-1.79), both 1.54 (1.21-1.96). Heart attack, heart failure or stroke: 1.35 (0.75-2.42), 2.20 (1.73-2.81), 2.08 (1.40-3.09).
key_findings.locator: Text, 7th paragraph; Table 1, rows 'Multivariable-adjusted HR'

key_findings.finding: Multivariable hazard ratios against cigarettes only: e-cigarette only 0.66 (0.46-0.94) for any disease and 0.61 (0.34-1.09) for heart attack, heart failure or stroke; both 1.01 (0.81-1.26) and 0.94 (0.65-1.36).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, columns 'Compared with Exclusive Smoking'
key_findings.note: The authors describe the e-cigarette contrast as 30 to 40% lower risk, 'only significant' for the broad outcome.

key_findings.finding: Authors' stated limits: self-reported non-adjudicated outcomes that could be misclassified; short follow-up for a slowly developing disease; a reference group that includes former cigarette smokers; analyses limited by few events in people who used e-cigarettes. They conclude that combining smoking with e-cigarette use does not reduce cardiovascular events and that quitting both products is required to ensure risk mitigation.
key_findings.locator: Text, 8th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Three of the four printed age-adjusted rates for any disease are 22% to 38% below the lowest crude rates the counts could give, and the fourth is above it (editors' calculation, assuming at most four years each): 764 cases among 14,832 people is at least 12.9 per 1,000 person-years against 8.0 printed; 12.5 against 9.7 (e-cigarette only); 21.8 against 14.8 (cigarettes only); but 15.2 against 17.1 (both). The age standardization is not described.
reporting_issues.locator: Table 1, row 'Incidence rate, per 1000 person-years'; footnote ‡
reporting_issues.consequence: The rates cannot be reproduced from the letter; cite the hazard ratios, and the rates only as age-adjusted values as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The mean pack-years are printed with standard deviations several times larger than the means (11.0 +/- 46.7; 15.7 +/- 32.2; 4.2 +/- 21.8), and the cigarette-only group's value is not given.
reporting_issues.locator: Text, 7th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The distribution is very skewed, so group means are a poor summary and the adjustment for pack-years (a linear and a squared term) may be driven by a few extreme values.

reporting_issues.issue: The hazard ratio of e-cigarette-only against cigarettes-only for any disease is printed identically (0.66, 0.46-0.94) in the age/sex/race-adjusted and the fully adjusted rows, although the two rows' ratios against neither differ (1.16 vs 1.00; 1.78 vs 1.53).
reporting_issues.locator: Table 1, 'Any cardiovascular disease' rows, column 'Exclusive e-Cigarette use' under 'Compared with Exclusive Smoking'
reporting_issues.consequence: Plausible by rounding (1.16/1.78 and 1.00/1.53 both give 0.65), but the identical intervals cannot be checked; low importance.

reporting_issues.issue: The closing sentence says quitting both products is required to mitigate risk, but the paper analyses no group that quit both, and its exclusive e-cigarette group did not differ detectably from the reference group; and it says combining does not reduce events although the interval for dual use against smoking alone (0.81 to 1.26) includes a 19% lower rate.
reporting_issues.locator: Text, 8th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should state the hazard ratios and intervals and leave out both inferences.

design_detail: Pooled analysis of individual participant data from eight Swedish prospective cohorts (the Swedish Collaboration on Health Effects of Snus Use), recruited 1978 to 2010 and followed to 2004 to 2013 through the national cause-of-death register. Men only, and only men who had never regularly smoked cigarettes: 169,103 men, 2,857,312 person-years, 10,928 deaths. Exposure was snus use reported once, at baseline; the comparison group was men who reported no tobacco use. Gamma-distributed shared-frailty survival models (random effect by cohort) with attained age as the time scale, adjusted for body mass index. Not a systematic review: the cohorts are those of the collaborating investigators.
can_establish: Whether, among Swedish men who had never regularly smoked cigarettes, men who reported using snus and no other tobacco at baseline died more often during follow-up than men who reported no tobacco use, after adjustment for age and body mass index, and how far that ratio moves across six sensitivity analyses.
cannot_establish: That snus itself causes the extra deaths (use reported once, main model adjusted for age and body mass index only, no pre-snus health measures, likely residual confounding by alcohol, education, physical activity and diet); absolute risks in each group (no group-specific rates are printed); anything about women, about people who smoke or smoked, about other smokeless products, pouches or vapes; or how snus compares with smoking (people who had ever regularly smoked cigarettes were excluded by design).

sample.recruitment: Eight Swedish cohorts recruited between 1978 and 2010: the Construction Worker Cohort (all workers in the construction industry, 279,897 men before exclusions, recruited 1978 to 1993), the Malmo Diet and Cancer Study, the northern Sweden MONICA study, the National March Cohort (participants in a charity walk), the Scania Public Health Cohort, the Screening Across the Lifespan Twin study (SALT), the Stockholm Public Health Cohort and the WOLF employee study. Seven collected tobacco use by self-administered questionnaire and one (SALT) by structured telephone interview (Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 4th paragraph; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men only (the authors say snus use is rare in women). Excluded from the 383,015 men in the cohorts: ever regular cigarette use (n = 202,171), age under 18 (6,697), missing body mass index (1,901) and missing tobacco information (3,143), leaving 169,103 (Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The analysed groups are men who never used tobacco, men who currently use snus and nothing else, and men who formerly used snus and nothing else.
sample.demographics: Mean age at entry 36 years (range 18 to 99): 29 (SD 11) in the current snus group, 38 (SD 16) in the never-used-tobacco group and 38 (SD 13) in the former snus group. Mean body mass index 24.1 to 25.0. In the current snus group 37.9% were in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2% of the never-used-tobacco group, and 52.6% had 10 to 12 years of education against 38.7% (Table 2). Ethnicity, income and occupation are not reported beyond the cohort descriptions.
sample.attrition: Follow-up was by linkage to national registers; losses to follow-up (emigration, for example) are not described. Mean follow-up was about 17 years per man (editors' calculation: 2,857,312 person-years divided by 169,103). Cohort follow-up ended between 2004 and 2013 (Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: The cohorts are those of the collaborating investigators, not a systematic selection, and the text calls all eight population-based although Table 1 lists an occupational cohort, a charity-walk sample, an employee study and a twin register. One cohort dominates: leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort removes 87% of the deaths in the current snus group (1,233 of 1,410) and 66% of those in the never-used-tobacco group (6,116 of 9,272) (editors' arithmetic from Tables 3 and 4). Excluding everyone who had ever regularly smoked cigarettes leaves a younger group (the current snus group averaged 29 years) who are mostly followed from early adult life; men who smoked and then switched are not in the analysis. Because the men were already using snus at baseline (prevalent use, not new use), any earlier harm that removed some of them before baseline cannot be seen (editors' point).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported current snus use at baseline in all eight cohorts, former use in six, weekly amount in six and duration in five (Table 1). Use was not updated during follow-up and was not checked against a biomarker. In the two cohorts without data on former use (Malmo and Scania), men who did not currently use snus were classed as never having used it, so the reference group there includes some former snus use (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported at baseline among men who currently use snus only. Amount in cans per week: under 4, 4 to 6, 7 or more. Duration: under 5, 5 to 9, 10 to 14, 15 or more years. Route: oral (snus is placed under the lip, Introduction, 1st paragraph). Brand, nicotine content and nitrosamine content of the snus were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Everyone who had ever regularly smoked cigarettes was excluded, so the comparison is snus-only against no tobacco. Smoking started after baseline is not tracked, and any use of cigars, pipes or other nicotine products in the reference group is not described. Alcohol intake is higher in the current snus group (Table 2) and was adjusted for only in a subset analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Men who formerly used snus (5,691; 4.8% of men in cohorts that recorded former use) were analysed as a separate group, with no information on when they stopped.

comparison.controls: Men who reported never using tobacco (n = 124,256; 73.5% of the sample).
comparison.matching: No matching. All models used attained age as the time scale and adjusted for body mass index. A sensitivity analysis in the six cohorts with the information (leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort and the Malmo study) added education, alcohol and physical activity; another added calendar year (Methods › Sensitivity analyses).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Beyond body mass index, no baseline health measures are used (no prior disease, blood pressure, blood lipids, mental health, diet, income); the cohorts' own baseline data were not harmonised for these. Snus use before baseline is not related to health before baseline, and smoking taken up after baseline is not tracked.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Alcohol was available in seven cohorts (all but the Construction Worker Cohort) as tertiles of grams per week; the snus group drank more (Table 2). Cigarette smoking was excluded by design at baseline; later smoking is unmeasured.

outcomes.instruments: Deaths from the Swedish National Cause of Death Register, coded to ICD-9 and ICD-10: all causes; cardiovascular disease (ICD-9 390 to 459, ICD-10 I00 to I99); cancer (ICD-9 140 to 208, ICD-10 C00 to C97); 'other causes' (every other death, for example respiratory disease, infection, accident, suicide) (Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Register-based death and cause coding, with a published validation of death certification cited. Cause of death was missing for part of the deaths: the cause-specific counts in Table 3 add to 9,722 of 10,928 deaths, so 1,206 (11%) have no classified cause (editors' arithmetic), although the Methods define 'other causes' as every death not coded cardiovascular or cancer.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is death during follow-up, expressed as a hazard ratio against men who never used tobacco. No non-fatal outcome, no cause-level detail within 'other causes' (for example suicide, accidents or respiratory disease) and no absolute risk is reported.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four mortality outcomes; Table 3 holds 40 hazard ratios and Table 4 another 24. The text does not designate a single primary estimate; all-cause mortality for current against never use leads the abstract.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted hazard ratios (aHR, adjusted for attained age and body mass index), current snus-only group against never used tobacco (Table 3): all causes 1.28 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.35; 1,410 deaths against 9,272); cardiovascular disease 1.27 (1.15 to 1.41; 443 against 3,444); cancer 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26; 332 against 2,660); other causes 1.37 (1.24 to 1.52; 511 against 2,098). Former snus-only group: all causes 1.15 (1.02 to 1.31); cardiovascular 1.13 (0.91 to 1.41); cancer 1.26 (1.01 to 1.57); other causes 1.14 (0.89 to 1.45). By weekly amount in the current group, all causes: under 4 cans 1.28 (1.16 to 1.41), 4 to 6 cans 1.17 (1.06 to 1.29), 7 or more 1.37 (1.25 to 1.50), p for trend 0.09; cardiovascular 1.44, 1.18, 1.17, p for trend 0.03; cancer 1.13, 1.17, 1.01, p for trend 0.22; other causes 1.24, 1.18, 1.65, p for trend 0.001. By duration, all causes: under 5 years 1.08 (0.88 to 1.32), 5 to 9 years 1.17 (1.00 to 1.36), 10 to 14 years 1.31 (1.12 to 1.52), 15 or more years 1.29 (1.20 to 1.38), p for trend 0.001; cardiovascular 0.98, 0.99, 1.16, 1.32, p for trend 0.001; cancer 0.68, 0.94, 1.08, 1.12, p for trend 0.11; other causes 1.13, 1.21, 1.46, 1.49, p for trend 0.001. Sensitivity analyses (Table 4, current against never, all causes / cardiovascular / cancer / other causes): leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort 1.42 (1.21 to 1.66) / 1.39 (1.05 to 1.84) / 1.52 (1.15 to 1.99) / 1.34 (0.97 to 1.86); follow-up capped at 10 years 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48) / 1.13 (0.93 to 1.38) / 1.24 (1.02 to 1.52) / 1.57 (1.35 to 1.83); extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity (two cohorts left out) 1.46 (1.22 to 1.75) / 1.56 (1.14 to 2.14) / 1.51 (1.12 to 2.03) / 1.20 (0.83 to 1.72); the other three analyses (first-year events removed, cohorts without former-use data removed, calendar year added) left the all-cause ratio at 1.28 and moved the cause-specific ratios by 0.00 to 0.03.
analysis.covariates: Attained age (as the time scale) and body mass index in every model. Education (three levels), alcohol (four levels) and physical activity (four levels) only in a sensitivity analysis restricted to six cohorts; calendar year in another. Smoking, diet, income and baseline disease were not adjusted for (smoking by exclusion at baseline only).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned in the article read.
analysis.selective_reporting: All six sensitivity analyses named in the Methods are reported, including the one that removes the statistical significance of the cardiovascular result (10-year follow-up). Gaps: the proportional-hazards test is named but its result is not printed; no results by cohort are shown, although one cohort supplies most deaths; no absolute rates by group.
analysis.power: Large for all-cause mortality (10,928 deaths) but thin in places: 13 cardiovascular deaths in the under-5-years group, and 158 deaths in the current snus group in the fully adjusted subset (Tables 3 and 4), so those intervals are wide.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among Swedish men who had never regularly smoked cigarettes, men who reported using snus and no other tobacco at baseline had 1.28 times the hazard of death from any cause over about 17 years of follow-up (1.20 to 1.35) compared with men who reported no tobacco, adjusted for age and body mass index only. The ratios were 1.27 for cardiovascular deaths, 1.37 for other causes and 1.12 for cancer (lower limit 1.00). The all-cause ratio rose with years of use (1.08 for under 5 years to 1.29 for 15 or more) but not clearly with weekly amount. The cardiovascular ratio fell to 1.13 (0.93 to 1.38) when follow-up was capped at 10 years, and the cancer ratio was higher (1.52) after leaving out the largest cohort. Men who formerly used snus also had a raised all-cause ratio (1.15).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that snus use among men is associated with higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, deaths from other causes and possibly cancer mortality, and the paper says 'if causal' for its public-health reading. Gaps: (1) the abstract and Key Messages do not carry the Discussion's own caution that the cardiovascular result is inconsistent across analyses and should be interpreted with caution (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); (2) the abstract says risks rose with duration but not with weekly amount, whereas Table 3 shows a significant trend by amount for cardiovascular deaths that runs the other way (1.44 under 4 cans, 1.17 at 7 or more; p for trend 0.03) and for other-cause deaths (p for trend 0.001), and the Discussion (6th paragraph) itself reports dose-response trends for other-cause deaths by both amount and duration; (3) the cancer ratio did not rise with duration (p for trend 0.11), which the Results text acknowledges but the abstract does not; (4) the Key Messages say the findings may help understand other non-smoked nicotine products such as e-cigarettes, which these data cannot show; (5) the Discussion's explanations for the excess of other-cause deaths (alcohol, self-harm, violence, risk-taking) are untested hypotheses, as no cause-level data are shown; (6) the Key Messages say associations were 'systematically' examined, but the cohorts were not systematically selected.

timeline.event: Bolinder et al. followed the Construction Worker Cohort for 12 years and reported about 40% higher overall mortality in men using snus only (odds ratio 1.4, 1.3 to 1.8), as cited in this paper. That cohort is also inside the pooled analysis, so the two are not independent.
Roosaar et al., a separate Swedish cohort, reported an odds ratio of 1.23 (1.09 to 1.40) for mortality in men who had ever used snus (current and former not separated), as cited in this paper.

Hansson et al., pooled analysis from the same collaboration (eight cohorts): no link with new heart attacks but higher short-term fatality, as described in this paper; a 2014 pooled analysis on stroke is described the same way.
Lee's updated review of epidemiological evidence on snus and health (appraised in this batch).
This pooled analysis: all-cause hazard ratio 1.28 for exclusive current snus use against no tobacco in 169,103 never-smoking Swedish men.
Systematic review of cancer risk among men and women using Swedish snus exclusively, against no tobacco (appraised in this batch).

replication.where_it_stands: The largest single analysis of snus and mortality found, and consistent in direction with two earlier Swedish reports (one of them drawing on the same construction-worker cohort). All the evidence it adds comes from Swedish men, mostly followed from early adulthood, with use measured once. Whether the excess is due to snus, to the people who choose it or to later smoking is not settled by this study; the authors themselves call for caution on causation.

funding.funder: Department of Public Health Sciences, Karolinska Institutet; Region Vasterbotten; Region Vasternorrland; the Joint Committee of County Councils in Northern Sweden (Visare Norr); the regional agreement between Umea University and Region Vasterbotten (ALF); the Swedish Society of Medicine. The paper states the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared.
funding.affiliations_note: The principal investigator of each contributing cohort provided the individual participant data (Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st paragraph), and the authors include those investigators; they are also authors of earlier snus reports from these cohorts. No tobacco, vape or pharmaceutical industry funding or tie is declared. The affiliations themselves were not in the page text read.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that records snus, cigarette and other nicotine use repeatedly through follow-up (so later smoking and stopping are counted), measures baseline health, alcohol, diet, income and physical activity in everyone, includes women, reports absolute death rates by group and by cause, and compares snus-only with people using nicotine replacement and with people who stopped all nicotine, so that the nicotine and non-nicotine parts of snus can be told apart. A randomised trial is not feasible for mortality.

domains.note: The main model adjusts for attained age and body mass index only. Men in the snus group drank more and had less education (Table 2), and diet, income, baseline illness and later smoking are unmeasured. The adjusted subset analysis (education, alcohol, physical activity) gave similar or larger ratios (1.46 against 1.42 when only the largest cohort was left out) but covers 11% of the snus-group deaths and still leaves other confounders, so confounding cannot be ruled out.

Self-reported at baseline, once, with no biomarker; former use unrecorded in two cohorts (those men sit in the reference group); amount and duration recorded in only six and five cohorts; use assumed stable over up to 26 years of follow-up.

Investigator-assembled cohorts, one of which supplies most deaths; occupational, charity-walk and twin samples; men already using snus at baseline (prevalent use); ever-smokers excluded, which is a design choice that limits the question to snus against no tobacco.
Changes after baseline (starting to smoke, stopping snus) are not tracked; they would push the estimate in opposite directions. The 10-year cap addresses misclassification only in part.

Men with missing body mass index or tobacco information were dropped (5,044); the cause of death is unclassified for 11% of deaths, and the share differs by group (11.5% of deaths in the never-used-tobacco group, 8.8% in the current snus group, 4.9% in the former group; editors' arithmetic), which can bias the cause-specific ratios. Covariates other than age and body mass index are missing for whole cohorts.
Death from a national register is complete and objective for all-cause mortality; cause coding is register-based, with the missing-cause problem recorded under missing data.

No registered protocol is mentioned and no primary estimate is named, but the main analysis is the obvious one and all stated sensitivity analyses are shown; results by cohort and the proportional-hazards test are not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because of confounding: the main estimate is adjusted for age and body mass index only, in a comparison between men who chose snus and men who used no tobacco, and the one fuller adjustment covers a minority of the data. The association with all-cause death is large in size of data and stable across the sensitivity analyses reported, so it is unlikely to be a chance finding in these cohorts; the study may be cited for the size and consistency of the association between snus-only use and mortality in Swedish men who never smoked, for the pattern by cause, duration and amount, and for the cardiovascular result's fragility; not for the claim that snus causes these deaths, for absolute risks, or for comparison with smoking.

key_findings.finding: 169,103 never-smoking men from eight Swedish cohorts, 2,857,312 person-years, 10,928 deaths. 73.5% had never used tobacco (n = 124,256), 23% currently used snus and no other tobacco (n = 39,156); 4.8% of men in the cohorts that recorded former use had formerly used snus and no other tobacco (n = 5,691 overall).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Exclusive current snus use against never use of tobacco, adjusted for attained age and body mass index: all-cause mortality aHR 1.28 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.35); cardiovascular disease 1.27 (1.15 to 1.41); cancer 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26); other causes 1.37 (1.24 to 1.52). Death counts in the current snus group were 1,410, 443, 332 and 511 (never-used group 9,272, 3,444, 2,660 and 2,098).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Exclusive former snus use against never use: all-cause aHR 1.15 (1.02 to 1.31); cancer 1.26 (1.01 to 1.57); cardiovascular 1.13 (0.91 to 1.41) and other causes 1.14 (0.89 to 1.45), both consistent with no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: By duration of use at baseline, all-cause aHR rose from 1.08 (0.88 to 1.32) under 5 years to 1.29 (1.20 to 1.38) at 15 years or more (p for trend 0.001); cardiovascular and other-cause deaths showed the same pattern (p for trend 0.001 each), cancer did not (p for trend 0.11). Few deaths sit in the shorter categories (for example 13 cardiovascular deaths under 5 years).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, duration rows; Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: By weekly amount, all-cause aHR was 1.28 (under 4 cans), 1.17 (4 to 6) and 1.37 (7 or more), p for trend 0.09. The cardiovascular ratio was highest in the lightest group (1.44, 1.18, 1.17; p for trend 0.03), the other-cause ratio highest in the heaviest (1.24, 1.18, 1.65; p for trend 0.001), and cancer showed no pattern (p for trend 0.22).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, amount rows
key_findings.note: The abstract says risks did not increase with weekly amount; the trends by amount differ by cause.

key_findings.finding: Leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort raised the ratios: all-cause 1.42 (1.21 to 1.66), cardiovascular 1.39 (1.05 to 1.84), cancer 1.52 (1.15 to 1.99), other causes 1.34 (0.97 to 1.86).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 4, first block

key_findings.finding: Capping follow-up at 10 years: all-cause aHR 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48), cancer 1.24 (1.02 to 1.52), other causes 1.57 (1.35 to 1.83), but cardiovascular 1.13 (0.93 to 1.38), no longer distinguishable from no difference. The authors say the cardiovascular result should be read with caution because of this inconsistency.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 4, 10-year block; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Additional adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity, in the subset of six cohorts that recorded them (the Construction Worker Cohort and the Malmo study left out): all-cause aHR 1.46 (1.22 to 1.75), cardiovascular 1.56 (1.14 to 2.14), cancer 1.51 (1.12 to 2.03), other causes 1.20 (0.83 to 1.72), on 158 snus-group deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 4, additional-adjustment block and footnote b

key_findings.finding: Baseline differences between the groups (Table 2): the current snus group was younger (mean 29 against 38 years), drank more (37.9% in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2%), and more often had 10 to 12 years of education (52.6% against 38.7%) than men who never used tobacco; body mass index was similar (24.1 against 24.6).
key_findings.locator: Table 2

key_findings.finding: The authors name residual confounding and single baseline measurement of exposure as weaknesses; they note that former snus use was not recorded in two cohorts and that excluding them changed the estimates only marginally; they describe their findings as supporting an association, with public-health relevance 'if causal'.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th and 10th paragraphs; Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' suggested explanations (nicotine effects on blood vessels and heart rhythm, nicotine-promoted tumour progression, poorer cancer survival, alcohol-linked self-harm and violence, risk-taking) are hypotheses; none was tested in these data.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th to 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding came from a university department, Swedish regional authorities and a medical society; funders had no role; no conflicts declared.
key_findings.locator: Funding; Conflict of interest

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give 383,015 men in the eight cohorts (which reconciles with the 169,103 analysed after the stated exclusions), but the male participants in Table 1 add to 383,025 (editors' arithmetic) and the table's total row prints 383,025.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: A 10-man discrepancy that does not touch the analysed sample; worth noting only because the flow cannot be reproduced exactly from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The cause-specific death counts in Table 3 add to 9,722 of the 10,928 deaths (3,970 cardiovascular, 3,074 cancer, 2,678 other), leaving 1,206 deaths (11%) without a classified cause; the share is 11.5% in the never-used-tobacco group, 8.8% in the current snus group and 4.9% in the former group (editors' arithmetic). The Methods define 'other causes' as every death except cardiovascular and cancer, which would include these.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 and footnote a; Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cause-specific ratios rest on deaths with a known cause, and the different shares of missing causes by group could shift them; the all-cause ratio is not affected. The 'other causes' category as analysed is not the one defined.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Discussion (1st paragraph) say risks rose with duration but not with weekly amount. Table 3 gives p for trend by amount of 0.09 (all causes), 0.03 (cardiovascular, with the highest ratio in the lightest group), 0.22 (cancer) and 0.001 (other causes); the Discussion (6th paragraph) separately says other-cause deaths show dose-response trends for both amount and duration.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about amount holds for all-cause and cancer deaths only. Any claim must state the pattern by cause rather than say there was no gradient with amount.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the mortality risks increased with duration; the cancer row of Table 3 has p for trend 0.11 with ratios of 0.68 to 1.12, and the Results text itself excludes cancer from the statement.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The duration gradient applies to all-cause, cardiovascular and other-cause deaths, not to cancer.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods cite a paper on the Fine and Gray competing-risks model as the reference for the Schoenfeld test of proportional hazards, and the result of that test is not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; reference 33
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the proportional-hazards assumption held cannot be judged; given the cardiovascular ratio's drop at 10 years of follow-up, a time-varying hazard ratio is plausible.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods call the eight cohorts population-based, but Table 1 lists a nationwide occupational cohort (construction workers), a charity-walk sample, an employee study and a twin register.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Generalisation to all Swedish men is weaker than the wording suggests; the construction workers supply most of the deaths.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7825961 (all sections, Tables 1 to 4 rendered as text, funding, conflict and author-contribution statements and reference list; Figure 1, the participant flow diagram, is an image and was not read; no supplementary material was seen)

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies (one nested case-control study) of current cigar smoking and mortality, published before June 2014. Searches: PubMed, EMBASE and ISI Web of Science (cigar terms combined with death or mortality; 399 records, 246 after removal of duplicates) plus handsearching of reference lists (3 further articles); two reviewers screened and extracted independently; 22 articles from 16 cohorts were included. Results are given descriptively as 'mortality ratios' (standardized mortality ratios, hazard ratios, incidence rate ratios and odds ratios, some calculated by the reviewers from printed counts) against never smokers or people who never used tobacco, for all-cause mortality and 17 cause-specific outcomes, with the emphasis on 'primary' cigar smoking (current, exclusive cigar smoking with no history of cigarette or pipe smoking) as against 'secondary' (with such a history), and on the two American Cancer Society cohorts (CPS-I, 1959-1972; CPS-II, 1982-1994). Current cigarette smokers are excluded by design. No protocol or registration is mentioned, no risk-of-bias tool is used, and no estimates are pooled. Read as the PMC full text (all sections and all 27 tables as text); the study-selection flow chart (Figure 1, an image) and Additional file 1 (the excluded references, a Word file) were not read.
can_establish: How mortality in people who currently smoked cigars (mostly white men in North America and Europe, in cohorts that began between the 1940s and the 1980s) compared with mortality in people who never smoked or never used tobacco, overall and by cause of death, by the number of cigars a day, by self-reported inhalation and, in one cohort, by years of smoking; and how those ratios differed between people with and without a history of cigarette or pipe smoking.
cannot_establish: A comparison with people who smoke cigarettes (cigarette smokers are excluded by design and the review tabulates no cigarette estimates); a pooled size of effect (nothing is pooled and most estimates are adjusted for age alone); effects in women, in younger adults or of current cigar products such as small, filtered or flavoured cigars and cigarillos (the cohorts are older and mostly large-cigar); effects of occasional smoking; non-fatal outcomes; or whether the excess is caused by cigars rather than by differences in alcohol, diet or social circumstances.

sample.recruitment: Cohorts of US government life-insurance policy holders (the Dorn study, about 250,000, mostly veterans of the First World War, questionnaire in the 1950s), American Cancer Society volunteers (CPS-I 442,455; CPS-II over half a million men, 1982; women were not asked about cigars), British civil servants (Whitehall) and others in Canada, Denmark, Sweden, Finland and the UK; vital status by follow-up or death-registry linkage (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: articles reporting mortality in people who currently smoked cigars at baseline, against never smokers or people who never used tobacco. Excluded (227 references, by the reasons the text gives): did not report mortality by cigar use 108; non-epidemiologic or non-human, including reviews 90; non-English 13; further publications of a cohort already included 7; unpublished meeting abstracts 3; cause of death not on the 2004 Surgeon General or 2012 IARC lists (prostate cancer, myeloma) 2; reference group included current or former cigarette smokers 2; an earlier American Cancer Society study of lifetime ever-use of cigars 2. The cigar-only and cigar-or-pipe studies are shown separately (Methods > Study selection, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Mostly white men in North America and Europe who smoked cigars in the 1960s or earlier; the predominant product was the large cigar; women appear in only a few cohorts (for example 18 of 265 cigar and/or pipe smokers in one Cook County, Illinois, cohort; 770 of 808 in the Copenhagen cohort as printed, see the reporting issues) (Discussion, 4th paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; each cohort's follow-up (years of enrolment and end of follow-up) is in Table 1.
sample.selection_effects: The search required the words 'death' or 'mortality' beside a cigar term, searched three bibliographic databases only (no registries, no grey literature), excluded non-English papers (13) without giving a reason, and stopped before June 2014. Most of the weight is carried by CPS-I and CPS-II, which are the only cohorts large enough to separate primary from secondary cigar smoking for most outcomes; other cohorts have few cigar smokers (for example 9 deaths among primary cigar smokers in Whitehall). Many cells for single cancers rest on a handful of deaths (for example 4 laryngeal cancer deaths in CPS-II).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported current cigar smoking at baseline. 'Primary' and 'secondary' are defined only in studies that asked about past cigarette or pipe smoking. In CPS-I, secondary cigar smokers were about twice as likely to report inhaling as primary cigar smokers (42.0% against 21.6%).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study categories, not recommendations: cigars per day (CPS-I 1-2, 3-4, 5 or more; CPS-II 1-2 and 3 or more; Dorn study under 5, 5-8, 8 or more; CPS-II heart disease 1, 2-3, 4 or more); self-reported inhalation (none, slight, moderate-to-deep in CPS-I; none or any in CPS-II); duration (under 25 years or 25 and more, CPS-II). Predominantly large cigars; no modern small, filtered or flavoured cigars.
exposure.polysubstance: Primary cigar smoking excludes anyone with a history of cigarette or pipe smoking; the cigar-and-pipe studies cannot separate the two products. Alcohol and smokeless tobacco are adjusted for in the CPS-II cancer analyses (Shapiro 2000) but not in the CPS-I estimates (age only).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (current cigar smoking at baseline; changes in smoking after baseline are not described).

comparison.controls: Never smokers or people who never used tobacco in each cohort; the review does not tabulate each study's exact reference-group definition.
comparison.matching: None at review level. The 'Adjustment' column of Tables 2-27 shows that most estimates are adjusted for age alone (CPS-I, Dorn, Whitehall, Swedish and Canadian cohorts); a few add residence, occupation, marital status, education, housing, body-mass index, blood pressure, cholesterol, alcohol, exercise, secondhand smoke, diet or family history (Sandler 1989, Shaper 2003, Jacobs 1999, Shapiro 2000, Chao 2002, Heineman 1995).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Alcohol, diet, social class and other tobacco use are unmeasured or unadjusted in most of the estimates, and the review does not discuss confounding by them beyond naming adjustment as a source of variation.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Cigarette smoking history is handled by restricting to 'primary' cigar smokers; alcohol is adjusted in the CPS-II cancer analyses only.

outcomes.instruments: Deaths from death certificates or registries, grouped by the International Classification of Diseases version used by each cohort (versions 7, 8 or 9 printed per estimate; none printed for Shanks 1998).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; cause-of-death misclassification and the changing coding systems over 1954-2000 are not addressed.
outcomes.operationalization: Mortality ratio (MR): the review's umbrella term for standardized mortality ratios, hazard ratios, incidence rate ratios and odds ratios. Confidence intervals were calculated by the reviewers for standardized mortality ratios (Breslow and Day) and for incidence rate ratios (Wald limits) where the studies gave counts only (Methods > Data extraction, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the results are descriptive and no summary test is made across outcomes.
