The count is all-cause mortality plus 17 cause-specific outcomes in Tables 4-27 (oral, oesophageal, stomach, liver, pancreatic, laryngeal, lung and bladder cancers, coronary heart disease, stroke, aortic aneurysm, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and single-study estimates for atherosclerosis, kidney, nasopharyngeal, colon and rectal cancers).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary cigar smoking against never smokers, all-cause mortality: CPS-I 1.08 (95% CI 1.05-1.12; 3,754 deaths); Whitehall 0.48 (0.25-0.93; 9 deaths). Across all cigar studies in Table 2 the current-cigar ratios run from 0.48 to 1.8. CPS-I by cigars per day (primary): 1-2 1.02 (0.97-1.07); 3-4 1.08 (1.02-1.15); 5 or more 1.17 (1.10-1.24); by inhalation: none 1.04 (1.00-1.08); slight 1.19 (1.09-1.30); moderate-to-deep 1.60 (1.38-1.84). Primary cigar smoking, CPS-I / CPS-II (men): oral cancer 7.92 (5.12-11.69) / 4.0 (1.5-10.3); oesophageal 3.60 (2.17-5.62) / 1.8 (0.9-3.7); laryngeal 10.02 (4.01-20.64) / 10.3 (2.6-41.0); lung 2.1 (1.63-2.65) / 5.1 (4.0-6.6); pancreatic 1.62 (1.22-2.11) / 1.3 (0.9-1.9); bladder 1.38 (0.89-2.04) / 1.0 (0.4-2.3); coronary heart disease 1.05 (1.00-1.11) / 1.30 (1.05-1.62; men aged 30-74); stroke (CPS-I) 0.96 (0.87-1.06); aortic aneurysm (CPS-I) 1.76 (1.29-2.35). Lung cancer in CPS-I by cigars per day (primary): 1-2 0.9 (0.54-1.66); 3-4 2.36 (1.49-3.54); 5 or more 3.4 (2.34-4.77); CPS-II: 1-2 1.3 (0.7-2.4); 3 or more 7.8 (5.9-10.3). Lung cancer by inhalation: CPS-I none 1.97 (1.48-2.57), moderate-to-deep 4.93 (1.80-10.72); CPS-II none 3.3 (2.3-4.7), inhalation 11.3 (7.9-16.1). Secondary against primary, CPS-I: lung cancer 6.29 (5.01-7.79) against 2.1; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 4.39 (3.02-6.16) against 1.42 (0.96-2.03). Editors' checks: the 227 exclusions in the text add to 227 (2+108+13+90+2+2+7+3) and 246 minus 227 plus 3 handsearched gives 22; the log-scale midpoints of the intervals in Tables 2-27 match the printed estimates within the asymmetry expected for small counts; two ranges quoted in the text do not match their tables (see the reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: Varies by estimate; see Comparison. Age alone for most.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The Methods say the review followed Institute of Medicine, MOOSE and Cochrane guidance; no protocol, registration or deviation is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The text quotes ranges that leave out table entries (see the reporting issues). Studies reporting only ever-use or non-mortality outcomes were left out by design. The authors list the outcomes that were significant for primary cigar smoking in CPS-I or CPS-II (all-cause, oral, oesophageal, pancreatic, laryngeal, lung, coronary heart disease, aortic aneurysm); stomach cancer (CPS-II 2.29, 1.49-3.51) and liver cancer are described in the Results but not split into primary and secondary, so they are not on that list. Publication bias is not discussed.
analysis.power: Low for single cancers and for the lowest amounts: for example 9 oesophageal cancer deaths in CPS-II, 4 laryngeal cancer deaths in CPS-II (1 in the 1-2 cigars a day cell), 0 deaths in some cells printed as an estimate of 0 with an interval of 0.00-0.00. The authors say the studies were often underpowered at the lowest levels of exposure.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the two large American Cancer Society cohorts, men who smoked cigars and had never smoked cigarettes or pipes died at higher rates than men who never smoked from all causes (8% higher in CPS-I), from cancers of the mouth and throat, oesophagus, larynx, lung and pancreas, from coronary heart disease (5% higher in CPS-I; 30% higher in CPS-II among men aged 30-74) and from aortic aneurysm, but not clearly from bladder cancer or stroke. For all-cause mortality and for lung cancer the ratios rose with cigars per day and with reported depth of inhalation; at 1-2 cigars a day the all-cause ratio was 1.02 and the lung cancer ratio 0.9 to 1.3. People with a history of cigarette smoking had higher ratios for lung cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. For mouth, oesophageal and laryngeal cancers, the ratios in people reporting no inhalation were raised in CPS-I (7.0, 3.4, 10.6) but with intervals that include 1 in CPS-II (3.2, 1.6, 4.2).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions say that cigar smoking carries many of the same health risks as cigarette smoking and that some risks 'can be as high as or exceed' those of cigarette smoking, especially at the highest amounts and depths of inhalation. The review excludes current cigarette smokers and tabulates no estimates for them, so this comparison is not a result of the review. The abstract also says risks for oral, oesophageal and laryngeal cancers were 'still highly elevated' without inhalation, which holds in CPS-I and is imprecise in CPS-II; the Discussion attributes the finding to cigar smoke being inhaled regardless of self-report, citing a single small lung-deposition study.

timeline.event: National Cancer Institute Monograph 9 (Shanks and Burns), the source of the CPS-I estimates that carry most of the weight here, as cited by the review.

International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded that cigar or pipe smoking causes cancers of the lung and upper aerodigestive tract and found evidence for pancreas, stomach and bladder, as cited in the Background.

European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC) cohort of 1,451 people who smoked only cigars: lung cancer hazard ratio 3.9, upper aerodigestive tract cancer 3.5, any tobacco-related cancer 1.6; described by the review as consistent, not re-read here.

INHANCE pooled analysis of 19 case-control studies: odds ratio 2.54 (1.93-3.34) for head and neck cancer in people who had never smoked cigarettes and ever smoked cigars; described by the review as consistent, not re-read here.

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive review whose authors themselves call for contemporary cohorts that include women, younger adults and current cigar products, with detail on cigar type, amount, inhalation and biomarkers. This card does not follow studies after the review's 2014 search.

funding.funder: No funding statement is printed. The four authors are at the Office of Science, Center for Tobacco Products, US Food and Drug Administration (affiliation as given in the article's page metadata; e-mail addresses at fda.hhs.gov). The Background says the review was done to inform potential regulatory approaches and future research, in the context of the agency's April 2014 proposed rule to extend its authority to cigars.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests. A disclaimer says the article is not a formal dissemination of information by the FDA and does not represent agency position or policy.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors work for the regulator of tobacco products. The Background cites an analysis of at least 9,000 deaths a year in the US from regular cigar smoking by a group that includes two of the four authors (reference 9, Nonnemaker et al., 2014, published ahead of print). The review's conclusions are not noticeably favourable or unfavourable to the regulator beyond the stated purpose.

what_would_settle_it: Contemporary cohorts of women and men, including people who smoke small, filtered and flavoured cigars, that measure amount, depth of inhalation and biomarkers of exposure (cotinine, a nitrosamine metabolite) and that analyse people who smoke cigars, people who smoke cigarettes and people who never smoked together, with the same adjustment for alcohol, diet and social circumstances; and individual-participant analyses of CPS-I and CPS-II to put numbers on a cigar-versus-cigarette comparison.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (general-population adult cohorts), exposure (current cigar smoking, split into primary and secondary), comparator (never smokers or people who never used tobacco) and outcomes (all-cause and listed cause-specific mortality) are specified (Methods, 1st paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph).
The review followed published guidance (Institute of Medicine, MOOSE, Cochrane) but mentions no written protocol, registration or deviations.
Inclusion is described as 'epidemiological studies'; all 22 are prospective cohorts (one nested case-control), a natural fit for mortality, but the choice is not explained.

Three databases with printed search strings and handsearching of reference lists, and the search is within 24 months of publication; but the strings require 'death' or 'mortality', 13 non-English papers were excluded without a stated justification, and no registries, grey literature or experts are described. No credit for 'partial yes' because the language limit is not justified (project reading of item 4, decision p-amstar2-item4).
Two reviewers screened independently at each stage and settled disagreements by discussion (Methods > Study selection, 1st paragraph).
Two reviewers extracted independently and compared entries (Methods > Data extraction, 1st paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The text accounts for all 227 exclusions by reason and refers to numbered web references w1-w227 in Additional file 1 (a Word file, not read), so a list exists; whether each exclusion is justified individually cannot be seen.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, cohort, follow-up years, size, number of cigar and/or pipe smokers, age range and effect measure, and each estimate's adjustment and ICD codes are in Tables 2-27; the exposure definitions are clear. Missing or inconsistent: each study's reference-group definition, sex mix for most, cigar type, and several cohort labels and counts that disagree between tables (see the reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No assessment of risk of bias, confounding or exposure measurement in individual studies; the Results only note variation in exposure definition, dose categories and adjustment.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

The authors chose not to pool because of differences in definitions, dose categories and adjustment, and because only CPS-I and CPS-II could give separate primary and secondary results (Results, 2nd paragraph).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations name narrow populations, older cohorts, large cigars, sparse data for some cancers and low power at the lowest exposure, but not confounding (most estimates are age-adjusted only), self-reported exposure measured once at baseline, or the mixing of five effect measures; the conclusion about cigarette smoking is not backed by a within-review comparison.

The primary-versus-secondary contrast is discussed (more inhalation and earlier lung damage from cigarettes are offered as explanations), but wide ranges within the same exposure group are not examined (all-cause 0.48-1.8; coronary heart disease 0.45-1.30 for current cigar smoking).
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not mentioned.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No competing interests declared; the authors' employer (the tobacco regulator) is printed and a disclaimer separates the paper from agency policy; no funding statement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are 'no' (no protocol; a search restricted by terms and language without justification; no risk-of-bias assessment; risk of bias not considered in the interpretation), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence in the review as a complete and unbiased summary. This is a judgment about the review, not about the cohorts: the estimates are printed with their adjustment, two reviewers screened and extracted independently, and the authors sensibly do not pool. The card can be cited for what the included cohorts reported, with each estimate's own adjustment, and for the review's account of its limits. It cannot be cited for a pooled size of effect, for completeness, for risk at low amounts, or for any comparison with cigarette smoking.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed (100 records), EMBASE (207) and Web of Science (92), 246 after duplicates, two reviewers independent at each stage, 227 excluded by stated reasons (108 no mortality by cigar use, 90 non-epidemiologic or non-human, 13 non-English, 7 further papers on cohorts already included, 3 abstracts, 2 causes not on the lists, 2 with cigarette smokers in the reference group, 2 an earlier study of lifetime ever-use), 3 added by handsearching, 22 articles from 16 cohorts.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Methods > Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1 (image, not read); Table 1

key_findings.finding: Definitions and design of the comparison: the main exposure is current exclusive cigar smoking (or cigar and/or pipe); current cigarette smokers are excluded; 'primary' means no history of cigarette or pipe smoking and 'secondary' means such a history; in CPS-I secondary cigar smokers were about twice as likely to report inhaling (42.0% against 21.6%); cigar-only and cigar-and-pipe studies are kept apart; the reference group is never smokers or people who never used tobacco.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Data extraction, 3rd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The 22 articles come from 16 cohorts (12 US, 5 UK, 1 Canada and 4 Nordic papers); four articles use the Dorn study, three CPS-II, two Whitehall; CPS-II excluded women because it did not ask them about cigars; the authors present results descriptively because exposure definitions, dose categories and adjustment vary and only CPS-I and CPS-II could separate primary from secondary cigar smoking for most outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality: primary cigar smoking 1.08 (1.05-1.12) in CPS-I (3,754 deaths) but 0.48 (0.25-0.93) in Whitehall (9 deaths); secondary 1.12 (1.06-1.18) in CPS-I; cigar-and-pipe primary 1.09 to 1.37 with intervals touching 1; CPS-I primary by cigars per day 1.02, 1.08, 1.17 (1-2, 3-4, 5 or more) and by inhalation 1.04, 1.19, 1.60 (none, slight, moderate-to-deep); Dorn study by cigars per day 1.04, 1.17, 1.49.
key_findings.locator: Results > All-cause mortality, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, larynx and lung, primary cigar smoking, CPS-I / CPS-II: oral 7.92 / 4.0; oesophageal 3.60 / 1.8 (second not significant); laryngeal 10.02 / 10.3; lung 2.1 / 5.1; ratios rise with cigars per day (for example oral cancer in CPS-I 2.12, 8.51, 15.94) and with inhalation; oesophageal ratios are flat across amount and inhalation in CPS-II (1.8 and 1.9 for 1-2 and 3 or more cigars a day; 1.6 and 1.0 without and with inhalation).
key_findings.locator: Results > Oral cancer, Esophageal cancer, Laryngeal cancer and Lung cancer, 1st paragraph each; Tables 4-7, 13-16

key_findings.finding: Reported no inhalation, primary cigar smoking: oral cancer 6.98 (4.13-11.03) in CPS-I and 3.2 (0.9-11.0) in CPS-II; oesophageal 3.4 (1.90-5.61) and 1.6 (0.7-4.1); laryngeal 10.6 (3.87-23.07) and 4.2 (0.5-37.1); lung 1.97 (1.48-2.57) and 3.3 (2.3-4.7). The Discussion says ratios were elevated 'particularly in CPS-I' and links this to cigar smoke being inhaled regardless of self-report (one lung-deposition study cited).
key_findings.locator: Results > Oral cancer, Esophageal cancer, Laryngeal cancer, Lung cancer, 1st paragraph each; Tables 5, 7, 14, 16; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lung cancer by amount and inhalation: CPS-I primary 0.9 (0.54-1.66) at 1-2 cigars a day, 2.36 at 3-4, 3.4 at 5 or more; CPS-II 1.3 (0.7-2.4) at 1-2 and 7.8 (5.9-10.3) at 3 or more; by inhalation CPS-II 3.3 (none) and 11.3 (any); duration in CPS-II 2.1 (under 25 years) and 5.9 (25 or more).
key_findings.locator: Results > Lung cancer, 1st paragraph; Table 16

key_findings.finding: Other outcomes, primary cigar smoking: pancreatic cancer 1.62 (1.22-2.11) in CPS-I and 1.3 (0.9-1.9) in CPS-II; bladder cancer 1.38 (0.89-2.04) and 1.0 (0.4-2.3); coronary heart disease 1.05 (1.00-1.11) in CPS-I, 1.30 (1.05-1.62) in CPS-II men aged 30-74 and 0.93 (0.72-1.21) at 75 and over; stroke 0.96 (0.87-1.06) in CPS-I; aortic aneurysm 1.76 (1.29-2.35) in CPS-I; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 1.42 (0.96-2.03) in CPS-I. Stomach cancer 2.29 (1.49-3.51) in CPS-II and liver cancer 3.1 and 7.2 in two cohorts are not split into primary and secondary.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pancreatic cancer, Bladder cancer, Coronary heart disease, Stroke, Aortic aneurysm, COPD, Stomach cancer, Liver cancer, 1st paragraph each; Tables 8, 10, 11, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25

key_findings.finding: Secondary against primary cigar smoking in CPS-I: lung cancer 6.29 (5.01-7.79) against 2.1; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 4.39 (3.02-6.16) against 1.42; the authors give different inhalation patterns and irreversible lung damage from past cigarette smoking as explanations and read the difference as a reason to isolate primary cigar smoking.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Tables 15 and 25

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: mostly white men in North America and Europe who smoked cigars in the 1960s or earlier; the predominant product is the large cigar, not today's range; limited data on stomach, colorectal and liver cancer; studies often underpowered at the lowest exposures. They call for contemporary cohorts including women, non-white people and younger adults, with detail on cigar type, number a day, inhalation and years of smoking, and biomarkers.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Conclusions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Consistency with other work, as described by the review: EPIC (1,451 people who smoked only cigars; lung cancer hazard ratio 3.9, upper aerodigestive tract cancers 3.5, any tobacco-related cancer 1.6, raised even without reported inhalation) and the INHANCE pooled analysis of 19 case-control studies (odds ratio 2.54 for head and neck cancer in never cigarette smokers who ever smoked cigars; not raised in ever cigarette smokers). These were not re-read.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusion: cigar smoking carries many of the same health risks as cigarette smoking, risks vary with cigars a day and inhalation and 'can be as high or higher' than those of cigarette smoking at the highest amounts and depths of inhalation, and risks of upper aerodigestive cancer remain highly elevated when no inhalation is reported. No cigarette-smoker estimates are tabulated.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Abstract > Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: The cigar-versus-cigarette conclusion is not a result of the review: current cigarette smokers are excluded by design (Methods > Data extraction, 3rd paragraph) and no cigarette estimates appear in any table or in the Results, yet the abstract and conclusions say cigar risks 'can be as high as or exceed' those of cigarette smoking.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim comparing cigars with cigarettes cannot rest on this review; any such comparison has to be an indirect juxtaposition with a cigarette cohort, labelled as such. Locators: Abstract > Conclusions; Conclusions, 1st paragraph.

reporting_issues.issue: Two ranges quoted in the text leave out the largest entry in the tables: all-cause 'ranged from 0.48 to 1.60' for current cigar smokers but Table 2 also gives 1.8 (1.40-2.20) for women in the Copenhagen cohort; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 'ranged from 0.79 to 4.39' but Table 25 gives 10 (2.30-48.00) for women in the same cohort and 3.7 for men.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote ranges from the tables, not the text. Locators: Results > All-cause mortality, 1st paragraph (last sentence but one); Results > COPD, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 25.

reporting_issues.issue: Cohort labels and counts disagree between tables: Shaper 2003 is the British Regional Heart Study in Table 1 but 'CPS-II' in Table 2; Chow 1992 is the Lutheran Brotherhood Insurance Society cohort with an incidence rate ratio in Table 1 but 'Dorn study' with a hazard ratio in Table 15; the Oslo Study (Haheim 1996) is listed under Finland in Table 1 and the text names no Norwegian cohort among the Nordic countries; Table 1 gives 808 cigar and/or pipe smokers for the Copenhagen cohort (770 of them women) while Table 2 gives 326 deaths in men and 185 in women, which cannot both hold.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which cohort an estimate belongs to, and so which estimates are independent, cannot be taken from the tables without the source papers. Locators: Table 1 (rows Shaper, Chow, Haheim, Lange); Table 2 (rows Shaper, Lange); Table 15 (row Chow 1992).

reporting_issues.issue: Several printed cause-of-death codes do not fit the cause named: the Swedish pancreatic cancer row in Table 11 carries codes 140-146, 148 and 161 (mouth, pharynx and larynx); the same code (ICD 7: 450) is printed for Kahn's aortic aneurysm row (Table 23) and his atherosclerosis row (Table 27), whose estimates differ (2.06 and 0.97); Kahn's oesophageal row (Table 6) is labelled ICD 8 although the other Dorn study rows are ICD 7; and Kahn's oral cancer row (Table 4) prints ICD 7 codes 140-150, which would take in the oesophageal code (150), so oral and oesophageal rows may overlap.
reporting_issues.consequence: The older estimates (Kahn 1966; Carstensen 1987) cannot be assumed to measure the cause named without the source papers. Locators: Tables 4, 6, 11, 23 and 27.

reporting_issues.issue: Two citations do not match the studies tabulated: reference 35, given for the 1997 Wald study of the British United Provident Association cohort, is an authors' reply published in the BMJ in 1998; and Heineman is dated 1995 in Table 1 and the tables but 1994 in reference 24.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Wald estimates (all-cause, lung cancer, coronary heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) come from a source the reader cannot check from the reference list. Locators: Table 1 (rows Wald, Heineman); References 24 and 35.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's 'strong dose trends' and 'still highly elevated' without inhalation hold in CPS-I; in CPS-II the oesophageal ratios are flat across amount and inhalation and the no-inhalation ratios for mouth, oesophageal and laryngeal cancers have intervals that include 1 (3.2, 1.6 and 4.2). The Discussion says 'particularly in CPS-I' but the abstract does not.
reporting_issues.consequence: State the no-inhalation finding as from CPS-I, with the CPS-II result beside it. Locators: Abstract > Results; Results > Oral cancer, Esophageal cancer, Laryngeal cancer; Tables 5, 7, 14.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4408600 (abstract, Background, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, competing interests, disclaimer and reference list; Tables 1-27 read as text; the author affiliation read from the page metadata). Figure 1 (the study-selection flow chart, an image) and Additional file 1 (a Word file listing the excluded references) were not read. The primary studies were not read.

design_detail: Editorial (American Journal of Public Health 2020;110(2):161-162), six authors. About two printed pages: an opening section, six headed sections, a conclusion and a call to action, seven references, a conflict-of-interest statement and a funding note; an online Appendix A (a non-exhaustive list of evidence of e-cigarette harm) was not read. No data, methods or search. It argues that the '95% less harmful' figure for e-cigarettes against cigarettes, which came from a July 2013 rating exercise by 12 experts, is no longer valid because products have changed and evidence of harm has accumulated. The 2013 exercise (Nutt et al., European Addiction Research 2014), the Public Health England and Royal College of Physicians reports, and the studies cited for harm are known here only as this editorial describes them.
can_establish: What the authors argue about where the '95% less harmful' figure came from and why it should no longer be relied on, which changes in products and which kinds of evidence of harm they point to, and what they concede.
cannot_establish: How much less harmful vaping is than smoking (the editorial offers no estimate), whether the evidence it cites is complete or fairly weighed (no search; the online appendix was not read), or whether the 2013 exercise was sound (not read).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (editorial). The 2013 exercise it describes: 12 experts in decision science, medicine, pharmacology, psychology, public health policy and toxicology rated the relative harm of 12 nicotine-containing products on 14 criteria covering harm to self and to others (opening section, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the authors choose the evidence.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The evidence is chosen by the authors: seven references in the text and a longer list in an online appendix that was not read. The editorial cites no study of exposure to toxicants in people who switched from smoking to vaping, and the harm it lists comes from cell and animal studies and short-term human measurements; the one outcome of heart attack or coronary disease is cited to a conference abstract that the authors call a preliminary report.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: Combustible cigarettes are the reference product of the figure under discussion; no comparison is made in this editorial.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: None. The 2013 exercise is described as an expert rating of products on 14 criteria; this editorial does not give the scores, the weights, or how the percentage was obtained.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Harm' in the figure under discussion is the result of an expert rating across criteria, as described; the editorial argues the rating lacked hard evidence for most products on most criteria.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported. Numbers in the text: 12 experts, 12 products, 14 criteria (2013); many e-cigarettes today reach a power output 10 to 20 times that of most over-the-counter 2013 models, up to and sometimes above 200 watts; liquids with protonated nicotine (nicotine salt) are available above 60 mg/mL. No source is given in the text for the power figures.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: The editorial is an argument for one position and presents the evidence of harm and not the evidence on lower exposure to smoke toxicants in people who switch (editors' note); a longer evidence list is in Appendix A, not read.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data. The editorial argues, from seven references and an unread appendix, that the 2013 rating exercise was described by its own authors as lacking hard evidence for most harms of most products on most criteria; that e-cigarettes and liquids on the market now differ from those of 2013 (higher power, thousands of flavours, nicotine salts); that evidence of harm from e-cigarette aerosol has accumulated in cells, animals and short-term human studies; and that e-cigarette use is linked to later smoking in young people. It also states that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and that the diseases they may die of are not yet known.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and conclusion say the 2013 estimate is invalid, cannot be valid today and should not be relied on; the call to action asks readers to expose it emphatically as an unreliable fact repeated until accepted. Gaps: (1) an estimate shown to lack hard evidence is not thereby shown to be wrong in size: the editorial offers no alternative figure and does not say that vaping is as harmful as smoking, apart from a conditional case of someone who would never have smoked; (2) section headings state harm categorically (e-cigarettes cause harm to cells; e-cigarettes harm the people who use them) on cell, animal and short-term human findings, while the conclusion speaks of potential harm; (3) the item on later smoking is conditional on causation and rests on a National Academies conclusion about ever trying cigarettes, which concerns starting to smoke, not the harm of vaping against smoking; (4) that nicotine salts probably raise dependence is the authors' inference; (5) the wording of the target drifts between 'less risky', 'less harmful' and 'safer'; (6) no evidence on lower toxicant exposure in people who switch is weighed. In the authors' favour, they concede the lung-cancer point, say the diseases are unknown, and call for evidence-based future estimates.

timeline.event: Nutt et al. publish the expert rating exercise held in July 2013 (12 experts, 12 products, 14 criteria); its authors list the lack of hard evidence for most harms as a limitation (as quoted in this editorial; the paper has no reference record here and was not read).
Public Health England evidence update (McNeill and colleagues) endorses the 95% figure, according to this editorial (not read).
Editors' list of critiques of the evidence for e-cigarette claims (McKee and Capewell, BMJ); not read for this card.
Royal College of Physicians report 'Nicotine without smoke' endorses the figure, according to this editorial (not read).
National Academies review of e-cigarette health effects, quoted in the editorial for the link to later smoking in young people.
This editorial: calls the figure invalid today.
UK government-commissioned evidence update states vaping carries a small fraction of the risks of smoking (read for the claim; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: An opinion piece whose factual premise about the origin of the figure is second-hand. Its main point, that the figure was not built on hard evidence and that products changed, is not disputed in the sources read for the claim; whether the true difference is large or small is what neither this editorial nor the 2013 exercise can show. The reply from those who defend the figure is not in this paper.

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health (U54DA036105, U54DA036151, U54HL12016, R01ES029435) and the Center for Tobacco Products of the US Food and Drug Administration. The note printed with the paper says the sponsor had no role in the preparation of this work.
funding.declared_conflicts: T. Eissenberg and A. Shihadeh are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and are named on a patent for a device that measures the puffing behaviour of people who use electronic cigarettes; as of September 2019 T. Eissenberg is also a consultant in litigation against the electronic cigarette industry. S. Jordt reports personal fees from Hydra Biosciences LLC and Sanofi SA and nonfinancial support from GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals, outside the submitted work.
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors share affiliation number 1 in the PMC text, with no institution named. No tobacco or vape industry funding of the editorial is stated; two authors are paid by lawyers in cases against those industries.

what_would_settle_it: A transparent, repeatable estimate of relative harm that sets out the outcomes, their weights and the evidence behind each, updated for current devices, liquids and patterns of use; with long-term cohort data on disease in people who only vape, against people who smoke and people who use neither.

domains.note: No search or criteria; seven references in the text and an online appendix of harm evidence that was not read.
Cited studies are described, not appraised; the heart attack item rests on a conference abstract that the authors call preliminary; several statements have no citation in the text.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The studies cited in the text are by others; the appendix was not read, so reliance on the authors' own work cannot be judged. The authors declare litigation consultancies and a patent.

Headings state harm categorically on mostly cell, animal and short-term evidence, and the dependence effect of nicotine salts and the later-smoking argument are inferences; the conclusion does say potential harm and the unknowns are acknowledged.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how harmful e-cigarettes are compared with smoking
domains.note: Only evidence of harm from e-cigarettes is presented; evidence on lower exposure to smoke toxicants in people who switch, and any estimate of the size of the difference, are absent apart from one concession on lung cancer.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an editorial (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The piece is a clear, openly argued opinion with its interests declared, and its central premise (the 2013 figure was not built on hard evidence and products have changed) is checkable against the sources it names. It is one side's case and not an appraisal of the evidence. Cite it for what the authors argue and concede, never for the size of any harm; a claim resting only on it stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: In July 2013 a group of 12 experts rated 12 nicotine-containing products on 14 criteria for harm to self and others, concluded that combustible cigarettes were the most harmful and that e-cigarettes were substantially less harmful, and the result was repeated in the popular media as e-cigarettes being 95% less risky or 95% less harmful than cigarettes.
key_findings.locator: Opening section (before the first heading), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The editorial states that the authors of the 2013 work listed as a limitation the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most criteria (quoted from page 224 of that paper, which was not read), and that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians endorsed and publicised the 95% assertion anyway.
key_findings.locator: Opening section, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Products have changed since 2013: many e-cigarettes reach a power output 10 to 20 times that of most 2013 over-the-counter models (up to and above 200 watts), producing more aerosol and exposing the person vaping and bystanders to more nicotine and other toxicants; thousands of flavours; widespread liquids with protonated nicotine, available above 60 mg/mL, that the authors say are less aversive to inhale, allowing higher nicotine concentrations and likely more dependence.
key_findings.locator: Today's Electronic Cigarettes Are Different, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Evidence asserted as unavailable in 2013: e-cigarette aerosols contain toxicants and are harmful to living cells in vitro and in vivo, including aldehydes, carcinogenic furans, chloropropanols and acetal compounds, and animals exposed to aerosol show adverse effects including in cardiovascular models. No source is cited for these statements in the text.
key_findings.locator: Electronic Cigarettes Cause Harm to Cells, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Harm in people: airway epithelial injury with and without nicotine in healthy young occasional cigarette smokers who used an e-cigarette (one cited trial report); wheezing associated with use; higher heart rate, blood pressure and platelet activation and lower flow-mediated dilation and heart rate variability; a preliminary report (a conference abstract) that people who vape may be at higher risk of heart attack and coronary artery disease.
key_findings.locator: Third headed section (harm in people), 1st paragraph; references 5 and 6

key_findings.finding: The editorial quotes the National Academies' conclusion that there is substantial evidence that e-cigarette use raises the risk of ever using cigarettes in youth and young adults, and argues that, to the extent first use of e-cigarettes causes later smoking in someone who would never have smoked, use could be considered as harmful as smoking for that person.
key_findings.locator: Electronic Cigarettes Increase Smoking Risk, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that lower toxicant content in aerosol than in smoke does not by itself show lower lethality, that propylene glycol is toxic when injected and that aerosol containing it and glycerol causes lung inflammation in people (no source cited), and that different toxicants may cause different diseases. They state there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, largely absent from the aerosol, and that what they may die of is part of the evidence still needed.
key_findings.locator: Electronic Cigarette Aerosol Is Not Harmless, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the 2013 estimate, which lacked evidence, cannot be valid today and should not be relied on further; future estimates should rest on the evidence now available and be revised as it accrues. The call to action names it an unreliable fact repeated until accepted and asks readers to highlight its provenance, the changes in products, the accumulated evidence of potential harm, the increased prevalence of use and the link to later smoking.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions; Call to Action

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests as printed: US NIH grants and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products (sponsor had no role); two authors are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and named on a patent for a puffing-behaviour device, one is also a consultant in litigation against the e-cigarette industry from September 2019; one author reports fees from two pharmaceutical companies and nonfinancial support from a third.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflicts of Interests

reporting_issues.issue: The figure under discussion is worded three ways: 95% 'less risky' and 'less harmful' in the opening section and the heading, and '95% safer' in the call to action. The 2013 exercise, as described, rated harm on 14 criteria.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Opening section, 1st paragraph; Call to Action)
reporting_issues.consequence: Safer, less risky and less harmful are different claims; our claim uses 'harmful' only, as the figure was described.

reporting_issues.issue: Statements on power output, flavours, cell and animal toxicity and lung inflammation from propylene glycol and glycerol carry no citation in the text; the supporting list is in an online Appendix A that was not read.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (sections 'Today's Electronic Cigarettes Are Different', 'Cause Harm to Cells', 'Aerosol Is Not Harmless')
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements cannot be anchored to a source from the article text; they are the authors' assertions here.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement on heart attack and coronary artery disease cites a conference abstract (J Am Coll Cardiol 2019;73(9 suppl 2):11) that the authors call a preliminary report.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (third headed section, harm in people; reference 6)
reporting_issues.consequence: Not usable as evidence of cardiovascular disease in people who vape; the cohort studies read for the claim on vapes and disease are the sources for that.

reporting_issues.issue: The nitrosamine and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon concession ('little doubt' that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by them) sits inside a section titled as showing the aerosol is not harmless.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Electronic Cigarette Aerosol Is Not Harmless)
reporting_issues.consequence: The editorial's own text grants part of the relative-harm claim it disputes; both halves belong in any summary of it.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6951374 (editorial, all sections, conflicts and funding statements, reference list; Appendix A, an online supplement, not read; the 2013 expert-rating paper cited as reference 1 not read)

design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of urinary biomarkers of nicotine and 49 other tobacco-related chemicals (50 in all, five classes: nicotine metabolites, tobacco-specific nitrosamines, metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, volatile organic compounds), measured once in a spot urine sample from adults in Wave 1 (2013-2014) of the PATH Study, a nationally representative US cohort. Four groups were compared: people who currently used only e-cigarettes, only cigarettes, both (dual use), or had never used any tobacco product. The paper evaluates exposure, not disease.
can_establish: How much nicotine and how much of 49 other tobacco-related chemicals (as urinary metabolites) was present, at one time point in 2013-2014, in US adults who used only e-cigarettes, only cigarettes, both, or no tobacco ever, after adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, marijuana use and second-hand smoke.
cannot_establish: Whether e-cigarettes caused any of the exposure (93% of the e-cigarette-only group were former smokers, and the groups are different people), what happens to one person's exposure after switching, whether exposure at these levels leads to disease (no health outcome was studied), or the exposure from the devices and liquids sold after 2014 (device generation was not recorded).

sample.recruitment: PATH Study Wave 1 (2013-2014): US household probability sample of noninstitutionalized civilian adults. Weighted response rate 54.0% for the household screener and 63.6% for the adult interview among those providing a urine sample. A stratified probability sample of 11,522 adults who gave urine was selected for laboratory analysis to represent diverse tobacco-use patterns; 6325 were excluded for not meeting the product-use criteria and 92 for creatinine outside the reference range (Methods › Data Source, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs). For the volatile-compound markers the four groups were 220, 2322, 769 and 1571 (the same order as above: e-cigarette only, cigarette only, dual, never), because of different laboratory batches (Methods › Data Source, 5th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Current product use meant everyday or some-days use of cigarettes, e-cigarettes or both; no current use of any other tobacco product; no nicotine replacement in the past 3 days. The cigarette-only and dual-use groups had smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime. The never group reported no lifetime use of any tobacco product. Urinary creatinine of 10 mg/dL or less, or above 370 mg/dL, was excluded.
sample.demographics: Weighted: most aged 35 to 54 years (38%), women (60%), non-Hispanic white (61%). Table 2: the e-cigarette-only group was 73% non-Hispanic white against 56% of the never group, 22% aged 55 or over against 31%, and 13% with a bachelor's degree or more against 31%.
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a single-wave analysis. Fewer than 4.6% of observations per biomarker were excluded for interfering substances. Some volatile organic compound results were still outstanding when the analyses were run, so the authors say weighted estimates for those markers may not represent the target population (figure legends).
sample.selection_effects: Only adults who gave a urine sample were eligible (the weighted adult-interview response rate for those providing urine was 63.6%), and the laboratory sample was deliberately stratified by tobacco-use pattern. The e-cigarette-only group is small (247) and 93% (229) had smoked cigarettes before; only 18 had never smoked cigarettes, too few to study separately (Discussion › Limitations). Estimates for the daily and some-days splits and for dual-use sub-groups rest on smaller numbers still, and some are flagged for unstable estimates (relative standard error above 30%).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported current use at the Wave 1 interview, classified as every day or some days. Table 2: 59% (161) of the e-cigarette-only group and 38% of the dual-use group reported using nicotine-containing e-cigarettes; 44% (122) of the e-cigarette-only group used flavored e-cigarettes. Device generation was not recorded (Discussion › Limitations); liquid nicotine content and puffing patterns are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as recorded, not recommendations. E-cigarette use every day: 56% (147) of the e-cigarette-only group and 20% (145) of the dual-use group. Mean e-cigarettes per day (composite measure): 1.3 (95% CI 0.9-1.7) in the e-cigarette-only group and 0.6 (0.3-0.9) in the dual-use group. Mean cigarettes per day: 15.4 (14.1-16.6) in the cigarette-only group and 15.1 (14.1-16.0) in the dual-use group (t = 0.34, P = .73). The former established smokers in the e-cigarette-only group had quit a mean of 3.5 years (SD 9.0) before the sample and had smoked a mean of 19.0 cigarettes per day (Results, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Other tobacco products and recent nicotine replacement were excluded by design. Past-30-day marijuana use differed by group (Table 2: never group 0.59%, e-cigarette-only 15%, dual 13%, cigarette-only 16%) and was adjusted for, as was self-reported weekly hours around other people's smoke. Alcohol, other drugs and diet were not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: None required: a single self-collected spot urine sample, shipped chilled overnight. The authors state that most of the biomarkers have short half-lives (mean 1.5 to 10 hours), so they mainly reflect recent use (Discussion › Limitations); the metals have half-lives of years (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

comparison.controls: People who had never used any tobacco product (n = 1655) as the reference group; the cigarette-only group as the comparison for the e-cigarette groups.
comparison.matching: None. Linear regression adjusted for urinary creatinine, age, sex, race/ethnicity and education, plus past-30-day marijuana use and weekly hours of second-hand smoke exposure; the figure legends add cigarettes per day and tobacco use status for some contrasts.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Smoking history of the e-cigarette-only group beyond the mean quit time and past cigarettes per day (no pack-years or time since quitting in the models as described); device and liquid characteristics; diet and environmental sources of metals and volatile compounds; no earlier biomarker value for anyone.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: In the never group 0.59% had used marijuana in the past 30 days against 13% to 16% of the three groups who used tobacco (Table 2); the models adjust for it.

outcomes.instruments: Highly selective mass spectrometric methods at the CDC Division of Laboratory Sciences; 50 urinary biomarkers in five classes. Total nicotine equivalents were the molar sum of cotinine and trans-3'-hydroxycotinine. Nine representative biomarkers are shown in the figures (nicotine equivalents, the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL, lead, cadmium, naphthalene, pyrene, acrylonitrile, acrolein, acrylamide). Limits of detection and half-lives are in eTable 1 (supplement, not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Objective laboratory measurement of exposure; concentrations below the limit of detection were replaced by the limit divided by the square root of 2, and biomarkers with more than 40% below the limit are flagged. Concentrations were corrected for urinary creatinine. A biomarker shows that a chemical entered the body, not which product it came from (second-hand smoke, diet and earlier smoking can contribute).
outcomes.operationalization: Exposure = geometric mean urinary concentration per mg creatinine in each group. No disease, symptom or risk outcome was measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni adjustment stated for the two-tailed tests (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 6th paragraph); the number of comparisons used is not given.

analysis.effect_sizes: Geometric means with 95% CIs, creatinine-corrected, and percent differences computed by the authors; every percentage in the text was recomputed from the printed means by the editors (editors' calculation: all within one percentage point of the text; acrylonitrile in the never group 66.8% against 'approximately 66%'). Total nicotine equivalents (nmol/mg creatinine): e-cigarette-only 2.000 (1.100-3.500), cigarette-only 27.90 (23.80-32.70), dual 43.70 (39.80-48.10). NNAL (pg/mg creatinine): never 0.921 (0.819-1.035), e-cigarette-only 4.887 (3.817-6.257), cigarette-only 203.5 (181.7-227.9), dual 262.6 (240.0-287.3). Lead (ng/mg): never 0.351, e-cigarette-only 0.432, cigarette-only 0.479, dual 0.500. Cadmium (ng/mg): never 0.149, e-cigarette-only 0.193, cigarette-only 0.277, dual 0.280.
analysis.covariates: Urinary creatinine, age, sex, race/ethnicity, education; past-30-day marijuana use; weekly hours of second-hand smoke exposure; cigarettes per day (figure legends). Forward stepwise selection with P < .20 or biological relevance. Missing covariates imputed as in the PATH restricted-use files guide.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned; the paper is a secondary analysis of restricted-use PATH biomarker files (analysis November 2016 to October 2017).
analysis.selective_reporting: Nine of 50 biomarkers are shown in figures and text; the full set is in eTable 2 (supplement, not read). The text gives counts for the rest (for example 17 volatile compounds lower in the e-cigarette-only group than in the cigarette-only group). The comparison of the e-cigarette-only and cigarette-only groups is presented for the every-day and some-days sub-groups separately in Figure 2 (values not extracted).
analysis.power: Not stated. The e-cigarette-only group (247) and its sub-groups are small, and several dual-use sub-group estimates are flagged as unstable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In US adults in 2013-2014, people who used only e-cigarettes had much lower urinary levels of nicotine metabolites (about 93% lower) and of the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL (about 98% lower) than people who only smoked cigarettes, lower levels of the markers for polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and most volatile compounds, and similar levels of nearly all metals; but higher levels than people who had never used tobacco for nicotine, all nitrosamines, four metals, one polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon and four volatile compounds. People who used both products had higher levels of most markers than people who only smoked, with about the same number of cigarettes per day.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Key Points conclude that exclusive e-cigarette use 'appears to result in' exposure to known tobacco-related toxicants, 'generally' lower than cigarette smoking, and that cigarettes alone or with e-cigarettes are associated with higher concentrations than e-cigarettes alone (Abstract; Key Points). The Key Points say the e-cigarette-only concentrations were lower than in the cigarette-only and dual-use groups, which the Results qualify: nearly all metals and three volatile-compound markers were statistically similar to the cigarette-only group. The Discussion suggests the exposures may be a conservative estimate for newer devices, citing other work, without data on device type.

timeline.event: Earlier short-term observational studies of people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes are described by the authors as showing lower levels of volatile compounds, nitrosamines and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (Introduction, 2nd paragraph, refs 8 to 12); a cross-sectional study of long-term e-cigarette and nicotine-replacement use is described as showing similar nicotine delivery and lower toxicant exposure than cigarette smoking (Discussion, 3rd paragraph). These studies were not read here.

Hartmann-Boyce et al.: secondary analysis of trials in which people who smoked were followed after switching to e-cigarettes; biomarker findings compared with continued smoking (card sc_hartmann_boyce_2023).

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the main contrast (lower nicotine, nitrosamine and combustion-product markers in people who only vape than in people who only smoke) is the same in the studies the authors cite and in the trial-based review read for this batch. This is the largest nationally representative cross-sectional comparison read here, from first-generation devices; it has not been repeated in this form with later devices in the sources read.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse (National Institutes of Health) and the Center for Tobacco Products, US Food and Drug Administration, with federal funds under contracts to Westat (HHSN271201100027C and HHSN271201600001C). The printed role-of-funder statement says staff from NIDA and FDA contributed to design and conduct, data management, analysis and interpretation, preparation, review or approval of the manuscript, and the decision to submit, but were not directly involved in collecting the data (Westat did that).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed in the corrected disclosure (the article was corrected on 24 June 2024 'to fix incomplete conflict of interest disclosures'): Goniewicz receives advisory board fees from Johnson & Johnson and grant support from Pfizer. Niaura reported paid consulting to the Government of Canada via Industrial Economics, an honorarium from Pfizer for a virtual meeting, other NIDA grants paid to his employers, salary from the Schroeder Institute (Truth Initiative), and, between mid-2015 and 2020, frequent unpaid communication with Juul Labs personnel and meals at some meetings outside the submitted work. No other disclosures. The original 2018 version of the disclosures was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors come from Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, Westat, the CDC Division of Laboratory Sciences (which ran the assays), the FDA Center for Tobacco Products, NIDA, the University of Minnesota Masonic Cancer Center and the Schroeder Institute. Public bodies that regulate or study tobacco funded the study and took part in the manuscript's preparation and approval. Industry ties as printed: one author reports advisory fees from Johnson & Johnson and grant support from Pfizer, and another reports an honorarium from Pfizer and unpaid contact with Juul Labs staff.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated urine and blood measurements in the same people before and after they stop smoking and start vaping (or not), with current devices, with the product's measured nicotine content recorded, with markers of short and long half-life reported separately, and with health outcomes followed in the same cohort (the later PATH waves can supply both).

domains.note: Adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, creatinine, marijuana, second-hand smoke and cigarettes per day. Prior smoking is not in the models as described: for long-lived markers (metals) a difference between the e-cigarette-only and never groups cannot be attributed to e-cigarettes, and any carry-over from prior smoking would push the e-cigarette-only group up, that is, against the finding that it was lower than the cigarette-only group.

Self-reported current use at one interview; only 59% of the e-cigarette-only group reported nicotine-containing products; people who used on some days were 44% of that group; device and liquid unknown.
Weighted response 54.0% (screener) and 63.6% (adult interview for those giving urine); stratified laboratory sample; 6325 of 11,522 excluded by product-use criteria (by design).
Not applicable to a single time point; people who had recently used nicotine replacement were excluded.
Fewer than 4.6% of observations dropped per biomarker for interfering substances; covariates imputed; below-limit values imputed; some volatile compound results were outstanding at analysis.
Objective, standardized mass-spectrometric assays at the CDC laboratory; but biomarkers measure exposure, not disease, and the supplement with limits of detection was not read.
Nine of 50 biomarkers shown in the main text; Bonferroni stated without the number of tests; no registered plan; the full set is in a supplement not read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The study is large for a biomarker survey, nationally representative, laboratory-measured and adjusted for the main sources of exposure other than prior smoking. The concerns are a single time point, a small e-cigarette-only group that is almost entirely former smokers, self-reported product use without device or nicotine content, and no health outcome. It may be cited for how the groups' urinary markers compared in 2013-2014 (including that people who only vaped had measurable nicotine and nitrosamine markers, far lower than people who smoked and higher than people who never used tobacco) and for the higher levels in dual use; it may not be cited for what happens to a person who switches, for exposure from current devices, or for any health effect.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6324349 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2, figure legends, references, author notes, funding and corrected conflict-of-interest statement; Figures 1 to 3 are images and their values were not extracted; supplement (eFigure, eTables 1 to 4, eMethods) not read)

key_findings.finding: Analytic sample 5105 adults: 247 current e-cigarette-only, 2411 cigarette-only, 792 dual-use, 1655 never used any tobacco (volatile-compound subsample 220, 2322, 769, 1571). Weighted response 54.0% for the household screener and 63.6% for the adult interview among those giving urine.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Source, 1st and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: 93% (229) of the e-cigarette-only group had previously smoked cigarettes; the former established smokers among them had quit a mean of 3.5 years (SD 9.0) before sampling and had smoked a mean of 19.0 cigarettes per day. 56% (147) used e-cigarettes every day and 44% (100) some days. Only 18 of the 247 had never smoked cigarettes.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Only 59% (161) of the e-cigarette-only group, and 38% (306) of the dual-use group, reported using nicotine-containing e-cigarettes; 44% (122) and 25% (208) used flavored ones.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows 'Use nicotine-containing e-cigarettes' and 'Use flavored e-cigarettes'
key_findings.note: The nicotine-content item is self-reported, and the comparisons include the whole e-cigarette-only group, with or without nicotine-containing products.

key_findings.finding: Second-hand smoke exposure (hours per week): never group 2.0 (95% CI 1.5-2.4), e-cigarette-only 7.9 (5.7-10.1), dual 20.0 (17.5-22.5), cigarette-only 18.9 (16.7-21.2). Past-30-day marijuana use: never group 0.59%, e-cigarette-only 15%, dual 13%, cigarette-only 16%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows 'SHS exposure' and 'Past 30-d marijuana use'

key_findings.finding: Against the never group, the e-cigarette-only group had higher levels of all major nicotine metabolites and total nicotine equivalents, all nitrosamines, 4 metals, 1 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon and 4 volatile-compound markers. NNAL was about 81% lower in the never group (0.921 vs 4.887 pg/mg creatinine; t = 7.73); lead about 19% lower (0.351 vs 0.432 ng/mg), cadmium about 23% lower (0.149 vs 0.193), pyrene about 20% lower, acrylonitrile about 66% lower (1.315 vs 3.959).
key_findings.locator: Results › Never Users vs e-Cigarette–Only Users, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within the e-cigarette-only group, people who used every day had higher levels of all major nicotine metabolites, 2 nitrosamines, 2 metals (lead and strontium) and 1 acrylonitrile marker than people who used on some days.
key_findings.locator: Results › Never Users vs e-Cigarette–Only Users, 2nd paragraph (eTable 3, not read)

key_findings.finding: Against the cigarette-only group, the e-cigarette-only group had lower total nicotine equivalents (2.000 vs 27.90 nmol/mg creatinine; about 93% lower; t = 8.53), NNAL (4.887 vs 203.5 pg/mg; about 98% lower; t = 27.96), cadmium (0.193 vs 0.277 ng/mg; 30% lower), naphthalene marker (about 62% lower), pyrene marker (47%), acrolein marker (60%; 108.0 vs 271.5), acrylonitrile marker (97%; 3.959 vs 123.9) and acrylamide marker (59%). Levels were statistically similar for nearly all metals except cadmium and for 3 volatile-compound markers (toluene, benzene, carbon disulfide). Overall: lower in all major nicotine metabolites, 2 minor alkaloids, all nitrosamines, 1 metal, all polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and 17 volatile compounds.
key_findings.locator: Results › e-Cigarette–Only Users vs Cigarette-Only Smokers, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The same pattern held when the every-day and some-days sub-groups were analysed separately (Figure 2, values not extracted).

key_findings.finding: The dual-use group had higher levels than the cigarette-only group of most markers, with similar cigarettes per day (15.1 vs 15.4): total nicotine equivalents 43.70 vs 27.90 nmol/mg creatinine (cigarette-only about 36% lower; t = 4.78), NNAL 262.6 vs 203.5 pg/mg (about 23% lower), pyrene marker 15% lower, acrolein marker 10% lower, acrylonitrile marker 15% lower. Lead and cadmium did not differ (lead 0.500 vs 0.479; cadmium 0.280 vs 0.277 ng/mg).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Results › Dual Users vs Cigarette-Only Smokers, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within the dual-use group, markers rose with how often people smoked: those who smoked every day and used e-cigarettes every day had higher levels of nicotine metabolites, all polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon markers and 15 volatile-compound markers than those who did both on some days; the authors flag these sub-group analyses as exploratory and the some-days groups as possibly reflecting the product last used.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dual Users vs Cigarette-Only Smokers, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' stated limits: device generation not recorded; cadmium in the e-cigarette-only group could remain from earlier smoking given the metal's long half-life and the 93% former-smoker share; most biomarkers have short half-lives (mean 1.5 to 10 hours); e-cigarettes may add exposures not measured here (nickel, chromium, flavoring compounds); the 2013-2014 devices were early-generation and the authors suggest newer devices may give higher exposure but cite one study of long-term use of later-generation devices with lower toxicant exposure than smoking.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the cigarette-only group's every-day cigarette use as '1975 (4) [81-87]'; the interval implies about 84%, so the '4' is a misprint.
reporting_issues.locator: Table 2, row 'Cigarettes' under 'Everyday use'
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the biomarker results; a reader copying the table would get a wrong percentage.

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Points say the e-cigarette-only concentrations were lower than in the cigarette-only and dual-use groups, but the Results and the abstract state that nearly all metals (all except cadmium) and three volatile-compound markers were statistically similar to the cigarette-only group.
reporting_issues.locator: Key Points, Findings; Results › e-Cigarette–Only Users vs Cigarette-Only Smokers, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should state the metals and the three volatile markers as 'similar', not 'lower'.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the regression estimated differences in non-creatinine-adjusted concentrations with creatinine as a covariate, while the reported geometric means are labeled creatinine-corrected (per mg creatinine). The covariate list in the Methods (creatinine, age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, marijuana, second-hand smoke) also differs from the figure legends, which add cigarettes per day and tobacco use status.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 4th paragraph; Figure 1 and Figure 3 footnotes
reporting_issues.consequence: Which version of the means each percentage refers to is not fully clear; the percentages recompute correctly from the printed creatinine-corrected means, which are the values to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: Daily cigarette smoking in the dual-use group is 83% (650) in Table 2 but 82% in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.locator: Table 2; Discussion, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Immaterial (probably weighted against unweighted); do not cite either figure without saying which.

reporting_issues.issue: Some volatile organic compound laboratory results were outstanding when the analyses were run, so the authors say weighted estimates for those markers may not reflect the target population.
reporting_issues.locator: Figure 1, 2 and 3 legends
reporting_issues.consequence: The volatile-compound percentages (acrolein, acrylonitrile, acrylamide) are the least settled numbers in the paper; cite them with that caveat.

design_detail: Systematic review with individual-participant-data (IPD) meta-analysis updating a 2007 review: randomized crossover or parallel trials of a single short bout of physical activity against a passive control in people abstaining from smoking for at least 2 hours and not using nicotine replacement or taking part in a cessation programme. Raw data were obtained for 19 of 20 eligible studies (7 parallel, 12 crossover; 14 published, 5 theses); two-stage and one-stage random-effects models of the post-intervention rating adjusted for baseline. Searches from 2004 to 31 May 2011, English only; not registered.
can_establish: Whether, and by roughly how many points on a 7-point scale, a single short bout of exercise lowers self-rated desire to smoke immediately afterwards compared with sitting, in laboratory studies of people abstaining for a few hours.
cannot_establish: How long the effect lasts (craving was rated only immediately or 5 minutes after the bout), whether exercise helps people stop or stay stopped, the effect in people in a quit attempt or using nicotine replacement (excluded), or an effect free of expectation (participants could not be blinded and the trials were not appraised for bias).

sample.recruitment: Searches of SportDiscus, MEDLINE, PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE and PsycINFO, the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group register and thesis databases, reference lists, SRNT abstracts 2007-11, list-serves and authors: 544 database records and 27 from other sources, 411 after duplicates, 58 abstracts, 36 full texts, 20 eligible, IPD for 19 (Figure 1, p. 29). The primary studies had 10 to 84 participants each; their characteristics are only in Table S1 (not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized crossover or parallel trials of acute physical activity against control, with strength of desire to smoke (SoD) or desire to smoke (DtS) on a 7-point scale and at least 2 hours of abstinence before baseline; published or unpublished. Excluded: people in a cessation programme or using NRT (because baseline craving may be low), other craving measures, no control group, insufficient or no abstinence (p. 27; Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Not reported in the main text (Table S1 not read); one study's mean age of 36 years is described as older than in the other studies (p. 34).
sample.attrition: One eligible study (8 participants) was left out because its IPD could not be obtained; four participants dropped from one published data set were restored from the raw data (pp. 28, 30). Attrition within trials is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: English only from 2004, with earlier studies taken from the 2007 review; titles screened by the first author alone (p. 28). Seventeen of the 19 included studies list at least one of the review's authors (editors' count from the reference list); the review is a collaboration of those authors pooling their raw data.

exposure.measurement: Supervised single bouts in a laboratory: moderate walking (8 studies), running (2), moderate cycling (9), vigorous cycling (2), light cycling (1) and isometric exercise (3); intensity set by perceived exertion or heart rate (p. 29).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single bouts of 5 to 40 minutes (p. 29); at least 2 hours without smoking before baseline; three-arm designs collapsed to two arms (exercise arms pooled; passive arms pooled).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 hours without smoking before baseline (inclusion criterion); actual durations and verification are in Table S1, not read.

comparison.controls: Passive conditions: sitting (16 studies), sometimes with an audio recording, a cognitive task, a video or body scanning; body scanning was coded as control although both studies of it found it lowered craving (pp. 29-30, 34).
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover or randomized parallel groups; baseline craving adjusted for.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (randomized).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: Single-item 7-point ratings of desire to smoke ('I have a desire for a cigarette right now') and strength of desire ('How strong is your desire to smoke right now?'); two studies' 0-5 ratings were rescaled to 1-7 (pp. 27-28).
outcomes.validity_norms: Widely used single items (Tiffany & Drobes; Mood and Physical Symptoms Scale), treated as continuous although ordinal (p. 28).
outcomes.operationalization: Post-intervention rating adjusted for baseline, taken immediately or 5 minutes after the bout (p. 29).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two outcomes with several sensitivity analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not possible for participants, who knew whether they exercised; not discussed.

analysis.effect_sizes: Baseline-adjusted differences in scale points (called standardized mean differences in the abstract and Results; the Methods derive mean differences and the one-stage model reports a mean difference). Two-stage random effects: SoD -1.91 (95% CI -2.59 to -1.22), 15 studies, 797 observations, I2 94.2%, Q 240.35; DtS -2.03 (-2.60 to -1.46), 17 studies, 837 observations, I2 92.0%, Q 201.02. One-stage: SoD -1.89 (-2.52 to -1.26 in Table 2; -2.53 in the text), SD of the random effect 0.850, 95% mid-range -3.56 to -0.22; DtS -2.03 (-2.54 to -1.51), SD 0.722, mid-range -3.45 to -0.62. Parallel trials only: SoD -1.78 (-3.17 to -0.40), I2 96.5%; DtS -2.27 (-3.82 to -0.72), I2 96.8%. Moderate intensity only: SoD -2.20 (-2.89 to -1.51), 13 studies; DtS -2.14 (-2.71 to -1.57), 16 studies. Published against unpublished: SoD -1.91 (-2.85 to -0.97) and -1.90 (-2.88 to -0.91); DtS -2.13 (-2.88 to -1.38) and -1.81 (-2.71 to -0.91). Single studies ranged from -0.22 to -4.54 (SoD) and -0.27 to -4.27 (DtS).
analysis.covariates: Baseline craving; in the one-stage model a fixed effect for study and a random intercept for participant.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA was followed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Both outcomes were analysed even where only one had been published (from the raw data). Moderators other than intensity were not analysed, although the authors call that analysis necessary.
analysis.power: Not addressed; heterogeneity very high (I2 89.7% to 96.8%).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Every included trial favoured exercise, with a baseline-adjusted difference of about 2 points on a 7-point craving scale immediately after a short bout, but with very large differences between studies, from a fraction of a point for isometric exercise to more than 4 points in a study with high baseline craving.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes there is “strong evidence that physical activity acutely reduces cigarette craving” (p. 26) and reports standardized mean differences. Gaps: (1) the effects are differences in scale points, not standardized; (2) strong evidence is asserted without any appraisal of trial bias, for unblinded self-ratings, from trials mostly run by the review's authors; (3) the Discussion calls the decrease moderate and the Conclusions call the effects large; (4) the claim that the reduction matches or exceeds that with NRT and glucose cites a review of nicotine receptor partial agonists (ref. 4) and the 2007 review; (5) nothing is shown about duration beyond minutes or about quitting.

timeline.event: Taylor, Ussher & Faulkner, systematic review of the acute effects of exercise on cravings (narrative synthesis), which this review updates.
Roberts et al., aggregate-data meta-analysis with 9 and 10 studies for the two craving measures and similar results (as described, p. 34); it shares most primary studies with this review.
This IPD meta-analysis.

replication.where_it_stands: The main pooled estimate of the immediate effect of a bout of exercise on craving. Agreement with the 2012 aggregate meta-analysis is not independent replication (shared studies). Quitting outcomes and the duration of the effect are outside its scope.

funding.funder: Internal institutional funds (Declarations of interest, p. 35).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no other direct or indirect support and no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries (p. 35).
funding.affiliations_note: Exeter, Peninsula College of Medicine and Dentistry, St George's London, Moffitt Cancer Center, Toronto, Surrey, West of England and Sheffield. Seventeen of the 19 included studies list at least one review author (editors' count), a conflict of a non-financial kind that the paper does not discuss.

what_would_settle_it: A registered randomized trial in people in a quit attempt comparing short bouts of exercise with an active attention control, with craving rated repeatedly for several hours afterwards and lapses recorded, run by investigators independent of the original trials.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (temporarily abstaining people who smoke, no NRT), intervention (short bouts of physical activity), comparator (passive control) and outcomes (SoD, DtS) specified.
No protocol or registration mentioned.
Randomized crossover and parallel trials, with the case for IPD from randomized trials set out (p. 27).

Six databases, a trials register, thesis databases, reference lists, conference abstracts, list-serves and authors, with the search string given; but English only without a stated reason (the date limit is explained as an update). Item 4 applied as written, as for other cards (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Titles screened by the first author alone; only abstracts were examined by two authors (p. 28).
IPD were obtained from the primary authors; who checked the data is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons are given by category in Figure 1; the list of excluded studies is in Table S2, which was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Designs, types and durations of exercise, control conditions, outcomes and timing are described in the text; participant characteristics only in Table S1 (not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The text says quality was examined but reports only that all studies were randomized (one by recruitment order); no assessment of allocation concealment or blinding.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Two-stage and one-stage random-effects IPD models adjusted for baseline, with crossover designs modelled with participant random effects; the mislabelling of mean differences as standardized does not change the method.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses by design (parallel only), intensity and publication status, none by risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The conclusion of strong evidence does not discuss bias in unblinded self-ratings or the authors' own studies.
I2 and Q reported; baseline craving, age and mode of exercise discussed; a moderate-intensity subgroup analysed (pp. 32-34).
Unpublished studies were included and compared with published ones, but no funnel plot or small-study test was done.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and absence of industry links stated; authorship of the included studies not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can only be judged from Table S2, which was not read. Critical items 2, 4, 9, 13 and 15 are not met, so confidence is critically low whatever item 7 shows. This concerns how far the pooled number can be trusted as an unbiased summary: the IPD methods are sound and every trial points the same way, but the trials were not appraised, the outcome is an unblinded self-rating taken minutes after exercise, and most trials come from the review's own authors.

key_findings.finding: Nineteen randomized trials with raw data (7 parallel, 12 crossover; 14 published and 5 theses); bouts lasted 5 to 40 minutes; studies had 10 to 84 participants; craving was rated immediately before and immediately after the bout, or 5 minutes after it in three studies; all controls were passive.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and quality assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Two-stage random-effects IPD meta-analysis: strength of desire -1.91 (95% CI -2.59 to -1.22), 15 studies, 797 observations (440 exercise, 357 control), I2 94.2%; desire to smoke -2.03 (-2.60 to -1.46), 17 studies, 837 observations (463 exercise, 374 control), I2 92.0%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Strength of desire; Desire to smoke; All eligible studies › Two-stage random-effects meta-analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 30); Tables 2 and 3 (p. 32)

key_findings.finding: One-stage model: strength of desire -1.89 (-2.52 to -1.26 in Table 2), SD of the random effect 0.850, so 95% of studies' true effects are expected between -3.56 and -0.22 points; desire to smoke -2.03 (-2.54 to -1.51), SD 0.722, range -3.45 to -0.62.
key_findings.locator: Results › One-stage individual participant data meta-analysis; Tables 2 and 3
key_findings.note: The text gives the lower limit for strength of desire as -2.53 (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Every study favoured exercise; the smallest effects came from the three studies of isometric exercise, two of whose intervals for strength of desire included zero (-0.55, -1.13 to 0.02; -0.22, -1.03 to 0.58), and the largest from a study with the highest baseline craving (-4.54 and -4.27).
key_findings.locator: Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 33-34); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 34) and last paragraph (p. 35)
