key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses agreed: parallel trials only -1.78 (-3.17 to -0.40) and -2.27 (-3.82 to -0.72); moderate intensity only -2.20 (-2.89 to -1.51) and -2.14 (-2.71 to -1.57); published and unpublished studies similar (-1.91 against -1.90 for strength of desire; -2.13 against -1.81 for desire to smoke).
key_findings.locator: Results › All eligible studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 30); Parallel arm studies; Studies investigating physical activity of moderate intensity (p. 32); Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Effect sizes were computed as baseline-adjusted mean differences between groups in post-intervention ratings on the 1-7 scale, although the abstract and Results call them standardized mean differences.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Data analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 28); Results › Two-stage random-effects meta-analysis (p. 30)

key_findings.finding: Eligibility required at least 2 hours without smoking before baseline and excluded people in a cessation programme or using NRT; the review sought effects on strong cravings such as those of the first hours and days of quitting.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Inclusion/exclusion criteria

key_findings.finding: Quality was reported only as randomization (one study allocated by recruitment order); publication bias was addressed by including unpublished studies, and reporting bias was judged not an issue because both outcomes gave similar results.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and quality assessment, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Funded by internal institutional funds; no industry links declared.
key_findings.locator: Declarations of interest

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results describe the pooled effects as standardized mean differences, but the Methods derive mean differences in post-intervention ratings, the one-stage model reports a mean difference, and the single-study values match raw differences in Table 1 (for example 2.10 against 6.58 points, effect -4.54).
reporting_issues.consequence: The effects are about 2 points on a 7-point scale, not about 2 standard deviations; any comparison with standardized effects elsewhere would be wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 16, 8 and 14 studies for the strength-of-desire analyses, while the text and Figure 2 give 15, 7 and 13.
reporting_issues.consequence: Study counts differ by one between table and text; the text and forest plot (15 studies) agree with each other.

reporting_issues.issue: The one-stage strength-of-desire interval is -2.53 to -1.26 in the text and -2.52 to -1.26 in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding-level discrepancy; no effect on interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: The unpublished strength-of-desire analysis cites refs. 28, 29, 50 and the unpublished Janse van Rensburg study, which has no strength-of-desire data (Table 1, NA), and omits Katomeri 2009 (ref. 27), an unpublished thesis that is in Figure 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; the pooled figure is presumably for refs. 27, 28, 29 and 50.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the craving reduction after exercise matches or exceeds that with NRT and glucose, citing refs. 4 and 11; ref. 4 is a Cochrane review of nicotine receptor partial agonists for stopping smoking.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison with NRT is unsupported in this paper and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls the decrease moderate, while the Conclusions call the effects large and the abstract calls the evidence strong.
reporting_issues.consequence: Inconsistent wording of the same result.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent; AI reader 120, first reader)
verification.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Haasova_2013_PhysicalActivityCravingsIPD_MA.pdf, pp. 26-37 (all pages read in a text extraction; pp. 30, 32 and 33 with Tables 2-3 and Figure 2 checked on the rendered pages, including every negative value); supplementary Tables S1-S2 and Figures S1-S4 not read; final published version

design_detail: Secondary analysis of the Cochrane living systematic review of electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation (data to January 2022), with protocol registered in advance (OSF). It regroups participants of nine studies by what they actually did after being given an e-cigarette (e-cigarette only, cigarettes only, both, neither) rather than by assigned arm, and compares biomarkers of potential harm: exhaled carbon monoxide (pooled by inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis where at least two studies allowed) and 25 other biomarkers (effect direction plots, because most were reported by single studies). Only one low-risk-of-bias study is among the nine and it contributes no pooled estimate.
can_establish: How biomarkers of exposure to combustion products compared, in nine short-term studies in which adults who smoked were given e-cigarettes, between groups defined by their later behaviour (e-cigarette only, cigarettes only, both, neither), with the direction and, for exhaled carbon monoxide, the size of the differences.
cannot_establish: That switching caused the lower values (the groups were formed by behaviour, not randomized, and 8 of 9 studies were at high risk of bias), that the differences last or lead to less disease (follow-up 1 week to 8 months, no clinical outcome), how much nicotine people took in (not analysed), or what happens outside trials and confinement units.

sample.recruitment: Studies of e-cigarette interventions given to adults who smoke, for smoking cessation (randomized trials, cross-over trials and non-randomized intervention studies), found in the Cochrane living review searches; countries Greece, Italy, Poland, the United Kingdom and the United States. Baseline participants per study (Table 2): Cobb 520, Cravo 419, Goniewicz 22, Ikonomidis 90, Kerr 55, McRobbie 40, Morris 79, Pacifici 34, Pulvers 40 (sum 1299).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Studies had to report exhaled carbon monoxide or any other known biomarker of potential harm at 1 week or longer from study start, with data available by observed or self-reported use of e-cigarettes and cigarettes. Where several time points existed, the longest follow-up was used.
sample.demographics: Not reported in this paper (see the parent Cochrane review).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; participant numbers in each regrouped comparison are not reported in the text (forest plots are images).
sample.selection_effects: Only 7 of the 49 parent-review studies with biomarker data reported them by actual product use, plus two newer studies. Behaviour-defined groups are self-selected after randomization (people who switched completely may differ from those who kept smoking). Two studies were confined units for 1 to 2 weeks. The abstainer comparison rests on one University of Glasgow document that appears to be a thesis (Kerr 2020: 12 abstainers, 16 in the e-cigarette group, 3 smoking).

exposure.measurement: Observed or self-reported use of e-cigarettes and cigarettes during each study, as extracted from the original reports; groups: e-cigarette only, cigarette only, both, neither.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as recorded, not recommendations. Device types by Table 2: cig-a-like (3 studies), refillable (3), pod (1), cartridge (1), not clear (1). Follow-up 1 week to 8 months (Cravo 1 week; Goniewicz 1 and 2 weeks; Morris 2 weeks; McRobbie and Pulvers 4 weeks; Ikonomidis 1 month; Kerr 12 weeks; Cobb 3 months; Pacifici 1, 4 and 8 months). In one study with 8-month values (the only one in Table 2 with that time point is Pacifici 2015) the cigarette group cut from 27 to 8 cigarettes per day and the dual group from 23 to 5 (Figure 1 and 2 legends). Nicotine content, flavours and puffing patterns are not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed at review level.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (exhaled carbon monoxide and urinary or blood markers at the study's follow-up point).

comparison.controls: Within each study, participants who smoked cigarettes only, who used an e-cigarette and cigarettes (dual use), or who used neither (abstainers; one study).
comparison.matching: None; unadjusted comparisons of behaviour groups (mostly absolute values at follow-up, some change from baseline).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Whatever drives who switches completely versus who keeps smoking (dependence, motivation, health); the authors note unmeasured confounding in the non-randomized groupings.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: Exhaled carbon monoxide (parts per million) and one blood carbon monoxide measure (carboxyhaemoglobin saturation); 25 urinary biomarker rows in Table 1 (mercapturic acids, the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites and other carcinogen metabolites); the abstract says 26.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors call these 'biomarkers of potential harm'; they measure exposure to combustion products and carcinogens, not disease. They deliberately did not analyse nicotine exposure, which they say is not necessarily a measure of harm.
outcomes.operationalization: Lower biomarker value = less exposure. For markers other than carbon monoxide, 'lower' is judged from an effect direction plot: two arrows when the 95% intervals or error bars did not overlap, one arrow when no interval or P value was given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; no formal test of 25 biomarkers.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled exhaled CO (inverse-variance random effects, RevMan 5): e-cigarette versus cigarettes, mean difference -9.57 ppm (95% CI -17.30 to -1.83), 3 studies; e-cigarette versus both, -4.40 ppm (-12.04 to 3.24), 2 studies; both versus cigarettes only, -1.91 ppm (-3.38 to -0.45), 2 studies. I-squared substantial in all, which the authors say reflects size rather than direction of effect (forest plots are images; abstract values used). Other biomarkers (Table 1): 12 of 13 lower with e-cigarette than cigarettes, 1 not different (NNN); e-cigarette versus both: 12 of 25 lower with e-cigarette, 5 lower with both, 8 unclear or inconsistent; both versus cigarettes only (one study): 12 of 13 lower with both, NNN not different.
analysis.covariates: None (unadjusted group comparisons); one included trial (Cobb 2021) used covariates in mixed models, reported without data.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Protocol registered in advance on OSF (https://osf.io/g6bw3/); deviations are not mentioned; the protocol was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Effect direction plots replace pooling for 25 biomarkers; the text notes Study 1 of Morris was shown because it was larger, and that Pulvers' two small groups (n = 6 and n = 21) were the ones compared.
analysis.power: Pooled analyses combine only 2 to 3 studies each; for carbon monoxide the baseline levels were low in all groups (figure legends).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In nine short-term studies (1 week to 8 months; 8 at high risk of bias; 2 industry-funded), exhaled carbon monoxide was lower in people who used only e-cigarettes than in people who kept smoking (by about 10 ppm in three studies, interval 1.8 to 17.3) and by a smaller amount in people who used both than in people who only smoked (about 2 ppm in two studies, 0.5 to 3.4). It was not clearly different between people who used only e-cigarettes and people who used both (interval -12.0 to 3.2). For other biomarkers, 12 of 13 were lower with e-cigarettes than with cigarettes, mostly from two industry-funded studies; against dual use, 12 of 25 were lower with e-cigarettes and 5 (all polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites, from a single 22-person study with no intervals) were higher.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that switching from smoking to vaping or dual use 'appears to reduce levels of biomarkers of potential harm significantly'. The Discussion adds that the studies showed no evidence that biomarkers rose in people who kept smoking while also using e-cigarettes, and that the findings fit other observational studies.

timeline.event: Goniewicz et al.: PATH cross-sectional comparison of urinary biomarkers in people who only vaped, only smoked, both, or neither (card sc_goniewicz_2018).

Akiyama and Sherwood systematic review of biomarker findings from nine clinical studies of e-cigarettes and heated tobacco products, cited by the authors as finding lower toxicant levels in people using e-cigarettes than cigarettes (not read here).
Parent Cochrane living review of e-cigarettes for smoking cessation (Hartmann-Boyce et al.), from which this analysis is drawn (not read here).

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (lower exhaled carbon monoxide and combustion-product markers with exclusive e-cigarette use than with continued smoking) is consistent across the studies pooled here and with the PATH comparison, but rests on short follow-up and mostly high-risk-of-bias studies. The reassurance about dual use rests on few studies; the 2023 paper itself calls for individual participant data and longer studies.

funding.funder: Oxford University Public Policy Challenge Grant; Cancer Research UK Tobacco Advisory Group Project Grant; core infrastructure funding from the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) for the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Review Group. No tobacco or e-cigarette industry funding is declared for the review.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: five authors declare none. Hajek provided consultancy to and received research funding from Pfizer. Bullen is an investigator on grants from the Health Research Council of New Zealand, the Australian NHMRC, the NZ Ministry of Health and Auckland Council, and has provided consultancy to J&J Japan on nicotine-replacement products. Rigotti has received royalties from UpToDate for chapters on electronic cigarettes and, outside e-cigarettes, has consulted for and received a research grant from Achieve Life Sciences.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors are at the University of Oxford (Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences; Department for Continuing Education), Queen Mary University of London (Wolfson Institute of Population Health), the University of Auckland, and Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. Two of the nine included studies (Cravo 2016, Morris 2022) are marked in Table 2 as tobacco or e-cigarette industry funded; no other funder of the included studies is named.

what_would_settle_it: Individual participant data from the trials, with biomarkers measured at several time points in people who switched completely, kept smoking, or did both, adjusted for baseline smoking, with device and nicotine content recorded, follow-up of at least a year, and clinical outcomes measured in the same people.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults who smoke given e-cigarettes; four behaviour-defined groups; carbon monoxide and listed biomarkers; follow-up of at least 1 week.
Protocol registered in advance on OSF and the parent Cochrane protocol exists; the registered plan was not read and deviations are not mentioned.
Randomized, cross-over and non-randomized intervention studies are included 'as per the parent review'; no reason is given here for mixing designs when regrouping by behaviour.

Seven sources (Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP); strategy and restrictions are in the parent review (not read); reference 5 (Kerr 2020) is a University of Glasgow document that appears to be a thesis; no reference-list searching is described here.
Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts; disagreements resolved by discussion or a third reviewer.
Study characteristics and risk of bias in duplicate in the parent review; for this analysis one reviewer extracted outcome data and a second checked it.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The main text gives no list of the 42 biomarker studies not used; the flow diagram is in the supporting information (not read) and a list may be in the parent review.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives device type, baseline N, groups, outcomes and time points, data type, risk of bias, industry funding and country; population, nicotine content and use patterns are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane methods in duplicate in the parent review, one overall judgment per study (8 high, 1 low); the tool is not named here and the judgments concern the original comparisons, not the behaviour-defined regrouping.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Table 2 flags tobacco or e-cigarette industry funding yes or no for each study (two yes); other funders are not named.

Inverse-variance random effects, with heterogeneity noted and pooling justified by consistent direction; but groups formed by post-randomization behaviour are combined as raw values or changes without adjustment, with 2 to 3 studies per estimate.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No sensitivity or subgroup analysis by risk of bias; 8 of 9 studies are rated high.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion states that the data come from short confinement studies or from non-randomized groupings open to unmeasured confounding; the 'high' ratings in Table 2 are not discussed in the text.
Substantial I-squared for exhaled carbon monoxide, said to reflect size rather than direction of effect.
Not tested because no pooled analysis had 10 studies; the parent review found no evidence of publication bias but could not rule it out.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Interests of each author and the review's funders are printed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can be judged only from the supporting information and the parent review, which were not read. On the items that can be judged, two critical items are 'no' (11: unadjusted pooling of behaviour-defined groups; 15: no publication-bias assessment, for a reason the authors give) and three are only partly met (2, 4, 9), which mechanically gives critically low confidence. This is a judgment about how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not about the authors' candour: they state the confinement and non-randomized-grouping limits and say what is missing (individual participant data, longer studies). The paper may be cited for the direction of the biomarker differences and for the pooled exhaled-carbon-monoxide differences as short-term, high-risk-of-bias findings; not for the size of any benefit of switching, for dual use being protective, or for any health outcome.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC10092879 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2, figure legends, declaration of interests, acknowledgements, references; Figures 1 to 3 are forest plots rendered as images and their values were not extracted, the pooled values are those printed in the abstract; Supporting information (flow diagram) not read; the parent Cochrane review not read)

key_findings.finding: Nine studies (1299 adults who smoked and were given e-cigarettes) were included: seven of 49 parent-review studies with biomarker data, plus two newer ones (Kerr 2020, Morris 2022). Settings: Greece, Italy, Poland, UK, US.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Overall risk of bias was high in 8 of 9 studies and low in 1 (Cobb 2021, 520 participants); two studies are marked as tobacco or e-cigarette industry funded (Cravo 2016, n = 419; Morris 2022, n = 79). Follow-up 1 week to 8 months; devices were cig-a-like, refillable, pod, cartridge or unclear.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, columns 'Overall risk of bias judgement', 'Tobacco or EC industry funding?', 'Outcomes available (time-point)', 'Device type'

key_findings.finding: Pooled exhaled carbon monoxide (ppm): e-cigarette only versus cigarettes only, mean difference -9.57 (95% CI -17.30 to -1.83), 3 studies; e-cigarette only versus both, -4.40 (-12.04 to 3.24), 2 studies; both versus cigarettes only, -1.91 (-3.38 to -0.45), 2 studies. Heterogeneity substantial in every comparison, said to reflect magnitude, not direction.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Findings; Results › Carbon monoxide, 1st paragraph; Figures 1 to 3 (images, values not extracted)
key_findings.note: Forest plots were images; the pooled values are those in the abstract.

key_findings.finding: Figure legends: baseline exhaled carbon monoxide was low in all groups; in one study with 8-month values the cigarette-only group cut from 27 to 8 cigarettes per day and the dual-use group from 23 to 5 (Table 2 suggests Pacifici 2015).
key_findings.locator: Figures 1 to 3, legends

key_findings.finding: The only data on abstainers (Kerr 2020, reference 5, a University of Glasgow document that appears to be a thesis): exhaled carbon monoxide at 12 weeks was 1 ppm (SD 1) in both the e-cigarette group (n = 16) and abstainers (n = 12); abstainers were 18.00 ppm lower than the cigarette group (n = 3; 95% CI -24.81 to -11.19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Carbon monoxide, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood carbon monoxide (carboxyhaemoglobin saturation) at day 14 in the confinement study of Morris et al. (study 1): e-cigarette versus cigarettes mean difference -7.13 (95% CI -8.41 to -5.85); e-cigarette versus both -2.56 (-3.81 to -1.31); both versus cigarettes -4.57 (-5.90 to -3.25). Participants used e-cigarettes only for days 1 to 9, then were randomized to e-cigarette, cigarettes or both for days 10 to 14.
key_findings.locator: Results › Carbon monoxide, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 footnote

key_findings.finding: Other biomarkers came from five studies (none on abstainers). Cigarette-only comparison (13 biomarkers): 12 lower with e-cigarettes, none higher, one (NNN) not different; Table 1 shows these rows rest on Cravo 2016 and Morris 2022 only, both industry-funded and rated high risk of bias.
key_findings.locator: Results › Other biomarkers, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, column 'EC versus CC'; Table 2

key_findings.finding: E-cigarette-only versus dual use (25 biomarkers): 12 lower with e-cigarettes, 5 lower with dual use (all five are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites, single-arrow entries from Goniewicz 2017, n = 22), 8 not different or inconsistent. Dual use versus cigarettes only (one study, Morris 2022; 13 biomarkers): 12 lower with dual use, NNN not different.
key_findings.locator: Results › Other biomarkers, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, columns 'EC versus EC + CC' and 'Dual use (EC + CC) versus CC'
key_findings.note: Three of the 12 'lower with e-cigarettes' rows (MHBMA, 3-hydroxyfluorene, 2-naphthol) carry single arrows (point estimates, no interval or P value).

key_findings.finding: In McRobbie 2015 a mercapturic acid marker (named '3-HMPA' in the text; see reporting issues) fell significantly in both the e-cigarette-only and dual-use groups over 4 weeks, with no between-group difference in the change (mean difference 194.00 ng/g, 95% CI -502 to 890); the authors say this was the only biomarker other than carbon monoxide with data that could have been meta-analysed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Other biomarkers, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' limits: data come from short confinement studies not readily generalizable, or from non-randomized groupings open to unmeasured confounding; for all outcomes but carbon monoxide data were very limited and precluded meta-analysis; products varied; no individual participant data; nicotine exposure not analysed; only one study gave data on abstainers.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd to 5th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The Results sentence on the single study comparing dual use with cigarettes says 12 of 13 biomarkers 'were lower in EC'; the abstract and Table 1 show they were lower in the dual-use group.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Other biomarkers, 2nd paragraph; Abstract › Findings
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence should read 'dual use'; cite the abstract's wording.

design_detail: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (including randomised cross-over trials) of oral nicotine pouches given to people who used tobacco or other non-pharmaceutical nicotine products, to help them cut down or stop; a second arm of the question, population-level time-series studies of pouch uptake and the prevalence of smoking or other product use, found no eligible study. Critical outcomes: smoking abstinence at four weeks or longer (strictest definition, missing counted as smoking), serious adverse events at one week or longer, and smoking prevalence; important outcomes included adverse events, tobacco-specific nitrosamines (NNAL), carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb), metals and inflammatory markers. Random-effects pooling was planned but nearly every comparison rests on one trial, so the review mostly reports single-trial risk ratios and mean differences; one two-trial pool exists (NNAL, higher against lower dose). Three summary-of-findings tables with GRADE ratings (pouches against minimal control, against nicotine replacement therapy, against e-cigarettes). Four small trials, 284 participants, searched to 13 January 2025; ten further trials are listed as ongoing. Risk of bias (Cochrane RoB 1 tool): three trials high, one unclear, none low.
can_establish: What the randomised evidence available by January 2025 contained on nicotine pouches as an aid to cutting down or stopping smoking: four small, short trials (7 days to 8 weeks) with between 0 and 4 people quitting in any arm of the trials that reported quitting, no serious adverse events recorded in any arm, and short-term biomarker differences from single trials. The review shows how thin the evidence was at that date.
cannot_establish: Whether nicotine pouches help people stop smoking (the comparison with continued smoking rests on 1 quit among 18 people against 0 among 9); how they compare with nicotine replacement therapy (no cessation or serious-event data for that comparison) or with e-cigarettes beyond one trial with 5 quits in all; effects beyond 8 weeks; effects on people who vape or use other products (all participants smoked); how often serious harms occur (no events in any arm of three small, short trials); effects on prevalence of smoking or other nicotine use (no study); effects of pouches bought by people outside trials; and anything about trials that reported after the January 2025 search, including the ten ongoing trials.

sample.recruitment: CENTRAL (2025 issue 1), MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO from 2000 to 13 January 2025, with ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO trials platform through CENTRAL; no language limit; experts contacted and reference lists checked; industry publications such as shareholder reports were not searched. The search found 1,476 records (488 unique), 29 full texts, 4 included trials (14 records), 15 excluded and 10 ongoing; the authors of two included trials (Avila 2024; NCT04250727) were contacted and replied (Methods › Search methods; Results › Results of the search). Three trials were in the USA and one in New Zealand. Search strategies and the characteristics of each trial are in supplements that were not opened.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: individual or cluster randomised trials and randomised cross-over trials in people currently using any tobacco or non-pharmaceutical nicotine product (not only pouches), of pouches given to help them cut down or stop, with tobacco or nicotine use at four weeks or longer, or biomarkers or adverse events at one week or longer. Time-series studies were sought for population-level prevalence and none was found. Excluded: quasi-randomised studies; 15 studies excluded at full text (8 ineligible outcomes, 4 ineligible intervention, 1 ineligible design, 1 duplicate, 1 observational study with no population-level analysis).
sample.demographics: Adults who smoked cigarettes at baseline in all four trials (average age 34 to 50 in the plain language summary; 14 to 23 cigarettes a day; mostly white in the trials that reported ethnicity). Three trials enrolled people not planning to quit; one (Caldwell 2010) included some people strongly interested in quitting or cutting down. At least three trials excluded people with recent use of other tobacco or nicotine products, pouches included, so most participants had not used pouches before. Three trials were in people aged over 21; the age cut-off of the fourth is unclear.
sample.attrition: Cessation was analysed with missing counted as smoking; other outcomes were complete-case, so cigarettes per day among people who kept smoking rest on 19 of 27 and 26 of 36 people. The review rated attrition and selective reporting low risk in all four trials. Avila 2024's registry lists cotinine, NNAL and 8-isoprostane, which were not analysed for lack of funding; the review says it does not treat this as a risk of bias.
sample.selection_effects: Four small trials of people who volunteered, 30 to 146 each. Two trials told people to use the product when they wanted to smoke rather than to quit, one told people to stop their usual brand (Rensch 2023), and three enrolled people not planning to quit, so quitting was not what most participants were asked to do. Products were supplied free. Only the tobacco-industry trial (Rensch 2023) contributes most of the biomarker data against continued smoking. The review was commissioned within an NIH and FDA tobacco regulatory science centre (CAsToR 3.0) whose steering committee commented on scope but, the review says, could not decide whether it is published or what it finds.

exposure.measurement: Allocation in the trial to pouches, or to a comparison product. Products named: nicotine pouches (2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 mg; original, mint and other flavours; brands include On!, Zyn and Zonnic), e-cigarette pods with 5% nicotine in tobacco or menthol flavour, snus (8 mg) and nicotine gum (4 mg). Product use was recorded in some trials (for example willingness to continue pouch use in NCT04250727); adherence was not synthesised.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported, not recommendations: Avila 2024 supplied products for four weeks with a choice of flavour and followed people to week 8; NCT04250727 supplied Zyn 3 mg or 6 mg, eight cans a week for four weeks, with a weekly check-in phone call; Rensch 2023 gave On! 2, 4 or 8 mg as much as wanted apart from three test-use occasions on the study day, with biomarkers at about day 7, against a no-tobacco group and a continue-smoking group; Caldwell 2010 was a cross-over of three products in random order. Follow-up across the four trials ran from 7 days to 8 weeks. In two trials people were told to use the product when they wanted to smoke.
exposure.polysubstance: At least three trials excluded recent use of tobacco or nicotine products other than cigarettes. Dual use of cigarettes and pouches occurred: two people in the 6 mg arm of NCT04250727 reported symptoms they or the investigators attributed to nicotine toxicity during dual use (one paused and resumed pouches; one stopped and withdrew).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Avila 2024: cigarette abstinence at week 8 (biochemically validated per the summary-of-findings table); NCT04250727: abstinence at week 4, carbon monoxide below 5 ppm. Rensch 2023 and Caldwell 2010 reported no smoking outcome.

comparison.controls: Minimal control (continue smoking as usual or no intervention: Avila 2024, 9 people; Rensch 2023), an e-cigarette (Avila 2024), a no-tobacco group (Rensch 2023), snus and 4 mg nicotine gum (Caldwell 2010, cross-over), and a lower-dose pouch (NCT04250727; Rensch 2023).
comparison.matching: Selection bias: low risk in Avila 2024, unclear in the other three (randomisation or concealment not described). Performance bias: low in Caldwell 2010, high in Avila 2024 and Rensch 2023 (unblinded, different levels of intervention), unclear in NCT04250727 (registry entry only). Detection bias: low in three (biochemical validation), high in Caldwell 2010 (no objective outcomes). Attrition, selective reporting and other bias: rated low in all four.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not examined; planned subgroups (flavour, nicotine dose, intensity of support) and sensitivity analyses (high risk of bias, industry funding) were precluded because no pool had more than two trials; the review notes only that the NNAL dose result did not change when the one high-risk, industry-funded trial was removed.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Use of other products outside the study was exclusionary at entry in at least three trials; use during the study was not synthesised. Comparisons between pouches and NRT or snus come from one cross-over trial with adverse-event outcomes only.

outcomes.instruments: Smoking abstinence at 4+ weeks (carbon monoxide validated where reported); serious and other adverse events at 1+ weeks, collected by self-report, a respiratory questionnaire (Avila 2024), Likert-scale side-effect ratings (Caldwell 2010), a registry list (NCT04250727) or a narrative report (Rensch 2023); NNAL and COHb plus 16 further urinary biomarkers in Rensch 2023; exhaled carbon monoxide in Avila 2024; cigarettes per day.
outcomes.validity_norms: Adverse events were recorded in four different ways and could not be pooled. Rensch 2023 gave a narrative report not split by arm: 56 of 146 people (38%) had 86 events, 76 mild and 10 moderate, headache most common (23 people), and 4 events judged related to the product. Rensch 2023 supplied 18 analysed biomarkers (NNAL, COHb and 16 others); Table 4 also lists nicotine equivalents and urine mutagenicity, which no analysis reports.
outcomes.operationalization: Quit = strictest abstinence definition at the longest follow-up of 4 weeks or more, missing counted as smoking. Serious adverse events = potentially life-threatening, needing hospital care, or causing disability or death; other medical problems (cough, headache, dry mouth) counted as adverse events. Each biomarker analysed separately, complete case. Zero-event cells handled by a 0.5 correction, which gives the printed risk ratio for 1 of 18 against 0 of 9.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six outcomes per summary-of-findings table; Rensch 2023 alone supplied 18 biomarkers, each reported with an unadjusted 95% interval, and the text lists which favoured which arm.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Review authors screened and extracted data in duplicate and assessed risk of bias in duplicate, and were not blinded to trial results. Within trials, detection bias was rated low in three of four trials because key outcomes were biochemically validated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Smoking abstinence (random-effects methods planned, single-trial risk ratios reported): pouch against minimal control at week 8, 1 of 18 against 0 of 9, RR 1.58 (95% CI 0.07 to 35.32), 27 participants, very low certainty (summary-of-findings table: 11 per 1,000 with minimal control against 18 per 1,000, interval 1 to 392; the control figure comes from the zero-event correction, since no control participant quit); pouch against e-cigarette at week 8, 1 of 18 against 4 of 18, RR 0.25 (0.03 to 2.02), 36 participants, 222 against 56 per 1,000 (7 to 449), low certainty; 6 mg against 3 mg pouch at week 4, 2 of 15 against 0 of 15, RR 5.00 (0.26 to 96.13), 30 participants, certainty not assessed. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: against minimal control MD -1.07 (-12.72 to 10.58), n = 19; against e-cigarette MD 5.32 (-2.16 to 12.80), n = 26; 6 mg against 3 mg, log-scale MD -0.20 (-0.27 to -0.13), n = 30. Serious adverse events: none in any arm (against minimal control 2 trials, 124 participants, very low; against e-cigarette 1 trial, 26, low; higher against lower dose 2 trials, 77). Any adverse event, 6 mg against 3 mg: 13 of 15 in each arm, RR 1.00 (0.76 to 1.32). Biomarkers against minimal control (Rensch 2023, 53 people, one week): NNAL MD -265.30 ng/g creatinine (-350.64 to -179.96), control mean 330; COHb MD -6.7% (-8.33 to -5.07), control mean 11.3%, very low certainty; 16 further biomarkers all favoured pouches with intervals excluding no difference. Against a no-tobacco group (Rensch 2023, 46 people): none of 18 biomarkers clearly differed. Higher against lower dose: NNAL SMD -0.16 (-1.87 to 1.56), I2 0%, 2 trials, 77 participants; COHb MD -0.40% (-1.19 to 0.39).
analysis.covariates: None. Planned subgroups by flavour, nicotine dose, support intensity and analysis type were precluded by too few studies.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol (published Issue 2, 2025; DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD016220), cited as the registration. The page has no section listing differences from the protocol and the protocol was not opened, so deviations, if any, cannot be listed; the Methods state which planned analyses (random-effects pooling, subgroups, sensitivity analyses, funnel plots, ROBINS-I, time-series synthesis) could not be done.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review rated selective reporting low risk in all four trials, and says Avila 2024's unreported registry biomarkers were not analysed for lack of funding; the Cochrane e-cigarette living review rates the same trial high risk for possible selective reporting for the same reason. The review notes that NCT04250727 is a registry record without a publication.
analysis.power: At most two trials contributed to any analysis and most outcomes had one or none. Events: 1 quitter among 27 people against minimal control; 5 quitters among 36 against the e-cigarette; 2 quitters among 30 for the dose comparison; no serious event in any arm. Every outcome carries serious imprecision.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Four small trials (284 people, 7 days to 8 weeks) are the whole randomised evidence in this review. Quitting smoking was reported by two trials: 1 of 18 people given pouches had quit at week 8 against 0 of 9 who were left to smoke as usual (RR 1.58, 0.07 to 35.32; very low certainty), and 1 of 18 against 4 of 18 given e-cigarettes (RR 0.25, 0.03 to 2.02; low certainty; about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate, interval from about 22 fewer to 23 more in 100 on the summary-of-findings figures); a third trial found 2 of 15 quitting at 6 mg against 0 of 15 at 3 mg at week 4 (RR 5.00, 0.26 to 96.13). None of these differences is distinguishable from chance. No serious adverse events were recorded in any arm of three trials, and other adverse events were reported in different ways (cough and breathlessness more often with pouches than e-cigarettes in the first week and similar by week four; 38% of the 146 people in Rensch 2023 had an event, mostly mild). Biomarker differences from single trials after about one week of use pointed lower with pouches than with continued smoking (NNAL 330 against about 65 ng/g creatinine implied; COHb 11.3% against about 4.6% implied, editors' arithmetic), with very low certainty, one of them from the tobacco-industry trial; 18 biomarkers against a no-tobacco group showed no clear difference. There is no randomised evidence on pouches against NRT for quitting, on people who vape, on follow-up beyond eight weeks, or on prevalence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says smoking abstinence may be slightly higher with pouches than no intervention and that people on pouches may be slightly less likely to quit than people on e-cigarettes; the conclusions say limited, short-term data did not identify serious health harms; the plain language summary says its key finding is no short-term serious health harms in three small studies, and that it was unclear whether pouches helped people quit relative to continuing as usual. Gaps: (1) 'may be slightly higher' rests on one person quitting among 18 against none among 9, with an interval from 0.07 to 35.32, which cannot show higher or lower; the summary-of-findings control risk (11 per 1,000) is an artefact of the zero-event correction; (2) 'slightly less likely' than e-cigarettes describes 1 against 4 quitters, a point estimate of 17 fewer in 100 with an interval that spans a large difference either way, from one unblinded trial; (3) the plain language summary says two small studies underlie the comparisons with continued smoking and with e-cigarettes, but both come from one trial (Avila 2024); (4) the key message that no short-term serious health harms were found is a statement about absence of recorded events in three small studies over 1 to 8 weeks, which the same summary says leaves it unclear whether serious harm is affected; (5) the Results outcomes paragraph says two trials reported serious events while the abstract and conclusions say three; (6) the review says the industry-funded trial's findings were consistent with independent trials, yet it is the only trial of NNAL and COHb against continued smoking, so no independent comparison exists for those outcomes; (7) the risk-of-bias text says all expected outcomes were reported while noting that Avila 2024 did not report registry-listed biomarkers.

timeline.event: Cochrane protocol published (Issue 2, 2025).
This review published in October 2025; search to 13 January 2025; four trials included and ten listed as ongoing; the authors say they know of no other systematic review with similar objectives.

The Cochrane living review of e-cigarettes for smoking cessation (search to January 2026) includes the same Avila 2024 trial as its only nicotine pouch comparison, with no cessation result for pouches.

replication.where_it_stands: Nothing here has been replicated: each quit result comes from one trial of 27 to 36 people (or 30 for the dose comparison), and the biomarker findings against continued smoking come from one industry-funded trial. The review states its own limits plainly (serious imprecision for every outcome, at most two trials per analysis) and lists ten ongoing trials. Trials completed after the January 2025 search, and the ongoing trials, are not covered here.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute of the US National Institutes of Health and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products (award 2U54CA229974), through the Center for the Assessment of Tobacco Regulation (CAsToR 3.0), which commissioned the review; the funders were not involved in the decision to submit for publication. No internal sources of support are listed. Of the four included trials, three were funded by philanthropic, academic or governmental bodies and one (Rensch 2023) by the manufacturer of the pouch tested (a tobacco company); the review says no review author was involved in any included trial.
funding.declared_conflicts: Review authors declare: payments from the Truth Initiative and the US FDA and grants from NIH, FDA, WHO and others (JHB); unpaid membership of the advisory board of a smoking cessation app (JB); honoraria, an unrestricted grant and travel from Pfizer and a panel honorarium from Johnson and Johnson, both makers of smoking cessation medicines (LS); a Pfizer research grant and membership of a Johnson and Johnson scientific advisory board, and consulting for the FDA, WHO and others on tobacco product toxicity (MLG); lecture payments and research grants from public and charity funders (NL); public grants and consultancy for the WHO (HJ). JHB, JB and JLB are Cochrane editors who took no part in the editorial process. No author declares funding from a tobacco, nicotine pouch or e-cigarette company (LS states he has never received any from alcohol, e-cigarette or tobacco companies). HTB, CLM, ADW and NT declare no conflicts. Two people with lived experience of pouches gave feedback on plans and write-up.
funding.affiliations_note: Author affiliations were not in the page text read for this card, apart from the declarations (University College London for JB; Cochrane roles).

what_would_settle_it: Adequately sized randomised trials of nicotine pouches against nicotine replacement therapy and nicotine vapes in people trying to stop smoking, with carbon monoxide or cotinine validated abstinence at six months or longer, serious adverse events and the amount of pouch use after quitting followed for as long as possible, registered outcomes, and funding independent of pouch makers; results from the ten ongoing trials; biomarker trials longer than a week and from more than one funder; and separate population-level work on uptake by people who never smoked, which these trials cannot address.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People using tobacco or other non-pharmaceutical nicotine products; oral nicotine pouches; comparators listed (other products, other pouch doses, medicines, placebo pouches, very low nicotine cigarettes, minimal control); smoking abstinence, serious adverse events and prevalence as critical outcomes; randomised trials and, for prevalence, time-series studies.

A Cochrane protocol (Issue 2, 2025) is cited as the registration and the Methods follow it by design; the page has no section on differences from the protocol and the protocol was not opened, so deviations cannot be checked.
Randomised, cluster-randomised and cross-over trials for benefits and harms (quasi-randomised excluded) and time-series studies for prevalence, with the reason for each stated.

Four databases and two registries to January 2025 with no language limit, experts contacted, reference lists checked, search strategy by an information specialist in a supplement (not opened); industry publications were not searched, and the authors say eligible trials may have been missed.
Two review authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts.
Two authors independently extracted outcome data and risk of bias information; study characteristics were extracted by one author.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 15 studies excluded at full text are listed in a supplement with reasons (the duplicate excluded from that list).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 4 and the text give country, arms, outcomes, risk of bias, participants, products and nicotine content, instructions, duration and follow-up for each of the four trials; full characteristics sit in a supplement that was not opened.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane RoB 1 tool (selection, performance, detection, attrition, selective reporting, other) by two independent assessors on the critical outcomes only; the selective-reporting rating for Avila 2024 is arguable (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding and author conflicts were extracted verbatim; the page states which trial was funded by a tobacco manufacturer and that the other three had independent funders (names are in the supplement).

Pooled only trials with the same comparator and outcome; one two-trial pool (NNAL) by generic inverse-variance random effects; single-trial risk ratios with a zero-cell correction; planned Mantel-Haenszel pooling was not possible. Almost all results are single-trial figures.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses could not be done; for the one pool the text says the NNAL result did not change when the single high-risk, industry-funded trial was removed.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision (very low for comparison with minimal control) and the Discussion states the limits; the abstract wording on direction of effect goes beyond what the certainty ratings support.
I2 0% for the single pool; the Methods set thresholds and state none was needed.
The review states there were too few studies for any formal assessment (no analysis pooled more than two trials); the ten ongoing trials are listed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Declarations for every author and the funder are given; no author was involved in an included trial.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical item is judged no; item 2 is only partly met, which AMSTAR 2 does not count as a flaw. AMSTAR 2 rates how the review was done, not how good its evidence is: here the evidence is four small trials, 284 people, one to eight weeks, three at high risk of bias, with at most two trials in any analysis and every outcome rated seriously imprecise. May be cited for: a plain statement that, by January 2025, randomised evidence on pouches for stopping smoking was one trial of 27 people against continued smoking and one of 36 against e-cigarettes, with 5 quitters in all, no recorded serious adverse events, and short-term biomarker differences from single trials. May not be cited for: any statement that pouches help or do not help people stop smoking, that they are or are not safe, or that they compare with NRT or vapes in effectiveness.

key_findings.finding: Included trials: four randomised trials, 284 participants (Avila 2024, USA, 45 people: pouch, e-cigarette, no intervention; Caldwell 2010, New Zealand, 63, cross-over of pouch, snus and 4 mg nicotine gum; NCT04250727, USA, 30: 6 mg against 3 mg Zyn pouches, registry record only; Rensch 2023, USA, 146, tobacco-industry funded: On! pouches of three strengths against a no-tobacco group and a continue-smoking group). All enrolled adults who smoked; three enrolled people not planning to quit; follow-up 7 days to 8 weeks. Ten ongoing trials are listed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Included studies, Table 4 (overview), Participants, Interventions and comparators; Results of the search

key_findings.finding: Pouch against minimal control (continue smoking as usual), abstinence at week 8: 1 of 18 people given pouches had quit against 0 of 9 with no intervention; RR 1.58 (95% CI 0.07 to 35.32), 1 trial, 27 participants (Avila 2024, high risk of bias). Very low certainty (downgraded two levels for risk of bias and two for imprecision). The summary-of-findings table prints 11 per 1,000 with no intervention and 18 per 1,000 with pouches (1 to 392), figures that come from the zero-event correction since no control participant quit. Among people who kept smoking, cigarettes per day at week 8: mean difference -1.07 (-12.72 to 10.58), 19 people with complete data (Avila 2024); the interval includes large differences in both directions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus minimal control › Smoking behaviour, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary of findings 1, row 1 and footnotes a and b
key_findings.note: The per-1,000 figures are not observed rates; the observed counts are 1 of 18 and 0 of 9.

key_findings.finding: Pouch against e-cigarette (5% nicotine pods), abstinence at week 8: 1 of 18 quit with pouches against 4 of 18 with e-cigarettes; RR 0.25 (0.03 to 2.02), 1 trial, 36 participants; 222 per 1,000 with e-cigarettes against 56 per 1,000 (7 to 449) with pouches, about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate (editors' subtraction). Low certainty (two levels for imprecision; 5 events in all); not downgraded for risk of bias because both arms were equally intensive although unblinded. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: MD 5.32 (-2.16 to 12.80), 26 people with complete data; exhaled carbon monoxide higher with pouches, interval including no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus e-cigarettes › Smoking behaviour and Biomarkers; Summary of findings 3

key_findings.finding: Higher against lower nicotine pouch (NCT04250727; registry record, unclear risk of bias), abstinence at week 4: 2 of 15 quit at 6 mg against 0 of 15 at 3 mg; RR 5.00 (0.26 to 96.13), 30 participants; certainty not assessed (a dose comparison was not a planned summary-of-findings comparison). Cigarettes per day (log scale) lower with 6 mg: MD -0.20 (-0.27 to -0.13), n = 30. Any adverse event 13 of 15 in each arm, RR 1.00 (0.76 to 1.32); two 6 mg participants reported nicotine toxicity symptoms during dual use of cigarettes and pouches.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Smoking behaviour and Adverse events; Table 5 (NCT04250727)

key_findings.finding: Serious adverse events: none in any arm in the trials reporting them. Against minimal control, 2 trials (Avila 2024; Rensch 2023), 124 participants, very low certainty (two levels for risk of bias, two for imprecision); against e-cigarettes, 1 trial, 26 participants, low certainty (imprecision); higher against lower dose, NCT04250727 and Rensch 2023, 77 participants; against a no-tobacco group, Rensch 2023, none. Follow-up 1 to 8 weeks. The authors conclude it is unclear whether pouches change the chance of a serious event.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events (ONP against minimal control; ONP versus e-cigarettes; ONP at different doses); Summary of findings 1 and 3; Plain language summary › What did we find?

key_findings.finding: Other adverse events (not pooled; Table 5): cough and shortness of breath were more frequent with pouches than with e-cigarettes in the first week of Avila 2024 (cough 5 against 3, breathlessness 6 against 1 people) and similar by week 4; Rensch 2023 reported 86 events in 56 of 146 people (38%), 76 mild and 10 moderate, headache most frequent (23 people), 4 judged related to the product (2 headaches, 1 nausea, 1 mouth irritation), not split by arm; Caldwell 2010 (63 people, rating scales) found side effects uncommon for pouch, snus and gum, with fewer reports of bad taste with pouches than snus or gum, and discontinuation for gastrointestinal symptoms by 1 person on pouch, 2 on gum and 1 on snus.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events; ONP versus snus; ONP versus nicotine replacement therapy; Table 5

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers against minimal control (Rensch 2023, tobacco-industry funded, high risk, 53 people, about one week): NNAL MD -265.30 ng/g creatinine (-350.64 to -179.96) from a control mean of 330; COHb MD -6.7% (-8.33 to -5.07) from a control mean of 11.3%; 16 further urinary biomarkers all favoured pouches with intervals excluding no difference. Very low certainty (risk of bias, imprecision). Against a no-tobacco group (46 people) none of 18 biomarkers clearly differed. Avila 2024 (19 people) found lower exhaled carbon monoxide with pouches than continued smoking, interval including no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus minimal control › Biomarkers; ONP versus no tobacco or nicotine product use › Biomarkers; Summary of findings 1, rows 3 and 4

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers, higher against lower dose: NNAL SMD -0.16 (-1.87 to 1.56), I2 0%, 2 trials (NCT04250727 and Rensch 2023), 77 participants, unchanged without Rensch 2023; COHb MD -0.40% (-1.19 to 0.39). Of 17 further biomarkers in Rensch 2023, point estimates for nine favoured the lower dose (intervals including no difference), four the higher dose, three the lower dose with intervals excluding no difference (HEMA, AAMA, GAMA) and one showed no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Biomarkers

key_findings.finding: Gaps in the evidence, as the review states: no study of prevalence of smoking or other nicotine use; no data on pouches for stopping or cutting down vaping, heated tobacco, snus or other products (all participants smoked); no data on metals or inflammatory markers; no trial with follow-up beyond 8 weeks; no abstinence result for the comparison with NRT; at most two studies in any analysis, so serious imprecision for every outcome; ten ongoing studies; industry publications not searched.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Outcomes; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review; Authors' conclusions

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias in the four trials: none low overall; Avila 2024, Caldwell 2010 and Rensch 2023 high, NCT04250727 unclear. Selection bias low in Avila 2024, unclear in the others; performance bias high in Avila 2024 and Rensch 2023 (unblinded, unequal intervention), low in Caldwell 2010, unclear in NCT04250727; detection bias low in three, high in Caldwell 2010; attrition, selective reporting and other bias low in all four.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding: Rensch 2023 was funded by the pouch manufacturer (a tobacco company); the other three trials by philanthropic, academic or governmental bodies. The industry trial reported no smoking outcome, no serious events, and the largest set of biomarker results. The review was funded by the US National Cancer Institute and FDA Center for Tobacco Products through CAsToR 3.0. The review says no author took part in an included trial.
key_findings.locator: Results › Included studies › Funding; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 2nd paragraph; Sources of support; Declarations of interest

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: eligible trials may have been missed through indexing or terminology; intention-to-treat with missing counted as smoking may underestimate absolute quit rates; other outcomes were complete case; industry reports were not searched; evidence reaches January 2025; future trials should compare pouches with NRT and nicotine e-cigarettes and measure abstinence and serious events as long as possible, ideally at six months or longer.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the review processes; Authors' conclusions › Implications for research

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says smoking abstinence may be slightly higher with pouches than no intervention. The data are one person who quit among 18 given pouches and none among 9 left to smoke (RR 1.58, 0.07 to 35.32); an interval this wide cannot show higher or lower. The summary-of-findings table prints a control risk of 11 per 1,000 although no control participant quit.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Synthesis of results, Smoking abstinence; Summary of findings 1, row 1; Results › ONP versus minimal control › Smoking behaviour
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim reports the counts (1 of 18, 0 of 9) and states that the result is not informative.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusions say people given pouches may be slightly less likely to quit than people given e-cigarettes. The data are 1 of 18 against 4 of 18 (RR 0.25, 0.03 to 2.02; 5 events, one unblinded trial); the table's own absolute figures (56 against 222 per 1,000) are not slight, and the interval spans a large difference either way.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Authors' conclusions; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 3rd paragraph; Summary of findings 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim reports the counts and the interval and does not use 'slightly'.

reporting_issues.issue: The plain language summary says its statement on quitting rests on two small studies; the comparisons with continued smoking and with e-cigarettes both come from one trial (Avila 2024), and the other trial that reported quitting (NCT04250727) compared two pouch strengths.
reporting_issues.locator: Plain language summary › What did we find?, 4th paragraph; Results › Outcomes
reporting_issues.consequence: One trial per comparison is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The key message in the plain language summary says no short-term serious health harms were found, while the same summary says it is unclear whether pouches change the chance of a serious event. The record is no serious event in any arm of three small trials lasting 1 to 8 weeks.
reporting_issues.locator: Plain language summary › Key messages and What did we find?
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim states no serious events were recorded and that the data cannot show frequency.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of trials reporting serious adverse events is two in the Outcomes paragraph (Avila 2024; Rensch 2023) but three in the abstract and conclusions and in the dose comparison, which includes NCT04250727; Table 4 lists no serious-event outcome for NCT04250727.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Outcomes, 'Of the critical outcomes'; Abstract › Synthesis of results; Results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Adverse events; Table 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Three trials with serious-event data is used, as in the abstract and the dose comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The review rates selective reporting low for Avila 2024 and says all expected outcomes were reported, while noting in the same paragraph and in Table 4 that biomarkers listed on the trial registry (cotinine, NNAL, 8-isoprostane) were not reported; the Cochrane e-cigarette review rates the same trial high risk of bias for selective reporting for the same reason.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Incomplete outcome data and selective reporting; Table 4 (Avila 2024)
reporting_issues.consequence: Flagged; the overall high risk for the trial does not change.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says the industry-funded trial's findings were consistent with independent trials, but Rensch 2023 is the only trial reporting NNAL and COHb against continued smoking, so no independent trial exists to compare for those outcomes.
reporting_issues.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 2nd paragraph; Results › ONP versus minimal control › Biomarkers
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding is reported beside the biomarker result; the consistency statement is not repeated.

reporting_issues.issue: Number and label slips: the adverse-event comparison for NCT04250727 is given as n = 15 where each arm has 15 (30 in all); Table 5 labels the 6 mg arm '5mg' in two rows; summary-of-findings comments label mean differences 'RR for 1 study'; 2-AN is expanded as 2-aminoadipic acid in the Results but 2-aminonaphthalene in Table 4; Table 4 lists nicotine equivalents and urine mutagenicity among Rensch 2023's outcomes but no analysis reports them; the Background gives the year of the US Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act as 2019 (the editors believe it is 2009 and have not checked); the Discussion refers to reviews of 'nicotine cigarettes' where e-cigarettes appear to be meant.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Adverse events; Table 5; Summary of findings 1, comments; Results › Included studies, Table 4; Background › Description of the intervention; Discussion › Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews
reporting_issues.consequence: Not used in any claim.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC12549188 (abstract, plain language summary, all three Summary of findings tables, background, methods, results [results of the search, Table 4 overview, participants, interventions, outcomes, funding, excluded studies, risk of bias, every synthesis section and Table 5], discussion, authors' conclusions, acknowledgements, contributions, declarations of interest, sources of support, registration and history read; the flow diagram and risk-of-bias figure are images and were not read; Supplementary materials 1 to 6 (search strategies, characteristics of included, excluded and ongoing studies, analyses, data package) and the reference list were not opened; the four trial reports themselves were not read)

design_detail: Report of the US Surgeon General (2006) on involuntary exposure to tobacco smoke (secondhand smoke), prepared by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Office on Smoking and Health. Initial chapters were written by 22 experts, consolidated into 10 chapters, reviewed by more than 40 peer reviewers, then by more than 30 scientists for scientific integrity, then by agencies of the US Department of Health and Human Services. Causal judgments use the same four-level hierarchy as the 2014 report (sufficient; suggestive but not sufficient; inadequate; suggestive of no causal relationship). Chapter 1 says the reviews cover evidence identified through search strategies set out in each chapter, that evidence on mechanisms was selectively reviewed, and that each chapter gives a review, a quantitative synthesis where appropriate and an assessment of sources of bias. Only chapter 1 was read (Preparation of the Report, Evidence Evaluation, Major Conclusions, the list of Chapter Conclusions for chapters 2-10, Methodologic Issues, Tobacco Industry Activities); chapters 2-10, where the searches and pooled analyses sit, were not, so the card uses the editors' narrative-review checklist and AMSTAR 2 is not applied.
can_establish: What the report's authors judged, level by level, about the health effects of secondhand smoke on children and on adults who do not smoke, which conclusions bear on the statement that there is no risk-free level of exposure, and how the report treats misclassification of exposure, confounding, meta-analysis, publication bias and industry-funded criticism.
cannot_establish: The size and certainty of any single effect beyond the pooled percentages that the conclusions quote (the chapters holding the studies and meta-analyses were not read), the completeness of the evidence, or anything newer than the report's cut-off dates (about 2005).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review of epidemiological, toxicological and mechanistic literature to about 2005).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Chapter 1 says search strategies are set out in each chapter and that an attempt was made to cover all health studies through specified target dates, with a list of later key references in an Appendix; mechanisms evidence was selectively reviewed (Evidence Evaluation, 4th paragraph). The strategies themselves were not read.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Not assessable from chapter 1. The report discusses publication bias for the lung-cancer meta-analyses (Methodologic Issues > Use of Meta-Analysis) and says tobacco-industry-funded research and criticism were handled where relevant to interpretation.

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited study. Chapter 1 describes exposure classification by questionnaire (the only way to cover a lifetime), biomarkers such as cotinine (recent exposure only) and air monitoring, and notes that questionnaire reports correlate only moderately with cotinine.
exposure.polysubstance: Secondhand smoke is mostly cigarette smoke, followed by pipes, cigars and other products (Methodologic Issues > Classification of Secondhand Smoke Exposure, 2nd paragraph). Active smoking by the person studied is a confounder and a source of misclassification, discussed in chapter 1.

comparison.controls: Varies by cited study: people with little or no exposure to secondhand smoke. The report notes that because exposure has been widespread, there are almost no truly unexposed people, which may bias estimates downward.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at the level of the report.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at the level of the report; confounding by lifestyle correlates of exposure is discussed (Methodologic Issues > Confounding).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed at the level of chapter 1 beyond misclassifying people who smoke as lifetime nonsmokers.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable: the report's own graded judgments (four levels).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Causal conclusions are the authors' judgments from the whole body of evidence using the criteria of consistency, strength, temporality and coherence; specificity is set aside as not relevant to secondhand smoke, and the criteria are not applied as a checklist (Evidence Evaluation, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As quoted in the chapter conclusions (not recalculated): lung cancer in people who never smoked, a pooled 20 to 30 percent increase in risk from living with a smoker; coronary heart disease, a pooled 25 to 30 percent increase from secondhand smoke exposure; sudden infant death syndrome, lower respiratory illness, middle ear disease, school-age respiratory symptoms and asthma, and lower lung function in childhood graded sufficient; no relative risks are given for the children's outcomes in chapter 1.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; not applicable to a report of this type.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed from chapter 1. The report discusses a possible small-study effect in one meta-analysis of 37 studies and cites a second analysis that found little evidence of it, and says efforts to find missing studies turned up nothing that would change the conclusions.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Chapter 1 shows graded conclusions: sufficient for secondhand smoke and sudden infant death syndrome, lower respiratory illness, middle ear disease, school-age symptoms and asthma, lower lung function, a small reduction in birth weight, lung cancer and coronary heart disease; suggestive for preterm delivery, childhood asthma onset, stroke (in 2006) and several others; inadequate for many outcomes, including fertility, spontaneous abortion, congenital malformations and children's cognitive and behavioural outcomes. The pooled increases quoted for adults are about 20-30% for lung cancer and 25-30% for coronary heart disease.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Major Conclusions state that secondhand smoke causes premature death and disease in children and in adults who do not smoke and that there is no risk-free level of exposure; chapter 1 gives no separate derivation for the second statement. The related chapter 2 conclusions are mechanistic (more than 50 carcinogens in sidestream and secondhand smoke; a raised urinary metabolite of a tobacco-specific carcinogen in nonsmokers; a prothrombotic effect; endothelial dysfunction; atherosclerosis in animal models) and the report adds that the overall cancer risk from secondhand smoke is lower than from active smoking because of a substantially lower carcinogenic dose.

timeline.event: Surgeon General's report on involuntary smoking, the topic this report returns to; this report says its reviews reaffirm and strengthen the 1986 findings.
US Environmental Protection Agency risk assessment of secondhand smoke, in which meta-analysis was central (as described in Methodologic Issues).
Surgeon General's report on active smoking, which introduced the four-level language used here and widened the list of diseases caused by smoking.

Surgeon General's report (card sc_hhs_2014): the stroke conclusion for secondhand smoke is graded sufficient, with an increase of about 20-30%, where the 2006 report graded it suggestive; this is stated in the 2014 report's chapter 8 conclusion as listed in its chapter 1.

replication.where_it_stands: A national scientific body's graded judgments on evidence to about 2005. The 2014 report updates stroke; this card does not follow newer studies.

funding.funder: Not stated in chapter 1. The report was prepared by the Office on Smoking and Health, National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, US Department of Health and Human Services (Preparation of the Report): a federal government report.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in chapter 1. The report states that tobacco-industry-funded research and criticism of the evidence are addressed where relevant and that it does not routinely identify industry sponsorship of publications unless that bears on interpretation.
funding.affiliations_note: Chapter authors and reviewers were not listed in the part read.

what_would_settle_it: For the statement that there is no risk-free level: studies that measure the dose-response of health outcomes (heart and blood vessels, children's airways) at the lowest exposures, with biomarkers rather than questionnaires, in populations where some people are truly unexposed. For the pooled increases: individual-participant analyses that handle misclassification of active smoking and background exposure explicitly.

domains.note: Chapter 1 says search strategies and target dates are set out in each chapter and that mechanisms evidence was selectively reviewed; the strategies were not read, so this is not judged as absent. Provisional until the chapters are read.

The report says each chapter assesses sources of bias, and chapter 1 discusses misclassification, confounding, meta-analysis and publication bias in detail, but no formal tool is named and the chapter-level appraisals were not read.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Not examined: authors and reference lists of chapters 2-10 were not read.
Graded conclusions are set apart from the narrative, but the statement that there is no risk-free level carries no stated derivation in chapter 1.

domains.domain: Balance of the epidemiological evidence against the criticism of it
domains.note: The report describes the industry-linked criticisms and a court challenge to one meta-analysis and explains why random misclassification and background exposure bias estimates toward the null; independent methodological critiques are summarized briefly, so their weight cannot be judged from chapter 1.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: only the summary chapter was read. Within it the report is explicit about its grading, names the main sources of bias and says pooled estimates may be more uncertain than their statistics suggest. The card can be cited for what the report concluded and at what level, for the pooled percentages the conclusions quote, and for its account of method. It cannot be cited for the underlying studies, for a threshold or a dose-response at low exposure, or for evidence after about 2005.

key_findings.finding: Process: initial chapters by 22 experts, consolidated into 10 chapters, more than 40 peer reviewers, more than 30 scientists and experts reviewing scientific integrity, then review by DHHS agencies; the report notes that publication lags mean newer studies exist and lists later key references in an Appendix.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Preparation of the Report, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Method: the report uses the criteria of consistency, strength, specificity, temporality and coherence; they are guidelines, not a checklist; specificity is set aside as not relevant; a small elevation of risk (for example spousal smoking and lung cancer) does not weigh against causality, but alternative explanations for small risks need full exploration; coherence draws on the larger literature on active smoking. Reviews cover evidence identified through search strategies set out in each chapter, with selective review of mechanisms evidence and specified target dates.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Evidence Evaluation, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1.4

key_findings.finding: Major Conclusions 1-3: secondhand smoke causes premature death and disease in children and in adults who do not smoke; children exposed are at increased risk of sudden infant death syndrome, acute respiratory infections, ear problems and more severe asthma, and smoking by parents causes respiratory symptoms and slows lung growth; in adults it has immediate adverse effects on the cardiovascular system and causes coronary heart disease and lung cancer.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Major Conclusions, conclusions 1, 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Major Conclusion 4: the scientific evidence indicates that there is no risk-free level of exposure to secondhand smoke. The Major Conclusions give no separate reasoning for it.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Major Conclusions, conclusion 4

key_findings.finding: Major Conclusions 5 and 6: many millions of Americans, children and adults, are still exposed in homes and workplaces; eliminating smoking in indoor spaces fully protects people who do not smoke from exposure, while separating smokers from nonsmokers, cleaning the air and ventilating buildings cannot eliminate exposure.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Major Conclusions, conclusions 5 and 6

key_findings.finding: Chapter 2 (toxicology) conclusions bearing on a lowest safe level: more than 50 carcinogens are in sidestream and secondhand smoke; sufficient evidence that secondhand smoke and its condensates cause tumours in laboratory animals; sufficient evidence that exposure of nonsmokers raises urinary levels of metabolites of a tobacco-specific lung carcinogen (NNK); the mechanisms of lung cancer are probably similar to those in smokers, with the overall risk compared with active smoking diminished by a substantially lower carcinogenic dose; sufficient evidence of a prothrombotic effect, of endothelial cell dysfunction, and of atherosclerosis in animal models; the evidence indicates multiple mechanisms of respiratory tract injury and mechanisms by which secondhand smoke could raise the risk of sudden infant death syndrome.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 2, conclusions 1-9

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 (reproductive and developmental effects): sufficient for sudden infant death syndrome (4) and for a small reduction in birth weight (6); suggestive for preterm delivery (5), for childhood cancer overall with exposure before and after birth (11), leukaemias (14), lymphomas (15) and brain tumours (16); inadequate for female fertility (1), spontaneous abortion (2), neonatal mortality (3), congenital malformations (7), children's cognitive functioning (8), behavioural problems (9), height and growth (10), childhood cancer from exposure in pregnancy alone (12) or in infancy alone (13), and other cancer types (17).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 5, conclusions 1-17

key_findings.finding: Chapter 6 (respiratory effects in children): sufficient for lower respiratory illnesses in infants and children (1; greatest from the mother's smoking, 2), middle ear disease (3), cough, phlegm, wheeze and breathlessness in school-age children (6), ever having asthma at school age (7), onset of wheeze illnesses in early childhood (8), persistent adverse effects on lung function across childhood from maternal smoking in pregnancy (11), and lower lung function in childhood from exposure after birth (12); suggestive for the natural history of middle ear effusion (4) and for onset of childhood asthma (9); inadequate for adenoidectomy or tonsillectomy (5) and for allergy (10).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 6, conclusions 1-12
