key_findings.finding: Chapter 7 (adult cancer): sufficient for lung cancer among lifetime nonsmokers, extending to all secondhand smoke exposure regardless of location (1); the pooled evidence indicates a 20 to 30 percent increase in lung cancer risk from living with a smoker (2); suggestive for breast cancer (3) and nasal sinus cancer (4); inadequate for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (5) and cervical cancer (6).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 7, conclusions 1-6

key_findings.finding: Chapter 8 (cardiovascular disease): sufficient for coronary heart disease morbidity and mortality in men and women (conclusion 1), with pooled relative risks from meta-analyses indicating a 25 to 30 percent increase in risk (conclusion 2); stroke suggestive but not sufficient (conclusion 3); studies of subclinical vascular disease, particularly carotid wall thickening, suggestive but not sufficient (conclusion 4).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 8, conclusions 1 to 4

key_findings.finding: Chapter 9 (respiratory effects in adults): sufficient for odor annoyance (1) and nasal irritation (2); suggestive for acute respiratory symptoms in people with asthma (4) and in healthy people (5), chronic respiratory symptoms (6), short-term decline in lung function in people with asthma (7), a small decrement in lung function from chronic exposure (9), adult-onset asthma (11), worsening of asthma control (12) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (13); inadequate for short-term lung function decline in healthy people (8), accelerated decline (10) and morbidity in people with the disease (14).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 9, conclusions 1-14

key_findings.finding: Chapter 10 (control of exposure): smoke-free workplaces are the only effective way to ensure that exposure does not occur in the workplace; total bans on indoor smoking in hospitals, restaurants, bars and offices substantially reduce exposure, up to several orders of magnitude with incomplete compliance and to elimination with full compliance; exposures cannot be controlled by air cleaning or mechanical air exchange; the home is becoming the predominant location of exposure.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 10

key_findings.finding: Misclassification of exposure: random misclassification tends to reduce the apparent effect; classifying some current or former smokers as lifetime nonsmokers would push the lung-cancer association upward when smoking clusters between spouses, but the report says analyses show this cannot fully explain the observed increase among lifetime nonsmokers married to smokers; because exposure has been widespread, there are almost no truly unexposed people, so estimates may be biased downward.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Methodologic Issues > Misclassification of Secondhand Smoke Exposure, 1st, 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Meta-analysis and publication bias: the authors pooled observational studies while recognizing that the uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what conventional statistics indicate, because of biases within the studies or in how they were selected; one analysis of 37 studies found smaller studies tended to give higher risks (a possible small-study effect), another found little evidence of publication bias, and intensive efforts to find missing studies turned up nothing that would alter published conclusions; the statistical significance of pooled estimates was not decisive for the causal conclusions.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Methodologic Issues > Use of Meta-Analysis, 3rd to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Confounding: potential confounders are not confounders unless they are associated with exposure and independently raise disease risk; socioeconomic status may lie on the causal pathway and adjusting for it can mislead; adults with more secondhand smoke exposure tend to have less healthful lifestyles in US and UK surveys, though how far this generalizes is uncertain; confounding matters more as the association weakens, and each disease chapter addresses it.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Methodologic Issues > Confounding, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Tobacco industry: the report says the industry has criticized the evidence repeatedly, funded or carried out research judged to be biased, and attempted to undermine key studies and sustain controversy; it identifies industry sponsorship of publications only where relevant to interpretation, and notes that papers acknowledging industry support criticized the lung-cancer meta-analyses.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Tobacco Industry Activities, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methodologic Issues > Use of Meta-Analysis, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Major Conclusion 4, that there is no risk-free level of exposure, is stated without a threshold analysis or a derivation in chapter 1. The nearest reasoning is in the chapter 2 conclusions (carcinogens present and taken up; prothrombotic effect and endothelial dysfunction; atherosclerosis in animal models) and the statement that cancer risk is lower than from active smoking because of a substantially lower carcinogenic dose.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim about what the statement rests on is the editors' reading of which conclusions bear on it; the report does not draw the link. Locators: Chapter 1 > Major Conclusions, conclusion 4; Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 2.

reporting_issues.issue: A sentence on efforts to find missing studies reads 'yielded little nothing that would alter published conclusions', which is garbled.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sense (little or nothing found) does not change the report's argument. Locator: Chapter 1 > Methodologic Issues > Use of Meta-Analysis, 5th paragraph.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 1 gives pooled percentages only for lung cancer (20-30%) and coronary heart disease (25-30%); the children's outcomes are graded without any relative risks in the part read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims on children's outcomes can state the grade, not a size of effect. Locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapters 5 and 6.

verification.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2006 (rptsmokeexp, rpt-smokeexp.ch1): Chapter 1 Introduction, Summary, and Conclusions in full (Preparation of the Report, Evidence Evaluation, Table 1.4, Major Conclusions, Chapter Conclusions for chapters 2-10, Methodologic Issues, Tobacco Industry Activities). Chapters 2-10, the Appendix and the cited studies were not read.

design_detail: Report of the US Surgeon General on smoking, fifty years after the first (1964) report. A multi-author federal report (15 chapters by 75 experts, more than 100 peer reviewers, more than 20 scientists reviewing for scientific integrity). Each chapter's authors weigh the whole body of evidence and grade their conclusions on a four-level hierarchy: sufficient to infer a causal relationship; suggestive but not sufficient; inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship; suggestive of no causal relationship. Chapter 3 names the criteria (consistency, strength, specificity, temporality, coherence) but gives no databases, dates or selection rules for the evidence behind the conclusions used here, so the card uses the editors' narrative-review checklist, not AMSTAR 2. Read on NCBI Bookshelf: chapter 1 (Major Conclusions and Chapter Conclusions, Table 1.1), chapter 5 on nicotine (all sections), and chapter 3 for how conclusions are graded. The other chapters were read only as far as chapter 1 lists their conclusions.
can_establish: What a national scientific report judged, level by level, about the diseases caused by smoking and about the effects of nicotine itself, and what kinds of studies the nicotine chapter describes under each conclusion.
cannot_establish: Whether the evidence base is complete (no search method is described), how any cited study would be rated on its own, or how much of the harm of smoking is due to nicotine as against the other substances in smoke: the report does not apportion it.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review of the literature up to about 2013). Chapter 5 draws on laboratory and animal experiments, trials of nicotine replacement, comparisons of smokeless tobacco with smoking, and population studies.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated for the conclusions used: chapter authors assemble the evidence they judge relevant and present the detail so that readers can judge it (Chapter 3).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence selection is by the chapter authors and is not documented. For nicotine alone, the human evidence is thin: the cancer discussion rests on one follow-up of long-term nicotine replacement (Lung Health Study) and on smokeless tobacco, so the graded conclusions lean on experimental studies and on comparisons between products that differ in more than nicotine.

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited study and is not appraised in the chapters read. Chapter 5 separates nicotine given alone (replacement medicines, laboratory experiments), nicotine in smokeless tobacco and e-cigarettes, and nicotine in cigarette smoke.
exposure.polysubstance: The central confounder is other tobacco constituents: in people who smoke, nicotine's own effects cannot be separated from those of the rest of the smoke, and the chapter says that smokeless tobacco findings may not carry over to inhaled nicotine.

comparison.controls: Varies by cited study: people who do not use tobacco, people who smoke, people who use smokeless tobacco or nicotine replacement, and animals given nicotine alone.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at the level of the report.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at the level of the report; the chapter itself says confounding makes causality hard to establish for adolescent smoking and later cognitive problems.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed at the level of the report.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable: the report's own graded judgments (four levels).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Sufficient' means the authors judge the evidence enough to infer a causal relationship; 'suggestive' means a possible but not sufficient basis; 'inadequate' means evidence that is sparse, of poor quality or conflicting. These are the authors' judgments, not a measured quantity.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited in the sections read (not recalculated): premature deaths attributed to cigarette smoking since 1964, more than 20 million; about 480,000 US deaths a year from smoking (above 400,000 for more than a decade); secondhand smoke and stroke, a 20-30% increase; preterm delivery with smoking, a 27% increase (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited); Swedish snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (1.02-1.43), with the cigarette figure misprinted (see reporting issues); a nicotine-patch trial in 250 pregnant women, birth weight 186 g higher (35-336) in the nicotine arm; Lung Health Study, 5,887 people enrolled, 3,220 followed 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with replacement use.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; not applicable to a report of this type.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed: no search method. The report itself says industry-funded studies of nicotine and cognition reported benefits almost exclusively and that authors' industry ties are often undisclosed in citing reviews (Chapter 5, Tobacco Industry Influence).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Chapter 5 shows that nicotine alone has been studied mainly in laboratory and animal experiments, in short trials of replacement medicines, and by comparing smokeless tobacco with smoking. For cancer, the animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to be a tumour-causing agent, genotoxicity data are mixed, and the one human follow-up of people who used replacement products long term was short; for the heart, the chapter reasons from known effects on heart rate and blood vessels and gives no graded conclusion; for dependence, it summarizes earlier reports and gives no new graded conclusion.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The chapter's six numbered conclusions: four graded sufficient (acute toxicity at high enough doses; activation of pathways through which smoking raises disease risk; lasting adverse effects of fetal exposure on brain development; adverse effects on maternal and fetal health in pregnancy, including preterm delivery and stillbirth), one suggestive (adolescent exposure and the brain) and one inadequate (cancer). The report's Major Conclusions attribute the US burden of tobacco-caused death and disease overwhelmingly to cigarettes and other combusted tobacco products. The chapter text calls adverse effects of adolescent exposure on cognition likely while the graded conclusion says only suggestive.

timeline.event: First Surgeon General's report on smoking; the 2014 report counts premature deaths attributable to smoking from this date.
Surgeon General's report concluding that cigarettes and other forms of tobacco are addicting and that nicotine is the drug in tobacco that causes addiction (as described in Chapter 5, Introduction).
Surgeon General's report on how tobacco smoke causes disease, covering the biology of dependence (as described in Chapter 5).
Surgeon General's report on tobacco use among young people (as described in Chapter 5).

replication.where_it_stands: A national scientific body's graded judgments as of about 2013, drawing on earlier reports for dependence. This card does not follow evidence published after the report. The report itself names the long-term effects of nicotine, compared with smoking and with no tobacco use at all, as information still needed.

funding.funder: Not stated in the chapters read. Per the reference record the author is the US Department of Health and Human Services and the publisher is the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: a federal government report.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the chapters read. The report treats tobacco-industry influence on the nicotine literature in Chapter 5 (Tobacco Industry Influence).
funding.affiliations_note: Chapter 3 says the report's editors have come from outside the federal government since 1979; the full author and reviewer lists were not read.

what_would_settle_it: Long-term follow-up of people who use nicotine without smoke (replacement medicines, smokeless tobacco, e-cigarettes) for cancer, cardiovascular and neurocognitive outcomes, compared with people who smoke and with people who use no tobacco, which the report itself says is needed; and human studies that can separate nicotine from the rest of the smoke for fetal and adolescent brain outcomes.

domains.note: No databases, dates or selection criteria are stated for the conclusions used; Chapter 3 describes authors assembling the relevant evidence. The search cannot be reproduced.

No formal appraisal tool, but the causal criteria and four-level hierarchy are explicit and chapter 5 names limits of individual bodies of evidence (confounding in adolescent studies, short follow-up in the Lung Health Study, a poorly documented human fatal-dose figure, mixed genotoxicity results).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Not examined in the sections read; the author and reference lists were not checked for concentration in one group.

Graded conclusions are set apart, but the chapter text on adolescents calls adverse effects likely while grading them suggestive, and the cardiovascular discussion reasons from mechanism without a graded conclusion.

domains.domain: Balance of the evidence on nicotine itself against the evidence on burning tobacco
domains.note: The chapter reports both the experimental evidence that nicotine is biologically active and the evidence that does not support nicotine alone as a tumour-causing agent. The under-represented side is long-term human data on nicotine without smoke, so the 'sufficient' conclusions lean on experimental studies and on comparisons between products.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative report (METHODS 5.3). The overall judgment follows the worst domain, the absence of any stated search. In the sections read, the report is explicit about its grading, names limits of the evidence, and says where nicotine-alone data are missing, so it can be cited for what the report concluded and at what level, and for the kinds of studies it describes under each conclusion. It cannot be cited for the size of an effect, for completeness of the evidence, or as an independent check of the studies it summarizes.

key_findings.finding: Major Conclusion 1: more than 20 million premature deaths can be attributed to cigarette smoking since the first Surgeon General's report in 1964.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Major Conclusions, conclusion 1

key_findings.finding: Major Conclusion 3: cigarette smoking is causally linked to disease in nearly all organs, to diminished health status in general and to harm to the fetus; research is still finding new diseases (the report names diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and colorectal cancer).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Major Conclusions, conclusion 3

key_findings.finding: Major Conclusion 4: secondhand smoke is causally linked to cancer, respiratory disease and cardiovascular disease, and to adverse effects in infants and children.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Major Conclusions, conclusion 4

key_findings.finding: Major Conclusion 9: the burden of death and disease from tobacco use in the United States is overwhelmingly caused by cigarettes and other combusted tobacco products, and rapid elimination of their use would dramatically reduce it. The report states this as a conclusion and does not apportion the burden between nicotine and the other constituents of smoke.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Major Conclusions, conclusion 9

key_findings.finding: Grading: Table 1.1 gives four levels (sufficient to infer a causal relationship; suggestive but not sufficient; inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship, because the evidence is sparse, of poor quality or conflicting; suggestive of no causal relationship). Causal judgments come from synthesizing all the evidence with the criteria of consistency, strength, specificity, temporality and coherence; the statistical significance of a meta-analysis has not figured directly in the inferences; conclusions are worded conservatively.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Table 1.1; Chapter 3 > Development of the Criteria for Causation; Evolution of the Application of the Criteria

key_findings.finding: Process: 15 chapters written by 75 experts, reviewed by more than 100 peer reviewers, with more than 20 scientists reviewing for scientific integrity. No search protocol, databases or dates are described for the conclusions used.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Development of the Report; Chapter 3 > Methods for Reviewing the Evidence

key_findings.finding: Chapter 11 conclusions (as listed in Chapter 1), all graded sufficient: smoking causes diminished overall health; cigarette smoking increases the risk of death from any cause in men and women; the relative risk of dying from cigarette smoking has increased over the last 50 years in US men and women.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 11, conclusions 1 to 3

key_findings.finding: Chapter 12 conclusions (as listed in Chapter 1): about 480,000 US deaths a year are attributable to smoking (above 400,000 a year for more than a decade); 5.6 million young people aged 0-17 are projected to die early of smoking-related illness; more than 20 million premature deaths since 1964 are attributed to smoking and secondhand smoke.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 12, conclusions 1 to 3

key_findings.finding: Chapter 8 conclusions (as listed in Chapter 1): secondhand smoke exposure causes stroke (sufficient), with an increase in risk of about 20-30%; smokefree legislation is followed by fewer coronary events in people under 65 (sufficient).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 8, conclusions 1 to 3

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 conclusion 1 (sufficient): at high enough doses nicotine has acute toxicity. Basis in the chapter: animal studies of lethal dose, trials of replacement medicines run at doses chosen to be safe, and case reports of poisoning; there is no systematic assessment of dose and response, and the commonly quoted human fatal oral dose is poorly documented (a literature search found no source for it).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Conclusions, conclusion 1; Toxicokinetics and Acute Toxicity

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 conclusion 2 (sufficient): nicotine activates multiple biological pathways through which smoking increases the risk of disease. The Evidence Summary describes pathways relevant to fetal growth, immune function, the cardiovascular system, the central nervous system and carcinogenesis, from experimental research.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Conclusions, conclusion 2; Evidence Summary, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 conclusion 3 (sufficient): nicotine exposure during fetal development, a critical window for brain development, has lasting adverse consequences for brain development. The Evidence Summary describes this as shown by experimental research. The supporting text inside chapter 5 is brief: one statement that nicotine targets neurotransmitter receptors in the fetal brain and may alter cell proliferation and synaptic activity (one cited review), a pointer to chapter 9 for the effects of prenatal exposure on the fetal nervous system (chapter 9 not read), and the Cognitive Function summary's statement that evidence shows adverse effects of cigarette smoke and of nicotine on fetal and adolescent brain development. No human study that separates nicotine from the rest of the smoke is described for the fetal brain in the chapter 5 sections read.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Conclusions, conclusion 3; Evidence Summary, 1st paragraph; Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Cognitive Function > Critical Periods of Exposure in the Nervous System, 1st paragraph; Cognitive Function > Summary

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 conclusion 4 (sufficient): nicotine adversely affects maternal and fetal health during pregnancy, contributing to adverse outcomes such as preterm delivery and stillbirth. Basis: inference about nicotine alone from smokeless tobacco studies (Sweden, India), trials of nicotine replacement in pregnancy, and experimental research, as the chapter states. For stillbirth the chapter notes that in the Swedish study the smoking-related risk fell markedly when antenatal bleeding and small-for-gestational-age deliveries were excluded while the raised risk for snus stayed the same, and reads this as suggesting that both involve nicotine but that other factors may also contribute to the risk in people who smoke. The Summary says the evidence supports a key role for nicotine in preterm delivery and stillbirth.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Conclusions, conclusion 4; Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Reproductive Health Outcomes (Fetal Growth Restriction; Preterm Delivery; Stillbirth, Perinatal Mortality, and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome; Summary)

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 conclusion 5 (suggestive, not sufficient): nicotine exposure during adolescence may have lasting adverse consequences for brain development. Basis: smoking in adolescence is associated with lasting cognitive and behavioural impairment, but confounding makes causality hard to establish; animal studies show adolescent-specific effects; effects after young adulthood are unknown.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Conclusions, conclusion 5; Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Cognitive Function > Critical Periods of Exposure in the Nervous System, 3rd, 8th and 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 conclusion 6 (inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship): nicotine and cancer risk. Basis: genotoxicity data are mixed; animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to cause tumours (one exception, sarcomas in one mouse strain) and it promotes tumours in some models, but not those driven by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; in people, the only study of people who used replacement products long term is the Lung Health Study (5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link to replacement use, short follow-up); smokeless tobacco raises oral, oesophageal and pancreatic cancer risk, less than smoking, and the oral route may not carry over to inhalation.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Conclusions, conclusion 6; Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Cancer (Genotoxicity; Experimental Animal Studies for Carcinogenicity; Human Studies; Summary)

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 Evidence Summary and Implications: previous reports reached causal conclusions on nicotine and dependence (1988, 2010, 2012); beyond replacement medicines, therapeutic roles for nicotine are not established; information is needed on the long-term risks of nicotine, including for reproductive health and adolescent cognitive development, compared with cigarette smoking and with no tobacco use at all; the report states that the evidence in this and other chapters and earlier reports shows long-term nicotine use may have adverse consequences for those exposed and clearly harms the developing fetus; the fetus is exposed to nicotine without the other smoke components if the mother uses non-smoked products; cancer, cardiovascular and neurocognitive outcomes are 'of concern'; the report calls for cautious messages for pregnant women, women of reproductive age and adolescents about smokeless tobacco and e-cigarettes as alternatives to smoking; all tobacco products contain toxicants, so all tobacco product use poses some health risks.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Evidence Summary, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Implications, 1st-3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Dependence (earlier reports, summarized in Chapter 5): nicotine is described as the major chemical component responsible for dependence in tobacco products (the 1988 report's conclusion is cited); the risk depends on the amount of nicotine delivered and the way it is delivered, and the potential for dependence rises with the rate of delivery, the rate of absorption and the concentration reached; not all forms of nicotine delivery pose an equal risk of establishing and maintaining dependence; nicotine replacement medicines designed to minimize dependence risk carry a low risk and are generally much easier to stop than tobacco products; cigarettes are engineered to raise the likelihood of dependence through contents and emissions beyond nicotine (for example acetaldehyde, ammonia compounds, menthol) and through design features. Chapter 5 has no numbered 2014 conclusion on dependence.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Introduction, 1st paragraph; Toxicokinetics and Acute Toxicity of Nicotine, 1st paragraph; Pathophysiology of Nicotine Addiction > Summary of Evidence from the 2010 Surgeon General's Report, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Heart and blood vessels: the chapter says the sympathomimetic effects of nicotine (on heart rate, contractility, coronary vascular resistance and insulin sensitivity) likely contribute to some extent to cardiovascular risk in people who smoke; tolerance develops to many effects with prolonged exposure; it is unclear whether short-term effects persist. Chapter 5 has no numbered conclusion on the heart.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Cardiovascular Diseases

key_findings.finding: Reproductive outcomes: Swedish population study (1999-2010), snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02-1.43), against a cigarette figure printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62-2.91 (misprinted); a trial of nicotine patches in 250 pregnant women found no difference in quit rates and a higher birth weight in the nicotine arm (186 g; 35-336), possibly because of less smoking, leading the chapter to a 'modest role' for nicotine in fetal growth; preterm delivery is raised about 27% with smoking and similarly with snus in Sweden; smokeless tobacco studies from India and Sweden show raised stillbirth.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Reproductive Health Outcomes > Fetal Growth Restriction; Preterm Delivery; Stillbirth, Perinatal Mortality, and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome; Summary

key_findings.finding: Lung development: primate and other animal studies consistently suggest nicotine may be the primary mediator of many adverse effects of maternal smoking on fetal lung development.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Lung Development > Summary

key_findings.finding: Cognition and industry influence: acute nicotine has modest cognition-enhancing effects in adult smokers during withdrawal; a meta-analysis of placebo-controlled studies found improvement in 6 of 9 cognitive domains in nonsmokers and in smokers abstinent for up to 2 hours; little is known about long-term effects. The chapter reports that industry-funded authors reported positive cognitive findings almost exclusively (Turner and Spilich 1997, as cited) and that for Alzheimer's disease industry-affiliated studies found a reduced risk with smoking while non-industry pooled estimates were neutral or showed higher risk (Cataldo 2010, as cited).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 > Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Cognitive Function (Effects of Nicotine on Cognitive Function in Healthy Adult Smokers and Nonsmokers; Tobacco Industry Influence)

key_findings.finding: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (chapter 7 conclusions, as listed in chapter 1): sufficient to infer that smoking is the dominant cause of the disease in men and women in the US and causes all elements of it, including emphysema and airway damage (conclusion 1); deaths from it have risen sharply in both sexes since 1964 and women's now exceed men's (conclusion 2). Suggestive, not sufficient, that women develop severe disease at younger ages (conclusion 3).
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 7 > Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, conclusions 1 to 3

key_findings.finding: Stopping, as far as chapter 1 lists it: the conclusion on people with cancer (chapter 6, conclusion 1, graded sufficient for the link between cigarette smoking and adverse outcomes in cancer patients) adds that quitting improves the prognosis of cancer patients; for age-related macular degeneration the report grades as suggestive, not sufficient, that stopping reduces the risk of advanced disease (chapter 10). No conclusion in chapter 1 gives the change in the risk of death, or of the main diseases, after stopping; the chapters on stopping and treatment were not read.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 1 > Chapter Conclusions > Chapter 6 > Adverse Health Outcomes in Cancer Patients and Survivors, conclusion 1; Chapter 10 > Eye Disease: Age-Related Macular Degeneration; Major Conclusions, conclusions 1 to 10

reporting_issues.issue: In the Swedish snus study of small-for-gestational-age births, the cigarette-smoking odds ratio is printed as 2.27 with a 95% interval of 2.62-2.91, so the point estimate lies outside its own interval (the snus figure, 1.21 with 1.02-1.43, is internally consistent).
reporting_issues.consequence: The cigarette comparator cannot be quoted; the primary study would have to be read to recover it. Locator: Chapter 5 > Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Reproductive Health Outcomes > Fetal Growth Restriction.

reporting_issues.issue: The chapter's concluding paragraph on adolescence says it is likely that nicotine exposure in adolescence adversely affects cognitive function and development, while the graded conclusion 5 is only suggestive.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims use the graded level (suggestive, not sufficient) and do not use 'likely'. Locators: Chapter 5 > Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Cognitive Function > Critical Periods of Exposure in the Nervous System, 8th paragraph; Chapter 5 > Conclusions, conclusion 5.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 5 discusses the heart and dependence at length but has no numbered, graded conclusion for either; the dependence conclusions are carried from the 1988, 2010 and 2012 reports.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim about nicotine and dependence or the heart cannot cite a 2014 graded conclusion. Locators: Chapter 5 > Conclusions; Pathophysiology of Nicotine Addiction; Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure > Cardiovascular Diseases.

verification.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2014 (surgsmoke50): chapter 1 (Major Conclusions, Chapter Conclusions, Table 1.1, Development of the Report), chapter 5 on nicotine (Introduction, Toxicokinetics and Acute Toxicity, Pathophysiology of Nicotine Addiction, Health Consequences, Tobacco Industry Influence, Evidence Summary, Conclusions, Implications) and chapter 3 (how the evidence is reviewed and conclusions graded). Figures were not read. Chapters 2, 4, 6-15 and the studies cited were not read.

design_detail: The Smokeless Tobacco monograph of IARC Monographs volume 100E (an expert Working Group's hazard evaluation of all smokeless tobacco products, oral and nasal, worldwide). Only the Smokeless Tobacco monograph was read, and within it section 5 (Evaluation), section 2 (Cancer in Humans, including the synthesis at 2.3) and the paragraphs of section 1 on Swedish snus. The chapter states that smokeless tobacco was previously evaluated (2004 meeting, published 2007) and that new data since then were incorporated; it describes no search, dates or selection process (the series' general procedures sit in a Preamble that was not read). The evaluation is a graded judgment (here 'sufficient evidence' and Group 1) for smokeless tobacco as a whole, not for snus separately.
can_establish: That an international Working Group judged the human evidence sufficient for smokeless tobacco as a class to cause cancers of the oral cavity, oesophagus and pancreas, and what the Swedish and Norwegian snus studies it cites found for each cancer, site by site.
cannot_establish: Whether Swedish snus in particular causes these cancers (the verdict pools snus with chewing tobacco, moist snuff, toombak, naswar and shammah, and the snus-specific studies are mixed); the size of any risk (a Group 1 classification says how sure the Working Group was that a hazard exists, not how large it is); how the risk compares with smoking; or any non-cancer outcome (the monograph covers cancer only). The chapter (published 2012) does not mention tobacco-free nicotine pouches. The chapter's tables (1.1 to 1.3, 2.1 to 2.14) are separate files and were not read.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (evaluation of published studies). Search, dates and inclusion criteria are not stated in the chapter; the text says new data since the 2004 evaluation 'have been incorporated' (opening paragraph). For oral cancer the chapter says it focuses on studies published since the previous monograph (2.1.1 › (a), 5th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Studies are set aside in text with reasons: for example three oral cancer case-control studies whose tobacco information probably came from medical records (possible ascertainment bias), and a US cohort with no adjustment for smoking (2.1.1 › (a) › (i) 2nd paragraph, (ii) 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Mainly men; the Swedish evidence is from a cohort of 279,897 to 343,822 male construction workers, a cohort of 9,860 men examined orally, and case-control studies; the Norwegian evidence from a cohort followed 35 years.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Studies are chosen by the Working Group, and the chapter says that because of the large body of evidence it concentrates on studies since 2007. Smokeless tobacco products differ greatly in content and use between regions, which the evaluation does not resolve.

exposure.measurement: Mostly 'ever' against 'never' use of a named product, usually defined as use for some minimal time such as a year (2.1.1 › (a), 5th paragraph); in the Nordic cohorts, tobacco habits at baseline only, with no information on later changes and no exclusion of cases in the first years of follow-up (2.1.1 › (a) › (i) 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Measured product content for Swedish snus: nicotine 0.5% to 1.7%, against 0.47% to 3.43% in 17 brands of US moist snuff (1.2.1, 2nd paragraph). Before 1983 Swedish snuff was fermented during manufacture, a process conducive to forming tobacco-specific nitrosamines (2.1.1 › (c) › (i) Northern Europe, 1st paragraph); newer pouch products, like Swedish snus, are made with extra controls to inhibit nitrosamine formation and are promoted as reduced risk (1.2.3, 1st paragraph; their levels are in Table 1.3, not read). Route: oral.
exposure.polysubstance: Confounding by smoking and alcohol is the chapter's central methodological point (2.1.1 › (a), 3rd and 4th paragraphs); studies were weighed by whether they restricted to non-smokers or adjusted for smoking, and some for alcohol.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; no study gave time since stopping (2.1.1 › (b) › (ii)).

comparison.controls: People who never used the product (or any tobacco) in each cited study.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not systematically discussed; the chapter flags missing adjustment for body mass index and alcohol in pancreatic cancer studies (2.3.1 › (d)) and for alcohol in the Swedish stomach cancer cohort (2.3.1 › (e)).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking and alcohol: see exposure.

outcomes.instruments: Cancer incidence and mortality at oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus (squamous and adenocarcinoma), pancreas, stomach, lung and other sites, from registers and case-control interviews.
outcomes.validity_norms: The Working Group notes problems study by study, in brackets: possible ascertainment bias from medical records, proxy interviews for fatal cancers such as oesophageal cancer, small samples (for example 132 cases and 320 controls in one Swedish study) and zero expected deaths in one US cohort.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is a statistically significant raised risk judged against confounding. 'Sufficient evidence' and 'Group 1' are IARC categories that express confidence that a hazard exists; the chapter does not define them (Preamble not read).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Oral cancer, northern Europe: four studies (Lewin 1998, Schildt 1998, Boffetta 2005, Rosenquist 2005) found no overall association with snus; Norwegian cohort HR 1.1 (0.5 to 2.4), age- and smoking-adjusted; Swedish construction workers, non-smokers, RR 0.8 (0.4 to 1.7); Swedish cohort of 9,860 men (Roosaar 2008), ever daily snus use RR 3.1 (1.5 to 6.6) adjusted for smoking, calendar period, residence and alcohol, and 2.3 (0.7 to 8.3) in never smokers; Swedish case-control study in non-smokers (Lewin 1998) OR 4.7 (1.6 to 13.8) for head and neck cancers combined; meta-analysis (Boffetta 2008, 11 oral cancer studies) overall 1.8 (1.1 to 2.9), USA 2.6 (1.3 to 5.2), northern Europe 1.0 (0.7 to 1.3); meta-analysis (Lee and Hamling 2009) never-smokers overall 1.72 (1.01 to 2.94, 9 studies) and Scandinavian snuff 1.01 (0.71 to 1.45, 4 studies). Oesophagus: Swedish construction-worker cohort (Zendehdel 2008) squamous cell carcinoma RR 3.5 (1.6 to 7.6) in non-smoking men using snuff only, against people who never used tobacco, adjusted for age and body mass index; Norwegian cohort RR 1.4 (0.6 to 3.2); Swedish case-control studies OR 1.4 (0.9 to 2.3, squamous), 1.2 (0.7 to 2.0, adenocarcinoma) and 1.2 (0.7 to 2.2, ever snuff); meta-analysis of five studies 1.6 (1.1 to 2.3); never-smokers in Scandinavia 1.92 (1.00 to 3.68, one study) and 1.10 (0.92 to 1.33) smoking-adjusted. Pancreas: Norwegian cohort (35 years) RR 1.67 (1.12 to 2.50, 45 cases), smoking- and age-adjusted, and 0.85 (0.24 to 3.07, 3 cases) in never smokers; Swedish construction-worker cohort (average follow-up 20 years, 83 pancreatic cancers), never-smoking current snus use RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6, 18 cases), adjusted for age and body mass index; the two cohorts pooled (Boffetta 2008) 1.8 (1.3 to 2.5). Stomach: Swedish construction-worker cohort (343,822 men, 33 years) significant excess of non-cardia stomach cancer among non-smoking snus-using men aged 70 and over, without alcohol adjustment. Lung: no significant association in the Swedish cohort of never smokers. Skin squamous cell carcinoma: RR 0.64 (0.44 to 0.95) with snuff dipping in the Swedish cohort.
analysis.covariates: Per cited study; the chapter highlights smoking and alcohol, and body mass index for pancreatic cancer.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a Working Group evaluation; the general procedure (Preamble) was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessed. The chapter reports null Nordic findings in text but its synthesis foregrounds the positive ones.
analysis.power: Not discussed generally; flagged for individual studies (for example zero expected oral cancer deaths in one US cohort).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The chapter's own text shows that for Swedish and Norwegian snus the oral cancer evidence is mostly null (four Nordic studies without an overall association; pooled northern European estimate 1.0, 0.7 to 1.3; the one Swedish cohort with a raised estimate, 3.1, 1.5 to 6.6, reached significance only with smokers included and gave 2.3, 0.7 to 8.3, in never smokers, an interval too wide to show either an increase or none), the oesophageal evidence rests on one significant cohort estimate (RR 3.5, 10 exposed cases per the 2023 review) among four Nordic studies, all above 1.0 but only one significant, and the pancreatic evidence on two cohorts, one of which was null in never smokers. The positive, robust findings for smokeless tobacco as a class come largely from products and populations outside Scandinavia (US moist snuff and chewing tobacco, South Asian products, toombak).
interpretation_gap.claimed: Section 5 states sufficient evidence in humans that smokeless tobacco causes cancers of the oral cavity, oesophagus and pancreas (Group 1); the synthesis says smokeless tobacco was positively associated with oral cancer in a cohort in northern Europe and several case-control studies, with elevated risks for every type studied including snus, and that there is good evidence for a causal association with pancreatic cancer. Gaps: (1) the verdict is for the class, not for snus; the chapter does not say it applies to Swedish snus and gives product differences (nitrosamine controls, nicotine content) in the exposure section; (2) the oral-cancer synthesis lists snus among elevated risks, whereas the chapter's detailed text finds no overall association in four Nordic studies, and the one Nordic cohort with a raised estimate was significant only when smokers were included (2.3, 0.7 to 8.3, in never smokers); (3) 'sufficient evidence' is a hazard category, not a measure of size, and nothing in the chapter compares risk with smoking; (4) the synthesis states that two European cohorts showed a significant increase in pancreatic cancer risk, without noting that the Norwegian cohort's estimate in never smokers was 0.85 (0.24 to 3.07, 3 cases).

timeline.event: Previous IARC evaluation of smokeless tobacco (2004 Working Group, published 2007): sufficient evidence for cancer of the oral cavity, as restated in this chapter; this chapter's evaluation names the oesophagus and pancreas as well.

Zendehdel et al., Swedish construction-worker cohort, oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma RR 3.5 (1.6 to 7.6), the Swedish evidence on which the oesophagus finding rests for snus (reported in this chapter).
Lee's industry-supported review concludes any cancer risk from snus is at most minimal and treats the pancreatic evidence as weak.

Systematic review of cancer risk among men using snus only, which cites this monograph as agreeing with its findings; oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma and pancreatic cancer rated moderate certainty, other sites lower.

replication.where_it_stands: The IARC classification of smokeless tobacco as carcinogenic to humans is the standing international hazard statement. For Swedish snus specifically it is neither confirmed nor refuted: the independent 2023 review rates oesophageal and pancreatic evidence moderate and the oral cancer evidence very low and null, while the industry-linked 2013 review reads the same Nordic studies as showing no clear risk.

funding.funder: Not stated in the chapter read (volume front matter and the Preamble were not read).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not stated in the chapter read; Working Group membership and declarations of interests are not part of this chapter.
funding.affiliations_note: Published by the International Agency for Research on Cancer as part of its Monographs series, and distributed on NCBI Bookshelf. Recorded as a flag: the Working Group's makeup and any ties of its members to the studies it weighs could not be checked from the chapter.

what_would_settle_it: Cancer-site-specific risk estimates for Swedish snus alone, from several independent cohorts that update tobacco use through follow-up and adjust for smoking, alcohol, body mass index and socio-economic position, with follow-up beyond age 70, reported as absolute risks beside the same cohorts' estimates for smoking; plus a monograph evaluation that classifies by product (snus separate from chewing tobacco and moist snuff) with the Working Group's reasoning and declared interests printed.

domains.note: The chapter states no search strategy, dates or criteria; it says new data since the 2004 evaluation were incorporated and focuses on studies since 2007. Study-by-study reasons for setting some aside are given. The series' Preamble was not read.
No formal tool, but each study's confounding by smoking and alcohol, ascertainment, proxy interviews and sample size are weighed in the text and some studies are excluded on those grounds.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Working Group membership and declarations of interest are not in the chapter; whether members authored cited studies could not be checked.
Data are reported before each synthesis, and the evaluation is a graded category stated separately; mechanisms are in a separate section (4), not read.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against harm
domains.note: Null findings are reported in the text, but the synthesis highlights positive associations and groups snus with products that show larger and more consistent risks; the under-represented side is the product-specific (snus) null evidence.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a Working Group evaluation (METHODS §5.3), and AMSTAR 2 is not used because the chapter states no systematic search and selection for the conclusions. The chapter is transparent about the studies behind each conclusion and the grading is a stated category; it may be cited for the Working Group's judgment about smokeless tobacco as a class, for the studies and numbers it reports on snus (to be checked against those studies, in most cases via the 2023 review), and for the measured nicotine content of Swedish snus; not for a claim about Swedish snus alone, for the size of any risk, or for a comparison with smoking.

key_findings.finding: Evaluation: sufficient evidence in humans for the carcinogenicity of smokeless tobacco; smokeless tobacco causes cancers of the oral cavity, oesophagus and pancreas; sufficient evidence in experimental animals; smokeless tobacco is carcinogenic to humans (Group 1). The evaluation does not separate products.
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 5. Evaluation, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Scope: smokeless tobacco was considered by a previous IARC Working Group in 2004 (published 2007); new data since then were incorporated; the previous monograph concluded sufficient evidence for oral cavity cancer.
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › opening paragraph; 2.1.1 › (a), 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Measured product content: nicotine in Swedish snus 0.5% to 1.7%, against 0.47% to 3.43% in 17 US moist snuff brands. Newer pouch products, like Swedish snus, are made with extra controls to inhibit nitrosamine formation and promoted as reduced risk. Swedish snuff made before 1983 was fermented, which favours nitrosamine formation.
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 1.2.1, 2nd paragraph; 1.2.3, 1st paragraph; 2.1.1 › (c) › (i) Northern Europe, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oral cancer, snus: four studies from northern Europe found no overall association (Lewin 1998, Schildt 1998, Boffetta 2005, Rosenquist 2005); one Swedish case-control study found no raised risk with either fermented or non-fermented snuff; the Swedish cohort of 9,860 men found RR 3.1 (1.5 to 6.6) for ever daily use, and 2.3 (0.7 to 8.3) in never smokers; a cohort of 280,000 construction workers gave 0.8 (0.4 to 1.7) in non-smokers; the Norwegian cohort 1.1 (0.5 to 2.4).
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.1 › (a) › (i) Cohort studies, 5th and 6th paragraphs; (c) › (i) Northern Europe, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Meta-analyses of oral cancer: overall RR 1.8 (1.1 to 2.9) in 11 studies, USA 2.6 (1.3 to 5.2) and northern Europe 1.0 (0.7 to 1.3) (Boffetta 2008); never smokers 1.72 (1.01 to 2.94) in 9 studies, Scandinavian snuff 1.01 (0.71 to 1.45) in 4 studies (Lee and Hamling 2009).
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.1 › (a) › (ii) Case–control studies, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Oral cancer synthesis: elevated risks for every type of smokeless tobacco studied, snus in northern Europe among them, with some studies in Scandinavia and the USA not positive; the Working Group concludes strong evidence that smokeless tobacco causes cancer of the oral cavity.
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.3.1 Oral use › (a) Oral cavity and pharynx, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Compare the four Nordic null studies and the positive Swedish cohort finding being in smokers only (2.1.1 › (a) › (i), 7th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Snus-induced lesions: Swedish men who had snus-induced lesions, followed 27 to 29 years, did not have a higher oral cancer risk than the whole Swedish population (not adjusted for smoking); more severe lesions were found in men using loose snus than portion-bag snus; lesions were less severe 24 weeks after a switch to a lower-pH, lower-nicotine product.
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.2 › (d) Types, 1st paragraph; (e) Reversal or progression of lesions, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oesophagus: Swedish construction-worker cohort, squamous cell carcinoma RR 3.5 (1.6 to 7.6) in non-smoking men using snuff only, against people who never used tobacco; Norwegian cohort 1.4 (0.6 to 3.2); two Swedish case-control studies OR 1.4 (0.9 to 2.3, squamous), 1.2 (0.7 to 2.0, adenocarcinoma) and 1.2 (0.7 to 2.2); of four northern European studies all estimates were above 1.0 but only the Swedish cohort's was significant; meta-analysis of five studies 1.6 (1.1 to 2.3); Scandinavian never-smoker estimate 1.92 (1.00 to 3.68, one study).
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.3 › (a) Overview, 5th, 8th and 10th paragraphs; (c) Types, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pancreas: Norwegian cohort (35 years follow-up) RR 1.67 (1.12 to 2.50, 45 cases) adjusted for smoking and age, and 0.85 (0.24 to 3.07, 3 cases) in never smokers; Swedish construction-worker cohort of never smokers (average follow-up 20 years; 83 pancreatic cancers), current snus use RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6, 18 cases) against people who never used any tobacco product, adjusted for age and body mass index, and 2.1 (1.1 to 3.8) in the group using 10 g a day or more (a study condition); the two cohorts pooled 1.8 (1.3 to 2.5). Synthesis: good evidence to support a causal association with smokeless tobacco.
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.4 › (b) Europe, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.3.1 › (d) Pancreas

key_findings.finding: Stomach: Swedish cohort of 343,822 men followed 33 years, significant excess of non-cardia stomach cancer among non-smoking snus-using men aged 70 and over, not adjusted for alcohol; other studies not significant; the Working Group did not consider the evidence strong enough to conclude causation. Lung: no significant association in Swedish never smokers.
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.5 › (a) Cancer of the stomach › (i) Cohort studies, 1st paragraph; (f) Lung › (iii), 2nd paragraph; 2.3.1 › (e), (f)

key_findings.finding: Other evidence in the chapter, from US products rather than Swedish snus: in a US cohort of former cigarette smokers followed 20 years, those who switched to smokeless tobacco had a higher lung cancer risk than those who quit tobacco entirely (RR 1.5, 1.2 to 1.7), and against people who never used any tobacco 5.6 for switchers and 3.9 for quitters.
key_findings.locator: Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.5 › (f) Cancers of the respiratory tract › (iii) Lung, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The oral cancer synthesis lists a cohort in northern Europe among the positive findings, but the cohort section says the Swedish cohort with 27 to 29 years of follow-up had significant positive findings among smokers only, and gives 2.3 (0.7 to 8.3) for never smokers.
reporting_issues.page: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.1 › (a) › (i), 6th and 7th paragraphs; 2.3.1 › (a)
reporting_issues.consequence: The synthesis reads more firmly than the cohort section for snus. The never-smoker estimate (2.3, 0.7 to 8.3) is imprecise rather than null, so the Nordic data neither confirm nor exclude a raised oral cancer risk from snus.

reporting_issues.issue: The lung cancer synthesis says switching from cigarettes to smokeless tobacco gave a risk of greater magnitude than quitting, and prints the figures as 3.9 versus 5.6; the cohort section gives 3.9 for quitters and 5.6 for switchers.
reporting_issues.page: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.3.1 › (f) Lung; 2.1.5 › (f) › (iii), 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The order of the two figures in the synthesis reads as reversed; use the cohort section's figures, and note they concern US products.

reporting_issues.issue: The same Swedish case-control estimate (OR 4.7, 1.6 to 13.8, in non-smokers) is described as head and neck cancer in one place and as oral cavity, pharynx and oesophagus cancers combined in another.
reporting_issues.page: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.1 › (a) › (ii), 4th paragraph; (c) › (i), 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The outcome definition of that estimate is unclear; it should not be quoted as an oral cancer estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Norwegian cohort is labelled snuff (snus) in the chapter. The industry-supported 2013 review (Lee) says critics noted its exposed group also included another smokeless product (skra).
reporting_issues.page: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Smokeless Tobacco monograph › 2.1.4 › (b) Europe, 1st paragraph; compare sc_lee_2013
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-source difference not resolved here; the Norwegian pancreatic estimate should not be taken as pure snus until its primary report is read.

verification.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/n/iarcmono100e/a008/ (Smokeless Tobacco monograph only: section 5 Evaluation; section 2 Cancer in Humans in full, including the synthesis; the Swedish-snus paragraphs of section 1; sections 3 and 4, all tables (1.1 to 1.3, 2.1 to 2.14, which are separate files) and the reference list were not read; the volume Preamble and Working Group list were not read)

design_detail: US National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) 1997-2004, a nationally representative household survey in which one randomly chosen adult per household is interviewed, linked to the National Death Index to 31 December 2006. Smoking status was therefore measured once, at interview, and deaths were followed forward (mean about 7 years, 1.3 million person-years). Analysis: age-stratified Cox models (hazard ratios with 99% intervals) adjusted for education, alcohol and body-mass index, with NHIS sample weights; survival from 25 to 80 years was then scaled to US national death rates for 2004. Read as the NEJM publisher HTML (text, Table 1, Table 2 and Figures 1-4 as images); the Supplementary Appendix (Tables S1-S3, a PDF) and the disclosure forms (a PDF) were not read.
can_establish: In a nationally representative US sample, how much higher the death rate was, overall and by cause, among adults who currently smoked cigarettes than among adults who had smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lives, and how the remaining excess varied with the age at which former smokers quit.
cannot_establish: That all of the excess is caused by smoking (unmeasured differences between groups cannot be excluded, though the authors argue they are small), the effect of the amount smoked or of products other than cigarettes, what happened to people who changed their smoking after the interview, or what quitting at a given age would do for one person.

sample.recruitment: Community: probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalized population (NHIS), interviewed 1997-2004. Black and Hispanic people were deliberately oversampled and the sample weights restore national proportions (Methods > Study Design, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults aged 25 or older at interview: 122,810 women and 94,107 men, of whom 9,058 women (761 died) and 5,611 men (544 died) were excluded for a missing variable such as education, smoking status, drinking status or cause of death (Methods > Study Design, 3rd paragraph). The NHIS frame leaves out about 7 million of 226 million US adults, chiefly people in long-term care, prisoners and active-duty military (Methods > Study Design, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Table 1: mean age in years, current / former / never-smoked groups, women 45.8 / 55.3 / 50.1, men 45.0 / 56.9 / 45.7. Current smokers more often drank alcohol, had less education and a lower body-mass index than the other groups; about two thirds of current and of former smokers had started before age 20 (Results > Characteristics of the Study Participants). Race is not tabulated in the text; adjusting for race changed the estimates little (not shown).
sample.attrition: Not a follow-up in the usual sense: deaths were found by matching survey records to the National Death Index (name, Social Security number and date of birth; success rate above 95%). The paper does not say whether the unmatched records were counted as alive.
sample.selection_effects: 6.8% of the interviewed adults (14,669 of 216,917) were dropped for missing variables, and their crude death proportion was slightly higher than in those kept (8.4% against 7.2% in women, 9.7% against 8.5% in men, editors' arithmetic from the printed counts). The NHIS leaves out incarcerated people, among whom smoking is more common; the authors expect little effect on the comparison between current smokers and people who never smoked. Smoking status was measured once, so people who quit after the interview stay in the current-smoker group.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at the NHIS interview, no biochemical check. Never smoked: fewer than 100 cigarettes in a lifetime. Former smoker: at least 100 cigarettes in a lifetime and none in the previous 5 years. Current smoker: the rest, plus former smokers who had quit within the 5 years before death, who were counted as current smokers to limit reverse causation (Methods > Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cigarettes only; the definitions count cigarettes and the paper does not mention cigars, pipes or smokeless tobacco. Table 1 gives the share of current smokers by cigarettes per day (women: under 10, 26.1%; 10-19, 30.9%; 20 or more, 41.6%; men: 22.0%, 23.6%, 52.7%) but no hazard ratio is given by amount smoked. Age at quitting was grouped 25-34, 35-44, 45-54 and 55-64 years (medians 29, 39, 49, 59).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol use (nondrinker, former, light, moderate-to-heavy) is adjusted for. Other tobacco products and other drugs are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Former smokers had been without cigarettes for at least 5 years by the paper's definition; the paper does not state the date that 5 years is counted back from for people still alive at the end of follow-up.

comparison.controls: People who had smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lifetime ('never smoked'): 67,524 women and 39,289 men.
comparison.matching: None. Age-stratified Cox models adjusted for education (3 levels), alcohol (4 levels) and body-mass index (3 levels); sample weights. The effect of the adjustment is described only as 'little' (data not shown).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No baseline health measures other than those adjusted for. Diet, physical activity, income, occupation and other tobacco use are not described as measured or adjusted. One sensitivity analysis (Table 2 footnote) excludes 1,795 women and 2,184 men with earlier heart disease, stroke or cancer.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Alcohol adjusted. Because 'never smoked' is defined by cigarettes alone, the group may include people who used cigars, pipes or smokeless tobacco; the paper does not say.

outcomes.instruments: National Death Index record linkage (death certificates); cause of death from the certificate, grouped as neoplastic (lung cancer, other cancers), vascular (ischemic heart disease, stroke, other), respiratory, other medical, and accidents and injuries.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note that cause-of-death misclassification, particularly at older ages, may raise some cause-specific ratios and lower others but does not affect the all-cause ratios (Discussion > limitations).
outcomes.operationalization: Death at ages 25-79 and survival from 25 to 80 years. 'Deaths attributable to smoking' are the excess of disease deaths in current smokers over what never-smoker disease death rates would give, after adjustment; accidents and injuries (about 7% of the excess) are left out of the attribution (Results > Mortality According to Smoking Status, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated. The paper uses 99% confidence intervals throughout, which are wider than 95% intervals. Twelve outcome rows per sex appear in Table 2, several of them sums of others; the main findings are far from 1, so multiplicity does not change them.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted hazard ratios (99% CI), current smokers vs people who never smoked, ages 25-79, women / men (Table 2): all causes 3.0 (2.7-3.3) / 2.8 (2.4-3.1); lung cancer 17.8 (11.4-27.8) / 14.6 (9.1-23.4); ischemic heart disease 3.5 (2.7-4.6) / 3.2 (2.5-4.1); stroke 3.2 (2.2-4.7) / 1.7 (1.0-2.8); respiratory disease 8.5 (6.1-11.8) / 9.0 (5.6-14.4); all cancers 3.2 (2.6-3.9) / 3.8 (3.1-4.8); all vascular 3.2 (2.7-3.9) / 2.6 (2.1-3.2); accidents and injuries 3.9 (2.4-6.2) / 2.1 (1.4-3.0). Deaths in the never-smoked and current-smoker groups (all causes): 2,190 and 1,579 in women, 1,283 and 2,030 in men. Probability of surviving from 25 to 80 years, scaled to 2004 US rates, never smoked vs current smokers: women 70% (99% CI 64-76) vs 38% (30-45); men 61% (55-67) vs 26% (18-33); about 11 years shorter in women and 12 in men. Years of life gained compared with continuing to smoke, by age at quitting 25-34 / 35-44 / 45-54 / 55-64: about 10 / 9 / 6 / 4; hazard ratio for those who quit at about 39 was 1.2 against 3.0 for those who continued. Editors' checks: Table 1 group sizes add to 113,752 and 88,496; the attributable percentages in Table 2 recompute within rounding from the printed counts; the survival gap at age 80 is 32 points in women and 35 in men.
analysis.covariates: Age (stratification), education, alcohol, body-mass index; sample weights. Race made no material difference (not presented). Not reported as adjusted: income, diet, physical activity, occupation, other tobacco.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned. The Notes say disclosure forms are on the publisher site (PDF, not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: Four checks are reported without numbers: the effect of the adjustment ('data not shown'), the effect of scaling death rates to national rates ('data not shown'), the exclusion of the first 2 years of follow-up ('data not shown'), and the adjustment for race ('not presented'). Hazard ratios for former smokers by age at quitting are in a supplement (Table S2) and appear in the main text only as bars in Figure 4 without printed values; this card does not quote them. One sensitivity analysis is printed (Table 2 footnote: all-cause ratios 3.1 in women and 2.8 in men after excluding recent quitters and people with earlier heart disease, stroke or cancer).
analysis.power: Large for all-cause and the main causes (15,715 deaths). Less precise for single causes: stroke in men 1.7 with a 99% interval of 1.0-2.8 (74 deaths in the never-smoked group, 66 in the current-smoker group).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among US adults aged 25-79 interviewed in 1997-2004, people who currently smoked cigarettes died at about three times the rate of people who had smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in the following 7 years on average. Most of the excess was from cancer, vascular and respiratory deaths, and the ratio was much larger for lung cancer (about 15-18) than for heart disease (about 3). Former smokers who quit younger had lower ratios, with a ratio of about 1.2 at quitting around age 39.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors conclude that people who smoke lose at least a decade of life and that quitting before age 40 cuts the risk of death 'associated with' continued smoking by about 90% (Abstract > Conclusions); the Discussion reads the small effect of adjustment as suggesting that the association is largely causal. The 90% figure is measured for the group that quit at 35-44 (median 39), with the 25-34 group looking like never smokers; the Results give no separate ratio for 'before 40'. Years gained are group differences read from survival curves, not what any one person would gain.

timeline.event: Fifty-year follow-up of male British doctors (Doll et al., BMJ 2004), cited by Jha et al. as showing a similar tripling of death rates and loss of about a decade of life; not read.

Prospective study of one million women in the UK (Pirie et al., Lancet, online October 2012) and a prospective cohort in Japan (Sakata et al., BMJ 2012; Jha's reference list prints the article number as e7903, the DOI is 10.1136/bmj.e7093), both cited by Jha et al. as giving similar results; not read.

A meta-analysis of other US cohorts (Thun et al., NEJM 2013;368:351-364, same issue; Jha's reference list prints the pages as 361-374), cited by Jha et al. as giving similar relative risks but lower absolute death rates because those cohorts are less representative of the US population; not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The authors describe the tripling of relative risk and the loss of about a decade as matching four other prospective studies; this card has not checked those studies. The estimates describe adults interviewed in 1997-2004 and followed to 2006; the Surgeon General's 2014 report (card sc_hhs_2014) judges, from the whole literature, that smoking increases all-cause mortality, as the report summarizes.

funding.funder: Fogarty International Center, US National Institutes of Health (grant TW007939-01); Canadian Institutes of Health Research (grant IEG-53506); Disease Control Priorities Project, Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (Notes). No tobacco-industry funding is printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: The Notes state that Dr. Jha holds an endowed faculty position at the University of Toronto and that the authors' opinions do not necessarily represent the agencies at which they work. The disclosure forms (PDF on the publisher site) were not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors are from the Centre for Global Health Research (Toronto), the US Food and Drug Administration, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the American Cancer Society and the University of Oxford. Two authors work at US federal tobacco-control agencies; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A contemporary, nationally representative cohort that measures smoking repeatedly (with a biochemical check), records the amount and duration of smoking and other tobacco products, adjusts for diet, physical activity and income, and prints every sensitivity analysis, so that people who quit at different ages can be compared with people who continued and with people who never used tobacco.

domains.note: Adjusted for education, alcohol and body-mass index; diet, physical activity, income and other tobacco use are not described as adjusted. The authors say adjustment barely moved the ratios, but the comparison is 'data not shown'; it is also unclear whether Table 2 shows the fully adjusted or the age-stratified ratios (see reporting issues).

One self-report at interview, no biochemical check. Never smoked means fewer than 100 cigarettes, so cigar, pipe and smokeless-tobacco use is not separated. Later quitting by some current smokers pushes the ratio toward 1. Former smokers who quit within 5 years before death are counted as current smokers, a rule that depends on the outcome; excluding them leaves the all-cause ratios at 3.1 and 2.8 (Table 2 footnote).
Probability sample of US households; 6.8% dropped for missing variables, with a slightly higher crude death proportion than those kept; institutionalized adults are outside the frame.
No intervention after the interview is described; changes in smoking after baseline are not tracked (a limitation the authors state).
Complete-case analysis after dropping 6.8% for missing variables; death follow-up by registry linkage with match success above 95%.
All-cause death from linked records is reliable; cause of death comes from certificates and may be misclassified, mainly at older ages (stated by the authors).
No registration or plan is mentioned; four sensitivity or adjustment results are 'data not shown' or 'not presented'; former-smoker ratios by age at quitting are in the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large, nationally representative cohort with linked death records, in which the main weaknesses are one baseline measurement of smoking, a limited set of adjusted variables, and sensitivity analyses that are described but not shown. None of these is likely to account for a threefold all-cause ratio or a 15-fold lung-cancer ratio, and the measurement problems mostly push the ratio toward 1. The card may be cited for the size of the all-cause and main cause-specific ratios, the survival difference to age 80 and the pattern by age at quitting in US adults interviewed in 1997-2004. It may not be cited for effects of the amount smoked, of cigars, pipes, smokeless tobacco or newer products, or as showing what one person would gain by quitting.

key_findings.finding: Cohort: 113,752 women and 88,496 men aged 25 or older at interview (of 216,917 interviewed 1997-2004), followed for a mean of about 7 years (1.3 million person-years) to 31 December 2006: 15,715 deaths (8,236 in women, 7,479 in men), of which 10,743 (5,122 in women, 5,621 in men) were at ages 25-79.
key_findings.locator: Results > Mortality According to Smoking Status, 1st paragraph; Methods > Study Design, 1st-3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: All-cause death at ages 25-79, current smokers against people who never smoked: adjusted hazard ratio 3.0 (99% CI 2.7-3.3) in women and 2.8 (2.4-3.1) in men. Deaths: 2,190 never-smoked and 1,579 current-smoker deaths in women; 1,283 and 2,030 in men. After excluding people who quit under 5 years before death (199 women, 222 men) and people with earlier heart disease, stroke or cancer (1,795 women, 2,184 men), the all-cause ratios were 3.1 and 2.8.
key_findings.locator: Results > Mortality According to Smoking Status, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (all-cause row and footnote)
Table 2, hazard ratio column

key_findings.finding: Deaths among current smokers counted as attributable to smoking (disease deaths only): about 62% (range 59-65) of all deaths in women and 60% (range 55-63) in men at ages 25-79; by cause, women / men: lung cancer 252 of 267 deaths (94%) / 324 of 348 (93%), ischemic heart disease 179 of 251 (72%) / 288 of 416 (69%), respiratory disease 182 of 206 (88%) / 167 of 188 (89%). About 7% of the excess mortality of smokers was from accidents and injuries, which are not attributed to smoking in the table.
key_findings.locator: Results > Mortality According to Smoking Status, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, attributable-deaths columns

key_findings.finding: Survival from 25 to 80 years, scaled to 2004 US death rates and adjusted for age, education, alcohol and body-mass index: never smoked vs current smokers, women 70% (99% CI 64-76) vs 38% (30-45); men 61% (55-67) vs 26% (18-33); current smokers' survival was shorter by about 11 years in women and 12 years in men. The authors give the gap at age 80 as now exceeding 30 percentage points for both sexes (32 in women, 35 in men from the printed figures).
key_findings.locator: Results > Mortality According to Smoking Status, 1st paragraph; Figure 2; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Benefit of stopping, compared with continuing to smoke, by age at quitting: 25-34 (median 29), survival nearly identical to never smoked, about 10 years of life gained; 35-44 (median 39), about 9 years gained, hazard ratio 1.2 against never smoked versus 3.0 for continuing, an excess risk cut by about 90%; 45-54 (median 49), about 6 years, excess cut by about two thirds; 55-64 (median 59), about 4 years. Figure 3 panels are labelled with the years gained (10, 9, 6, 4); Figure 4 shows the hazard ratios as bars without printed values.
key_findings.locator: Results > Benefits of Smoking Cessation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figures 3 and 4

key_findings.finding: Remaining excess after quitting at about 39: hazard ratio 1.2, which the authors call substantial: about 1 in 6 of such former smokers who die before age 80 would not have died at the death rates of people who never smoked. Among former smokers, lung cancer carried the highest hazard ratio (Table S3, supplement, not read).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Results > Benefits of Smoking Cessation, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline (Table 1): current / former / never-smoked groups, women 23,839 / 22,389 / 67,524; men 23,348 / 25,859 / 39,289. About two thirds of current and former smokers started before age 20. Among current smokers, 41.6% of women and 52.7% of men reported 20 or more cigarettes a day. The ratio of former to current smokers at ages 65-69 was 2 to 1 in women and 4 to 1 in men.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results > Characteristics of the Study Participants

key_findings.finding: Comparison with other studies, as the authors describe them: the tripling of relative risk and the loss of about a decade are similar to four other studies (male British doctors, a UK women's study, a meta-analysis of other US cohorts, a Japanese study); women's risks are about 50% greater than in the 1980s studies; absolute death rates here are much higher than in other US studies because the NHIS is more representative of the US population.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations the authors state: confounders beyond the few recorded; incarcerated adults outside the survey; fewer deaths than in recent studies; cause-of-death misclassification (not affecting all-cause); smoking measured only at baseline, so some current smokers later quit; former smokers' excess may be overestimated because some quit when ill; quitters may differ from never smokers.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: It is unclear which ratios Table 2 shows. The table title, Methods and Abstract say the hazard ratios are adjusted for education, alcohol and body-mass index, yet the Results sentence says adjustment 'had little effect on these age-stratified hazard ratios', with the comparison 'data not shown'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either way the authors say the two sets are close, but the paper does not let a reader compare them; claims quote the ratios as 'adjusted for age, education, alcohol and body-mass index' as the Methods state. Locators: Methods > Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Results > Mortality According to Smoking Status, 1st paragraph; Table 2 title.

reporting_issues.issue: Four checks are given without numbers: effect of adjustment, effect of scaling death rates to national rates, exclusion of the first 2 years of follow-up (a reverse-causation check) and adjustment for race.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claims that these did not change the results cannot be verified from the text; the Supplementary Appendix (not read) may hold some. Locators: Methods > Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Results > Mortality According to Smoking Status, 1st paragraph; Results > Benefits of Smoking Cessation, 2nd paragraph.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results sentence on the survival analysis lists adjustment for 'age, educational level, and adiposity' and omits alcohol, while the Methods and the Figure 2 legend include alcohol consumption.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably an omission in one sentence; the Methods and figure legend are taken as correct. Locators: Results > Mortality According to Smoking Status, 1st paragraph; Methods > Statistical Analysis, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 legend.

reporting_issues.issue: The rule that former smokers who quit within the 5 years before death are counted as current smokers depends on the outcome, and the paper does not say how it applies to people still alive at the end of follow-up or what date the 5 years is counted from for the definition of a former smoker.
reporting_issues.consequence: It could raise the current-smoker death rate relative to a classification made only at the interview; the printed sensitivity analysis (Table 2 footnote) leaves the all-cause ratios at 3.1 and 2.8, so the effect appears small. Locator: Methods > Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 2 footnote.
