reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract's conclusion that quitting 'before the age of 40 years' cuts the excess risk by about 90% is measured in the group that quit at 35-44 (median 39); no ratio for quitting before 40 as a whole is given. The Discussion's last sentence restates it as about 90% of the decade of life lost.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims quote the 90% as 'quitting at about 39' and the years gained by age band. Locators: Abstract > Conclusions; Results > Benefits of Smoking Cessation, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph.

reporting_issues.issue: Two entries in the reference list do not match the cited papers: the Thun et al. NEJM paper is printed as 'smoking-related deaths' with pages 361-374 (the journal gives 'smoking-related mortality', 351-364), and the Sakata et al. BMJ paper has the article number e7903 (its DOI, 10.1136/bmj.e7093, gives e7093).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the papers are identifiable. Checked against the journals' pages on 2026-10-18. Locator: References 20 and 21.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128: abstract, methods, results, discussion, notes (funding), reference list, and Table 1, Table 2 and Figures 1-4 read as images in the app's browser (Figure 4 has no printed values). The Supplementary Appendix (Tables S1-S3) and the disclosure forms, both PDFs, were not opened.

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD420251062250) of human studies of the health effects of Swedish snus and tobacco-free oral nicotine pouches. PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews were searched up to 25 July 2026, English only, with six search terms (the full strategy is in an online resource that was not read). 2,215 records, 1,241 after duplicates, 102 read in full, 66 studies included: 54 on snus and 15 on pouches (some studies count in both). Results are narrated outcome by outcome, with no pooling and no certainty grading. Study quality was scored with the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) tools and risk of bias rated with CLARITY, NOS-xs and Joanna Briggs Institute tools; per-study ratings are in an online resource that was not read. Biomarker studies, studies of people who use several products, reviews and non-English papers were excluded.
can_establish: What human studies of snus and of tobacco-free nicotine pouches had been published by July 2026 under the review's criteria: how many, of what design, where, and with what follow-up; what each reported for blood pressure, heart rate, metabolic, respiratory, oral, mental-health, cancer, pregnancy and smoking-reduction outcomes; and, above all, how thin the pouch evidence is (15 studies, the longest 6 months, none following disease or death).
cannot_establish: That snus or pouches cause any listed outcome (the review itself says its observational designs prevent causal conclusions); the size of any risk (no pooling, no grading, no absolute risks); how either product compares with smoking for any disease; long-term effects of pouches (none measured); anything about women or about countries outside Scandinavia for snus (most studies are of Swedish and Norwegian men); and independent replication (several cohorts, notably the Swedish construction-worker cohort, feed many of the 66 'studies'). The review's abstract and conclusions say more than its printed estimates show (see reporting issues).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Databases: PubMed (330 records), Scopus (638), EMBASE (1,078) and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (169), searched up to 25 July 2026 with 'nicotine pouch', 'tobacco free nicotine pouch', 'oral nicotine pouch', 'snus', 'Swedish moist snuff' and 'health'; no reference-list, register or grey-literature search is described (Methods › Search Strategy; Results › Study Selection, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: controlled, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort, observational and prospective studies of people aged 12 and over who currently or formerly used snus or tobacco-free pouches, reporting acute or chronic health effects, cancer or nicotine dependence, in English. Excluded: letters, commentaries, reviews, protocols, other languages, other products (cigarettes, e-cigarettes, heated tobacco, nicotine gum, sprays, patches), and papers on chemical composition, methods, markets or regulation; at full-text stage, studies of tobacco products in general or smokeless tobacco without separating snus or pouches, studies of people who use several products, and studies of biomarkers of exposure or potential harm (Methods › Eligibility Criteria; Study Selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). No list of the 36 studies dropped at full-text stage is given in the page text (Figure 1 is an image and was not read).
sample.demographics: Mostly men in Scandinavia: 40 of 66 studies were set in Sweden and 6 in Norway; many include men only. The 15 pouch studies are five short crossover trials of 30 to 42 adults (four in adults who smoke, one in people who use snus or pouches), a 24-week trial of oral health (n printed as 155; the sex counts sum to 100), an 8-week pilot (n = 45), a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start), a national cohort (n = 5,556), three cross-sectional surveys in Saudi Arabia (n = 489, 1,214 and 831; where sex is given, almost all men) and three Swedish oral-health studies (n = 23 to 272) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. The review notes that four controlled studies lost more than 20% of participants (Results › Quality of the Studies, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: English only; four databases; six search terms including 'health'; no grey literature or reference-list search described. Biomarker studies and studies of people who use several products were removed at full-text stage, which removes the studies that most directly compare toxicant exposure from pouches with exposure from cigarettes and the many people who use more than one product. Several of the 66 are reports from the same Swedish cohorts or pooled analyses that contain them (for example the construction-worker cohort appears in Luo 2007, Hergens 2007, Arefalk 2012 and in the pooled analyses of Araghi, Hansson, Hergens and Yang), so '66 studies' overstates independent evidence. The largest pooled mortality analysis of men who use snus (Byhamre 2021, 169,103 men) is not among the included studies; only Byhamre 2017 (metabolic syndrome) is.

exposure.measurement: In primary studies, mostly self-reported use of snus or pouches; the review says all but one observational study relied on self-report, and few measured use more than once (Results › Quality of the Studies, 1st paragraph). In the crossover trials the product and nicotine strength were assigned.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesised. Product content cited in the Introduction from other papers: nicotine 12.8 mg per snus pouch and 1.79 to 47.5 mg per tobacco-free pouch, set beside 1.64 to 2.28 mg per cigarette (Introduction, 2nd paragraph, citing Lawler 2020 and Mallock 2024); the cigarette figure is of a different kind (a per-cigarette quantity of unstated type) and is not comparable with content per pouch. Crossover trials used single exposures of 30 to 60 minutes; the longest pouch follow-up is 6 months. Route: oral.
exposure.polysubstance: People who use several products were excluded at full-text stage, yet included studies enrolled smokers (the pouch switching and craving trials), people who currently or formerly used snus (Alizadehgharib 2026, Rosa 2025) and groups combining snus and pouches (Miluna 2022); some limitations lists note dual use as unmeasured. Attribution of an outcome to the pouch alone is therefore not possible for several of the 15 pouch studies.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at review level.

comparison.controls: Varies by study: people who never used tobacco in the cohorts; continuing cigarettes in the switching trials; a placebo pouch and nicotine gum in one 9-hour trial; no comparison group in the three Saudi Arabian symptom surveys and in the 6-week plaque study.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not assessed at review level; the Discussion lists diet, exercise, education, income and concurrent tobacco use as possible confounders that differ between studies (Discussion, 1st paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking is adjusted or restricted in many cohorts; for pouches, smoking history is a design feature of the trials (all enrolled people who smoked) and uncontrolled in the surveys.

outcomes.instruments: Per primary study: blood pressure and heart rate, arterial stiffness, hospital and register diagnoses (heart failure, stroke, diabetes, cancer, pregnancy outcomes), questionnaires (asthma symptoms, mental health, withdrawal and craving scales such as the QSU-Brief), and dental and mucosal examinations.
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality by NIH tools: controlled studies scored 6 to 12 of 14 ('fair' and 'good'); observational studies 5 to 9 of 14 ('fair'); case-control studies 6 to 8 of 12 ('fair'). Risk of bias mostly moderate, one cross-sectional study high (Results › Quality of the Studies; Risk of Bias). The review states that none of the observational studies justified its sample size or blinded outcome assessors.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is any association reported in a primary study. The text often calls a non-significant estimate 'increased' or 'reduced' risk (examples in reporting issues), so 'association' in this review does not reliably mean a statistically supported difference.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no pooling). Dozens of outcomes are narrated, each from a handful of studies, with no correction for multiplicity and no weighting by study size.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Both authors screened independently. Who extracted data and who rated quality is not stated in the Methods; the author-contribution statement says both authors analysed the data.

analysis.effect_sizes: Snus, from primary studies as printed in the review (hazard, odds or risk ratios against never use unless stated): heart failure 2.08 (1.03 to 4.22) and 1.28 (1.00 to 1.64) in two cohorts; fatal heart attack in men who never smoked 1.28 (1.06 to 1.55) and non-fatal 0.91 (0.81 to 1.02); pooled acute heart attack 1.04 (0.93 to 1.17); pooled stroke 1.04 (0.92 to 1.17), 1.52 (1.01 to 2.30) for total stroke in people who use snus and never used any tobacco (another cohort); death from cardiovascular disease 1.70 (1.01 to 2.87) in that cohort; hypertension death 1.64 (1.36 to 1.98) and heart-failure death 1.75 (1.17 to 2.62), coronary death 1.10 (0.76 to 1.59) in a cohort of 4,222 men; pooled atrial fibrillation 1.07 (0.97 to 1.19), 1.18 (1.03 to 1.35) in one cohort; type 2 diabetes 1.49 (1.04 to 2.15), 1.15 (1.00 to 1.32), 1.34 (0.65 to 2.7) and 1.00 (0.47 to 2.11) in four studies; asthma 1.49 (1.20 to 1.85); non-affective psychosis 1.22 (1.00 to 1.48), schizophrenia 1.03 (0.70 to 1.54); Parkinson's disease pooled 0.41 (0.28 to 0.61); pancreatic cancer 2.0 (1.2 to 3.3) in the construction-worker cohort against 0.96 (0.83 to 1.11) in a pooled analysis of nine cohorts; rectal cancer 1.40 (1.09 to 1.79) in men who use snus only, colorectal no association; oral cancer 0.90 (0.74 to 1.09) pooled; stillbirth 1.6 (1.1 to 2.3), preterm stillbirth 2.1 (1.3 to 3.4), very preterm birth 1.38 (1.04 to 1.83), intellectual disability in offspring 1.28 (1.06 to 1.52), small for gestational age 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17), preschool asthma or wheeze 1.06 (0.96 to 1.18). Pouches: acute single-use crossover (n = 30), systolic pressure from 1% lower to 3% higher, diastolic 4.5% to 7.4% higher and heart rate from 3% lower to 3.2% higher at 30 minutes, by strength; symptom prevalence in surveys with no comparison group (for example 28.4% rapid or irregular heartbeat, 66.7% bloating); oral lesions 79% and hyperkeratosis 65% among people who use pouches against 89% and 79% among people who use snus (n = 126 and 63); cigarettes per day 15.0 to 8.3 over 8 weeks in a pilot of 45; odds of quitting smoking 1.29 (1.04 to 1.59) for fruit-flavoured and 1.04 (0.82 to 1.28) for mint-flavoured pouches in a 6-month online cohort. No confidence intervals are printed for several results.
analysis.covariates: Per primary study; not synthesised.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD420251062250 is cited. The article was received on 29 August 2025 and the search ran to 25 July 2026; no deviation from the protocol or search update is described, and the registration was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract foregrounds adverse associations and omits lower estimates the Results report (Parkinson's disease pooled 0.41, 0.28 to 0.61; reflux in people who use snus daily 0.77, 0.64 to 0.93; hand eczema), which the Discussion does list. No assessment of selective reporting in primary studies.
analysis.power: Not assessed. The review notes that only four controlled studies justified sample size and no observational study did.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 66 studies, mostly cohorts of Swedish men, the estimates for snus are mixed: some are raised with intervals that exclude 1 (heart failure, fatal heart attack, some cohorts' type 2 diabetes, stillbirth and preterm birth, asthma, oral lesions, rectal cancer in men who use snus only), many span 1 (pooled stroke 1.04, atrial fibrillation 1.07, pooled pancreatic cancer 0.96, schizophrenia 1.03, small for gestational age 1.05, preschool asthma 1.06) and some are lower (Parkinson's disease, reflux in daily use, hand eczema). For pouches, 15 studies show small acute blood-pressure and heart-rate changes in single-use crossover trials, symptom surveys without comparison groups, and oral findings in small samples, none longer than 6 months and none following disease or death.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract and Conclusions: current literature 'confirms' negative health consequences of regular snus use, listing increased risk of asthma, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, heart failure, stroke, type 2 diabetes, metabolic disorder, pancreatic and rectal cancer, a weak association with schizophrenia and non-affective disorders, and, after maternal use, small-for-gestational-age births and preschool asthma. The Discussion says pouches increased blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms and oral changes, and that snus use gave no cardiovascular-disease mortality finding. Gaps: (1) atrial fibrillation, stroke, pancreatic cancer (pooled), schizophrenia, small for gestational age and preschool asthma are named as increases though the printed pooled estimates have intervals spanning 1 (or, for schizophrenia, are close to 1); (2) the Discussion's 'no cardiovascular mortality finding' sits beside printed cardiovascular, hypertension and heart-failure death estimates above 1 in the Results; (3) the limitations paragraph says observational designs prevent establishing causality while the Conclusions say the literature 'confirms' harm; (4) respiratory and gastrointestinal 'increases' for pouches come from three Saudi Arabian surveys without comparison groups.

timeline.event: IARC Monograph 100E classifies smokeless tobacco as a class as carcinogenic to humans; it does not mention tobacco-free nicotine pouches.
Pooled analysis of eight Swedish cohorts on mortality in men using snus only (169,103 men); not among the 66 studies of this review.
Systematic review of snus and cancer with graded certainty, which excluded industry-linked studies; reviews were excluded from this review, so it is not cited.
Laboratory comparison of harmful constituents in two nicotine pouch brands with smokeless tobacco and nicotine replacement products; cited in this review's Introduction and Discussion.
Laboratory measurement of nicotine and tobacco-specific nitrosamines across pouch brands; cited in this review's Introduction.

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review in this batch that covers both snus and pouches. Its snus sections largely re-narrate Swedish cohorts already covered by the graded 2023 cancer review and the 2021 mortality pool, so they are not independent confirmation, and its abstract is firmer than its estimates. Its pouch inventory, 15 human studies, none longer than 6 months, is its distinctive and most reliable contribution.

funding.funder: Medical University of Lodz, Poland (grant 503/0-149-03/503-01-001), as printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors are at the Department of Immunopathology, Faculty of Medicine, Medical University of Lodz. The review does not report who funded the 66 included studies (AMSTAR 2 item 10); only one included trial (Thornley 2009, a 9-hour crossover trial of a pouch against nicotine gum and placebo) is noted in Table 1 as funded by the product's manufacturer. The Discussion calls for tobacco-industry-independent trials of pouches, citing another review. A 2026 scoping review in this batch (Travis) identifies the oral-health trial listed here as Liu 2025 (switching to on! pouches) as Altria-funded, which this review does not say. Recorded as a flag: who funded the other pouch studies could not be checked from the review.

what_would_settle_it: A review with a registered protocol, a justified and wider search (including biomarker studies and people who use more than one product, reported separately), a list of excluded studies, duplicate extraction, funding of included studies and overlapping cohorts tabulated, and results pooled or graded by outcome. For the products themselves: independent, registered cohorts of people who use only pouches or only snus, women included, followed for years, with biomarker and disease outcomes, reported beside people who smoke and people who use no nicotine.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people aged 12 and over who use snus or pouches), exposure, outcomes and designs are stated, but no comparator is specified; several included designs have none.
PROSPERO CRD420251062250 is cited. No deviations are described, although the manuscript was received in August 2025 and the search ran to July 2026; the registration was not read.
Controlled, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort, observational and prospective designs are listed with no reason for including each.

Four databases and a stated date, but English only without justification, six search terms including 'health', and no reference-list screening, registers, grey literature or experts described. Judged 'no' on the project's reading of item 4 (decision p-amstar2-item4). The full strategy is in Online Resource 1, not read.
Both authors selected independently; disagreements were settled by discussion.
The Methods list the data extracted but do not say that two people extracted or that one checked the other; the contribution statement says both analysed the data.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Counts only (102 read in full, 66 kept). No list of the 36 excluded studies is referenced in the page text; Figure 1 is an image and was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, setting, participants, sample size, measured variables and limitations for each study; exposure (product, brand, amount) and follow-up length are not systematically given, and some entries contain errors (for example 366,381 men with n = 336,381).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: NIH tools scored every study and CLARITY, NOS-xs and Joanna Briggs tools rated risk of bias, covering confounding, selection and measurement; the Joanna Briggs quasi-experimental checklist was used for 'observational studies', which it was not designed for, and per-study risk ratings are in Online Resource 2 (not read). Overall: mostly moderate.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not tabulated; one manufacturer-funded trial is noted in Table 1's limitations column.
The authors say heterogeneity prevented a meta-analysis (Discussion, 8th paragraph).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Most studies were rated moderate risk and the limitations paragraph says quality was 'not always satisfactory' and that observational designs prevent causal conclusions, but no result is qualified by it and the abstract and Conclusions say the literature 'confirms' harm.

The Discussion attributes inconsistent findings to differences in products, patterns and intensity of use, designs and confounders, and the limitations paragraph lists brand, nicotine and flavour variety.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias and selective reporting are not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: University grant stated; no competing interests declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 rates three critical items 'no' (the search, the list of excluded studies, and risk of bias in interpretation) and a fourth (the protocol) only partly met, which makes the review critically low confidence: it should not be relied on as an accurate and comprehensive summary of the studies. Item 7 and part of item 9 rest on an online resource and a figure that were not read, but the page text gives no sign of either being enough to change the rating. It may be cited for the inventory it gives (counts, designs, countries, durations, and the statement that pouch evidence is thin and short), for the printed estimates of single studies (to be checked against those studies), and for the limitations its authors state; not for its conclusion that the literature confirms harm, for any claim of direction where the abstract and the printed estimates differ, for any comparison with smoking, or as independent confirmation of the Swedish cohort findings.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 2,215 records (PubMed 330, Scopus 638, EMBASE 1,078, Cochrane 169), 1,241 after duplicates, 102 read in full, 66 included; 54 studies on snus and 15 on pouches (some in both); 40 set in Sweden, 8 in the USA, 6 in Norway, 3 in Saudi Arabia, 5 international. Search to 25 July 2026, English only.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph; Results › Study Selection, 1st paragraph; Results › Study Characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Quality and risk of bias: controlled studies scored 6 to 12 of 14 on the NIH tool (three open-label, four with more than 20% drop-out, five explaining randomisation); observational studies 5 to 9 of 14 ('fair'), all but one using self-reported snus or pouch use, none justifying sample size or blinding assessors; case-control studies 6 to 8 of 12. Most studies were rated moderate risk of bias; one cross-sectional study was rated high.
key_findings.locator: Results › Quality of the Studies, 1st paragraph; Results › Risk of Bias, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pouch evidence base (15 studies): five short crossover trials of 30 to 42 adults (blood pressure, heart rate, craving, abuse potential; one 9-hour trial funded by the manufacturer), a 24-week trial of oral health (n printed as 155; sex counts sum to 100), an 8-week pilot (n = 45), a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start), a national cohort (n = 5,556), three cross-sectional symptom surveys in Saudi Arabia (n = 489, 1,214, 831) and three Swedish oral-health studies (n = 23 to 272). The longest follow-up is 6 months; no study follows disease or death.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Health Effects Associated with Tobacco-Free Oral Nicotine Pouches, all subsections
key_findings.note: Counts of designs are the editors' reading of Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Pouch heart and blood pressure effects: in a single-use crossover study of 30 people who use snus or pouches, changes measured 30 minutes after use were, by strength, systolic pressure -1% (6 mg), +3% (9 mg) and +1.4% (11.2 mg), diastolic +4.5%, +7.4% and +3.9%, and heart rate -3%, +3.2% and -0.2%; in a survey with no comparison group 28.4% of people who use pouches reported rapid or irregular heartbeat.
key_findings.locator: Table 6; Results › Pouches › Cardiovascular System, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text calls the 11.2 mg product snus and gives its heart-rate change as +0.2%; Table 6 labels it a pouch and gives -0.2%.

key_findings.finding: Pouch symptoms in Saudi Arabian surveys without comparison groups: bloating 66.7%, nausea 47.9%, heartburn 46.7%, difficulty breathing 40.5%, frequent cough or wheeze 27.8%, any psychological effect 39.3%, taste or smell change 36.7%, dry mouth 39.8%.
key_findings.locator: Table 6; Results › Pouches › Gastrointestinal Health, Respiratory System, Oral Health and Mental Health, 1st paragraphs
key_findings.note: Prevalence in people who use pouches only; no estimate of what share of a comparable group without pouches would report the same symptoms.

key_findings.finding: Pouch oral findings: among 272 young Swedish adults, oral lesions 79% and hyperkeratosis 65% in people who use pouches (n = 126) against 89% and 79% in people who use snus (n = 63); erythema 44% and mucosal ulcers 2% in the pouch group; gingival recession 45% against 52%. After 23 dentists switched from snus to pouches, snus lesion severity fell from 95.7% to 69.6% and gingival irritation from 43.5% to 4.3%. In a randomized trial of adults who smoked (n printed as 155), gingival and bleeding indices were 20% to 30% lower at 12 and 24 weeks after switching to pouches than with continued smoking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pouches › Oral Health, 1st paragraph; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Pouch smoking outcomes: lower urge to smoke than baseline but higher than after a cigarette (QSU-Brief), mixed by strength, in two small crossover trials; higher craving at 5 minutes after pouches (3 mg and 6 mg) than after cigarettes in one; 8-week pilot, cigarettes per day 15.0 to 8.3, one of 12 on pouches quit; 6-month cohort, quitting odds 1.29 (1.04 to 1.59) for fruit-flavoured and 1.04 (0.82 to 1.28) for mint-flavoured pouches; 9-hour trial, odds of temporary abstinence against gum 2.8 (0.8 to 8.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pouches › Nicotine Dependence, Smoking Reduction and Cessation, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Snus and the heart: heart failure HR 2.08 (1.03 to 4.22) in 1,076 older men and 1.28 (1.00 to 1.64) in construction workers; fatal heart attack in never-smokers aRR 1.28 (1.06 to 1.55), non-fatal 0.91 (0.81 to 1.02); pooled heart attack 1.04 (0.93 to 1.17); pooled stroke 1.04 (0.92 to 1.17) but death after stroke HR 1.32 (1.08 to 1.61); pooled atrial fibrillation 1.07 (0.97 to 1.19); in people who use snus and never used any tobacco, total stroke 1.52 (1.01 to 2.30) and cardiovascular death 1.70 (1.01 to 2.87); in never-smoking men followed in one cohort, hypertension death 1.64 (1.36 to 1.98), heart-failure death 1.75 (1.17 to 2.62), coronary death 1.10 (0.76 to 1.59), stroke death 1.12 (0.74 to 1.70).
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Cardiovascular System, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Snus and diabetes or metabolic disorder: type 2 diabetes 1.49 (1.04 to 2.15), 1.15 (1.00 to 1.32), 1.34 (0.65 to 2.7, ever use), 1.18 (0.48 to 2.9, current use), and 1.00 (0.47 to 2.11) in Swedish and 0.91 (0.75 to 1.10) in Norwegian men; higher odds with higher weekly use in one study; metabolic disorder with high-dose use 1.6 (1.26 to 2.15).
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Metabolic Disorders, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Snus and cancer: pancreatic 2.0 (1.2 to 3.3), oral 0.8 (0.4 to 1.7), lung 0.8 (0.5 to 1.3) in the construction-worker cohort; pooled nine cohorts: oral 0.90 (0.74 to 1.09), pancreatic after smoking adjustment 0.96 (0.83 to 1.11), rectal 1.40 (1.09 to 1.79) in men who use snus only, no clear association for colorectal; colon 1.08 (0.91 to 1.29), described as a positive association.
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Risk of Cancer Development, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 5

key_findings.finding: Snus, pregnancy and offspring: stillbirth aOR 1.6 (1.1 to 2.3), preterm stillbirth 2.1 (1.3 to 3.4), very preterm birth 1.38 (1.04 to 1.83), moderately preterm 1.25 (1.12 to 1.40), intellectual disability 1.28 (1.06 to 1.52), small for gestational age 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17), preschool asthma or wheeze 1.06 (0.96 to 1.18); offspring asthma 1.94 (1.23 to 3.10) when a parent used snus before conception (children of mean age 9).
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Pregnancy Complications and Offspring's Health, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Snus and smoking reduction: in a trial of 150 adults who smoked, cigarettes per day after 8 weeks fell from 15 to 1.5 with complete switching, from 14.7 to 11.7 with partial switching and rose from 14.1 to 15.6 with continued smoking; in a double-blind placebo trial of 319 men, 63.9% against 67.7% halved smoking at 24 weeks (OR 0.81, 0.48 to 1.36), and one-week quit odds at 36 weeks were 2.7 (1.0 to 7.3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Snus › Nicotine Dependence, Smoking Reduction and Cessation, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' stated limitations: many studies of men only; few data on pouches; self-reported use; no meta-analysis because of heterogeneity; most studies from Scandinavia and Swedish snus differs from products elsewhere; observational designs prevent establishing causality; brands, nicotine content and flavours vary; quality 'not always satisfactory'. Conclusion: too little data to clearly determine the health effects of pouches.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists a 'weak association' of snus with schizophrenia and non-affective disorders; the text gives schizophrenia aHR 1.03 (0.70 to 1.54) and non-affective psychosis aHR 1.22 (1.00 to 1.48).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › Snus › Mental Health, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates a null schizophrenia result.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract names atrial fibrillation, stroke and pancreatic cancer as increased with snus use. The pooled atrial fibrillation estimate is 1.07 (0.97 to 1.19), the pooled stroke estimate 1.04 (0.92 to 1.17) and the pooled pancreatic estimate 0.96 (0.83 to 1.11); the raised estimates come from single cohorts. The text describes colon cancer HR 1.08 (0.91 to 1.29) as a positive association and oral and lung cancer RR 0.8 (0.4 to 1.7; 0.5 to 1.3) as reduced risk.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › Snus › Cardiovascular System, 3rd paragraph; Risk of Cancer Development, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Directions are asserted where intervals span 1; the abstract cannot be cited for these outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says maternal snus use increased the risk of a newborn small for gestational age and of asthma in preschool age; the text gives 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17) and 1.06 (0.96 to 1.18). The one significant asthma result (1.94, 1.23 to 3.10) is for school-age children of parents who used snus before conception.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › Snus › Pregnancy Complications and Offspring's Health, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Null results are reported as increases in the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says snus use gave no cardiovascular-disease mortality finding, but the Results print cardiovascular death HR 1.70 (1.01 to 2.87), hypertension death 1.64 (1.36 to 1.98) and heart-failure death 1.75 (1.17 to 2.62), and fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06 to 1.55).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph; Results › Snus › Cardiovascular System, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion and Results disagree; the Results numbers are the better guide.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists a reduced risk of rheumatoid arthritis among people who use snus; the Results give OR 1.0 (0.8 to 1.2) for developing rheumatoid arthritis and only lower disease activity scores among people who already had it.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph; Results › Snus › Autoimmune Disorders, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A null risk result is reported as a reduction.

reporting_issues.issue: Respiratory and gastrointestinal 'increases' attributed to pouches come from symptom surveys with no comparison group; blood-pressure 'increases' come from one crossover study whose changes run from -1% to +3% (systolic) by strength. Oral mucosal findings in Miluna 2022 are from snus and pouches analysed as one group.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 (Miluna 2022); Table 6
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion's statement that pouches increased these outcomes is not supported by comparisons in the studies reviewed.

reporting_issues.issue: In the snus cardiovascular text the 11.2 mg product in Renard 2025 is called snus and its 30-minute changes are given as systolic +1.4%, diastolic +3.9% and heart rate +0.2%; Table 6 gives the same systolic and diastolic figures for 'Nordic Spirit 11.2 mg ONP' with a heart-rate change of -0.2%. A scoping review in this batch describes a five-product study in people who use snus that appears to be the same study, with both an 11.2 mg pouch and an 11.2 mg snus.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Snus › Cardiovascular System, 1st paragraph; Table 6
reporting_issues.consequence: The same numbers are attributed to two different products and the sign of the heart-rate change differs; the primary paper was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints 366,381 men with n = 336,381 for Nordenvall 2011, n = 155 for Liu 2025 with 44 men and 56 women (100), and n = 489 for Aldali 2026 with 381 men and 14 women (395); the text cites Munafo 'et al. 2007' for a study listed as 2016. The three quality tables list 67 appraisals against 66 included studies because Rasouli 2017 (a Swedish case-control and a Norwegian cross-sectional study) is appraised twice.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1; Tables 3 and 4; Results › Snus › Mental Health, 1st paragraph; Results › Quality of the Studies, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors with no effect on the findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction sets nicotine per pouch (12.8 mg snus; 1.79 to 47.5 mg tobacco-free pouches) beside 1.64 to 2.28 mg per cigarette.
reporting_issues.consequence: Content per pouch and a per-cigarette quantity of unstated kind are not comparable; use Mallock 2024 for the pouch measurements.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12403-026-00812-w: all sections, Tables 1 to 6 (read as HTML table pages) and the funding, competing-interest and contribution statements; Figure 1 (image), Online Resources 1 and 2 (supplementary files, not opened) and the reference list were not read

design_detail: Update, by one author, of his own 2011 review of epidemiological evidence on snus and health, limited to cancers, circulatory disease and oral conditions. Searches were 'updated to 18 November 2012' and nine new publications were found; databases, search terms and selection criteria are not given in this paper (methods are 'as previously described' in the 2011 review, which was not read). Results are summarised narratively, with one small meta-analysis (fixed and random effects) of 13 published relative risks or odds ratios for heart attack or ischaemic heart disease in never-smoking Swedish men, and a second of fatal and non-fatal heart attack in five studies. The update was supported by a snus manufacturer and the author is a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry.
can_establish: How this author, with these funders, read the epidemiological evidence on snus and cancer, heart attack, heart failure and oral disease as of November 2012, and what his pooling of published heart-attack estimates in never-smoking Swedish men gives under his choices of studies and exclusions.
cannot_establish: Whether snus is harmful or harmless: the search and selection are not described in this paper, the cited studies are not appraised against a standard, null and positive findings are not scrutinised alike, the pooling mixes designs and adjustment sets and drops one estimate after the fact, the evidence stops in 2012 (before the 2020 pooled mortality analysis and the 2023 cancer review), and the comparison with smoking is asserted more than shown.

sample.recruitment: Search of unnamed sources 'updated to 18th November 2012' following the 2011 review; no databases, terms or flow of records are given. 'Results are only summarized for health effects where new relevant publications could be identified' (Methods, Results). The update was prompted by two recent publications the author regarded as major new findings, one on pancreatic cancer and one on heart attack (Background, 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated in this paper. For the heart-attack pooling: male never smokers only, and earlier results from the same cohorts that were superseded by later reports were left out of Table 1. One estimate (the Construction Workers Study interviews of 1971 to 1974) was later left out of a second pooling because of differences in the type of snus, limited and ambiguously coded questionnaire data, and its being based only on fatal cases (Results › Circulatory disease, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Swedish men, almost entirely. The Construction Workers Study contributed 88% of the person-years in the pooled heart-attack analysis (Results › Circulatory disease, 4th paragraph). Other samples are local population surveys, hospital-based case-control studies and registers.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence is selected by the author; the update is built on his own earlier reviews and was triggered by two papers he judged important. The citations are mainly Swedish cohort and case-control studies, and the direct evidence on several outcomes (for example the oesophagus and stomach) is carried from the 2011 review and not shown here.

exposure.measurement: Current or ever use of snus as recorded in each cited study (questionnaire or interview at baseline in cohorts; interview in case-control studies). Exposure is mostly a single recording and the review does not discuss that limitation for the null findings.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesised. The text states that nicotine exposure from snus is similar to, and perhaps somewhat greater than, that from smoking (Background, 1st paragraph, citing earlier physiological studies). Route: oral.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled by analysing male never smokers and, separately, all men with adjustment for smoking; the pancreatic and heart-disease conclusions differ between these in some studies.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: People who never used snus (and, in the never-smoker analyses, never smoked), in each cited study.
comparison.matching: Adjustment varies by study from none or age only to six factors (Table 1, adjustment column).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed systematically. The author raises confounding by socio-economic status, alcohol, area of residence and health care for the positive findings, much less for the null ones.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Alcohol is raised as a possible confounder for one Norwegian study only (Results › Pancreatic cancer, 2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Published estimates of cancers (pancreas, oral cavity and oropharynx, colon, rectum, anus, acoustic neuroma), survival after cancer, heart attack and ischaemic heart disease (fatal and non-fatal), heart failure, periodontitis and caries.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed. Outcomes are taken as the cited studies defined them.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is a significantly raised risk estimate in the cited studies; 'unassociated' is used where estimates were not significant, without intervals being weighed against the size of a risk that would matter.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (single author, no duplicate selection or extraction described).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pancreatic cancer (earlier review of nine North American and two Scandinavian studies on smokeless tobacco): smoking-adjusted RR 1.07 (0.71 to 1.60) in seven studies and 1.23 (0.67 to 2.31) in never smokers in five; the Scandinavian cohort of construction workers 2.00 (1.20 to 3.30) in never smokers and 0.90 (0.70 to 1.20) smoking-adjusted; the Norwegian cohort 0.85 (0.24 to 3.07) in never smokers and 1.67 (1.12 to 1.50 as printed) smoking-adjusted; the two combined 1.61 (0.77 to 3.34) in never smokers and 1.20 (0.66 to 2.20) smoking-adjusted. New: pooled analysis of 11 case-control studies of smokeless tobacco other than snus, none in Scandinavia, OR 0.98 (0.75 to 1.27) for ever use and 0.62 (0.37 to 1.04) for smokeless tobacco only. Oropharyngeal cancer (2011 review): RR 1.01 (0.71 to 1.45, 4 estimates) in never smokers, 0.97 (0.68 to 1.37, 7 estimates) smoking-adjusted. Colon (153 exposed cases) and rectal (97) cancer in 336,381 construction workers: no association shown, intervals not given in the text; anal cancer 1 case. Acoustic neuroma (451 cases, 710 controls): current snus OR 0.94 (0.57 to 1.55), former 1.22 (0.71 to 2.10), current smoking 0.41 (0.23 to 0.74). Survival after any cancer in 40,320 [sic] male construction workers: all-cause RR 1.13 (1.05 to 1.20) for snus only, 1.21 (1.17 to 1.25) for smoking only, 1.17 (1.12 to 1.22) for both; cancer-specific RR 1.15 (1.05 to 1.26) for snus only, 1.15 (1.10 to 1.21) for smoking only. Heart attack or ischaemic heart disease in never-smoking Swedish men, 13 estimates: fixed-effect RR 1.07 (0.98 to 1.16), heterogeneity p = 0.06; random-effects 1.06 (0.91 to 1.23); without the 1971 to 1974 construction-worker estimate (1.35, 1.13 to 1.62, fatal cases only) 12 estimates: fixed 1.00 (0.91 to 1.10), random 1.00 (0.88 to 1.13). Pooled analysis of eight cohorts (cited): incidence RR 1.04 (0.93 to 1.17), short-term fatality OR 1.28 (0.99 to 1.68). Five studies: fatal cases RR 1.31 (1.09 to 1.58), non-fatal 0.89 (0.79 to 1.00), ratio 1.48 (1.19 to 1.84). Heart failure: construction workers RR 1.28 (1.00 to 1.64, 75 cases); Uppsala cohort 2.08 (1.03 to 4.22, 14 cases). Periodontitis and caries: no raised risk after adjustment for age, sex and sociodemographic variables in random population samples.
analysis.covariates: Per cited study (Table 1 lists: age; age and residence; age, exercise, health, illness, residence, socio-economic status; age, BMI, cholesterol, education, leisure and physical activity; none). Many cited estimates are adjusted for age only.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results are given only for conditions with a new publication since 2011. The heart-attack pooling drops the only significantly raised estimate in a second pooling on grounds given after the data were in; the 13-estimate result is also shown. Confidence intervals are missing for the colorectal and some other findings.
analysis.power: Not discussed for the null findings: several heart-attack estimates rest on fewer than 10 exposed cases (for example 0, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8 cases among the eight pooled cohorts), and cancers such as anal cancer on one case.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The paper summarises nine publications since 2011. For pancreatic cancer it reports no new snus study, only a pooled analysis of other smokeless tobacco products, with an earlier two-cohort summary showing a wide interval. For heart attack, the 13-estimate pooling gives 1.07 (0.98 to 1.16), 1.00 when one estimate is dropped, while fatal heart attacks were raised (1.31, 1.09 to 1.58) and non-fatal ones slightly lower (0.89) in five studies. Death after a cancer diagnosis was raised in men who used snus only (1.13 all causes, 1.15 cancer-specific) about as much as in men who smoked only (1.21 and 1.15). Heart failure was higher in two small analyses.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the new evidence 'further undermines' the argument that snus raises pancreatic cancer risk, extends the list of cancers unassociated with snus (oropharynx, oesophagus, stomach, lung, now colorectal and acoustic neuroma), and says that even if some adverse effects exist they are far less than those of smoking; the conclusions say any cancer risk is at most minimal. Gaps: (1) there is no new snus study on pancreatic cancer, and the pooled analysis said to undermine the argument concerns other forms of smokeless tobacco, with no Scandinavian study; (2) 'unassociated' is read from non-significant estimates, several from few cases and one-time exposure measures, and no interval is given for colorectal findings; (3) no oesophagus, stomach or lung data are shown in this update, so their listing rests on the 2011 review; (4) 'far less than smoking' is not shown here for cancer survival, where cause-specific mortality ratios are the same for snus only and smoking only (1.15 and 1.15); (5) the sentence in the Discussion that effects if any are probably no more than 1% of those of smoking is carried over from the 2011 review without derivation; (6) positive findings are met with critique of method (confounding, exposure group, follow-up), null findings with much less; (7) the stated preference to treat the 1971 to 1974 construction-worker estimate as an outlier is argued after the fact.

timeline.event: European Commission scientific committee report on smokeless tobacco cited the pancreas as a target organ; the author calls its reading misleading because it reported only the significant associations.

The author's comprehensive review and meta-analysis of snus and health, which this paper updates; its 'scant support for any major adverse health effects' conclusion is restated in the Background (not read).
Pooled analysis of eight Swedish cohorts on heart attack (Hansson et al.): no raised incidence, higher short-term fatality (OR 1.28, 0.99 to 1.68), as cited here.
This update (searches to 18 November 2012).
Pooled analysis of eight Swedish cohorts on mortality: higher all-cause (HR 1.28), cardiovascular (1.27) and cancer (1.12) death in men using snus only against men who never used tobacco.
Systematic review of cancer risk among men using snus only, with industry-linked and industry-sponsored studies excluded by design; found graded evidence of higher risk for some cancers.

replication.where_it_stands: A decade-old, single-author update that supplies the industry-supported reading of the 2000s and early 2010s evidence. Its main specific findings (no overall heart-attack incidence signal in never-smoking men; fatal heart attack and post-cancer mortality raised) have been reproduced in direction by later pooled analyses (byhamre_2021), and its reading of pancreatic and oesophageal cancer is disputed by the 2023 independent review (valen_2023). Newer data now exist that this paper could not include.

funding.funder: Supported by Swedish Match (a snus manufacturer); some of the earlier reviews underpinning it were supported by Philip Morris Products and the European Smokeless Tobacco Council (Acknowledgements). The paper states the sponsor had no involvement in the planning, execution or writing of the manuscript or the decision to submit it.
funding.declared_conflicts: The author is a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry; he describes the paper as an independent scientific assessment, the views being his alone (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, who also wrote, alone or with co-authors, several of the earlier reviews on which the conclusions rest (the 2011 review on snus, and earlier reviews on smokeless tobacco and circulatory disease, oral disease, pancreatic cancer and cancer in general). Industry support is declared for this update and for some of those reviews; the text read does not say which. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the findings; every finding of this review is set beside independent work on the same question in the claim.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a registered protocol, named databases, explicit criteria, duplicate selection and extraction and a standard bias assessment of every cohort, applying the same scrutiny to null and positive estimates, by authors and funders without tobacco-industry ties (or with an independent second team repeating the extraction); and individual-participant pooling of the Swedish and Norwegian cohorts with tobacco use updated through follow-up, which exists in part in the 2020 and 2023 papers.

domains.note: A search date is given but no databases, terms, criteria or selection process; the methods are by reference to the 2011 review.

Some studies are criticised in text (confounding by alcohol, mixed exposure group, long follow-up without updating, interview-year coding in the construction-worker data) but there is no standard bias assessment of any cited study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The conclusions rest on the author's own earlier reviews and meta-analyses (the 2011 review and four earlier reviews on specific diseases), some supported by tobacco companies and an industry council.
Mostly separated, but 'far less than smoking', 'at most minimal' and the 1% of smoking figure are asserted rather than shown here, and policy opinions about switching are included in the Discussion.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against harm
domains.note: Findings of harm are examined closely for method flaws; null findings from small, single-baseline-measure cohorts are taken at face value; the pooling that removes the one significantly raised estimate is justified after the fact. The side under-represented is the evidence of harm.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The paper is explicit about its funders and declares the author's industry ties, and it prints the underlying numbers for its pooling, which can be rechecked; but selection is unsystematic, the cited studies are not appraised alike, and the author relies on his own earlier work. It may be cited as the industry-supported author's reading of the evidence to 2012, for the numbers it reports from primary studies (to be checked against those studies), and for the heart-attack pooling as an unweighted-by-quality summary; not as evidence that snus is harmless, and never alone.

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests as printed: the update was supported by Swedish Match, with some earlier reviews supported by Philip Morris Products and the European Smokeless Tobacco Council; the sponsor is stated to have had no involvement; the author is a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry and calls the work an independent scientific assessment.
key_findings.locator: Competing interests; Acknowledgements

key_findings.finding: Search updated to 18 November 2012 after the 2011 review; nine new relevant publications identified; methods otherwise 'as previously described'.
key_findings.locator: Methods; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pancreatic cancer: no new study of snus. A pooled analysis of 11 case-control studies of other smokeless tobacco, none in Scandinavia, gave OR 0.98 (0.75 to 1.27) for ever use and 0.62 (0.37 to 1.04) for smokeless tobacco only, against never use of tobacco; earlier combined Scandinavian cohorts gave 1.61 (0.77 to 3.34) in never smokers and 1.20 (0.66 to 2.20) smoking-adjusted. The author concludes the evidence for a link was weak and is weaker.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pancreatic cancer, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Colorectal cancer in 336,381 male construction workers followed to 2007: no association of snus-only use with colon (153 exposed cases) or rectal (97) cancer, age- and BMI-adjusted; intervals not printed; anal cancer, 1 exposed case. Acoustic neuroma: current snus OR 0.94 (0.57 to 1.55), current smoking 0.41 (0.23 to 0.74).
key_findings.locator: Results › Colorectal cancer; Acoustic neuroma

key_findings.finding: Oral cancer: 16 men with oral squamous cell carcinoma at the exact site of snus use in seven hospitals (a case series); the author notes there is no comparison information on site distribution; earlier pooled oropharyngeal estimates were close to 1 (1.01 and 0.97); a follow-up of 1,115 people with the snus-related oral lesion found no cancers at the lesion sites.
key_findings.locator: Results › Oral cancer, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Survival after a cancer diagnosis in construction workers: all-cause RR 1.13 (1.05 to 1.20) for snus only, 1.21 (1.17 to 1.25) for smoking only, 1.17 (1.12 to 1.22) for both, against never tobacco; cancer-specific RR 1.15 (1.05 to 1.26) for snus only and 1.15 (1.10 to 1.21) for smoking only; stage at diagnosis not controlled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Survival from cancer

key_findings.finding: Heart attack or ischaemic heart disease in never-smoking Swedish men: 13 estimates pooled, fixed-effect RR 1.07 (0.98 to 1.16), heterogeneity p = 0.06, random-effects 1.06 (0.91 to 1.23); leaving out the construction-worker interview estimate of 1971 to 1974 (1.35, 1.13 to 1.62, fatal cases only) gives 12 estimates, fixed 1.00 (0.91 to 1.10), random 1.00 (0.88 to 1.13). Several of the 13 estimates are adjusted for age only.
key_findings.locator: Results › Circulatory disease, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Case fatality: in five studies, fatal heart attack RR 1.31 (1.09 to 1.58) and non-fatal 0.89 (0.79 to 1.00), ratio 1.48 (1.19 to 1.84); in the pooled eight-cohort analysis incidence RR 1.04 (0.93 to 1.17) and short-term fatality OR 1.28 (0.99 to 1.68), with the Construction Workers Study 88% of person-years. The author asks whether the fatality excess is a direct effect or confounding.
key_findings.locator: Results › Circulatory disease, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Heart failure: Construction Workers Study RR 1.28 (1.00 to 1.64) in never smokers with 75 exposed cases, no dose-response by daily amount; Uppsala cohort RR 2.08 (1.03 to 4.22) with 14 exposed cases, smokers and non-smokers combined.
key_findings.locator: Results › Circulatory disease, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Periodontitis and dental caries: random population samples of one Swedish city at three time points showed no raised risk after adjustment for age, sex and sociodemographic variables.
key_findings.locator: Results › Periodontitis and dental caries, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author's conclusions: adverse health effects of snus have not been clearly identified; any cancer risk is at most minimal and much less than for smoking; snus might adversely affect survival from cancer; reports of increased fatal heart attack and heart failure need investigation. He restates that any effects on cancer or circulatory disease, if they exist, are probably no more than 1% of those of smoking (a figure from the 2011 review) and that switching should improve the health prospects of smokers who cannot give up nicotine.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: The Norwegian cohort's smoking-adjusted pancreatic cancer estimate is printed as 1.67 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.50): the upper limit is below the point estimate.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Pancreatic cancer, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A misprint. IARC Monograph 100E (sc_iarc_2012) prints the same estimate as 1.67 (1.12 to 2.50; 45 cases), so the upper limit is very probably 2.50; this was not checked against the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the additional evidence 'further undermines' the pancreatic cancer argument, but the text states there are no new studies of pancreatic cancer and snus; the new pooled analysis concerns smokeless tobacco other than snus, with no Scandinavian study.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › Pancreatic cancer, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The new evidence is indirect for snus; a claim must not present it as a new snus finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The Construction Workers Study's non-fatal heart-attack estimate is given as RR 0.70 (0.48 to 1.02) in the text and as 0.94 (0.83 to 1.06) in Table 2 for the same earlier report.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Circulatory disease, 4th paragraph; Table 2 (Hergens et al. row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The non-fatal estimate for the main cohort is uncertain by about a quarter; the primary paper must be checked before it is quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: Heterogeneity of p = 0.06 is called significant, although significance is defined as p < 0.05 elsewhere in the same section.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Circulatory disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the choice to drop one estimate rests on this heterogeneity and on three explanations given for that estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives 40,320 male construction workers in the cancer-survival study, whereas the cited paper's title (in the reference list) gives 40,230.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Survival from cancer, 1st paragraph; reference list
reporting_issues.consequence: A transposition; the cited paper's number is 40,230 (also used in the 2023 review).

reporting_issues.issue: The rendered reference list is unnumbered and at least one citation (the 'strong' cohort studies cited for pancreatic cancer) does not match the reference in the matching position.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Pancreatic cancer, 2nd paragraph; reference list
reporting_issues.consequence: Numbered citations in this paper cannot all be traced to a reference with certainty; findings here are attributed by the study names the text gives.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4029226 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, competing interests and acknowledgements read; the reference list was read but is rendered without numbers; the 2011 review that supplies the methods was not read)

design_detail: Cochrane living systematic review of randomised controlled trials (and randomised cross-over trials) in which adults who smoked were given a vape (electronic cigarette), or advice to use one, or a comparison condition. Random-effects Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios (RR) with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman intervals when three or more studies were pooled and heterogeneity was above zero (Wald-type intervals otherwise); risk differences (RD) for serious adverse events, used for the first time in this update; mean or standardised mean differences for biomarkers. Primary outcomes: abstinence at six months or longer (strictest definition, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking, biochemical validation preferred), adverse events and serious adverse events at one week or longer. Three summary-of-findings tables with GRADE ratings: nicotine vapes against nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), against non-nicotine vapes, and against behavioural support only or no support. 80 completed trials, 29,861 participants, searched to 1 January 2026; nine trials are new in this update; non-randomised and single-arm studies were removed in this update as pre-specified. Risk of bias (Cochrane RoB 1 tool): 12 trials low, 27 unclear, 41 high. This is the sixth living update; first published 2014.
can_establish: The average effect, as of January 2026, of being offered a nicotine vape (supplied by the trial in most cases) on not smoking at six months or longer, in adults who smoked and joined randomised trials, compared with NRT, with non-nicotine vapes, and with behavioural support only or no support; and the counts of adverse and serious adverse events over trial follow-up (up to about two years), with the certainty the authors give each.
cannot_establish: Health effects beyond two years; effects of vaping outside trials, in adolescents (all trials were in adults) or in people who never smoked; effects of a particular device type, flavour or nicotine strength (planned subgroup analyses could not be run); whether the result differs against combination NRT specifically (the pooled subgroup is imprecise and inconsistent, see key findings); absolute numbers still vaping or still smoking at six months or longer (the page gives relative figures; the forest plots are images); products containing cannabis or illicit products (outside the review); and the blinded effect against behavioural support or no support, which cannot be blinded.

sample.recruitment: Monthly searches; this update searched CENTRAL (2025 issue 12), MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO to 1 January 2026 (dates from 2004), with ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO trials platform searched through CENTRAL; the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group Specialised Register was searched only to 1 February 2023, when it stopped being maintained; conference abstracts from the Society for Research on Nicotine and Tobacco to the March 2025 meeting, reference lists and contact with trial authors were added (Methods › Search methods). This update screened 1,902 records after removing duplicates, retrieved 102 full texts and added nine completed trials (with 43 new linked articles) and seven ongoing trials (Results › Results of the search). Trials took place in 13 countries: USA 40, UK 16, Australia 6, Greece 5, Italy 3, New Zealand 2, Canada 2, and one each in Belgium, Finland, the Netherlands, Korea, Switzerland and Turkey. Search strategies and the characteristics of each included trial are in supplements that were not opened.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomised controlled trials and randomised cross-over trials in which people who smoked cigarettes were randomised to a vape (or an intervention to promote vaping) or to a control condition, any age, motivated or not to quit, pregnancy allowed; the trial had to set out to measure an eligible outcome (cessation at six months or longer, adverse events, serious adverse events, biomarkers, product use, patterns of vaping and smoking). Excluded in this update: single-arm and other non-randomised studies (dropped as pre-specified because of the number of randomised trials; September 2025 protocol update). 37 studies excluded at full text across updates are listed with reasons in a supplement; the authors say the list covers those most likely to need explanation, not every exclusion.
sample.demographics: All trials were in adults who smoked cigarettes. Twenty-three trials enrolled only people not motivated to quit, 29 only people motivated or willing to quit, five people with some motivation, two limited interest, two people interested in cutting down, one people willing to replace cigarettes with vapes, one did not require motivation, and motivation was not stated in 17. Thirty-four trials recruited specific groups: 13 on a physical health condition (heart attack, cancer, HIV, periodontitis, awaiting surgery, smoking-related chronic disease, obesity), three on serious mental illness, three on people in or after alcohol or drug treatment, three on people who both smoke and vape; one trial recruited people using homeless services and three more recruited at-risk or socially deprived groups; single trials recruited an African-American sample, pregnant women, people who had failed a recent quit attempt, people who had failed to quit with medicine, people who found quitting difficult, people attending an emergency department, veterans and veterans awaiting surgery.
sample.attrition: People lost to follow-up counted as still smoking. Attrition risk of bias (high if more than half were lost overall or follow-up differed by more than 20 points between arms): low in 59 trials, high in 8, unclear in 13. Per-trial loss to follow-up is in the supplementary characteristics, which were not opened.
sample.selection_effects: People who agreed to be randomised, most often given a vape free with instructions to use it in place of cigarettes, so the pooled result is the effect of being offered a vape, not of buying one; three trials enrolled people who already vaped and told them to keep their own device, and one gave advice without a device. Trials are mostly from the USA and UK. Six of the review authors are authors of included trials and, by the review's account, took no part in decisions about those trials. Unpublished data may be missing, and five of the six funnel plots (pools of 10 or more studies) were asymmetric. Industry-funded trials (8) are flagged in the review and tested in sensitivity analyses.

exposure.measurement: Allocation in the trial: a vape, nicotine or non-nicotine, usually supplied by the study; or advice on how to use one. Devices, where enough was reported to judge: 27 trials refillable, 20 cartridge (typically lower nicotine delivery), two both, 14 pod, three disposable, two standard research devices, one high and low wattage, one pre-filled tank; the rest did not report. Use of the allocated product at six months or longer was reported by 10 trials.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported in Table 1, not recommendations: for example 7.2 mg cartridges for 12 weeks, or 7.2 mg for 6 weeks then 5.4 mg for 6 weeks (Caponnetto 2013), 36 mg and 8 mg (Cobb 2021), Vuse devices of 4.8%, 1.5% and 3% (Kanobe 2022), 18 mg/mL and 6 mg/mL (Kimber 2021). How long each trial supplied the device, the intensity of support and the nicotine strength used in the pooled trials are in the supplementary characteristics, which were not opened. Planned subgroups by device type, instructions for use, support intensity and participant type could not be run because there were too few trials in each; the text names the device type when reporting pooled results.
exposure.polysubstance: Three trials recruited people in or after alcohol or drug treatment and three people with serious mental illness; results for these groups were not analysed separately. Several trials added a vape to NRT, varenicline, cytisine or very low nicotine cigarettes (reported as add-on comparisons). Cannabis vaping is outside the review; the authors say illicit products or products containing other active substances such as THC may have different harm profiles.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Cessation at the longest follow-up of at least six months from the start of the intervention (intention to treat; strictest definition; biochemical validation preferred). Follow-up across the 80 trials ran from about a week to 24 months; 34 trials reported abstinence at six months or longer.

comparison.controls: NRT (single form, combination, or form unclear), non-nicotine vapes, behavioural support only or no support, varenicline, cytisine, NRT plus bupropion, heated tobacco, oral nicotine pouches, advice to use a vape against no such advice, and head-to-head comparisons of nicotine dose, flavour, device type, nicotine salt against freebase nicotine, and wattage. Non-nicotine vapes were also compared as an intervention in themselves.
comparison.matching: Random sequence generation: low risk in 47 trials, unclear in 33, none high. Allocation concealment: low in 40, unclear in 37, high in 3. Performance bias: low in 45, high in 24, unclear in 11. Detection bias: low in 60, high in 12, unclear in 8. Selective reporting: low in 48, high in 8, unclear in 24. In the comparison with behavioural support or no support the review states that blinding was not possible and support differed between arms; it rates the evidence down two levels for risk of bias. Table 1 rates one trial in that comparison (Eisenberg 2020) low risk overall, which sits oddly with the text saying all contributing trials were high risk (see reporting issues).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomisation balances baseline traits within each trial on average. Subgroups run at review level: pregnancy and NRT type (combination, single-form, unclear) in the NRT comparison. Planned subgroups by support intensity, device type, instructions and participant type were not run.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Use of cessation aids outside the study was not extracted at review level. In the NRT comparison, four trials gave combination NRT (patch plus another form), five gave single-form NRT and two did not state the form; the review notes that combination NRT is the more effective comparator and should be used where possible.

outcomes.instruments: Abstinence at six months or longer (biochemical validation, for example breath carbon monoxide, preferred); adverse events and serious adverse events at one week or longer (self-report; serious events also from medical records), as defined by trial authors; carbon monoxide, blood pressure, heart rate, blood oxygen, lung function and toxicant biomarkers; use of the allocated product at six months or longer; four patterns of vaping and smoking at six months or longer (vaping only, neither, both, smoking only).
outcomes.validity_norms: Of the 80 trials, 35 contributed to pooled adverse event analyses (18 more gave data that could not be pooled), 48 reported serious events, and 28 reported carbon monoxide. The share of reported quits that were biochemically verified is not given on the page (per-trial detail is in the supplements).
outcomes.operationalization: Quit = strictest abstinence definition at the longest follow-up of at least six months, missing counted as smoking. Adverse events were counted among people available for follow-up, not those randomised. Serious events were analysed as risk differences so that trials with no events in either arm could be included. One trial measured safety outcomes but had not reported them in the text available (Skelton 2022).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The authors follow Cochrane guidance for living reviews and do not adjust for multiple testing, while noting that repeatedly updating meta-analyses raises the issue. Nine primary results (three outcomes in each of three main comparisons) plus dozens of secondary analyses across 25 numbered comparison groups (biomarkers, lung function, product use, vaping and smoking patterns).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Review authors screened in duplicate and extracted outcome data and risk of bias in duplicate (study characteristics by one author); they were not blinded to trial results. Within trials, detection bias was judged low when cessation was biochemically verified or the intensity of the intervention was similar between groups; 12 trials were rated high for detection bias.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cessation at six months or longer (random-effects RR, 95% CI, I2): nicotine vape against NRT 1.61 (1.23 to 2.12), 55%, 11 trials, 4,114 participants, 6 per 100 with NRT against 10 per 100 (7 to 13) with a vape; against non-nicotine vape 1.34 (1.05 to 1.69), 0%, 7 trials, 1,918, 6 against 8 per 100 (6 to 10); against behavioural support only or no support 1.75 (1.39 to 2.20), 13%, 11 trials, 7,214, 5 against 9 per 100 (7 to 11). Adverse events: against NRT 0.95 (0.72 to 1.24), 72%, 8 trials, 3,107, 41 against 39 per 100 (30 to 51); against non-nicotine vape 1.01 (0.95 to 1.08), 0%, 6 trials, 909, 46 against 46 per 100 (44 to 50); against behavioural support or no support 1.22 (1.00 to 1.49), 58%, 11 trials, 2,801, 43 against 52 per 100 (43 to 64). Serious adverse events (RD): against NRT 0.01 (-0.01 to 0.02), 0%, 10 trials, 4,045, 6 against 7 per 100 (5 to 8); against non-nicotine vape 0.00 (-0.01 to 0.01), 0%, 11 trials, 1,786, 2 against 2 per 100 (1 to 3); against behavioural support or no support 0.00 (-0.00 to 0.01), 0%, 18 trials, 5,032, 3 against 3 per 100 (3 to 4). Sensitivity (Table 2): cessation against NRT without the two high-risk trials 1.74 (1.30 to 2.34) and without the one industry-funded trial 1.72 (1.23 to 2.39); against non-nicotine vape without the one high-risk trial 1.40 (1.09 to 1.81) and without the one industry-funded trial 1.28 (1.01 to 1.64); against behavioural support or no support without the one industry-funded trial 1.53 (1.30 to 1.79). Absolute figures are the summary-of-findings values; the 'about N more in 100' differences stated elsewhere on this card are editors' subtraction of those values.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Subgroups run: pregnancy (one trial) and type of NRT in the comparator arm (combination, single-form, unclear) for the NRT comparison. Planned subgroups by support intensity, device type, instructions and participant type were not run (too few trials). Sensitivity analyses removed trials at high risk of bias and trials with tobacco or vaping industry funding, for every outcome where trials remained.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol published in 2012; methods changes between updates are pre-specified through an Open Science Framework registry (osf.io/upgjc) and listed in a supplementary document (Supplementary material 10), which was not opened. Changes visible on the page include the living-review approach from 2020, a continued-use outcome added in 2021, single-arm and non-randomised studies dropped (September 2025 protocol update), risk differences for serious events used for the first time in this update, new outcomes on vaping and smoking patterns, and new comparisons added in 2021 and 2026.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review rated 8 of 80 trials high risk and 24 unclear for selective reporting, noting that some are recent trials whose publications are incomplete. One trial (Skelton 2022) measured safety outcomes without reporting them; NCT03277495 was rated high risk because its final design differed from the pre-specified one without justification; Ioakeimidis 2018 (conference poster, quit rates in the vape arm differing between two sources) was rated high risk on other bias. Funnel plots were drawn for six pools of 10 or more studies and five were asymmetric.
analysis.power: Serious adverse events: fewer than 300 events in the NRT and the behavioural-support comparisons (downgraded one level) and fewer than 100 in the non-nicotine vape comparison (downgraded two levels); many trials had no events in either arm (5 of 12 against non-nicotine vapes, 10 of 18 against behavioural support or no support). The comparison with non-nicotine vapes has fewer than 300 quits overall and was downgraded one level for imprecision. Cessation pools: 11, 7 and 11 trials.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In randomised trials, adults who were offered a nicotine vape were more likely to be not smoking at six months or longer than adults offered NRT: about 10 in 100 against 6 in 100 (RR 1.61, 1.23 to 2.12; 11 trials; about 4 more in 100, interval 1 to 7 more; rated high certainty by the review, though its own funnel plot for this outcome is asymmetric and I2 is 55%). Against non-nicotine vapes: 8 against 6 in 100 (RR 1.34, 1.05 to 1.69; 7 trials; 2 more in 100, interval 0 to 4; moderate certainty). Against behavioural support only or no support: 9 against 5 in 100 (RR 1.75, 1.39 to 2.20; 11 trials; about 4 more in 100, interval 2 to 6; low certainty because the trials could not be blinded and support differed). Advice to use a vape without being given one showed no clear difference (RR 1.02, 0.88 to 1.19; 2 trials; 2,652 participants). Serious adverse events showed no clear difference in any of the three comparisons (7 against 6 per 100 with NRT, moderate certainty; 2 against 2 per 100 with non-nicotine vapes, low; 3 against 3 per 100 with behavioural support or no support, very low), with many trials recording none. Any adverse event: no clear difference against NRT (39 against 41 per 100, low certainty, I2 72%) or non-nicotine vapes (46 against 46 per 100, moderate); more with a nicotine vape than behavioural support or no support (52 against 43 per 100, very low certainty, interval touching no difference). Use of the allocated product at six months or longer could not be pooled against NRT (I2 95%; in three of five trials more people kept using the vape than NRT); the review pooled patterns of use (vape only RR 4.40, 1.27 to 15.28; neither vape nor cigarettes RR 0.49, 0.26 to 0.91; I2 78% and 31%). Follow-up in the pooled safety data runs to about two years at most; the review says longer-term effects are unknown.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and plain language summary state high-certainty evidence that nicotine vapes increase quit rates against NRT, moderate against non-nicotine vapes and low against behavioural support or no support, and that serious events are probably similar to NRT and that no clear serious short-term harm was found; the plain language summary adds that regulated vapes do not expose people to the same levels of chemicals as cigarettes. The Discussion says the tobacco and vaping industry trials did not influence the conclusions, that comparisons with NRT isolate the effect of the sensory and behavioural elements of vaping, and that the review process is robust. Gaps: (1) the high-certainty label for the NRT comparison carries no downgrade although the review's own funnel plot for that outcome is asymmetric (11 trials) and I2 is 55%, above the 50% line its Methods call substantial; the same comparison's adverse-event outcome was downgraded for I2 of 72%, and the Discussion says asymmetry may reflect publication bias or between-study differences; (2) the abstract gives the absolute gain against behavioural support or no support as two in 100 (interval 2 to 6), while its own summary-of-findings table (5 to 9 per 100) gives four in 100; (3) 'industry trials did not influence the conclusions' holds for the three cessation outcomes (each pool has at most one such trial) but not for lung-function results against behavioural support, where the estimate moved on removal, and many sensitivity analyses could not be run because every trial was industry-funded or high risk; (4) the sensory-and-behavioural explanation is not tested in the trials, which also differ in nicotine delivery, device choice, flavour, support and use of the product; (5) the chemical exposure statement rests on biomarker outcomes with one to a few trials per comparison and, for some (NNAL against non-nicotine vapes and against behavioural support), I2 of 96% to 99%, not on health outcomes; (6) the Results text says adverse events against NRT are 'probably' not different while the review rates that outcome low certainty; (7) the text says every trial in the behavioural-support comparison is at high risk of bias, but Table 1 rates Eisenberg 2020 low and Table 2 gives a one-trial result after removing high-risk trials.

timeline.event: First version of this Cochrane review (Issue 12, 2014).
Update with 11 new trials; 'reduction' removed as an outcome (covered by a separate review).
