Companion Cochrane review of nicotine replacement therapy against control (search 2017), the comparator condition in several vape trials.
Update with 35 new studies; living review protocol adopted; the strength of evidence for existing comparisons increased.
Update with 17 new included studies; certainty changed for some primary outcomes.
Cochrane review of ways of using NRT (combination, dose, preloading), whose combination arms are the comparator in some vape trials.
Certainty for cessation against behavioural support or no support raised from very low to low.
Two updates (January and November); non-randomised studies dropped in the protocol update of September 2025.
This update: nine new trials, searches to 1 January 2026, conclusions unchanged.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the cessation result (vape better than NRT, than non-nicotine vape and than behavioural support or no support) has been stable across successive living updates, and the review's Discussion lists other meta-analyses that point the same way (relative risks of about 1.5 to 1.7 against NRT) alongside two whose intervals include no difference (relative risks 1.17 and 1.42). Those reviews draw on many of the same trials, so they are not independent confirmations. The NRT result rests on 11 trials, six at low risk of bias; the combination-NRT subgroup is imprecise and inconsistent (see key findings); no trial has yet reported follow-up beyond two years in the safety pools. Eight of 80 trials had tobacco or vaping industry support, and the review authors state they have no such funding.

funding.funder: Cancer Research UK (grant PICCTR-2024/100012 for this update; earlier updates also CRUK project grants); NIHR infrastructure funding for the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group; University of Oxford and Cochrane internal awards. The addition of new outcomes on vaping and smoking at six months or longer was supported by the National Cancer Institute of the US National Institutes of Health and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products (award 2U54CA229974). The funders were not involved in the decision to submit for publication. The authors state they receive no funding from tobacco or vaping industries.
funding.declared_conflicts: Six review authors are authors of included trials (RB, Begh 2021; CB, Bullen 2013 and others; PH, Hajek 2019 and 2022; JLB and CN, Pope 2024; HM, several) and each states they took no part in eligibility, extraction, risk of bias or GRADE decisions for those trials. CB reports travel and conference expenses paid by Kenvue/Johnson and Johnson Asia (a maker of NRT), employment by the University of Auckland and roles with bodies that hold policy positions on e-cigarettes. NAR reports research funding from Achieve Life Sciences (a cytisinicline developer) and a grant to test the long-term safety of the drug. HM's employer holds a contract to deliver smoking cessation services in which vapes are used for some quit attempts. CN is Editor-in-Chief of Nicotine and Tobacco Research, a journal that publishes work relevant to the review. NL holds grants from the NIHR, Cancer Research UK, local authorities, NIH/FDA and Action on Smoking and Health and is involved in two ongoing trials. PH provided commentary for the Science Media Centre. JHB and TT hold Cochrane editorial roles and were not involved in the editorial decision. The others declare none known or no relevant interests. Funding of the 80 trials (Table 1 and Results › Funding): 8 report tobacco or vaping industry support (Caponnetto 2013 and Caponnetto 2023, the latter from Philip Morris Products SA; Cravo 2016, Fontem Ventures; Edmiston 2022, Altria; Kanobe 2022, RAI Services Company; Rose 2023, a NIDA grant with lead-author ties to Foundation for a Smoke-Free World, Philip Morris International, Altria and JUUL Labs; Russell 2021, the e-cigarette or alternative nicotine products industry; Xu 2023, JUUL Labs), 66 report none, 6 do not report. One of the eight (Caponnetto 2013) is described in the text only as funded by an anti-smoking charity.
funding.affiliations_note: Author affiliations were not in the page text read for this card; the sources of support name Queen Mary University of London (HM, PH), the University of Auckland (CB) and the University of Oxford, and the declarations name Massachusetts General Hospital (NAR).

what_would_settle_it: Larger and longer trials that test the same newer devices against combination NRT (patch plus a fast-acting form) and against other first-line medicines, with registered outcomes, quit status verified by a biochemical test and follow-up of 12 to 24 months or more; trials that make the comparison with behavioural support less open to bias (for example matched contact time or objectively verified outcomes at all visits); serious-event data from trials powered to detect rare events and reported by arm; trial registry follow-up and unpublished-result checks to settle the funnel plot asymmetry; head-to-head trials of device type, nicotine delivery and flavour to allow the planned subgroup analyses; and independent funding for a larger share of trials.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults who smoked, any age and motivation; vapes or advice to use them; comparisons with NRT, non-nicotine vapes, behavioural support or no support and others; abstinence at six months or longer, adverse events and serious adverse events; randomised trials.

A 2012 Cochrane protocol, with updates to the methods pre-specified on an Open Science Framework registry and differences from the protocol and between updates documented in a supplement (Supplementary material 10, not opened), so the justification for each deviation was not checked here.
Randomised and randomised cross-over trials; single-arm studies dropped, with the reason given (editorial feedback and the growth of randomised evidence).

CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO to January 2026, registries through CENTRAL, conference abstracts, reference lists, contact with trial authors, monthly searching; publication date limit (2004) justified; strategies are in Supplementary material 1 (not opened). The Specialised Register was not searched after February 2023; direct database searches ran across the whole period.
Two review authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts.
Two authors independently extracted outcome data and risk of bias information with a piloted form; study characteristics were extracted by one author.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: A supplement lists 37 studies excluded at full text across all updates with reasons, but the authors say it does not cover every study excluded.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives arms, numbers randomised, follow-up, motivation, population, overall risk of bias, industry funding, country and NRT type for all 80 trials; device, nicotine strength, duration of supply and support intensity sit in Supplementary material 2, which was not opened.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane RoB 1 tool (random sequence, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and of outcome assessors, incomplete data, selective reporting, other) by two independent assessors, with Tobacco Addiction Group rules for blinding and attrition.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Study funding was extracted; Table 1 flags tobacco or vaping industry support and the text names the funder of each of the eight.

Random-effects Mantel-Haenszel models with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman intervals, risk differences for rare events, I2 reported, cross-over trials handled by published methods; trials with multiple arms not combined unless the authors did.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses removing high-risk trials and industry-funded trials for every outcome (Table 2), though many could not be run because all trials were high risk or industry-funded.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE downgraded the behavioural-support comparison by two levels for risk of bias and the Discussion explains why; the interpretation of industry funding and of the funnel plots is arguable (see reporting issues).

I2 reported throughout; subgroups by pregnancy and NRT type; heterogeneity described as driven by size more than direction of effect where that applies; the adverse-event outcome against NRT was downgraded for I2 of 72%.

Funnel plots for the six pools of 10 or more studies; five showed some asymmetry and were not treated as grounds for downgrading, with asymmetry attributed to publication bias or between-study differences.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Declarations for each author, authors' roles in included trials, and funders of the review are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical item is judged no and two non-critical items are partly met (7 and 8), which AMSTAR 2 does not count as flaws. AMSTAR 2 rates how the review was done, not how good its trials are: 41 of 80 trials were at high risk of bias overall, every trial in the comparison with behavioural support or no support was treated as unblinded with unequal support, the serious-event pools rest on few events, and five of six funnel plots were asymmetric. Six review authors are authors of included trials (declared; they did not take part in decisions on those trials). May be cited for: the pooled cessation, adverse-event and serious-event figures with the review's own certainty ratings, set beside the sensitivity analyses and the points in the key findings. May not be cited for: long-term health effects of vaping, effects in adolescents or in people who never smoked, the combination-NRT comparison as settled, or the statement that industry trials did not influence any result.

key_findings.finding: Nicotine vape against NRT, abstinence at six months or longer: RR 1.61 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.12), I2 55%, 11 trials, 4,114 participants. Summary of findings: 6 per 100 with NRT against 10 per 100 (7 to 13) with a nicotine vape, about 4 more in 100 (interval 1 to 7 more). The review rates this high certainty with no downgrade. Six of the 11 trials were at low risk of bias, three unclear and two high; devices were two cartridge, five refillable, one pod, one disposable, one mixed and one not specified.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Direct comparisons between nicotine EC and other pharmacotherapies › Cessation, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings 1
key_findings.note: The 6 (or 5) per 100 baseline is the review's assumed quit rate, not the trials' observed control-group rate: the table footnote says the control risk is based on assumed quit rates with limited behavioural support (the review's reference 1), and the vape figure is that baseline multiplied by the relative effect; the observed rates are in forest plots that were not read.

key_findings.finding: Subgroups and sensitivity for the NRT comparison: the pregnancy trial (Hajek 2022) did not differ from the rest (P = 0.89). Split by NRT type, 4 trials used combination NRT, 5 single-form and 2 unclear, with little evidence of a subgroup difference (P = 0.11, I2 55.1%; P = 0.52 comparing combination with single-form only). Without the one industry-funded trial (Russell 2021) RR 1.72 (1.23 to 2.39), I2 56%; without the two high-risk trials RR 1.74 (1.30 to 2.34), I2 55%. For the combination-NRT subgroup Table 2 gives RR 1.95 (1.01 to 3.73), I2 74%, after removing high-risk trials and RR 1.90 (0.87 to 4.15), I2 74%, in the industry-removed column (that subgroup contains no industry-funded trial, so this is read as the main subgroup value); the subgroup estimates in the main analysis are in a forest plot image that was not read.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Cessation › Subgroup and sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (rows Analysis 1.1 and 1.2)
key_findings.note: The reading of the 1.90 (0.87 to 4.15) value as the main combination-NRT subgroup result is the editors' inference from the table layout.

key_findings.finding: Funnel plots: six pools had 10 or more studies and five showed some asymmetry, including the NRT cessation pool (11 trials) and the behavioural-support cessation pool (11 trials). The authors say plots with this few studies are not diagnostic, that asymmetry could reflect unpublished small trials that showed no benefit or differences between trials, and that they did not downgrade for publication bias but will keep monitoring. The Methods define I2 above 50% as substantial; the NRT cessation pool has 55% and was not downgraded for inconsistency, while adverse events in the same comparison (72%) were.
key_findings.locator: Results › Reporting biases; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Synthesis methods

key_findings.finding: Adverse events and serious adverse events, nicotine vape against NRT: any adverse event RR 0.95 (0.72 to 1.24), I2 72%, 8 trials, 3,107 participants, 41 against 39 per 100 (30 to 51), low certainty (imprecision and inconsistency); without the one high-risk trial RR 0.90 (0.71 to 1.14), I2 66%. Serious events RD 0.01 (-0.01 to 0.02), I2 0%, 10 trials, 4,045, 6 against 7 per 100 (5 to 8), moderate certainty (fewer than 300 events); without the two high-risk trials RD 0.01 (-0.01 to 0.03). No trial in either pool was industry-funded. Trials that could not be pooled: Hajek 2019 found nausea more often with NRT and throat or mouth irritation more often with the vape; Bonafont Reyes 2022 (COPD) reported a trend to fewer breathlessness and COPD symptoms with the vape without detail.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events, 1st paragraph and Sensitivity analyses; Serious adverse events, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Narrative summary of unpooled studies; Summary of findings 1

key_findings.finding: Use of vapes and cigarettes at six months or longer against NRT (none industry-funded except where stated): use of the allocated product could not be pooled (I2 95%, five trials, one industry-funded); in three of five more people in the vape arm kept using it than in the NRT arm, and in Russell 2021 and Lee 2018 there was no difference. Vaping without smoking was more frequent in the vape arms (RR 4.40, 1.27 to 15.28; I2 78%; 2,776 participants); neither vaping nor smoking was less frequent (RR 0.49, 0.26 to 0.91; I2 31%); smoking without vaping RR 0.76 (0.58 to 1.01), I2 83%, 4 trials, 2,543; concurrent vaping and smoking was higher in the vape arm in three of four trials and not pooled. Absolute counts are in forest plots that were not read.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Study product use; Long-term nicotine EC and combustible cigarette use
key_findings.note: These patterns are relative figures only on the page; the proportion of each arm still vaping is not given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Nicotine vape against non-nicotine vape, abstinence at six months or longer: RR 1.34 (1.05 to 1.69), I2 0%, 7 trials (five cartridge, two refillable), 1,918 participants; 6 against 8 per 100 (6 to 10), about 2 more in 100 (interval 0 to 4). Moderate certainty: not downgraded for risk of bias (one high-risk trial; removing it gave RR 1.40, 1.09 to 1.81), downgraded one level for imprecision (fewer than 300 quits). Without the one industry-funded trial (Caponnetto 2013) RR 1.28 (1.01 to 1.64).
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Cessation › Versus non-nicotine, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Analysis 8.1); Summary of findings 2
key_findings.note: The 6 (or 5) per 100 baseline is the review's assumed quit rate, not the trials' observed control-group rate: the table footnote says the control risk is based on assumed quit rates with limited behavioural support (the review's reference 1), and the vape figure is that baseline multiplied by the relative effect; the observed rates are in forest plots that were not read.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events and serious events, nicotine against non-nicotine vape: any adverse event RR 1.01 (0.95 to 1.08), I2 0%, 6 trials, 909 participants, 46 against 46 per 100 (44 to 50), moderate certainty (imprecision). Serious events RD 0.00 (-0.01 to 0.01), I2 0%, 11 trials, 1,786, 2 against 2 per 100 (1 to 3), low certainty (fewer than 100 events, downgraded two levels); five of 12 trials reporting serious events had none. Of the trials that could not be pooled, two found similar adverse event rates (Caponnetto 2013, Tuisku 2024) and two reported more events with the nicotine vape (Felicione 2019, Tseng 2016). Industry funding: one trial in the any-adverse-event pool and two (Caponnetto 2013, Rose 2023) in the serious-event pool; removing them made no change to either result (Table 2: RR 1.01, 0.95 to 1.08; RD -0.00, -0.01 to 0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events › Versus non-nicotine; Serious adverse events › Versus non-nicotine EC; Summary of findings 2; Table 2 (Analyses 8.2 and 8.3)

key_findings.finding: Nicotine vape against behavioural support only or no support, abstinence at six months or longer: RR 1.75 (1.39 to 2.20), I2 13%, 11 trials (five refillable, three cartridge, three pod), 7,214 participants; 5 against 9 per 100 (7 to 11), about 4 more in 100 (interval 2 to 6). Low certainty: downgraded two levels for risk of bias because blinding was not possible and the vape arm received more support. One trial in the pool was industry-funded (Xu 2023, JUUL Labs); without it RR 1.53 (1.30 to 1.79). One trial (Pulvers 2020) measured quits at six months in the vape arm only and could not be pooled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Cessation › Versus behavioural support or no support, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2 (Analysis 9.1); Summary of findings 3
key_findings.note: The 6 (or 5) per 100 baseline is the review's assumed quit rate, not the trials' observed control-group rate: the table footnote says the control risk is based on assumed quit rates with limited behavioural support (the review's reference 1), and the vape figure is that baseline multiplied by the relative effect; the observed rates are in forest plots that were not read.

key_findings.finding: Adverse and serious events, nicotine vape against behavioural support only or no support: any adverse event RR 1.22 (1.00 to 1.49), I2 58%, 11 trials, 2,801 participants, 43 against 52 per 100 (43 to 64), very low certainty (risk of bias and imprecision). Serious events RD 0.00 (-0.00 to 0.01), I2 0%, 18 trials, 5,032, 3 against 3 per 100 (3 to 4), very low certainty; ten of 18 trials reported none. Twelve further trials gave adverse event data that could not be pooled, with mixed direction by symptom (for example more throat irritation, cough and dry mouth in vape arms of some trials, fewer respiratory symptoms in others). Industry support: one trial (Cravo 2016) in the any-adverse-event pool and two (Edmiston 2022, Cravo 2016) in the serious-event pool; the review says removing them did not affect interpretation (Table 2 gives RR 1.26, 0.96 to 1.66, I2 60%, for any adverse event without the industry-supported trial).

key_findings.finding: Advice to use a vape without being given one, against no such advice: RR 1.02 (0.88 to 1.19), I2 0%, 2 trials (Martinez 2021, low risk, in people who already vaped; Elling 2023, high risk), 2,652 participants; no clear difference, and unchanged without Elling 2023. A third trial (Vickerman 2022, 52 participants) found more adverse events with the advice (RR 1.27, 0.72 to 2.26) and no serious events. None was industry-funded.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Advice to use EC to stop smoking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Vape added to other treatments: nicotine against non-nicotine vape with NRT in both arms RR 1.77 (1.07 to 2.94), I2 0%, 2 trials (both high risk), 1,039 participants. Nicotine vape plus NRT against NRT alone: three trials could not be pooled (I2 83%), driven by a cartridge-device trial (Morphett 2022a, high risk); the other two (refillable devices) gave RR 3.57 (1.96 to 6.51), I2 0%, 980 participants. Nicotine vape plus cytisine against cytisine alone RR 1.39 (0.96 to 2.01), 1 trial, 597 participants. Non-nicotine vape as an add-on to NRT RR 1.67 (0.50 to 5.53), 1 trial, 624.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › EC as an adjunct to other interventions; Non-nicotine EC › Cessation

key_findings.finding: Other active comparators (each one or two trials, none pooled): nicotine vape against cytisine RR 1.56 (1.06 to 2.30), 508 participants (Walker 2023); against varenicline RR 0.31 (0.11 to 0.82), 54 participants (Ioakeimidis 2018, conference presentation, high risk, data inconsistencies); non-nicotine vape plus varenicline against nicotine vape RR 0.73 (0.53 to 1.01), 305 participants (Tuisku 2024, low risk); against NRT plus bupropion RR 0.89 (0.44 to 1.81), 38 participants. Non-nicotine vape against NRT RR 0.99 (0.64 to 1.54), I2 36%, 2 trials, 314 participants; against behavioural support or no support RR 1.59 (0.80 to 3.19), 2 trials, 388.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Narrative summary of unpooled studies; Non-nicotine EC › Cessation

key_findings.finding: Head-to-head comparisons of nicotine vapes, with abstinence at six months or longer (one trial each): higher against lower nicotine strength RR 2.50 (0.80 to 7.77), 260 participants (Cobb 2021, low risk); choice of flavours against tobacco flavour only RR 0.80 (0.54 to 1.16), 566 (Xu 2023, JUUL Labs funded, high risk); nicotine salt against freebase nicotine RR 1.25 (0.85 to 1.83), 285 (Russell 2021, industry funded); higher against lower wattage RR 0.72 (0.30 to 1.74), 267 (NCT03113136, high risk). All intervals include no difference. Device type could not be tested.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Direct comparisons between different nicotine EC conditions

key_findings.finding: Nicotine vape against oral nicotine pouches: one small trial (Avila 2024, 26 participants in the comparison, high risk of bias for possible selective reporting, follow-up about two months). No cessation outcome; no serious events in either arm (RD 0.00, -0.14 to 0.14); carbon monoxide fell more in the vape arm, interval including a greater fall with pouches (mean difference -12.44, -28.82 to 3.94 ppm); cough and shortness of breath were reported more often in the pouch arm early, similar by week four. Nicotine vape against heated tobacco: two trials, adverse events RR 0.86 (0.68 to 1.10), 220 participants (Caponnetto 2023, Philip Morris funded); no cessation result.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Nicotine EC versus other tobacco/nicotine products used for stopping combustible tobacco use; Table 1 (Avila 2024)

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers and physiology against NRT and other comparisons (short follow-up, few trials): breath carbon monoxide fell more with a nicotine vape than NRT (mean difference -1.98 ppm, -3.78 to -0.18; 5 trials, 385 participants, none industry-funded); heart rate, systolic blood pressure and oxygen saturation showed no clear difference (2 trials, 166 participants, wide intervals); toxicant biomarkers come from a single trial against NRT; carbon monoxide against behavioural support or no support was too heterogeneous to pool (I2 93%; 13 of 14 trials favoured the vape); NNAL against non-nicotine vapes and behavioural support had I2 of 99% and 96% and was not pooled; against behavioural support, FEV1 SMD 0.12 (-0.10 to 0.34), changing to -0.01 (-0.40 to 0.39) after removing the two industry-funded trials.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Carbon monoxide; Heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation; Toxicants; Lung function; Table 2 (Analysis 9.16)

key_findings.finding: Funding of the 80 included trials: 8 report tobacco or vaping industry support (Caponnetto 2013 and Caponnetto 2023, Cravo 2016, Edmiston 2022, Kanobe 2022, Rose 2023, Russell 2021, Xu 2023), 66 report none, 6 do not report. One industry-funded trial sits in each of the three cessation pools (Russell 2021 in the NRT pool, Caponnetto 2013 in the non-nicotine pool, Xu 2023 in the behavioural-support pool); removing it left the cessation estimates positive in each (RR 1.72, 1.28 and 1.53). Eight trials carry the asterisk in the review; the text names an anti-smoking charity as the only funder of one (Caponnetto 2013), and Rose 2023 is flagged because its lead author declared industry support although the trial was funded by NIDA. In the safety pools none of the trials against NRT was industry-funded; the non-nicotine pools held one (any adverse event) and two (serious events) and the support pools one (Cravo 2016) and two (Cravo 2016 and Edmiston 2022), with no change in the review reading when they were left out.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Funding; Table 1; Table 2
key_findings.note: The text says 75 trials reported funding information; 8 plus 66 is 74, as Table 1 shows with 6 not reported.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias across the 80 trials (RoB 1): overall 12 low, 27 unclear, 41 high; random sequence generation low in 47, unclear in 33; allocation concealment low in 40, unclear in 37, high in 3; performance bias low in 45, high in 24, unclear in 11; detection bias low in 60, high in 12, unclear in 8; attrition low in 59, high in 8, unclear in 13; reporting low in 48, high in 8, unclear in 24. The 12 low-risk trials include Bullen 2013, Cobb 2021, Courtney 2025, Eisenberg 2020, Hajek 2019, Hajek 2022, Kerr 2020, Lee 2018, Lee 2019, Martinez 2021, Myers-Smith 2022 and Tuisku 2024.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: imprecision remains the main limit; longer-term health effects are unknown and the review includes safety data to two years only; the trials tested regulated nicotine vapes, and illicit or THC-containing products may have different harm profiles; intention-to-treat analysis limits conclusions about biomarkers in people by their later vaping or smoking; the field and devices are changing quickly and there is a time lag between devices on the market and trial devices; planned subgroups by device type could not be run; unpublished data may be missing; searches for this update ran to 1 January 2026.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review; Limitations of the review processes; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice and for research

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the absolute gain for a nicotine vape against behavioural support only or no support as two more quitters per 100 (interval 2 to 6). The summary-of-findings table gives 5 per 100 against 9 per 100 (7 to 11), which is four more per 100, and the interval of 2 to 6 matches that. The Discussion repeats 'two to six' as a range.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Synthesis of results, 3rd paragraph; Summary of findings 3; Discussion › Summary of main results, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary-of-findings figures (5 against 9 per 100, about 4 more, interval 2 to 6) are used.

reporting_issues.issue: High certainty is given for the cessation comparison with NRT with no downgrade, although the review's own funnel plot for this outcome is asymmetric (11 trials) and I2 is 55%, above the 50% line the Methods define as substantial. In the same comparison the adverse-event outcome was downgraded for inconsistency at I2 72%. The Discussion attributes asymmetry to publication bias or between-study differences and does not downgrade for either.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods › Synthesis methods; Results › Reporting biases; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Summary of findings 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim reports the review's high rating beside the asymmetry and I2 and proposes one level lower on the editors' reading; the senior author decides.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says all trials in the comparison with behavioural support or no support were at high risk of bias, but Table 1 rates Eisenberg 2020 low risk overall (nicotine vape plus counselling against counselling), and Table 2 gives a result for removing high-risk trials from that comparison (cessation RR 8.51, 0.46 to 156.44; adverse events RR 1.29, 1.15 to 1.45; serious events RD -0.01, -0.05 to 0.03; I2 not estimable in each, which fits a single remaining trial) where an all-high-risk pool would show no such row.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Nicotine EC versus non-nicotine EC, behavioural support or no support, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Eisenberg 2020); Table 2 (Analyses 9.1 to 9.3)
reporting_issues.consequence: Not used; the claim treats the pool as predominantly high risk and notes that the single low-risk trial result is too imprecise to read.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text describes adverse events against NRT as probably not different, while the abstract, summary-of-findings table and Discussion rate this outcome low certainty (wording that fits 'may be similar'); the Discussion says the rating was lowered from moderate in this update because inconsistency rose.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Adverse events (EC against NRT), 1st paragraph; Abstract › Synthesis of results; Discussion › Summary of main results, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Low certainty used.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that tobacco and vaping industry studies did not influence the conclusions because conclusions were unchanged when they were removed. That holds for the three cessation outcomes, but for lung function against behavioural support or no support the point estimate moved on removal (FEV1 SMD 0.12 to -0.01), and Table 2 shows that many sensitivity analyses could not be run because every trial was industry-funded or high risk.
reporting_issues.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the review processes, 3rd paragraph; Results › Lung function; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim states the industry sensitivity result for cessation only.

reporting_issues.issue: The Funding section says 75 studies reported funding information, with 8 reporting industry support and 66 none; 8 plus 66 is 74, and Table 1 shows 6 trials with funding not reported (80 minus 6 is 74).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Description of studies › Funding, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: 8, 66 and 6 are used.

reporting_issues.issue: Caponnetto 2013 carries the industry-funding asterisk, but the text names only the Lega Italiana AntiFumo (an anti-smoking charity) as funder; the reason for the flag is not stated on the page (the supplementary characteristics, not opened, may say).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Description of studies › Funding; Table 1 (Caponnetto 2013)
reporting_issues.consequence: Counted as one of the eight flagged trials, with the discrepancy noted.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary-of-findings footnote for the nicotine against non-nicotine vape cessation row says the imprecision downgrade was because the interval spans harm and no difference; the cessation interval (1.05 to 1.69) does not, and the Results text gives the reason as fewer than 300 events. Separately, footnotes in all three tables describe the assumed risk for adverse events as a mean of 'quit rates', and the serious-event row of table 3 is labelled a risk ratio where the text and abstract give a risk difference.
reporting_issues.locator: Summary of findings 1 to 3, footnotes and serious adverse events rows; Results › Cessation › Versus non-nicotine, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Wording only; the Results text reason (fewer than 300 events) is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The text for the heated-tobacco carbon monoxide sensitivity analysis gives a mean difference of -20, while Table 2 gives -0.20 (-3.23 to 2.83); and for FEV1/FVC against behavioural support the text repeats the main interval (-0.47 to 2.50) for a new estimate of 0.20, while Table 2 gives SMD 0.20 (-1.08 to 1.48).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Nicotine EC vs heated tobacco, 4th sentence; Lung function (EC against behavioural support), 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Analyses 6.3 and 9.17)
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 2 values taken; neither enters a claim.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives follow-up of 3 months for Courtney 2025, a trial listed in the pooled cessation analysis at six months or longer against NRT; it gives 9 months for Bonevski 2025 and 3 months for Bonevski 2021. The text on the page does not explain the follow-up used for each trial's cessation result (per-trial details are in the unopened supplements).
reporting_issues.locator: Table 1 (Courtney 2025); Results › Cessation, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Flagged for the senior author; the pooled result is used as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts of trials in the NRT add-on comparison differ within the same paragraph: 'three studies' for cessation, 'four trials' contributing adverse event data, then 'pooling all three studies' for the same outcome; five studies provided serious event data.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › EC as an adjunct to other interventions › Nicotine EC and NRT › Cessation, Adverse events and Serious adverse events
reporting_issues.consequence: Not used in any claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says comparisons with NRT isolate the effect of the sensory and behavioural elements of vaping and comparisons with non-nicotine vapes isolate the effect of nicotine; the trials do not test either explanation, and vape and NRT arms also differ in nicotine delivery, flavours, device choice, how much each product is used and the support offered.
reporting_issues.locator: Discussion › Cessation, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Mechanism statements are left out of the claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The absolute cessation figures in all three summary-of-findings tables (6, 6 and 5 per 100 in the comparison arm) are built from an assumed quit rate for NRT or support with limited behavioural support (the table footnote cites the review's reference 1), not from the control-group rates observed in the pooled trials; the non-nicotine vape table repeats the NRT wording for a different comparator. The tables label the row 'Study population'.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claims give these figures as the review's illustrative absolute effects and say the baseline is assumed; the relative risks are the observed pooled results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Authors' conclusions in the abstract call the evidence for more (non-serious) adverse events against behavioural support or no support low certainty, while the abstract's own results paragraph, the summary-of-findings table (risk of bias and imprecision) and the Discussion rate it very low.
reporting_issues.consequence: Very low is used, as the table and results give it.

reporting_issues.issue: For any adverse event against behavioural support or no support, the text says the result was not sensitive to leaving out the one industry-supported trial (Cravo 2016), but Table 2 gives RR 1.26 (0.96 to 1.66), I2 60%, against 1.22 (1.00 to 1.49) in the main analysis, so the interval then includes no difference (its lower limit was already 1.00). For serious events against support (Analysis 9.3), Table 2 prints I2 not estimable in the industry-removed column although two industry-supported trials out of 18 were removed, which should leave a poolable set; that cell may be misaligned.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events › Versus behavioural support or no support, last sentence; Serious adverse events › Versus behavioural support or no support; Table 2 (Analyses 9.2 and 9.3)
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim states the 1.26 (0.96 to 1.66) result beside the main 1.22 (1.00 to 1.49) and rests the serious-event statement on the review text, not on the Table 2 cell.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC13506250 (abstract, plain language summary, all three Summary of findings tables, background, methods, results [results of the search, included studies with Table 1 parsed programmatically for all 80 rows, participants, interventions, outcomes, funding, excluded studies, risk of bias, all syntheses including the Table 2 sensitivity analyses, reporting biases], discussion, authors' conclusions, acknowledgements, contributions, declarations of interest, sources of support, what's new and history read; the forest plots, funnel plots, flow diagram and risk-of-bias figures are images and were not read; Supplementary materials 1 to 17 (search strategies, characteristics of included, excluded, awaiting and ongoing studies, analyses, living-review protocol, changes in methods between updates, data not contributing to meta-analyses) and the reference list were not opened)

design_detail: Secondary analysis of the adult interview of Wave 1 (12 September 2013 to 14 December 2014) of the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) Study, a US national probability survey of tobacco use. Compares adults who used only e-cigarettes, every day, with adults who smoked only cigarettes, every day, on four yes/no dependence questions and on time to first use after waking. Weighted analyses with replicate weights; logistic regression (odds ratios, cigarette group relative to e-cigarette group) and linear regression of log time to first use.
can_establish: How often adults in the US in 2013 to 2014 who used only e-cigarettes daily, and adults who smoked only cigarettes daily, gave answers that indicate dependence on their own product, and how much the gap between the groups changes when age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and poverty status are taken into account.
cannot_establish: Whether the products differ in how dependence-forming they are (one time point; 145 of the 156 people in the e-cigarette group were former established cigarette smokers, so lower scores may reflect who ends up using only e-cigarettes); dependence in people who use both products, who are most of the people in the survey who had used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days; any effect of device type, liquid or nicotine strength (described but not analysed); dependence in people who never smoked; or how dependence changes over time.

sample.recruitment: Nationally representative household survey (PATH Study Wave 1 adult interview); the authors say the survey oversampled people who use tobacco, young adults and black adults, and that weighted analyses account for this. Analysis sample drawn from 32,320 adult observations in Wave 1; the 3586 eligible observations are 5.9% weighted of that total. The e-cigarette group is 4.6% and the cigarette group 95.4% of the weighted analysis sample.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults whose use of one product, e-cigarettes or cigarettes, was exclusive, daily, established and current. Excluded: people who used either product in the past 30 days and whom PATH also classed as currently using any other tobacco product, on an established or experimental basis; for the cigarette group also people who had used any other tobacco product on an established basis in the past 12 months but no longer did (Methods › Ascertainment of Study Population). Figure 1 (flowchart with the counts at each step) is an image; its values were not extracted.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (unweighted n, weighted %): e-cigarette group (n=156) vs cigarette group (n=3430): men 46.7% vs 46.8%; non-Hispanic white 84.8% vs 74.0%; education beyond high school 57.1% vs 40.7%; below the poverty level 14.6% vs 35.0%; use of their product allowed anywhere at any time in the home 61.9% vs 26.5%. Age bands were similar, with 27.5% vs 19.9% aged 25 to 34. The paper marks race/ethnicity, education, poverty and home rules as differing between groups (Rao-Scott chi-square, p < 0.01).
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a single wave. The survey response rate and any missing answers on the dependence items are not reported in the paper.
sample.selection_effects: The e-cigarette group is small (156) and, by the authors' own account, the most dependent subgroup of people who vape: only 6.8% of adults who had ever tried e-cigarettes used them daily (alone or with other products), against 23.8% of adults who had ever tried a cigarette and smoked daily. Most adults who had used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days also used other products and were left out. 92.9% of the e-cigarette group (145 of 156) were former established cigarette smokers, so the group is largely made of people who stopped smoking. The data are from 2013 to 2014.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported current use, classified into 'exclusive', 'daily' and 'established' by PATH's derived variables from the survey answers; no biological verification (the authors recommend cotinine in future studies). In the e-cigarette group: 151 of 156 (96.3% weighted) used a rechargeable device most of the time, 124 (76.5%) could refill it, 150 (95.8%) usually used a product that contained nicotine, and of the 151 rechargeable devices 52 (37.9%) used cartridges (Methods › Ascertainment of Study Population, 5th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not compared. Amount per day could not be compared because the units for e-cigarettes and cigarettes in PATH are not comparable; duration of use could not be computed because the age variables are categorical. Nicotine concentration, device type and flavour were not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Exclusive use of one tobacco product was imposed by design (see inclusion criteria). Alcohol, cannabis and other drug use were not considered.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (current daily use).

comparison.controls: Adults who smoked only cigarettes, every day (n=3430), as the comparison for adults who used only e-cigarettes every day (n=156). There is no group that used no nicotine.
comparison.matching: No matching. Regression adjustment for age (7 bands), sex, race/ethnicity (2 levels), education (3 levels) and poverty status (2 levels); the time-to-first-use model also adjusts for smoking rules inside the home (3 levels).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of dependence on cigarettes in the e-cigarette group before they changed products (the study is cross-sectional), no length of time using each product, no amount used per day, no age of starting, and no mental-health or other-substance measures. Who succeeds in moving to e-cigarettes only, and who stays with cigarettes, is a selection the study cannot separate from the effect of the product.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Four PATH yes/no items, worded for the person's own product: considers self addicted; ever has strong cravings; found it difficult in the past 12 months to refrain from using in places where it was prohibited; ever felt really needed to use. Plus self-reported time to first use after waking, analysed in Fagerstrom bands and as a log-transformed continuous variable.
outcomes.validity_norms: The four items were chosen because the other PATH dependence items use a 1 to 5 scale with unlabelled middle points, which the authors found hard to interpret. They are single items, not a validated dependence scale or diagnosis, and are not combined into a score. The authors cite time to first use as a strong predictor of difficulty quitting. The Penn State Electronic Cigarette Dependence Index described in their introduction was not used.
outcomes.operationalization: Dependence is what people said about themselves: more 'yes' answers and a shorter time to first use are read as more dependent. No clinical diagnosis, withdrawal measure or nicotine level was used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; a significance level of 0.05 was used for all analyses. All five outcomes differed with intervals well away from no difference (adjusted odds ratio intervals from 1.92 to 14.32).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (interviewer-administered survey answers; blinding not reported).

analysis.effect_sizes: Weighted percentages answering yes (e-cigarette group vs cigarette group): addicted 77.2% vs 94.0%; strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9%; difficult to refrain where prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6%; really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5% (Table 2, all p < 0.0001). Odds ratios, cigarette group relative to e-cigarette group, unadjusted and adjusted (95% CL): addicted 4.63 (3.05 to 7.02) and 6.92 (4.46 to 10.73); strong cravings 2.48 (1.66 to 3.70) and 2.85 (1.92 to 4.23); difficult to refrain 6.80 (3.08 to 15.04) and 6.39 (2.85 to 14.32); really needed 3.06 (1.92 to 4.86) and 3.89 (2.36 to 6.40) (Table 3). Time to first use after waking: within 5 minutes 15.1% vs 24.0%; 6 to 30 minutes 49.4% vs 44.7%; 31 to 60 minutes 24.6% vs 19.2%; over 60 minutes 10.9% vs 12.1% (Table 2). Geometric mean minutes (95% CL): e-cigarette group 23.46 (19.47 to 28.27) vs cigarette group 19.25 (18.25 to 20.30) unadjusted; 29.16 (24.39 to 34.87) vs 20.03 (18.66 to 21.49) adjusted. Editors' calculation: ratio of geometric means 1.22 unadjusted and 1.46 adjusted.
analysis.covariates: Age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, poverty status; for time to first use also home smoking rules. Not adjusted: length of use, amount used, age of starting, history of smoking, mental health, other substances, device or liquid features. Weighted with PATH replicate weights (Fay's balanced repeated replication, coefficient 0.30), SAS SURVEY procedures.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned in the paper.
analysis.selective_reporting: Four of the PATH dependence items were used and the rest set aside because of their response scales (stated reason); results of the unused items are not shown. All five chosen outcomes are reported, in the same direction. The categorical comparison of time-to-first-use bands is given as percentages without a test; only the continuous comparison is tested.
analysis.power: Not discussed. The e-cigarette group is 156 people, so intervals are wide (for example adjusted odds ratio for difficulty refraining 2.85 to 14.32; geometric mean 24.4 to 34.9 minutes).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among US adults in 2013 to 2014 who used only one product every day, those who only vaped were less likely than those who only smoked to say they were addicted (77.2% vs 94.0%), to have strong cravings (72.8% vs 86.9%), to have found it hard to go without in places where use was prohibited (5.6% vs 28.6%) or to feel they really needed it (71.5% vs 88.5%), and on average they first used their product later after waking (adjusted geometric mean about 29 vs 20 minutes). The differences held after adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and poverty. The majority of the e-cigarette group still gave a dependence answer on each item except difficulty refraining. Time to first use was not later in every band: the share waiting more than 60 minutes was similar (10.9% vs 12.1%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that adults who only vape, every day, are less dependent on their product than comparable adults who smoke, and the discussion adds that the dependence reported for e-cigarettes is 'not negligible' and that over three quarters called themselves addicted (Discussion, 1st paragraph). Gaps: (1) 'less dependent' rests on four self-report items and one timing question from a single time point, not a validated scale; (2) the e-cigarette group is nearly all former cigarette smokers (92.9%), so the contrast mixes the product with who ends up on it; (3) the discussion reads the lower share of daily use among people who tried e-cigarettes (6.8% against 23.8% for cigarettes) as suggestive of differential dependence potential, which is a different dataset (cited to Kasza et al.) and not a result of this analysis; (4) the abstract says the results agree with earlier studies without saying that most were convenience samples from internet surveys, which the introduction itself says could attract people favourable to e-cigarettes.

timeline.event: Farsalinos et al.: 111 former smokers using e-cigarettes, longer time to first use and lower self-rated dependence on e-cigarettes than on their earlier cigarettes (as described in the introduction; not read).
Etter and Eissenberg: lower dependence in people who use e-cigarettes than in people who smoke, in an internet convenience sample (as described in the introduction; not read).

Foulds et al.: 3609 former smokers who used only e-cigarettes reported less dependence on e-cigarettes than on their earlier cigarettes, retrospectively and in an online convenience sample (as described in the introduction; not read).
Rostron et al.: National Adult Tobacco Survey 2012 to 2013, fewer dependence symptoms in exclusive daily e-cigarette than exclusive daily cigarette use (as described in the introduction; not read).
This analysis of PATH Wave 1 (2013 to 2014): the first PATH-based comparison; the authors call for follow-up with later waves, biomarkers and device and liquid features.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (lower self-reported dependence in daily e-cigarette-only than in daily cigarette-only groups) agrees with the earlier studies the authors cite, including one national survey, but all are single-time-point comparisons of mostly former smokers, and the earlier ones are mostly convenience samples. This card covers only the 2013 to 2014 data; later waves and newer devices are not covered by this paper.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIH) and the Center for Tobacco Products of the US Food and Drug Administration (P50-DA-036107) for three authors; National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, NIH (UL1 TR000127) for one author. The paper states the content is solely the authors' responsibility.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the author manuscript text read.
funding.affiliations_note: The PMC text lists affiliation numbers 1 to 3 without institution names. J. Foulds, a co-author, is the first author of reference 25, the earlier e-cigarette dependence questionnaire study that this paper extends. No tobacco or vape industry funding is stated.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated measurement, in the same people before and after they move from cigarettes to e-cigarettes only, and in people who stay with cigarettes, using a dependence scale validated for each product, nicotine biomarkers such as cotinine, and recorded device and liquid features; plus the same measures followed over time in people who start vaping without having smoked.

domains.note: Adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and poverty only. The groups differ in who they are (92.9% of the e-cigarette group are former cigarette smokers), and length of use, amount used, age of starting, smoking history, mental health and other substances are not controlled.
Self-reported exclusive daily use classified by PATH algorithms, no biomarker; devices and liquids are described but not compared.
National probability sample with weights, but the comparison is restricted to exclusive daily use, which the authors say selects the most dependent people who vape; the e-cigarette group is only 156.

Home rules about where each product may be used differ strongly between groups (use allowed anywhere: 61.9% vs 26.5%) and affect time to first use; adjusted for in that model only. Quit support and treatment are not recorded.
Item non-response and survey response rate not reported.
Single self-report items worded for each product and a timing question, not a validated dependence scale; the time to first use depends on where the product may be used.
Four of the survey's dependence items were chosen for interpretability; results for the others are not shown and no analysis plan is mentioned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A consistent difference across five self-reported measures in a nationally representative sample, but the comparison is between people who differ in history and in who they are, the adjustment is limited to a few sociodemographic variables, and the outcomes are single items. Citable for what adults who only vaped daily and adults who only smoked daily said about their dependence in 2013 to 2014, and for the authors' own point that dependence on e-cigarettes was not negligible. Not citable for the dependence-forming potential of the products, for dual use, or for any device feature.

key_findings.finding: Sample: of 32,320 adult observations in PATH Wave 1, 3586 (5.9% weighted) were eligible: 156 who used only e-cigarettes every day (4.6% weighted) and 3430 who smoked only cigarettes every day (95.4% weighted).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Ascertainment of Study Population, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of the 156 in the e-cigarette group, 145 (92.9%) were former established cigarette smokers, 10 (6.7%) former experimental cigarette smokers and 1 (0.4%) had never used cigarettes or any other tobacco product. Devices: 151 (96.3% weighted) rechargeable, 124 (76.5%) refillable, 150 (95.8%) usually containing nicotine; of the 151 rechargeable, 52 (37.9%) used cartridges.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Ascertainment of Study Population, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: All four yes/no dependence items were answered yes less often by the e-cigarette group than the cigarette group: addicted 77.2% vs 94.0%; strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9%; difficult to keep from using where prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6%; felt really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5% (weighted; all p < 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Adjusted odds ratios for the cigarette group relative to the e-cigarette group (95% CL): addicted 6.92 (4.46 to 10.73); strong cravings 2.85 (1.92 to 4.23); difficult to refrain 6.39 (2.85 to 14.32); really needed 3.89 (2.36 to 6.40). Unadjusted: 4.63, 2.48, 6.80, 3.06. Adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and poverty status.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Time to first use after waking: within 5 minutes 15.1% (e-cigarette group) vs 24.0% (cigarette group); over 60 minutes 10.9% vs 12.1%. Geometric mean 29.16 minutes (24.39 to 34.87) vs 20.03 (18.66 to 21.49) after adjustment (home smoking rules added); 23.46 (19.47 to 28.27) vs 19.25 (18.25 to 20.30) unadjusted.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Tables 2 and 3
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: ratio of geometric means 1.22 unadjusted, 1.46 adjusted.

key_findings.finding: The groups differed on race/ethnicity, education, poverty and home rules: below the poverty level 14.6% (e-cigarette group) vs 35.0% (cigarette group); education beyond high school 57.1% vs 40.7%; product use allowed anywhere at any time in the home 61.9% vs 26.5%; not allowed anywhere 21.0% vs 47.8%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: The authors state that dependence on e-cigarettes was not negligible: over three quarters of the e-cigarette group considered themselves addicted. They also state that only 6.8% of adults who had ever tried an e-cigarette used them daily, against 23.8% of adults who had tried a cigarette and smoked daily, and that the exclusive daily comparison therefore picks the most dependent people who vape.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: amount per day could not be compared because the units differ; most adults who had used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days also used other products and were excluded; duration of use could not be computed; device and liquid features were not analysed and are called for in future work, with biomarkers such as cotinine and later PATH waves.
key_findings.locator: Study limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: The odds ratios in the abstract and Table 3 are for the cigarette group relative to the e-cigarette group (a value above 1 means the cigarette group answered yes more often); this is stated only in a Table 3 footnote and in the wording of the abstract.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader who takes the odds ratios as 'e-cigarette relative to cigarette' reverses the direction; claims should state the direction in words, and give the percentages (Table 2) before the ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: The time-to-first-use comparison is given two ways. The categorical distribution (Table 2) has no test statistic and shows the e-cigarette group less often in the within-5-minutes band but with a similar share above 60 minutes (10.9% vs 12.1%); the tested comparison is the continuous geometric mean, adjusted additionally for home smoking rules, which differ strongly between the groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's 'longer time to first use' rests on the adjusted geometric mean; the band percentages show a shift in the middle bands more than at both ends.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says most of the cigarette group have not had post-secondary education (59.3%); Table 1 gives 16.5% and 42.9% for the two lower bands, which add to 59.4%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding only; no effect on interpretation.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5868349 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 to 3 as text, reference list, funding; Figure 1 is an image and its counts were not extracted; no supplement)

design_detail: Laboratory chemical analysis of commercial products, not of people or cells (the schema has no design for a laboratory analysis of products; 'in-vitro' is the nearest). A German federal risk-assessment institute bought 46 tobacco-free pouch products online between January and May 2021 and measured nicotine (gas chromatography, triplicate), the pH of an aqueous extract and the calculated free-base share, and four tobacco-specific nitrosamines (liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry; one pouch per product, a single screening analysis). It also recorded what the packs printed about nicotine content and warnings. No people, no nicotine uptake and no comparison product (snus, nicotine gum, e-cigarette or cigarette) were measured.
can_establish: How much nicotine, which pH and what calculated share of free-base nicotine were in 44 nicotine pouches (and none in 2 nicotine-free pouches) that a German laboratory bought online in January to May 2021; which tobacco-specific nitrosamines were found at trace levels in some of them and the amounts measured; and how the strength printed on the packs (a milligram figure, a score or a word) related to the measured content.
cannot_establish: What people take in when they use pouches (no uptake, blood or urine measurement; the share extracted in use is taken from another study); whether any pouch is harmful, or less harmful than snus, nicotine replacement products or cigarettes (no health outcome and no other product was measured here); what the market as a whole contains (a convenience sample bought online in 2021, not weighted by sales); the exact nitrosamine amounts (one pouch per product, a single analysis, most results at or near the quantification limit); what other substances the pouches hold (metals, aldehydes, flavouring and other constituents were not measured, as the authors say); or whether products sold now match those bought in 2021.

sample.recruitment: Convenience sample of products (not people): bought January to May 2021 from German online shops or online shops in other countries that ship to Germany; 46 different products from 20 producers (Material and methods › Nicotine pouches, chemicals and standard substances, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria beyond availability are stated. Two products labelled nicotine-free were included as comparison pouches. The number of packs or batches bought per product is not stated.
sample.demographics: Not applicable (products).
sample.attrition: None: all 46 products were measured for nicotine and screened for nitrosamines; the two nicotine-free pouches showed none (Table 2 lists only nicotine-containing products).
sample.selection_effects: Convenience sample, not weighted by sales, bought online in 2021. The authors say the higher contents than in earlier studies of large US brands are partly because they also bought from smaller brands in online shops (Discussion, 1st paragraph). Contents of the most widely sold products and of products sold after 2021 may differ; one product was a free sample with no label at all.

exposure.measurement: Total nicotine by liquid-liquid extraction of one complete pouch (adapted from WHO TobLabNet SOP 4) and gas chromatography with flame ionisation, triplicate; pH of a 10 mL aqueous extract with a calibrated meter, duplicate (the water was not degassed, so dissolved carbon dioxide may have lowered pH); free-base share calculated from pH with the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation (pKa 8.01), not measured. NNN, NNK, NAT and NAB by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (ISO 21766:2021) with isotope-labelled standards, one pouch per product, a single screening analysis. Validation: precision below 10%; mean recoveries 102.9% to 126.1% for nicotine and 110.2% to 127.2% for the nitrosamines; detection limits 0.12 (NNN), 0.12 (NNK), 0.22 (NAT) and 0.34 (NAB) ng per pouch (Material and methods; Results › Results of method validation).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Measured product content, not a dose: nicotine 1.79 to 47.5 mg per pouch (median 9.48, interquartile range 5.50 to 16.6); wet weight median 0.643 g (interquartile range 0.455 to 0.718); pH of extract median 8.8 (interquartile range 8.2 to 9.8; range 5.5 to 10.5); calculated free-base share median 86% (interquartile range 62% to 98%) (Results › Nicotine contents, pouch weights and pH of extracts, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph). No use, route or duration was studied; the products are placed between lip and gum.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (products). Only nicotine, pH and four nitrosamines were measured; other constituents were not.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (products).

comparison.controls: Two products labelled nicotine-free are the only reference inside the study. No snus, nicotine gum or lozenge, e-cigarette or cigarette was measured. The Discussion's comparisons with them use figures from other studies (its references 25 to 27) obtained on other bases.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a product analysis; what was not measured: uptake by people, saliva or urine nitrosamines, other constituents, product ageing, and batch-to-batch variation.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Chemical analyses above; visual inspection of packs for printed nicotine content (milligram per pouch or per gram), a strength score or word, hazard pictograms under EU classification and labelling rules, and warnings for minors and for pregnancy.
outcomes.validity_norms: Method validation is summarised in the main text and detailed in a supplement that was not read. Results for nitrosamines are described by the authors as coming from a single measurement with unsteady precision at the instrument's lower limit (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: No harm outcome. Content is compared with earlier laboratory studies, with EU thresholds for hazard labels (2.5 and 16.7 mg per gram) and with a European Food Safety Authority reference dose for nicotine in food.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive; no hypothesis tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; no second checker of the label coding is described.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes. Nicotine per pouch: 1.79 to 47.5 mg, median 9.48 (interquartile range 5.50 to 16.6); two pouches above 40 mg (43.4 and 47.5 mg, both printed as 50 mg per pouch); pH median 8.8; free-base share median 86%. Nitrosamines (ng per pouch, Table 2): detected in 26 of 44 nicotine pouches; NNN in 24 (9 below the quantification limit of about 0.4), highest 12.9 (text) or 13 (table); NNK in 3 (0.5, 0.9, 5.4); NAT in 6 (3 below the quantification limit), highest 2.7; NAB in 5 (2 below the quantification limit), highest 5.6. Counted from Table 1 by the AI reader (not stated in the text): 8 of 44 pouches under 5 mg, 19 above 10 mg, 8 above 20 mg; among the 12 products with a milligram figure and its unit printed, measured content was at or below the printed figure in 11 (up to about 40% below) and above it in 1 (7.09 against 6 mg).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (a laboratory screening).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 46 products are listed in Table 1 and every product with a detected nitrosamine in Table 2. The supplement with validation data and the toxicity-category calculation was not read; Figures 2 and 3 (images) were not read.
analysis.power: Not applicable (no tests). The sample is a convenience sample of 46 products.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a convenience sample of 46 pouches bought online in 2021, nicotine ranged from 1.79 to 47.5 mg per pouch (median 9.48); most extracts were alkaline with a calculated free-base share around 86%; 15 of 44 nicotine-containing products printed a milligram content, 38 used a score or word for strength, 4 gave no indication, and the contents behind the scores were neither explained nor shared between brands (a product scored 1 of 5 held 7.14 mg while products scored 5 of 5 held 5.72 to 6.66 mg, Table 1); traces of tobacco-specific nitrosamines (up to about 13 ng NNN and 5.4 ng NNK per pouch) were found in 26 products, mostly at or near the quantification limit, from one analysis of one pouch each. Nothing was measured in people, and no snus, nicotine replacement product or cigarette was measured in the same study.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract and Conclusion: some pouches' nicotine content 'alarmingly high'; nitrosamines in the pouches 'of serious concern'; strength labels 'misleading'; pouches 'may potentially be a reduced risk alternative' for people who smoke or use some other oral tobacco products. Discussion: the contents are 'expected to induce and maintain addictive behaviour'; nicotine is toxic on ingestion; with an assumed 60% uptake the lowest-content pouch exceeds a food-regulation reference dose 22-fold; the nitrosamine amounts are much lower than in most cigarettes and in snus but 'still problematic'. Gaps: (1) addictiveness, toxicity and uptake were not measured, and the 22-fold figure is an extrapolation from content using an uptake share from another study; (2) 'serious concern' about nitrosamines rests on trace amounts from a single analysis, while the Discussion itself says the amounts are much lower than in cigarettes and snus; (3) 'misleading' rests on missing and non-comparable strength indicators, not on printed milligram figures being wrong (11 of 12 with a unit were at or below the printed figure, counted from Table 1); (4) the comparison with snus, replacement products and cigarettes uses other studies' figures on other bases, such as smoke yield per cigarette under an intense puffing regime. In the authors' favour, they state the single measurement, the unsteady precision at the lower limit and that the effect on public health is unclear.

timeline.event: Earlier laboratory analyses described in this paper's Discussion (not read): a study of pouches from larger US brands found up to 6.73 mg nicotine per pouch with a similar free-base share, and a manufacturer's study found up to 11.9 mg per pouch and no nitrosamines quantified, with a quantification limit the authors call much less sensitive than theirs.

Laboratory comparison of harmful constituents in two variants of one pouch brand with snus, moist snuff and nicotine replacement products, designed and funded by the maker of that brand, whose employees wrote it; no nitrosamines quantified in the pouches at a limit of 0.01 microgram per gram (see its card).
Scoping review of pouch studies reports analyses of pouch contents from the US and Germany and separates findings by industry funding.

replication.where_it_stands: A single laboratory survey of one set of products. Nobody has re-measured these products; other laboratories have measured other products with different ranges, so the contents are best read as a description of what could be bought, not as a fixed property of pouches.

funding.funder: Intramural funding of the German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR), SFP grant no. 1322-772, as printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none declared (as printed). Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed.
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors are in the BfR Department of Chemical and Product Safety, Berlin. The Introduction says the institute was asked by the German Federal Ministry of Food and Agriculture to assess potential risks of new nicotine pouches, and this chemical characterisation was the first step of an intramural project (Introduction, 5th paragraph). No tobacco, vape or pouch industry funding is stated; the paper notes that most earlier pouch studies were done by manufacturers (Introduction, 4th paragraph).

what_would_settle_it: Replicated measurements (several packs and batches per product, blanks and spiked controls, results shown with and without recovery correction) of nicotine, nitrosamines and other constituents in a sales-weighted sample of pouches, measured in the same laboratory beside snus, nicotine replacement products and cigarettes, and repeated over time; plus measurements in people who use pouches (nicotine uptake, blood and urine markers of nicotine and nitrosamines) beside people who smoke, people who use snus and people who use no nicotine.

domains.note: Convenience sample of 46 products bought online in 2021 from 20 producers; not weighted by sales; packs or batches per product not stated. It describes what could be bought then, not what is mostly used.

Adapted WHO method, triplicate means with standard deviations, validation reported; mean recoveries up to 126.1% with no statement in the main text on correction; extract pH measured in water that was not degassed; free-base share calculated, not measured.

One pouch per product, a single screening analysis; NNN below the quantification limit in 9 of 24 positive products; recoveries 110% to 127%; the authors state unsteady precision at the lower limit. The two nicotine-free products showed none, a weak negative control.

Visual inspection with no second checker described; Table 1 omits the unit for three printed values (20, 20 and 25 mg); the comparison of scores and words with measured content is in Figure 3 (an image, not read).
No snus, replacement product or cigarette was measured; the Discussion's comparisons come from other studies on other bases (per pouch against smoke yield per cigarette).
Two counts differ by one from the tables; evaluative words in the abstract go further than what was measured; the main text itself is open about the single nitrosamine measurement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for a laboratory analysis of commercial products (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to this design; the overall judgment cannot be less severe than the worst domain. The nicotine, pH and label results are transparent and sound within a non-representative sample, while the nitrosamine amounts and the comparison with other products are weak. Citable for the measured nicotine content and labelling of these 46 products in 2021 and for traces of nitrosamines in some of them; not for contents of the market as a whole, exact nitrosamine amounts, uptake, harm, or a ranking against snus, replacement products or cigarettes.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 46 pouch products from 20 producers bought January to May 2021 from online shops (German or shipping to Germany); 44 contained nicotine and 2 were labelled nicotine-free. Nicotine, pH, weight and four tobacco-specific nitrosamines were measured; label content and warnings were recorded.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Material and methods › Nicotine pouches, chemicals and standard substances, 1st paragraph; Results › Product labelling, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nicotine content ranged from 1.79 to 47.5 mg per pouch, median 9.48 mg (interquartile range 5.50 to 16.6); two pouches (numbers 45 and 46) held more than 40 mg; median pouch weight 0.643 g. No nicotine was detected in the two nicotine-free products.
key_findings.locator: Results › Nicotine contents, pouch weights and pH of extracts, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: A convenience sample; the authors say the higher contents than earlier studies of large US brands partly reflect the inclusion of small online brands.

key_findings.finding: All but one extract was alkaline; median pH 8.8 (interquartile range 8.2 to 9.8; range 5.5 to 10.5); calculated free-base share median 86% (interquartile range 62% to 98%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Nicotine contents, pouch weights and pH of extracts, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The free-base share is calculated from extract pH with a published pKa, not measured, and the water was not degassed.

key_findings.finding: Labelling: of the 44 nicotine-containing products, 15 printed the nicotine content in milligrams per pouch or per gram; 38 used a score or a word for strength (29 scores, 28 words by the text); 4 gave no strength indication; all but 3 carried a warning for people under 18 and 10 a warning against use in pregnancy. The authors say the contents behind the scores are neither explained nor harmonised between brands.
key_findings.locator: Results › Product labelling, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Relationship between labelled and measured nicotine contents, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Some products with a measured content above 16.7 mg per gram (the EU threshold for the 'toxic' pictogram) carried neither that pictogram nor the 'harmful' one. Counted from Table 1 by the AI reader: 16 pouches were above 16.7 mg per gram; 7 of the 44 carried the 'toxic' pictogram, 23 the 'harmful' one and 14 neither.
key_findings.locator: Results › Product labelling, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Tobacco-specific nitrosamines were detected in 26 of the 44 nicotine pouches (none in the two nicotine-free ones): NNN in 24 (9 below the quantification limit), NNK in 3, NAT in 6, NAB in 5. Highest per pouch: NNN 12.9 ng, NNK 5.4 ng, NAT 2.7 ng, NAB 5.6 ng. Results were mostly below or close to the quantification limits and come from a single analysis of one pouch per product.
key_findings.locator: Results › TSNAs in nicotine pouches, 1st paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Comparison figures given by the authors but not measured in this study: up to 1190 ng NNN and 120 ng NNK per pouch of spit-free snus; 2 ng NNN per gram of a nicotine gum in a 2005 study and none in a lozenge; 33 to 323 ng NNN and 40 to 246 ng NNK per cigarette in smoke under an intense puffing regime. The authors conclude the pouch amounts are much lower than most cigarettes and snus, but 'still problematic' next to the traces in replacement products.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Other studies, other measurement bases (content per pouch against smoke yield per cigarette); not a head-to-head result.

key_findings.finding: Authors' reading: the nicotine content of some pouches is 'concerning' and expected to induce and maintain dependence; with an assumed uptake of 60% of the content, a 60 kg person's reference dose for nicotine in food would be exceeded 22-fold by the lowest-content pouch; pouches are 'under discussion' as a risk-reducing alternative to smokeless tobacco or smoking because of lower toxicant levels, but the overall effect on public health is unclear and the appeal to young people unknown. They call for limits on nicotine, labelling in milligrams per pouch, purity and quality control, and research on uptake.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st, 5th and 6th paragraphs and the list that follows; Conclusion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Interpretation, not measurement: uptake, dependence and toxicity were not studied here.

key_findings.finding: Earlier laboratory studies described by the authors: up to 6.73 mg per pouch in larger US brands, and up to 11.9 mg per pouch in a manufacturer's study, in which no nitrosamines were quantified in the four pouches investigated (a quantification limit of 10 ng per gram, less sensitive than this study's). The authors say most earlier studies were done by manufacturers.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Key messages box

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls some nicotine contents 'alarmingly high' and nitrosamines 'of serious concern'. The paper measured contents only: nothing in people, no uptake, no health outcome, no comparison product. Its own Discussion says the nitrosamine amounts, mostly at or near the quantification limit from a single analysis, are much lower than in most cigarettes and snus.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite for measured content; the evaluative words are the authors' opinion and carry no measured harm.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says labels of nicotine strength 'on most products are misleading'. The results show missing or non-comparable strength indicators; where a milligram figure with a unit was printed, measured content was at or below it for 11 of 12 products (counted from Table 1), with one product 18% above.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › Product labelling; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding is that labels are mostly uninformative or not comparable between brands, not that printed milligram figures were wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts in the text differ by one from the tables: descriptors of strength on '28 products' in Results, 27 rows with a word in Table 1; NNN or NNK 'quantifiable' in '17 products' in the Discussion, 18 in Table 2 (15 with a quantified NNN, 3 with a quantified NNK, none in common).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Product labelling, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Tables 1 and 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use the table values.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives no unit for three printed nicotine values ('20 mg', '20 mg', '25 mg'); the two '20 mg' products measured 5.72 and 6.24 mg per pouch (17.8 and 18.7 mg per gram) and the '25 mg' product 27.9 mg per pouch.
reporting_issues.consequence: The labelled-against-measured comparison cannot be read from the table for these three; a per-gram label would fit the two '20 mg' products.
