key_findings.locator: Chapter 14 › Main findings › Use of heated tobacco products in England, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Chapter 14 › Main findings › Cochrane review, 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Chapter 14 › Implications, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Harm perceptions (Chapter 15). In 2021, 44.7% of 11 to 18 year olds (ASH-Y) accurately perceived vaping as less harmful than smoking, 32.4% thought the harms about the same, 3.6% more harmful and 19.3% did not know; among adults who smoke (Smoking Toolkit Study) 34.1% accurately perceived vaping as less harmful, 32.1% about the same, 11.9% more harmful and 22% did not know. 13.9% of adults who smoke or vape (ASH-Adult) correctly said that none or a small amount of smoking's risk came from nicotine. A systematic review of 32 articles (29 studies) found that information about the reduced harms of vaping relative to smoking raised the perception that vaping is less harmful, information about absolute harms raised perceptions that vaping is harmful, and the US EVALI outbreak raised harm perceptions, including inaccurate ones relative to smoking; 21 studies found that perceptions predicted later vaping and, in limited evidence, smoking behaviour. The Summary states 'Risk of bias was high for all included studies'.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 15 › Main findings › Young people’s harm and other perceptions of vaping in England, 1st paragraph; Chapter 15 › Main findings › Adult smokers’ and vapers’ harm perceptions of vaping in England, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 15 › Main findings › Interventions to change perceptions, 1st paragraph; Chapter 15 › Main findings › Vaping harm perceptions predicting changes in behaviour, 1st and 13th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusions (Chapter 16). The authors write that weaknesses in the choice of assessments and biomarkers, populations, groups and exposure, and study designs 'all limit the conclusions that we can draw'. They restate their 2015 statement that vaping 'is at least 95% less harmful than smoking' (smoking at least 20 times more harmful) and write that the estimate 'remains broadly accurate' at least over short term and medium term periods, while noting that summarising relative risks across products, behaviours and biomarkers 'can be simplistic and misinterpreted'; they suggest the statement that vaping poses 'only a small fraction of the risks of smoking' may be a better summary and repeat that vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked. They list 61 evidence statements (not printed on the pages read) that follow the National Academies' level definitions and involve 'a great deal of expert judgement'. Research recommendations include a common set of biomarkers, standard definitions of who is studied, agreed protocols and pre-registration. Implications: the authors say evidence from stop-smoking services and the Cochrane living review (not covered in their report) shows that vaping is effective for stopping smoking; higher absolute exposure than not using nicotine reinforces discouraging uptake by people who have never smoked; since the July 2021 cut-off new studies have been published, and the authors recommend a continual updating approach.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 16, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 16 › Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 16 › Recommendations for research, 1st paragraph; Chapter 16 › Overall implications, 1st, 2nd and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Main findings page (a separate GOV.UK page). It calls the report 'the most comprehensive to date', with a main focus on 'a systematic review of the evidence on the health risks of nicotine vaping', and says it 'provides the most robust evidence on health risks of vaping to date'. Overall conclusions (four bullets): in the short and medium term vaping poses a small fraction of the risks of smoking; vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked; evidence is mostly limited to short and medium term effects and studies of vaping for more than 12 months are necessary; more standardised methods would improve interpretation. Biomarkers of toxicant exposure: significantly lower exposure to harmful substances from vaping than from smoking, as shown by biomarkers associated with the risk of cancer, respiratory and cardiovascular conditions; similar or higher exposure than from not using nicotine products; no significant increase of toxicant biomarkers after short-term secondhand exposure to vaping among people who do not smoke or vape. Biomarkers of potential harm: only limited conclusions could be drawn, but 'better-run studies' of short and medium term risks 'found no major causes of concern'. Vaping among adults who have never smoked 'remained very low' (0.6% to 0.7% in 2021).
key_findings.locator: Main findings page › 1. The review, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2. Health risks, 1st paragraph; 2.1 Overall conclusions, 1st to 4th bullets; 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure, 1st to 3rd bullets; 2.3 Biomarkers of potential harm, 2nd and 3rd sentences of the paragraph; 3.2 Adults, 3rd bullet

reporting_issues.issue: Follow-up beyond 12 months is described three ways. Chapter 7 says follow-up in the exposure review ran from 8 days to 12 months and that 'we were unable to summarise findings on longer term' vaping exposure. Chapter 5 cites 'medium to longer term studies (up to 2 years)' for nicotine exposure. Chapter 10 rates exposure as lower for vaping than smoking with moderate evidence at 'long-term exposure (more than 12 months)'. The studies behind the longer periods are not named on the pages read.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 7 › Evidence reviewed, 6th paragraph; Chapter 5 › Main findings › Nicotine intake, 4th paragraph; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Biomarkers of respiratory diseases, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: For follow-up length, the safe statement is that the pooled exposure analyses cover up to 12 months; any longer-term exposure result in the Summary needs the full report's tables before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 10 reports that spirometry showed no detrimental effects at acute, short-to-medium or long-term (more than 12 months) exposure. A few paragraphs later it concludes there is 'insufficient evidence' from spirometry, FeNO, oscillometry, bronchoscopy and imaging on whether vaping affects lung function at those durations. The first reads as a finding of no effect; the second says the studies cannot tell.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 10 › Main findings › Respiratory tests and imaging, 2nd and 6th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the insufficient-evidence conclusion for lung function. The no-detrimental-effects sentence describes what small, mostly short studies found; it is not evidence that there is no effect.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 10 says there was 'limited evidence that vaping negatively affects lung function among adults with asthma', but its Conclusions section says differences in designs, diagnoses and measurements in the asthma studies 'prevent us from making any conclusions'.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 10 › Main findings › Asthma, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Conclusions, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The asthma result is at most a limited signal of harm from 4 small studies; the Summary does not make clear whether its authors treat it as a conclusion.

reporting_issues.issue: The COPD section gives spirometry results from two articles drawn from one group of patients (small numbers) and then states 'limited evidence' for fewer COPD exacerbations; exacerbations are not among the results listed. The Conclusions add that improvements 'seem mainly to be among participants who switched to exclusive vaping', a subgroup finding. The Summary says the update is the 5-year follow-up reported 'by the same study group' that supplied the National Academies' limited-evidence conclusion, so it adds follow-up of one cohort, not a second cohort.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 10 › Main findings › Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Conclusions, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat COPD improvement after switching as one small cohort followed for up to 5 years, with spirometry results given and the exacerbation result not shown in the Summary.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 8 says larger studies found lower HDL cholesterol in people who use no nicotine than in people who vape and smoke; Chapter 11 says that in large samples HDL was significantly higher in people who use no nicotine than in people who vape and smoke. The studies are not named. Higher HDL in people who do not smoke is the usual direction, so Chapter 8 may have the direction reversed (reader's inference).
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 8 › Main findings › Oxidative stress, 3rd paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Cholesterol, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite neither sentence for the direction of HDL differences. Chapter 8's two pooled cross-sectional analyses, which found no difference in HDL between people who vape and either comparison group, are the only consistent statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The Main findings page says that 'better-run studies' of short and medium term risks 'found no major causes of concern'. The Summary does not say which studies were judged better run, how, or how many. Its chapters say most studies had methodological concerns (Chapters 7, 8, 10 and 11), rate lung-function evidence insufficient, and say most of the biomarker-of-harm studies 'cannot inform us about the medium or long term' risks.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 7 › Implications › Methodological improvements needed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 8 › Implications › Need to distinguish between biomarkers of potential harm from smoking or vaping from other sources, 1st paragraph; Chapter 10 › Main findings › Respiratory tests and imaging, 6th paragraph; Main findings page › 2.3 Biomarkers of potential harm, 3rd sentence of the paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: For biomarkers of potential harm, cite the chapter-level statements with their evidence levels, not the sentence about better-run studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 16 says the 'at least 95% less harmful' estimate 'remains broadly accurate' for the short and medium term. The pages read show no calculation from the review's results to that figure: the pooled reductions printed for individual exposure biomarkers run from 58% to 94%, nicotine exposure does not differ significantly from smoking in five pooled comparisons, some markers are higher than in people who use no nicotine, and no disease outcome is pooled. The authors themselves say such summaries 'can be simplistic and misinterpreted' and that their evidence levels involve 'a great deal of expert judgement'.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Tobacco specific nitrosamines, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Volatile organic compounds, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 16 › Evidence statements, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the figure as the authors' judgement, with their qualifiers (short and medium term; not risk-free), and not as a result of this review's analyses.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 8 concludes that switching 'might improve endothelial function in the longer-term'. The only supporting human study described is a single RCT of 4 weeks (Chapter 11 says 'after one month'). Chapter 11 says pulse wave velocity may improve after a sustained switch but 'the longest follow-up reported was only 4 months'. The Main findings page calls studies of vaping for more than 12 months necessary.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 8 › Main findings › Endothelial function, 3rd and 7th paragraphs; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Endothelial function, 1st paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Peripheral resistance and arterial stiffness, 1st paragraph; Main findings page › 2.1 Overall conclusions, 3rd bullet
reporting_issues.consequence: In this review 'longer-term' for these outcomes means 1 to 4 months, not the more than 12 months the authors elsewhere call necessary.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 16 refers to 61 evidence statements that are not printed on the pages read. Level words appear in the chapter text (for example 'conclusive evidence' of lower carcinogen exposure; substantial evidence of comparable nicotine exposure in experienced adults; moderate evidence of similar exposure up to 2 years) without the number of studies, designs or risk-of-bias ratings behind each, and the authors say the framework involves expert judgement.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 16 › Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 5 › Main findings › Nicotine intake, 4th paragraph; Chapter 9 › Main findings › Cancer risks, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite a level word together with the counts and designs given in the same chapter, and check the numbered statement in the full report before relying on its wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The review's two questions, as printed in Chapters 7 and 10, concern biomarkers associated with the risk of disease and disease outcomes in people with existing conditions. Neither question asks about new disease in people who did not already have it. Chapter 11 nevertheless says that 'to date there is still no available evidence' on clinical cardiovascular outcomes. The Summary names no individual study, so it is unknown whether cohort or cross-sectional studies of heart or lung disease were searched for or excluded. A PATH Study cohort report of new respiratory conditions had been published before the July 2021 cut-off (card sc_xie_2020), and one on cardiovascular disease after it (card sc_berlowitz_2022).
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 7 › Evidence reviewed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 10 › Evidence reviewed, 1st paragraph; Chapter 11 › Main findings › Comparisons with other reports, 1st paragraph; Chapter 16 › Overall implications, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: 'No available evidence' here describes what this review found with its questions and cut-off; it should not be cited as meaning that no such studies exist. Whether such studies were searched for is in the unread Methods.

design_detail: Commentary (Drug and Alcohol Review 2022;41(7):1493–1498; received 12 May 2022, revised 19 June 2022, accepted 25 June 2022), four authors. About two and a half printed pages of text in six numbered sections (introduction; vaping and smoking cessation; vaping as a gateway to smoking; comparative harms of vaping and smoking; net public health effects of vaping; conclusion), one figure (US high-school smoking and vaping trends, drawn from CDC youth survey data), 54 references and a conflict-of-interest statement; no funding statement. No data, methods or search. Its target is the 2022 report to the Australian Department of Health by Banks and colleagues, 'Electronic cigarettes and health outcomes: systematic review of global evidence' (its reference 1, not read), the report on which the 2023 journal article in this library is based (card sc_banks_2023); the 2023 article appeared later and is not discussed. Every study cited is known here only as this commentary describes it. Commentary appraised with the editors' checklist.
can_establish: What four Australian authors argued in 2022 against the Australian report's conclusions and methods: that it did not compare the harms of vaping with those of continuing to smoke, did not weigh net population effects, underrated the trial evidence on stopping smoking, read the link between youth vaping and later smoking as causal while setting aside observational evidence on quitting, and gave weight to self-reported nicotine-only cases in the 2019 lung-injury outbreak; and which evidence they cite for each point.
cannot_establish: Whether the report's conclusions are wrong (the commentary appraises none of the evidence it cites and describes no search); how much less harmful vaping is than smoking, or what vaping does to rates of heart disease, lung disease or cancer (it cites no study of disease incidence, and its cancer figure is a modelled estimate as cited); and whether the 2023 journal article answered or changed any of the points (not discussed).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the authors say they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings (Introduction, 4th paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The 54 references are chosen to set out evidence against the report. For the health effects of switching from smoking, seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited for cardiovascular and respiratory benefit (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42) and one of the two cell studies (reference 44) share authors: at least one of Polosa, Caponnetto, Cibella, Campagna, Morjaria and Caruso appears in each author list as printed; the two others are a four-week switching study (reference 37) and an online survey of airway infections (reference 43). Cancer risk is cited to two studies that, by their titles, estimate risk from emissions (references 49 and 50); youth trends to US survey data and simulation models; quitting to trials, a network meta-analysis, reviews of cohort studies and population surveys. No study of the incidence of heart attack, stroke, chronic lung disease or cancer in people who vape is cited.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, except that the lung-injury paragraph turns on whether people who reported using only nicotine products had also used THC products (Comparative harms, 10th paragraph).

comparison.controls: No comparison of its own. The commentary argues that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine compares it with the much greater risk of continuing to smoke, because most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (Comparative harms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The journal version of the review it critiques takes people who neither smoke nor vape as the main comparison and gives its reasons (card sc_banks_2023).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: None.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is argued from the toxicant content of aerosol against smoke, exposure biomarkers, short-term cardiovascular and respiratory measures after switching, cell studies and modelled cancer potency; the net public health effect from simulation models; effectiveness for quitting from trials, meta-analyses and surveys.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Figures as cited: the 2021 Cochrane review, moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement therapy (RR 1.53); one trial in people unable to stop smoking by conventional methods, relative risk 6.4 (95% CI 1.5 to 27.3, p = 0.01) at 6 months against nicotine replacement; a network meta-analysis of 171 trials ranking vaping the most effective single treatment, with a wide interval; people who vape daily two to eight times more likely to stop smoking than people who smoke and do not vape; fewer than 1 in 100 adults in Australia who had never smoked vaped in the previous 12 months (2019); smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals against fewer than 100 detectable chemicals in aerosols; 14% of EVALI patients denied using THC; lifetime cancer risk from vaping estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking; no evidence of harm in studies up to 2 years in the Cochrane review (few studies); in one US model 1.8 million premature deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060; in one UK estimate 50,000 additional people stopped smoking with a vaping product in 2017. Figure 1 labels, read from the image: past-30-day smoking among US high-school students 22.3% in 2004 and 1.9% in 2021, a decline of '1% per year' from 2004 to 2013 and '1.4% per year' from 2013 to 2021; past-30-day vaping 27.5% at its 2019 peak and 11.3% in 2021.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: By its own statement the commentary sets out only evidence inconsistent with the review. Harms rated in the review's 2023 journal version (card sc_banks_2023), such as dependence, poisoning, burns and acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure in people who smoke, are not discussed, and no cited study is appraised.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data. The commentary argues, from 54 references, that the report did not compare vaping with continuing to smoke; did not consider net public health effects (all but one of the simulation models cited find benefits exceed harms); rated the trial evidence on quitting as limited where the 2021 Cochrane review rated it moderate certainty; used 'evidential double standards', reading observational associations between youth vaping and later smoking as causal while setting aside observational and population evidence on quitting, although in the authors' reading adjusted studies and population trends point to a common liability or to diversion from smoking; and gave weight to the 14% of lung-injury patients who reported only nicotine products, a self-report the authors consider unreliable. On harm it cites lower toxicant content and exposure, short-term cardiovascular and respiratory improvements after switching (mostly from studies sharing authors), cell studies and a modelled cancer risk, and it says that human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited and that the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion (p. 1495) states that, contrary to the review, the evidence suggests vaping nicotine is an effective aid to stopping smoking, substantially less harmful than smoking tobacco, diverting young people away from smoking, and likely to bring a major net public health benefit if widely available to adults in Australia who smoke. Gaps: (1) 'substantially less harmful' rests on exposure, short-term and modelled evidence, the kinds the review set aside for clinical outcomes, and no study of disease incidence is cited; (2) the diversion claim rests on population time trends and survey comparisons, associations of the kind the authors say the review over-read for the gateway; (3) the statement that lower biomarkers in people who switch confirm harm reduction is cited to two studies that, by their titles, compare exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional (references 30 and 31); (4) the sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites two human studies (references 39 and 40, by their titles) and no animal study; (5) the overlap of authors behind most of the switching evidence is not mentioned. The 2023 journal version of the review states that the uptake findings were similar after adjusting for factors including risk-taking (Results › Smoking behaviour, 1st paragraph, in the saved PMC text read for card sc_banks_2023), which the commentary, written about the 2022 report, does not address. In the authors' favour, they acknowledge the wide interval of the network meta-analysis, the mixed results of observational cohorts, limited human evidence on cardiovascular outcomes, possible risk from nicotine in people with heart disease, the unknown effects of flavourings and the small number of trials followed to 2 years.

timeline.event: BMJ analysis questioning the evidence behind the 2015 English report and the origin of its 95% figure; not cited by this commentary.
National Academies report: the starting point of the Australian review's umbrella part (card sc_banks_2023); not cited by this commentary.

Cochrane review update (Hartmann-Boyce et al., 2021): moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement therapy, RR 1.53 (as cited here; no reference record; not read).

Banks et al., report to the Australian Department of Health, 'Electronic cigarettes and health outcomes: systematic review of global evidence' (dated 7 April 2022 in reference 13 of the 2023 article): the target of this commentary (reference 1 here; no reference record; not read).
This commentary (received May, accepted June 2022).
UK evidence update stating that vaping carries a small fraction of the risks of smoking; published after this commentary was accepted and not cited by it.

Journal article based on the 2022 report: keeps 'limited evidence' for quitting with clinical support and 'strong evidence' for uptake of smoking by young people who vape; its text and reference list, as saved for card sc_banks_2023, do not cite this commentary.

replication.where_it_stands: A published critique of the Australian review that argues mainly about the question and the comparison (relative harm against continuing to smoke; net population effect) and about evidence standards, not with new data. On disease, it and the review do not disagree about rates of heart attack, stroke or cancer, which neither has; they disagree about which comparison and which kinds of evidence should count. No reply from the review's authors has been found: the 2023 journal article does not cite it.

funding.funder: No funding statement is printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Dr Colin Mendelsohn was a board member of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association (ATHRA), a registered health promotion charity, from October 2017 to January 2020, and Dr Alex Wodak is a board member of ATHRA. ATHRA accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry to get established; the funding ceased in March 2019. Mendelsohn and Wodak were directors of ATHRA in March 2018 when it received a donation from Knowledge Action Change Communications, a private sector public health agency in the UK; the donation was sourced from a surplus arising from the Global Forum on Nicotine conference in May 2017. Knowledge Action Change Communications is legally separate from Knowledge Action Change (KAC). KAC has received two grants from tobacco companies: in 2012 a small development research grant from Nicoventures (then owned by British American Tobacco) to evaluate a nicotine delivery device in Scottish prisons, conducted with the Scottish Prison Service and publicly declared; and in 2018 a grant from the Foundation for a Smoke-Free World, which is funded by an annual grant from Philip Morris International, specifically for preparing The Global State of Tobacco Harm Reduction report; under the Foundation's bylaws and pledge agreement, Philip Morris International and the tobacco industry are precluded from any influence over how the Foundation spends its funds or focuses its activities. Mendelsohn is the author of the book Stop Smoking Start Vaping (Aurora Press) and has never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; Wodak has never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies. Professors Wayne Hall and Ron Borland have no interests to declare.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations as printed: general practice, Sydney (Mendelsohn); St Vincent's Hospital Sydney, Alcohol and Drug Service (Wodak); University of Queensland, Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research, Brisbane (Hall); School of Psychological Sciences, University of Melbourne (Borland). None of the four appears among the authors printed in the reference list (lists are cut after six names). Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount: the commentary argues for wider access to vaping for adults who smoke, and two authors held governance roles in an association that took vape-retail seed funding until March 2019; both state they have never received payments from e-cigarette or tobacco companies, and the other two authors declare no interests.

what_would_settle_it: On the comparison: long-term cohorts that report disease and death separately for people who only vape, people who smoke, people who both smoke and vape, people who stopped smoking with and without vaping, and people who never used nicotine, so that the comparison with smoking and the comparison with no nicotine can both be read from the same data. On evidence standards: a rule set in advance, applied to both quitting and starting to smoke, on which designs count as causal evidence and how residual confounding is handled. On the lung-injury outbreak: product testing linked to cases rather than self-report.

domains.note: No search or criteria; the authors set out the evidence they find inconsistent with the review.

Cited studies are described, not appraised. Some statements carry no citation (most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers; faster declines in adult smoking in the UK and US); the biomarker statement cites two group comparisons of exposure; the in vitro and animal statement cites two human studies; the overlap of authors behind most of the switching evidence is not noted.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the four authors appears among the names printed in the 54 references (author lists are cut after six names).

Firm wording ('highly implausible', 'confirmed', 'diverting young people') rests on associations, time trends and modelling; some limits are acknowledged (wide interval, mixed cohort results, limited cardiovascular evidence, unknown effects of flavourings).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how harmful vaping is compared with smoking and with using no nicotine
domains.note: Only evidence favouring vaping for adults who smoke is presented, by design; harms such as dependence, poisoning, burns and acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure are not discussed, and the comparison with people who use no nicotine is not addressed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, as for the other critiques in this monograph (cards sc_eissenberg_2020 and sc_mckee_2015). The commentary is openly argued, says it sets out only evidence inconsistent with the review, and declares its authors' interests in detail; it is one side's case and appraises none of its sources. Cite it for what its authors argue about the review's question, comparison and evidence standards, never for the size of any harm or benefit; a claim resting only on it stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: The commentary critiques the review of vaping by Banks and colleagues funded by the Australian Department of Health, cited as the 2022 report to the Department (reference 1), whose stated aims were to examine contemporary evidence on the health outcomes of nicotine and non-nicotine e-cigarette use and to integrate it with systematic reviews on smoking uptake and cessation to guide policy and practice.
key_findings.locator: 1 Introduction, 1st paragraph; reference 1

key_findings.finding: In the authors' view the review failed its aims because it did not compare the relative risk of the harms of vaping with those of cigarettes, did not consider the net public health impact of vaping, ignored evidence that vaping is effective for stopping smoking, and confused causation and correlation for youth vaping and cigarette smoking. They add that it used 'evidential double standards', accepting a causal reading of observational associations for the gateway hypothesis while rejecting similar observational evidence on cessation, and took a sceptical attitude to trials showing that vaping helps people stop smoking. They state that they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings.
key_findings.locator: 1 Introduction, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Against the report's conclusion of limited evidence that, in the clinical context, freebase nicotine e-cigarettes may be more efficacious than nicotine replacement therapy, the authors cite the 2021 Cochrane review (moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement, RR 1.53), other meta-analyses that agree but differ in confidence, one trial in people unable to stop by conventional methods (relative risk 6.4, 95% CI 1.5 to 27.3, at 6 months), a network meta-analysis of 171 trials ranking vaping the most effective single treatment (they note its wide interval calls for larger trials), two reviews of higher-quality cohort studies after mixed cohort results, population surveys in Australia, the US and the UK, people who vape daily being two to eight times more likely to stop, and faster declines in adult smoking where vaping is more common (no source given for the last).
key_findings.locator: 2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 1st to 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Against the report's claim of strong evidence that e-cigarettes increase uptake of smoking in people who do not smoke, particularly young people, the authors argue that the association is most likely explained by a common liability to risk-taking; that more rigorous prospective studies adjusting for shared risk factors found the association largely disappears (one paper cited, reference 18); that population studies suggest vaping diverts young people from smoking, with US youth smoking falling faster from about the time vaping became popular (Figure 1, from CDC survey data: past-30-day smoking in high-school students 22.3% in 2004 and 1.9% in 2021); that most young people who vape smoked first and most vaping by people who have never smoked is experimental and transient; and that fewer than 1 in 100 adults in Australia who had never smoked vaped in the previous 12 months in 2019.
key_findings.locator: 3 Vaping as a gateway to smoking, 1st to 5th paragraphs (the 1st begins on p. 1493); Figure 1

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the review does not address relative risk, and that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine should compare it with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke tobacco, because the vast majority of people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (no source given).
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: They write that harm reduction from vaping rests on substantially lower exposure to toxins and carcinogens in vapour than in smoke (references 28 and 29) and is confirmed by considerable reductions in biomarkers of harm in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch (references 30 and 31); that smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals and solid particulate matter while vaping aerosols generally have fewer than 100 detectable chemicals, most at far lower concentrations (reference 29); that chemicals found in vapour but not in smoke do not appear to pose a significant hazard when inhaled (a 2020 UK Committee on Toxicity statement); and that the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown and could carry risk, with no harm shown so far and ongoing monitoring needed.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular: most effects of vaping are consistent with the known effects of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis); nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease; cardiotoxic constituents of smoke are absent from vapour or much lower (one review, reference 34). Human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited; two studies showed sustained falls in blood pressure in people who switched to vaping and one showed better vascular function after 4 weeks. Respiratory: vaping is likely to be far less harmful to the lungs (a narrative review), with improved symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer respiratory infections reported in people who switched. In vitro and animal studies are said to find effects generally far smaller than from smoke.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 6th to 9th paragraphs; references 34 to 45
key_findings.note: Seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited (references 35, 36, 38 to 42) and one of the cell studies (44) share authors; the in vitro and animal sentence cites references 39 and 40, which are human studies by their titles.

key_findings.finding: The authors call it highly implausible that nicotine vaping caused the 2019 US EVALI outbreak, which they say was strongly linked to vitamin E acetate added to black-market THC vaping oils and disappeared after it was removed from the illicit supply chain (CDC, reference 46); they argue that the 14% of patients who denied using THC and had vaped nicotine do not prove a link with nicotine products, because many patients who denied vaping THC were later found to have done so and no other causal agent has been identified in nicotine e-liquids (references 47 and 48; no numbers given).
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: On the basis of the reduced number and dose of carcinogens in vapour, lifetime cancer risk from vaping has been estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking (references 49 and 50, which by their titles estimate cancer potency or lung cancer risk from emissions and particle measurements); the Cochrane review detected no evidence of harm in studies up to 2 years, although the studies were few and longer ones are needed.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 11th and 12th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that the key public health question is the net population effect, a function of the harm difference between vaping and smoking, effectiveness for stopping smoking and uptake by people who smoke and who do not; that numerous modelling studies, with one exception, conclude benefits considerably exceed harms, evaluating net effects under a wide range of assumptions about uptake, quitting and the reduction in harm compared with smoking; one US model estimated 1.8 million premature deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060, and one UK estimate put the additional people who stopped smoking with a vaping product in 2017 at 50,000.
key_findings.locator: 5 Net public health effects of vaping, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: contrary to the review's conclusions, the authors write, the evidence suggests that vaping nicotine is an effective aid to stopping smoking, that vaping is substantially less harmful than smoking tobacco, that it is diverting young people away from smoking, and that vaping by people who smoke is likely to have a major net public health benefit if widely available to adults in Australia who smoke.
key_findings.locator: 6 Conclusion

key_findings.finding: The commentary does not mention the 95% figure or any other overall estimate of relative harm apart from the modelled cancer estimate, cites no study of the incidence of heart attack, stroke, chronic lung disease or cancer in people who vape, and does not engage with the reasons for the review's choice of comparison group or its exclusion of biomarker studies (both stated in the 2023 journal version, card sc_banks_2023).
key_findings.locator: Whole text (editors' reading)

key_findings.finding: Interests as printed: two authors were or are board members of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association, a registered health promotion charity that accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry until March 2019 and in March 2018 a donation from Knowledge Action Change Communications (legally separate from Knowledge Action Change, which has received a 2012 grant from Nicoventures, then owned by British American Tobacco, and a 2018 grant from the Foundation for a Smoke-Free World, funded by Philip Morris International); one author wrote the book Stop Smoking Start Vaping; both state they have never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; the other two authors have no interests to declare. No funding statement.
key_findings.locator: Conflict of interest

reporting_issues.issue: The biomarker sentence says reduced biomarkers of harm in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch confirm harm reduction, but the two studies cited (references 30 and 31) are, by their titles, comparisons of nicotine, carcinogen and toxicant exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1494 (4 Comparative harms, 3rd paragraph; references 30 and 31)
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as evidence of lower exposure in group comparisons, as cited, not of lower harm or of change within people who switched; the studies were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites references 39 and 40, which by their titles are human studies (a randomised cessation trial and a follow-up of people with asthma who switched); neither of the other two (44 and 45) is, by its title, an animal study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about animal studies has no animal study behind it in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Those who vape daily are two to eight times more likely to quit' is cited jointly to three studies (references 14 to 16), one of which is, by its title, a time-series analysis of national prevalence; which study gives which figure is not said.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1493 (2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 7th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be traced to a study from this text.

reporting_issues.issue: 'More rigorous prospective studies' in which the vaping-smoking association largely disappears are cited to a single paper (reference 18).
reporting_issues.page: p. 1494 (3 Vaping as a gateway, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: One re-analysis as cited, not a body of studies; not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The phrases attributed to 'the Banks review' ('limited evidence ... may be more efficacious' for quitting; 'strong evidence' for uptake of smoking) come from the 2022 report (reference 1); the 2023 journal version words these judgments differently (limited evidence that freebase nicotine e-cigarettes with clinical support are as efficacious as, or in Box 4 more efficacious than, nicotine replacement; strong evidence that young people who have never smoked or do not smoke and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking and to become regular smokers).
reporting_issues.page: p. 1493 (2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 1st paragraph; 3 Vaping as a gateway, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The critique should be described as a critique of the 2022 report; it cannot be assumed to quote the 2023 article.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf in the senior author's DrugEncyclopedia uploads (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493–1498: all six sections, Figure 1, the conflict-of-interest statement and the 54 references), text extracted once with pdftotext -layout; pages 1493 to 1496 checked on the rendered image (Figure 1 labels read from the image); none of the cited sources read, including the 2022 report it critiques. For the comparison with the 2023 journal article, the saved PMC text used for card sc_banks_2023 was searched.

design_detail: Consensus committee report (13 members; chair David L. Eaton) commissioned by the US Food and Drug Administration through a contract with the National Academies, to review the health effects of e-cigarettes, smoking initiation and cessation, and harm reduction. Chapter 2 says the committee's approach 'incorporated major attributes of systematic reviews': a six-database search (collection from 1 February to 31 August 2017, no limits on date, language or country), predefined inclusion criteria (peer-reviewed original research on humans, animals or cells), study assessment by one committee member followed by whole-committee discussion, and a narrative synthesis. Findings are worded on a six-level scale (conclusive, substantial, moderate, limited, insufficient, no available evidence) and listed as 47 numbered conclusions. No pooled estimate is reported; the committee calculated one risk ratio itself (Chapter 10). A population model (Chapter 19) projects possible net effects. The report says it did not systematically review the health effects of individual constituents (nicotine, humectants, certain metals), which it takes from other literature. AMSTAR 2 is used because the report states a systematic search and selection (Chapter 2, Literature Search; Appendix B, Literature Search; Box B-2) for the studies behind the conclusions used here (Chapters 4, 9, 10, 11 and 18).
can_establish: What an expert committee concluded, at what stated level of evidence, about each of 47 questions on e-cigarettes as of a literature collection that ended on 31 August 2017; which kinds of studies (designs, sizes, follow-up) sat under each conclusion; and which outcomes had no human studies at all.
cannot_establish: The size of any risk or of any difference between e-cigarettes and smoking (the level of evidence 'does not indicate the size, magnitude, or importance of the effect', Chapter 2); anything published after August 2017 (including the PATH Study cohort papers on heart and lung disease in this batch); which studies were excluded and why (no list or count is printed); the health effects of nicotine itself (not systematically reviewed); long-term effects, since the longest human health follow-ups described are one to two years.

sample.recruitment: Searches in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO (ProQuest), MEDLINE (Ovid) and Embase (Ovid) between 1 February and 31 August 2017 with the terms e-cigarette(s), electronic cigarette(s), electronic nicotine delivery, electronic nicotine device, vape, vaping and e-liquid (MeSH term added in PubMed and MEDLINE), plus special searches on dependence, smoking initiation, cessation (reviews and original studies) and smoking reduction. Appendix B gives the first series of six searches (1 to 6 February 2017) and the dependence search (14 July to 31 August) as five databases, the smoking-transition searches (to March or May 2017) as six or seven, and 641 further unique results from updates to 31 August. For smoking transitions the committee first assessed existing systematic reviews and then added newer studies. A professional research librarian helped; titles and abstracts were screened with criteria developed in a preliminary title-and-abstract review (Chapter 2, Literature Search; Appendix B, Literature Search).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Box B-2: human, animal or cell studies; exposure to e-cigarettes or their products; any physiological response or biological effect as outcome; peer-reviewed original research. For the harm-reduction chapter: studies of people who switched from smoking were included only if e-cigarette use was the treatment condition and smoking the positive control; studies that calculated risk from known toxicant risks in other settings were excluded; cross-sectional studies and case reports were excluded from the health-outcome analysis (15 longitudinal or crossover studies); studies that compared people who use e-cigarettes with historical data from other studies were excluded for dual use and secondhand exposure (Chapter 18, Evidence Review: Methods).
sample.demographics: Not summarised across the report. Chapter 9 gives mean ages of 23 to 39 years in the short-term clinical studies (healthy adults, mostly without hypertension or diabetes risk factors) and 33 to 54 years in the longer-term studies, with recruitment sites in Italy, Greece, Poland, Sweden and several US cities.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at report level; in the studies described, losses to follow-up were large in some (for example 17 of 40 in a 24-month study of people not intending to quit; the Catania cohort in Chapter 9 has 'a relatively large loss of study participants during follow-up').
sample.selection_effects: Literature collection ended on 31 August 2017 (the smoking-transition searches ran to March or May 2017, plus updates), so the report predates the large national cohorts (such as the PATH Study papers in this batch). Chapter 4 mentions nicotine-salt devices only briefly: a chemical analysis of one pod product, and a clinical pharmacokinetic study of a prototype developed by Philip Morris Products S.A. Most human studies were small, short and in healthy adults, mostly with first- or second-generation devices. Six of the 17 respiratory studies came from one research group, and most of the benefit studies from one region of Italy (Chapter 11). The committee prioritised human studies for its most structured assessments and used animal and cell studies as supporting evidence. Peer-reviewed papers only; no grey-literature or registry search is described.

exposure.measurement: E-cigarette devices and e-liquids as used in each study, from first-generation 'cigalikes' to tank and variable-power devices; exposure assessed by biomarkers of exposure (urinary nicotine equivalents, cotinine, the tobacco-specific nitrosamine metabolite NNAL, volatile organic compound metabolites, exhaled carbon monoxide), laboratory emissions, and in some cohorts by self-report.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Inhaled aerosol. In the study conditions read: e-liquid nicotine from none to 36 mg/ml in controlled sessions of 10 to 15 puffs or ad libitum use of 60 to 90 minutes; switching studies lasted from 5 days to 12 weeks (one randomized study of 48 people followed for 8 months), and observational cohorts up to 24 months. The Chapter 4 synthesis says nicotine yield increases with device power, e-liquid nicotine concentration and puff duration.
exposure.polysubstance: Chapters separate people who have never smoked, people who currently or formerly smoked, dual use and exclusive e-cigarette use; the report says dual use may confer benefit only if it is transitional and that the health effects of dual use over the long term are not known (Chapter 18). Cannabis vaping is not part of the report's scope.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Laboratory sessions often required hours of abstinence from smoking or e-cigarette use (Chapter 9). In free-living switching studies compliance was checked by exhaled carbon monoxide or self-report and was incomplete (in the 12-week Cravo trial 40.2% were compliant, defined as self-reported smoking no cigarettes on 80% or more of study days) (Chapter 4; Chapter 18).

comparison.controls: Varies by study: smoking as positive control, no use, nicotine-free e-cigarettes, sham puffing, nicotine replacement, and continued smoking. The committee's own list of preferred comparison groups for future studies is people who continue to smoke, people trying to quit with other evidence-based treatments, and people who use no tobacco products including e-cigarettes (Box S-4, Recommendation 15-2).
comparison.matching: Crossover designs in most short-term clinical studies; matching in a few cohorts (for example, a hypertension cohort matched for age, sex and blood-pressure stability). Not applicable at report level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Chapter 9 notes that the Moheimani 2017 comparison did not adjust for sociodemographic characteristics or cardiovascular risk factors; Chapter 10 notes no consideration of complete smoking history or confounders in the Manzoli data, and that the e-cigarette group in Franco 2016 was on average 10 years older than the other groups.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking history is the main concern raised in the chapters read. The respiratory chapter names dual tobacco or cannabinoid use, secondhand smoke exposure and prior tobacco use as confounders to consider (Chapter 11, Optimal Study Design, 2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Biomarkers of exposure and potential harm; heart rate, blood pressure, arterial stiffness, flow-mediated dilation; spirometry and symptom questionnaires; self-reported adverse events; in animals and cells, cytotoxicity, inflammation and DNA damage.
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was judged qualitatively (design, sample, comparison groups, statistics, outcome measures, confounding, loss to follow-up, sponsorship); no named risk-of-bias tool, per-study rating or reliability data are printed for the health-effect studies. For the Franco 2016 micronucleus study the chapter notes that evidence on the assay's reliability was not presented.
outcomes.operationalization: 'No available evidence' means no studies at all; 'insufficient' means mixed findings or a single poor study; 'limited', 'moderate', 'substantial' and 'conclusive' describe a direction of effect with increasing support (Box S-2; Chapter 2, Conclusions).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. The committee calculated one risk ratio itself, for 'any cancer' reported among serious adverse events over 24 months in the Manzoli cohort: 2/97 for e-cigarette only against 3/363 for smoking only, risk ratio 2.49 (95% CI 0.42 to 14.72), which the chapter calls 'extremely limited by sample size' and of low quality (Chapter 10). Ranges quoted from single studies include a fall in the urinary nitrosamine metabolite NNAL of 57% after one week and 64% after two weeks in 20 people who switched (Chapter 18). The conclusion levels themselves do not carry effect sizes.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at report level.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is described. The Statement of Task (summarised in Summary Box S-1; Chapter 1 not read) set the scope; inclusion criteria were developed through a preliminary title-and-abstract review (Appendix B); no deviations are discussed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be checked: no list or count of excluded studies, and the number of studies behind most conclusions is not stated. The sponsorship table for included studies is in an online supplement that was not read.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Human studies quoted for exposure and short-term health outcomes range from 13 to 420 people; the Manzoli cohort is given as 932 or 1,355, and a cross-sectional survey of college students (Loukas) as 5,468 (Chapters 9, 10, 11, 18).

interpretation_gap.results_show: As of studies to August 2017: no human studies of clinical heart disease, stroke or atherosclerosis (Conclusion 9-1), of cancer (10-1) or of respiratory disease (11-1) in people who use e-cigarettes; short-term rises in heart rate (substantial) and diastolic blood pressure (moderate) after nicotine intake; lower exposure to many toxicants and carcinogens in people who completely switched from smoking (conclusive) in studies of 13 to 420 people lasting 2 to 12 weeks; limited evidence of better lung function in adults with asthma and fewer exacerbations in adults with COPD after switching, mostly from one research group; moderate evidence of more cough and wheeze in adolescents in four cross-sectional studies; no available evidence (long-term) and insufficient evidence (short-term) on health outcomes in people who use both products.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary says laboratory tests, in vitro tests and short-term human studies 'suggest that e-cigarettes are likely to be far less harmful than combustible tobacco cigarettes', while 'the absolute risks of the products cannot be unambiguously determined' and long-term effects are not yet clear; it also says e-cigarette constituents are 'not inert' and likely to have some negative health effects on their own. The Chapter 18 synthesis says all but one human study showed significant short-term improvements in people who smoked and switched, and calls the improvement consistent across all studies, which is stronger than the studies it describes (see reporting issues). Statements about nicotine itself (minimal cancer risk; likely higher cardiovascular risk in people with existing heart disease) are not graded conclusions.

timeline.event: McKee and Capewell, 'Evidence about electronic cigarettes: A foundation built on rock or sand?' (BMJ), is cited by the committee in Chapter 18 for concerns about using e-cigarettes for harm reduction (continued use of a product with its own risks, possible increases in smoking, and terms of engagement with the tobacco industry). It was not read for this card.

McNeill and colleagues, Nicotine vaping in England: 2022 evidence update, commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; an independent review with a later search date (card sc_mcneill_2022).

Banks and colleagues' umbrella and systematic review takes this report as its starting point; 112 of its 400 publications come from it, so the two are not independent (card sc_banks_2023). It rates clinical heart disease and cancer 'no available evidence' and rates the certainty of cardiovascular and respiratory findings low or very low.

replication.where_it_stands: Not independently replicated as a review. A later umbrella review (Banks 2023) uses this report's studies as a base, so it is not independent of it. On clinical heart disease and cancer its 'no available evidence' ratings describe the 2017 literature; later cohort studies exist (see sc_berlowitz_2022 and sc_xie_2020) but were outside its search. A critique of the later review (Mendelsohn 2022) is listed in the library and was not read.

funding.funder: US Food and Drug Administration. The front matter on the book's landing page prints the sponsor statement: support under contract number HHSF223201610054C between the National Academy of Sciences and the US Department of Health and Human Services (Food and Drug Administration), and adds that opinions in the report do not necessarily reflect the views of any organization or agency that provided support. The FDA's Center for Tobacco Products asked the National Academies to convene the committee (Summary, opening, 7th paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: No statement of committee members' financial interests, or of how they were managed, appears in the pages read (landing page, committee list, Reviewers, Preface, Summary, Chapter 2, Appendix B, Appendix F biosketches). Appendix B says that where committee members co-authored studies under review, members who did not take part in the study reviewed them independently; committee members Goniewicz and St.Helen are authors of studies reviewed in Chapters 4, 5, 9, 10 and 18. Chapter 2 (footnote 3) and Appendix B say the committee recorded each study's sponsor (industry, government or federal agency, other, not stated) and any other industry involvement in an online table, which was not read. The Reviewers page lists one reviewer employed by British American Tobacco Research and Development Centre, as printed, and a reviewer (Hecht) who is an author of a study reviewed in Chapter 18. In the chapter text, some studies are named by commercial product (blu, SKYCIG, Vype ePen, Green Smoke) and one trial's product is described as developed by Fontem Ventures B.V.; the sponsors are in the unread table.
funding.affiliations_note: Committee members are from US universities and medical centres (Washington, South Carolina, Roswell Park, USC, Connecticut, Johns Hopkins, Michigan, Columbia, UC Davis, Harvard/MGH, Brown, UCSF), as printed in the committee list. The commissioning agency regulates e-cigarettes as tobacco products (Summary, opening, 7th paragraph).

what_would_settle_it: An update of the same review with a search beyond 2017 that includes the large longitudinal cohorts and any trials with clinical endpoints, with a registered protocol, duplicate screening, a published list of excluded studies, study-level risk-of-bias ratings, and comparison groups named in advance (people who continue to smoke, people using other cessation treatments, and people using no tobacco products). The committee itself lists such studies as research needs (Boxes S-3 to S-5).

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: The Statement of Task names populations (people who use the products, vulnerable groups, people exposed to secondhand aerosol), the exposure and the outcomes; Box B-2 lists exposure and outcome but no comparator. Comparison groups are chosen chapter by chapter.
No protocol is described; inclusion criteria were developed during a preliminary title-and-abstract review (Appendix B).

Chapter 2 and Appendix B explain the design hierarchy (randomized trials, controlled studies, prospective cohorts and crossover trials, case reports for injuries), why human studies were prioritised, and why animal and cell studies were used as supporting evidence.

Six databases, search terms and syntax printed (Boxes B-1A to B-7), no language or date limits; no reference-list, registry, grey-literature or expert search is described, and the databases differ between Chapter 2 (six for the whole period) and Appendix B (five for the first series).
Titles and abstracts were reviewed against criteria; the number of reviewers is not stated.

One committee member made the initial review of the studies for a set of outcomes, and the full committee then discussed each assessment (Chapter 2). That is a consensus check, not independent duplicate extraction as AMSTAR 2 defines it; a more lenient reader could judge it differently.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list, no count of full texts assessed or excluded, and no reasons are printed in Chapter 2 or Appendix B; only counts of unique search results are given.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Chapter text and Tables 4-2, 9-1, 9-2 and 11-1 give device, e-liquid, sample, setting, protocol, follow-up and outcomes (tables are images and were not extracted; the chapter text was read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Qualitative appraisal that names confounding, sampling, loss to follow-up, outcome operationalization and sponsorship (Appendix B, Quality Assessment); no tool is named and no per-study judgments are shown.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Chapter 2 (footnote 3) and Appendix B say sponsorship of every included study was recorded in an online supplement table, which was not read.
No meta-analysis; existing meta-analyses were assessed for the smoking-transition questions.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The level-of-evidence scale is tied to study quality and the chapters name limits of each body of evidence (for example Chapter 9: no adjustment for sociodemographic factors in some studies; Chapter 11: one research group, retrospective selection).
Differences between studies are discussed (for example heart-rate findings by device generation and nicotine delivery; inconsistent systolic blood pressure findings).
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed in the chapters read.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The FDA contract is printed; no statement of the committee members' own interests or of how they were managed was found in the pages read; Appendix B describes how studies co-authored by members were reviewed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 10 can be judged only from the online sponsorship table, which was not read; it is non-critical and cannot change the overall rating. The rating rests on two critical items judged 'no' from the pages read: no protocol (item 2) and no list or count of excluded studies (item 7). AMSTAR 2 was built for reviews of intervention trials and gives 'critically low' to any review with more than one critical flaw; here the flaws are reproducibility and reporting ones in a transparent consensus report, and the rating does not say the graded conclusions are wrong. The report may be cited for the committee's judgment and its stated level of evidence, for the kinds and sizes of studies under each conclusion, and for the places where it says no human studies existed (clinical heart disease, cancer, respiratory disease, long-term dual use); not for effect sizes, for completeness of the literature, for anything after August 2017, or as independent confirmation of the later reviews that start from it.

verification.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML of NBK507171 (nap24952), read 2026-10-18 in a browser tab: landing page (sponsor statement and suggested citation), committee list, Reviewers, Preface, Summary in full with Boxes S-1 to S-5, Summary Annex (all 47 conclusions), Chapter 2 in full, Appendix B in full with Box B-2, Appendix F (biosketches), Chapter 4 (nicotine exposure sections in detail, nicotine salts, synthesis), Chapter 5 (introduction, carbonyl compounds, minor alkaloids, tobacco-specific nitrosamines, other toxicants, synthesis, metals; not humectants or flavorings in full), Chapter 9 in full, Chapter 10 (opening, optimal study design, epidemiology, case reports and synthesis; the animal and in vitro sections only skimmed), Chapter 11 (human studies, synthesis and conclusions, vulnerable populations; the animal and in vitro sections only skimmed), Chapter 18 in full. Not read: Chapters 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12 to 17 and 19 to 21, Appendixes A, C, D and E, Boxes B-1A to B-1F and B-3 to B-7 (search syntax), the tables and figures (shown as images), the online sponsorship supplement and the PDF. Reader 72 reads Chapters 3 and 8.

key_findings.finding: Mandate and method: Chapter 2 says the Statement of Task charges the committee with a 'comprehensive and systematic assessment and review of the literature' (the Summary's Box S-1 words the task as a comprehensive review of the literature on constituents, human health effects, initiation and cessation, and harm reduction). The committee searched six databases between 1 February and 31 August 2017 with no date, language or country limits (3,494 unique results in the first series, plus special searches on dependence, smoking initiation, cessation and smoking reduction, and 641 more through updates), assessed studies against criteria developed in a preliminary screen, and states it 'identified more than 800 peer-reviewed scientific studies' for the report. The Preface says that, where feasible, the committee applied the most important attributes of systematic review methodology.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Box S-1; Chapter 2, 1st paragraph and Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Appendix B › Literature Search, all subsections; Box B-2; Preface, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Appraisal: one committee member made an initial review of all studies for a set of outcomes, then the whole committee discussed each assessment, weighing design, sample, setting, comparison groups, statistics, outcome measures, confounding, loss to follow-up, other sources of bias and sponsorship; studies co-authored by committee members were reviewed by members who did not take part; case reports and animal or cell studies were assessed by modified approaches; existing reviews of smoking transitions were assessed with methods adapted from published guidelines. No named tool, per-study rating or list of excluded studies is printed; the sponsorship of each included study is recorded in an online table.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 2 › Literature Review and Quality Assessment › Health Effects Literature, 1st to 3rd paragraphs and footnote 3; Smoking Transitions Literature, 1st paragraph; Appendix B › Quality Assessment (all subsections) and External Influences

key_findings.finding: Scale of evidence: conclusive (many supportive findings from good-quality controlled studies, no credible opposing findings), substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality observational studies or controlled trials), moderate (several findings from fair-quality studies), limited (supportive findings from fair-quality studies, or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion), insufficient (mixed findings or a single poor study; no conclusion can be made) and no available evidence (no studies). The committee states that the level 'does not indicate the size, magnitude, or importance of the effect' and that conclusions of insufficient or no available evidence 'do not imply a direction'. Across the 47 conclusions the Annex lists 8 conclusive, 10 substantial, 8 moderate, 12 limited, 4 insufficient and 5 no available evidence (reader's count of the Annex).
key_findings.locator: Summary › Box S-2; Chapter 2 › Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Summary Annex

key_findings.finding: Headline: laboratory tests of ingredients, in vitro tests and short-term human studies 'suggest that e-cigarettes are likely to be far less harmful than combustible tobacco cigarettes', but 'the absolute risks of the products cannot be unambiguously determined' and the long-term effects, of particular concern for young people who become dependent, are not yet clear. The Summary also says e-cigarettes contain constituents that are 'not inert' and likely to have some negative health effects on their own, and that, because the risks of smoking are so great, the net effect depends on the relationship between e-cigarette use and smoking as well as on the products' own risks. The net public health effect depends on three factors: effect on initiation of smoking by young people, effect on cessation by adults, and intrinsic toxicity. Final observations: compared with cigarettes, e-cigarettes contain fewer toxicants, can deliver nicotine in a similar manner, show significantly less biological activity in a number of in vitro, animal and human systems and might be useful as a cessation aid to people who use them exclusively; but young people who begin with e-cigarettes are more likely to move to smoking, e-cigarettes can explode, and e-liquids are dangerous and can be fatal. 'Much of the research on e-cigarettes suffers from methodological flaws', and many areas are unstudied.
key_findings.locator: Summary, opening paragraphs 1, 2 and 5; Summary › Final Observations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Context from national surveys (Summary): youth e-cigarette use in 2016 was substantially higher than cigarette smoking; adult use was relatively low compared with youth use and adult smoking; most adults who use e-cigarettes report currently using other tobacco products; few adults begin using e-cigarettes without already smoking. In the cardiovascular studies of Chapter 9, all participants were current smokers in seven studies and some were in five more.
key_findings.locator: Summary, opening paragraph 4; Chapter 9 › Evidence from Human Studies of Cardiovascular Effects, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nicotine exposure: highly variable and dependent on product and how the device is operated (Conclusion 4-1, conclusive); nicotine intake among adults experienced with e-cigarettes can be comparable to that from cigarettes (4-2, substantial). Behind them: 27 acute clinical studies of nicotine exposure (17 in people who smoke with no or little experience of e-cigarettes and 12 in people with experience; these add to 29, so two studies appear in both groups, a reader's inference), in which blood nicotine in people new to e-cigarettes was much lower than from their usual cigarettes and in experienced people could reach the range of a typical cigarette; and seven switching studies, of which three reported no significant change in nicotine exposure and four suggested that some e-cigarettes were ineffective nicotine delivery devices compared with cigarettes. The Chapter 4 synthesis adds that nicotine yield rises with device power, e-liquid nicotine and puff duration. The Summary states that nicotine causes dependence and addiction.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Constituents, 1st paragraph and Conclusions 4-1 and 4-2; Chapter 4 › Exposure to Nicotine and Nicotine Derivatives from E-Cigarettes, 3rd paragraph; Clinical Studies with E-Cigarette-Naive Smokers, 1st and last paragraphs; Clinical Studies in people experienced with e-cigarettes (the section after the one on people new to them), 1st and last paragraphs; Switching Studies, last paragraph; Synthesis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other toxicants: most products contain and emit numerous potentially toxic substances besides nicotine (5-1, conclusive); the number and amount vary widely with product and operation (5-2, conclusive); except for nicotine, under typical conditions of use, exposure to potentially toxic substances is significantly lower than from combustible tobacco cigarettes (5-3, substantial). Chapter 18 presents four direct comparisons: one calculation from published data found levels of selected toxicants in smoke 9 to 450 times those in aerosol, assuming 15 puffs per cigarette; one measured 150 chemicals and found toxicants 82 to more than 99% lower per puff in the e-cigarette aerosol; one found about 1,500 times more harmful or potentially harmful constituents in smoke; one compared 11 metals (higher in the aerosol for four, within the smoke range for five, lower for two). The Summary says that, taken together, the aerosol contains fewer numbers and lower levels of toxicants than smoke, and that exposure from flavorings and humectants depends on the characteristics of the person using the product and of the device.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Constituents, Conclusions 5-1 to 5-3 and closing paragraph; Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 1st paragraph; Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels in E-Cigarettes and Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and Synthesis

key_findings.finding: Nitrosamines and carbonyls: tobacco-specific nitrosamines were found in e-liquids and aerosol at low levels, 'typically at levels similar to' those in pharmaceutical nicotine products (the chapter says this is probably attributed to pharmaceutical-grade nicotine); one study of 12 brands found two nitrosamines in aerosol from all but three, and another, of three liquids, found none in 100-puff aerosol. Carbonyls such as formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein were found in aerosol and were in most cases lower than in smoke (for example 86 to 544 times lower for three carbonyls in one comparison), but very high formaldehyde levels were also reported, one study estimated formaldehyde exposure comparable to a cigarette, and levels varied widely between brands and between samples of the same product.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Tobacco-Specific Nitrosamines, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Carbonyl Compounds, 2nd to 11th paragraphs; Chapter 10, opening, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Metals: aerosol contains metals from the coil, other parts of the device and the liquid (5-4, substantial); the number of metals could be greater than in cigarette smoke, except for cadmium, which is markedly lower (5-5, limited). The chapter notes few, mostly small studies of first- and second-generation devices, metal levels that 'can be substantially high in some instances', one biomarker study of 64 people supporting an inhaled contribution to the internal dose of chromium and nickel, and no study of the health effects of metals from e-cigarettes except one cell study of copper nanoparticles.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Constituents, Conclusions 5-4 and 5-5; Chapter 5 › Metals, 6th and 8th paragraphs and Synthesis

key_findings.finding: Exposure falls when people switch completely (18-1, conclusive). The Synthesis says all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure to potentially toxic chemicals in people who substituted e-cigarettes for cigarettes, and that nicotine intake among people experienced with e-cigarettes was comparable to that from cigarettes. Examples: a 5-day randomized study of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29 to 95% lower and exhaled carbon monoxide 27 to 89% lower after partial or complete switching; people who used both products and replaced half their cigarettes had 7 to 38% reductions and 1 to 20% higher nicotine equivalents); 20 people switched for two weeks (NNAL 57% lower after one week and 64% after two; total nicotine and some polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites unchanged at one week); 40 people followed for four weeks, 33 of whom were using e-cigarettes at the end (48% only e-cigarettes, 52% both products; exhaled carbon monoxide 80% lower with e-cigarettes only and 52% lower with both products; the acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 79% and 60% lower); a cross-sectional comparison of 181 people in five groups (36 or 37 each) in which long-term exclusive e-cigarette use had lower NNAL than every other group, while nitrosamine and volatile-compound metabolites in people who used both products were similar to those in people who only smoked. Studies ranged from 13 to 420 people with follow-up of 2 to 12 weeks, apart from one randomized study of 48 people followed for 8 months. The 12-week trial of a manufacturer's product (developed by Fontem Ventures B.V., per Chapter 18) had 40.2% compliance in its unconfined phase.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Harm Reduction, Conclusion 18-1; Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 2nd to 10th paragraphs and Synthesis; Chapter 4 › Switching Studies, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Short-term health outcomes after complete switching (18-2, substantial). The Synthesis says all but one of the human studies showed significant short-term improvements in respiratory, cardiovascular and oral outcomes, in most studies in relatively small numbers of people; 21 of 27 in vitro studies and 3 of 5 animal studies favoured e-cigarettes as less harmful and none found them more harmful. One 2-week pilot of 20 people found a statistically significant increase in gum inflammation after switching. For people who keep smoking while using e-cigarettes: no available evidence on long-term illness or death compared with smoking only (18-3) and insufficient evidence on short-term outcomes (18-4); the chapter adds that on average they do not smoke fewer cigarettes (though among them e-cigarettes 'may help maintain smoking reduction') and that those who do not reduce smoking are very unlikely to reduce risk and may be exposed to additional effects of e-cigarettes.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Harm Reduction, Conclusions 18-2 to 18-4; Chapter 18 › Health Risk Profile, last paragraph (Wadia 2016); Toxicity in In Vitro and Animal Studies, 1st paragraph; Synthesis; Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Use E-Cigarettes Concurrently, Synthesis

key_findings.finding: Harm-reduction framing: the committee says e-cigarettes 'have not been theoretically or experimentally proven to be safe' but may be less harmful alternatives to smoking in at least some scenarios; those who switch completely would be expected to gain more than those who keep smoking, and dual use may confer benefit only if it is a transitional state; the evidence about harm reduction suggests that across a range of studies and outcomes e-cigarettes 'pose less risk to an individual than combustible tobacco cigarettes'.
