Modeling (Summary): a net public health benefit in the short run if adult cessation increases, substantially less and negative under some scenarios at 50 years, and net harm in the short and long terms if the products do not increase adult cessation.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 18, opening, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Summary › Harm Reduction, last paragraph; Summary › Modeling, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Heart and circulation: no available evidence whether e-cigarette use is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral artery disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis (9-1); heart rate rises shortly after nicotine intake (9-2, substantial); diastolic blood pressure rises (9-3, moderate); limited evidence for short-term rises in systolic blood pressure, oxidative stress markers, endothelial dysfunction, arterial stiffness and autonomic changes (9-4); insufficient evidence for long-term changes in heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac geometry and function (9-5). Behind them: 13 short-term clinical studies (2010 to 2017; mostly crossover; healthy adults aged 23 to 39 on average) and three longer studies (a 34-person cross-sectional study; a randomized cessation trial analysed as a cohort, 183 people; a record-based cohort of 89 hypertensive patients); none measured clinical or subclinical atherosclerosis outcomes. The chapter says the five studies finding no heart-rate change (2010 to 2014) used first- or second-generation devices with small or no rises in nicotine biomarkers, and the five finding a rise (2015 to 2017) used tank-style or participants' own devices or showed a nicotine rise; effects were generally smaller than with cigarettes but closer for some products with higher nicotine intake; diastolic pressure rises were similar in size to those after a cigarette.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Human Health Effects, Conclusions 9-1 to 9-5; Chapter 9 › Characterization of Disease Endpoints and Intermediate Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Evidence from Human Studies of Cardiovascular Effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Heart Rate, 1st paragraph and Synthesis; Blood Pressure, Synthesis; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Cancer: no available evidence whether e-cigarette use is associated with intermediate cancer endpoints in humans, compared with smoking or with no tobacco use (10-1); the chapter says the literature is 'devoid' of rigorous epidemiology on intermediate cancer endpoints, let alone cancer. The two human studies that refer to cancer were a 24-month cohort in which 'any cancer' was reported under serious adverse events (presumably self-reported; 2/97 e-cigarette only, 3/363 smoking only, 0/37 using both; committee-calculated risk ratio 2.49, 95% CI 0.42 to 14.72, called extremely limited by sample size and low quality) and a 65-person micronucleus study of cells scraped from the mouth (micronucleated cells 21% higher, and total micronuclei 133% higher, in people who used e-cigarettes than in people who neither smoked nor used them, against 160% and 633% higher in people who smoked; the e-cigarette group was on average 10 years older and the chapter notes no evidence on the assay's reliability). Limited evidence from animal studies using intermediate biomarkers that long-term use could increase cancer risk, and none from long-term animal bioassays (10-2); limited evidence of mutagenicity or DNA damage (10-3); substantial evidence that formaldehyde and acrolein can cause DNA damage (10-4), which supports biological plausibility but not a risk estimate. The statements about nicotine itself are not graded conclusions.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Human Health Effects, Conclusions 10-1 to 10-4; Chapter 10 › Optimal Study Design, 1st paragraph; Epidemiology, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Synthesis; Chapter 4 › Synthesis, 2nd paragraph; Summary › Constituents, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lungs: no available evidence whether e-cigarettes cause respiratory disease in humans (11-1); limited evidence for better lung function and symptoms in adults who smoke and have asthma after switching completely or partly (11-2) and for fewer COPD exacerbations (11-3), from small studies selected retrospectively, mostly one region of Italy, with the one randomized trial (12 weeks) finding no lung-function difference; moderate evidence for more cough and wheeze in adolescents and an association with asthma exacerbations (11-4), from four cross-sectional self-reported studies; limited animal and cell evidence of harm (11-5). The chapter says studies of long-term effects on chronic respiratory symptoms are 'completely lacking', that results are unclear whether use instead of smoking in people with COPD may be beneficial, neutral or harmful, and, in its synthesis, that nicotine-containing e-cigarettes can have short-term adverse effects on lung defences (mucociliary clearance, urge to cough, cough sensitivity; moderate evidence, not carried to a numbered conclusion). The Summary adds that use instead of smoking by people with existing respiratory disease 'might be less harmful'.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Human Health Effects, Conclusions 11-1 to 11-5 and closing paragraph; Chapter 11 › Clinical and Epidemiological Studies in Humans › the section on people who use combustible tobacco products, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Respiratory Symptoms in Adolescents; Synthesis and Conclusions, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Vulnerable/Susceptible Populations › COPD, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other conclusions listed in the Summary: acute endothelial cell dysfunction (7-1) and oxidative stress (7-2) substantial; symptoms of dependence on e-cigarettes substantial (8-1), dependence risk and severity lower than for cigarettes moderate (8-2), product characteristics an important determinant moderate (8-3); periodontal improvement after switching limited and oral cell damage limited (12-1, 12-2); pregnancy outcomes no available evidence and fetal development insufficient (13-1, 13-2); explosions, burns, poisoning from e-liquids and fatal exposure conclusive (14-1 to 14-3); indoor air nicotine and particulate matter conclusive (3-1) and nicotine and other constituents on indoor surfaces limited (3-2); secondhand nicotine and particulate exposure lower than from smoking, moderate (18-5). The Summary's closing statement on health effects: e-cigarettes are 'not without physiological activity in humans', and the long-term implications for illness and death are not yet clear. Chapters 3, 7, 8 and 12 to 14 were not read.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Constituents and Human Health Effects and Harm Reduction, Conclusions 3-1, 3-2, 7-1 to 8-3, 12-1 to 14-3, 18-5; Summary › Human Health Effects, closing paragraph; Summary Annex

key_findings.finding: Smoking initiation and cessation (listed for completeness; Chapters 16 and 17 not read): e-cigarette use increases the risk of ever using cigarettes among young people (16-1, substantial), the frequency and intensity of later smoking (16-2, moderate) and, in the near term, its duration (16-3, limited); limited overall evidence that e-cigarettes may be effective cessation aids (17-1); moderate evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes beat nicotine-free ones in randomized trials (17-2); insufficient evidence against no treatment or approved treatments (17-3); moderate evidence from observational studies that more frequent use goes with a higher likelihood of cessation, while the overall observational evidence is mixed (17-4). The Summary states that, taken together, e-cigarettes might cause young people to move on to smoking and might increase adult cessation.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Initiation and Cessation, Conclusions 16-1 to 17-4 and closing paragraph; Summary Annex

key_findings.finding: Research needs (Boxes S-3 to S-5): study the stability and heated by-products of e-liquid ingredients; indoor air quality and secondhand exposure in vulnerable groups; particle deposition in the airways; longitudinal cohorts of young people with little or no smoking; abuse-liability testing; and in clinical and epidemiological studies comparison groups of people who continue to smoke, people who try to quit with other evidence-based treatments, and people who use no tobacco products including e-cigarettes. The Summary says gaps were found in every aspect of the committee's work.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Research Recommendations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Boxes S-3, S-4 and S-5

reporting_issues.issue: The harm-reduction synthesis says all but one human study showed significant short-term improvements in people who smoked and switched, and that the improvement was consistent across all studies, but studies described in the same section report no significant change (Cibella 2016: no differences in spirometry except one flow measure; D'Ruiz 2017: non-significant improvements in lung volumes; Szołtysek-Bołdys 2014: no significant changes in arterial stiffness, blood pressure or heart rate; Cravo 2016: no clinically significant product-related findings, which is absence of harm rather than improvement).
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched › Health Risk Profile, 3rd, 4th, 8th and 14th paragraphs; Synthesis, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Conclusion 18-2 (substantial) should be cited with its level and with the sizes and durations of the studies behind it, not as a finding that every study improved.

reporting_issues.issue: The same study of arterial stiffness (Szołtysek-Bołdys 2014) is described differently in two chapters: Chapter 9 reports that the stiffness index fell after a cigarette (p = 0.006) but not after an e-cigarette; Chapter 18 says there were 'no significant changes' after the cigarette while printing p = 0.0056 and p = 0.010 for the same comparison, and gives 6.75 as the after value and 6.56 as the before value, the reverse of Chapter 9.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 9 › Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, Endothelial Function, and Arterial Stiffness, 4th paragraph; Chapter 18 › Health Risk Profile, 14th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the cigarette comparison in this study cannot be taken from Chapter 18.

reporting_issues.issue: Cibella 2016 (300 people, Catania group) is described as an observational study of people not intending to quit who were invited to switch in Chapter 11, and as a 1-year randomized controlled trial in which groups of 'quitters', 'reducers' and 'failures' are compared in Chapter 18; Chapter 9 describes the Farsalinos 2016 Catania cohort as a randomized trial also analysed as a cohort, with the same three labels and nicotine arms (the chapters do not say whether it is the same trial).
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 11 › Clinical and Epidemiological Studies in Humans, 1st paragraph; Chapter 18 › Health Risk Profile, 3rd paragraph; Chapter 9 › Evidence from Human Studies, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Groups formed by what people did after assignment are not randomized comparisons; the design behind the limited conclusions 11-2 and 11-3 is hard to pin down from the report.

reporting_issues.issue: The Manzoli cohort is described as 932 people with end-of-follow-up groups of 363, 97 and 37 (which add to 497) in Chapter 10, and as 1,355 people with 343 using e-cigarettes only and 319 using both products in Chapter 18.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 10 › Epidemiology, 1st paragraph; Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Use E-Cigarettes Concurrently, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators behind the committee's own risk ratio for cancer cannot be reconciled from the report.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 9 counts 13 short-term clinical studies and three longer studies (16) but then refers to 15 studies; its totals (356 + 306 = 662 participants) agree with the three longer studies (34 + 183 + 89 = 306). It also says five studies enrolled people experienced with e-cigarettes but cites two.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 9 › Evidence from Human Studies of Cardiovascular Effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The study count behind the cardiovascular conclusions is uncertain by one; the participant total is consistent with 16 studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 2 and the opening of Appendix B give six databases (including Embase) for 1 February to 31 August 2017, but Appendix B's account of the first series of six searches (1 to 6 February 2017, 3,494 results) and of the dependence search lists five (no Embase), the cessation review search lists seven, and the databases for the 641 update results are not listed.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 2 › Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Appendix B › Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Health Effects of E-Cigarettes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; E-Cigarettes and Transitions to and from Combustible Tobacco Cigarette Smoking; Literature Updates
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether Embase was searched for the health-effects and exposure literature.

reporting_issues.issue: Conclusion 5-3 (lower toxicant exposure) closes the Chapter 5 synthesis, which cites no comparison studies; the direct comparisons are partly in Chapter 5's carbonyl and metals sections and mainly in Chapter 18, which Chapter 5 itself points to. Chapter 5 also reports one study estimating formaldehyde exposure comparable to a cigarette.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 5 › Synthesis; Chapter 5 › Carbonyl Compounds, 2nd and 6th paragraphs; Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels, Synthesis
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Chapter 18 for the four direct comparisons and Chapter 5 for the variability and the high-formaldehyde reports.

reporting_issues.issue: The synthesis of Chapter 11 states moderate evidence of short-term adverse effects of nicotine-containing e-cigarettes on lung defence mechanisms, but none of the five numbered respiratory conclusions (11-1 to 11-5) carries it.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 11 › Synthesis and Conclusions, 3rd paragraph; Conclusions 11-1 to 11-5
reporting_issues.consequence: The graded short-term lung-defence finding is not in the Annex's list of 47 conclusions and cannot be cited by number.

reporting_issues.issue: Statements on nicotine itself (minimal cancer risk from e-cigarette nicotine; likely higher cardiovascular risk in people with existing disease; uncertain risk in people without) are not graded conclusions and rest on other literature that the committee says it did not review systematically.
reporting_issues.locator: Summary › Constituents, 1st paragraph; Chapter 2 › Smoking Transitions Literature, 2nd paragraph; Chapter 4 › Synthesis, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite these as the committee's reading, not as graded evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Chapter 4 text gives 419 enrolled in the 12-week Cravo trial; Chapter 18 gives 420 people who smoke.
reporting_issues.locator: Chapter 4 › Switching Studies, 4th paragraph; Chapter 18 › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one participant.

design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analysis of randomised and quasi-randomised trials that compared one way of using nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) with another in people motivated to quit smoking: combination (patch plus a fast-acting form) against a single form; fast-acting forms against patch; patch dose and duration; gum dose; fixed against as-needed dosing; NRT started before the quit date (preloading); free against purchased NRT. Primary outcome: abstinence at 6 months or longer (strictest definition, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking); secondary: cardiac adverse events, serious adverse events and withdrawals due to treatment, where reported. 68 completed trials, 43,327 participants, search 29 April 2022. Seven summary-of-findings tables with GRADE ratings. NRT against placebo or no NRT, and NRT against other drugs, are covered by separate Cochrane reviews. This is an update of a 2019 review (Lindson et al.); the 'What's new' table says four studies were added while the abstract and Results say five.
can_establish: The average relative effect on abstinence at 6 months or longer of one way of using NRT against another, in people motivated to quit who joined randomised trials, as of an April 2022 search: combination against single forms, fast-acting forms against the patch, patch dose, and with less certainty gum dose, preloading and duration of use.
cannot_establish: Whether NRT works against no NRT (a separate review); how often side effects or serious events occur with each way of using NRT (cardiac events, serious events and withdrawals were measured variably, rarely reported by arm and rated low or very low certainty); effects in people who smoke fewer than about 15 cigarettes a day (the authors say there is little evidence), in adolescents (one trial) or outside trials; the three comparisons that rest on one small trial (type of fast-acting NRT; 16-hour against 24-hour patch use; gum duration); whether results differ by funder (not assessed); effects beyond 6 to 12 months.

sample.recruitment: Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group Specialised Register (CENTRAL 2022 issue 3, MEDLINE to 5 April 2022, Embase to week 14 of 2022, PsycINFO to 4 April 2022, hand-searched conference abstracts; ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO trials platform as indexed in CENTRAL), searched 29 April 2022, with no limit on date or language; this update screened 805 records after removing duplicates and read 96 in full (Methods › Search methods; Results › Results of the search). Studies were run in the USA (41), Europe (15), Australasia (4), Canada (2), China (2), South Africa (2), South America (1) and several continents (1). Median study size 401 (range 45 to 3,575). Participants were typically adults averaging about 44 years; the most common source was the community (32 trials), usually volunteers answering media advertisements, with others from clinics, quit-lines, worksites or earlier studies (Results › Included studies, Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomised, cluster-randomised and quasi-randomised trials of any form, dose, duration or schedule of NRT against another variation of NRT use, in people of any age who smoked and were motivated to quit, with a cessation outcome at 6 months or longer. Excluded: cross-over trials; trials without a cessation outcome or with follow-up under 6 months; trials aimed at cutting down rather than quitting; trials in which an arm had an extra component that could not be separated from the NRT difference; NRT against placebo (separate review) and NRT against other drugs (separate reviews); 51 excluded studies are listed with reasons.
sample.demographics: Adults averaging about 44 years. Seven trials targeted specific groups: adolescents (Moolchan 2005), people over 50 (Hall 2009), men in a workplace (Kornitzer 1987), people with current alcohol dependence (Cooney 2009) or a history of it (Kalman 2006), adults with post-traumatic stress disorder (Dennis 2016) and people with a smoking-related disorder or an illness that raises the risk of one (Berlin 2011). The average was 20 or more cigarettes a day in 48 of the 61 trials that reported it (79%); the highest mean was 38. The authors say the conclusions apply to adults who smoke about 20 or more cigarettes a day and that there is little evidence for fewer than 15.
sample.attrition: People lost to follow-up counted as still smoking. Attrition risk of bias: low in 39 trials, unclear in 22, high in 7 (six with more than half of participants lost: Caldwell 2014, Dennis 2016, Dignan 2019, Krupski 2016, Leung 2019, Rose 2009; and Hughes 1999, ended early by its sponsor). Per-trial attrition sits in the risk-of-bias tables, which were not read trial by trial.
sample.selection_effects: People motivated to quit who agreed to be randomised, mostly heavier smokers recruited by advertisement or from clinics. Only trials with 6 months or more of follow-up and a cessation outcome are in. The authors say unpublished data may be missing, that reference lists were not screened uniformly across versions, and that manufacturers were written to only for the first version. Thirty-eight of the 68 trials involved a manufacturer as funder, supplier of product or employer of authors (editors' count, see funding).

exposure.measurement: Allocation in the trial to a way of using NRT (type, combination, dose, duration, schedule, timing or price). Adherence by arm was not synthesised.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported, not recommendations. Patch trials compared 25 mg with 15 mg (16-hour patches), 21 mg with 14 mg and 42/44 mg with 21/22 mg (24-hour patches), and courses from 2 to 52 weeks. Gum trials compared 4 mg with 2 mg, fixed hourly use with use as craved, and 50 with 10 weeks. Combination NRT means a patch plus a fast-acting form (gum, lozenge, nasal or oral spray, inhaler). Preloading trials started NRT before the quit date while participants still smoked: 2 weeks in seven trials, 3 weeks in one and 4 weeks in one, mostly with patches alone.
exposure.polysubstance: Two trials enrolled people with alcohol dependence (Cooney 2009; Kalman 2006); other substance use was not analysed. Post hoc sensitivity analyses leaving out trials in vulnerable groups did not change the combination, patch-dose or fast-acting-against-patch results.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinence at 6 or 12 months after baseline (a 6-week window allowed; 12-month data used where available), using the strictest definition each trial gave and preferring sustained abstinence and biochemical validation.

comparison.controls: Another way of using NRT, not placebo or no treatment: a single form (patch alone, a fast-acting form alone, or a choice of one), a lower or shorter or later course, or the same product on a different schedule or price. Trials in which the arms differed in more than NRT use (Tulloch 2016, LeBlanc 2017, Berlin 2011) were reported singly and not pooled.
comparison.matching: Randomised. Random sequence generation was low risk in 30 of 68 trials, unclear in 37 and high in 1 (Kupecz 1996, allocation by month of recruitment); allocation concealment low risk in 28 and unclear in 40. Blinding was often impossible when forms differ: low risk in 21 trials, unclear in 23, high in 24.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline traits are balanced by chance within each trial. Results by dependence were pooled only for the gum-dose trials, in a post hoc split into lower- and higher-dependence people by each author's own definition (Garvey 2000 and Kornitzer 1987 sit in both subgroups).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Use of other cessation aids outside the trial was not extracted by the review.

outcomes.instruments: Abstinence at 6 months or longer, validated biochemically where available (for example carbon monoxide); cardiac adverse events as defined by trial authors (fast or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, palpitations, heart attack, stroke); serious adverse events; withdrawals due to treatment, each only where reported.
outcomes.validity_norms: In Walker 2011 only 34% of claimed quits were verified; the main analysis used verified quits (63/706 against 49/704), with sensitivity analyses using extrapolated (161/706 against 136/704) and self-reported (143/706 against 133/704) rates, all pointing the same way.
outcomes.operationalization: Quit = the strictest abstinence definition each trial reported, with missing counted as smoking. Other side effects (for example local irritation) were not extracted. Serious events were analysed as the trial authors defined them; one trial's events were found only on ClinicalTrials.gov, not in the paper (Schlam 2016).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four outcome types (cessation, cardiac events, serious events, withdrawals) across 13 comparison groups and many subgroups; the authors call the subgroup and sensitivity analyses checks on consistency, and the gum-dose dependence split is labelled post hoc.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The review authors did not blind themselves to trial results or arms (stated). Within trials, blinding was low risk in 21 of 68, unclear in 23 and high in 24; the authors did not rate high risk when blinding was impossible but face-to-face contact was similar or abstinence was biochemically verified.

analysis.effect_sizes: Fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI for abstinence at 6 months or longer. Combination against single form: RR 1.27 (1.17 to 1.37), I2 12%, 16 studies, 12,169 participants; against patch alone 1.24 (1.13 to 1.37), 13 studies, 9,552; against a fast-acting form alone 1.30 (1.09 to 1.54), 6 studies, 2,364; against a choice of one form 5.16 (1.18 to 22.59), 1 study, 253. Fast-acting form against patch: 0.90 (0.77 to 1.05), I2 0%, 8 studies, 3,319 (inhaler 0.59, 1 study; nasal spray 0.90, 2; lozenge 0.94, 3; gum 0.58, 2). Patch dose: 21 against 14 mg (24-hour) 1.48 (1.06 to 2.08), 1 study, 537; 25 against 15 mg (16-hour) 1.19 (1.00 to 1.41), I2 0%, 3 studies, 3,446; 42/44 against 21/22 mg 1.09 (0.93 to 1.29), I2 38%, 5 studies, 1,655. Gum 4 against 2 mg: 1.43 (1.12 to 1.83), I2 63%, 5 studies, 856; higher-dependence 1.85 (1.36 to 2.50), 4 studies, 618; lower-dependence 0.77 (0.49 to 1.21), 3 studies, 238 (post hoc, subgroup difference P = 0.002). Preloading: 1.25 (1.08 to 1.44), I2 0%, 9 studies, 4,395; without the five high-risk trials 1.16 (0.93 to 1.46), 4 studies, 1,444. Absolute figures (Summary of findings): 137 against 174 per 1,000 for combination (160 to 187); 164 against 148 per 1,000 for fast-acting form against patch (126 to 172); 167 against 248 for 21 against 14 mg; 123 against 146 for 25 against 15 mg; 238 against 260 for 42/44 against 21/22 mg; 136 against 170 for preloading. No tau-squared or prediction interval (fixed-effect model).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Subgroups by NRT type and, for gum dose, by dependence (post hoc); sensitivity analyses removing high-risk trials, removing trials in vulnerable groups (post hoc) and, for Walker 2011, varying the verification assumption.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A 'Differences between protocol and review' section lists one deviation: post hoc sensitivity analyses excluding trials in vulnerable groups, added at peer review. The protocol itself is not cited on the page and was not read, and no registration number is given. The fixed-effect model is described as chosen a priori.
analysis.selective_reporting: The Methods name no selective-reporting domain among the risk-of-bias items (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, other). Safety outcomes were extracted only for cardiac events, serious events and withdrawals, and were often missing or not split by arm (for example Piper 2009 reported serious events without arm; Schlam 2016's appeared only on the trial registry). Funnel plot only for one comparison (16 studies).
analysis.power: Most comparisons rest on one to three trials. Harm outcomes had fewer than 100 events in most comparisons, which the authors rated down two levels for imprecision; the two comparisons rated high certainty for quitting (combination against single form; fast-acting form against patch) pool 16 and 8 trials with I2 of 12% and 0%.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across randomised trials of people motivated to quit, combination NRT (patch plus a fast-acting form) was followed by more people abstinent at 6 months or longer than a single form: 174 against 137 per 1,000, about 4 more in 100 (RR 1.27, 1.17 to 1.37; 16 trials; consistent across comparators; unchanged without high-risk trials). A fast-acting form alone against the patch showed no clear difference (148 against 164 per 1,000, about 2 fewer in 100, interval 4 fewer to 1 more; RR 0.90, 0.77 to 1.05; 8 trials). Higher patch doses did better than lower in two of three dose comparisons (21 against 14 mg: about 8 more in 100 from one trial; 25 against 15 mg: about 2 more in 100, interval touching no difference) and not for 42/44 against 21/22 mg. Gum 4 mg against 2 mg favoured the higher strength overall (RR 1.43, 5 trials) but only in higher-dependence people (RR 1.85 against 0.77). Preloading favoured early use (about 3 more in 100; RR 1.25) but the interval included no difference once five high-risk trials were removed (RR 1.16). No clear difference for patch duration, combination duration, tapering, fixed against as-needed dosing, gum duration, free against purchased NRT, or participant- against clinician-selected NRT, mostly from one or two small trials. Safety data were sparse: serious events 1 per 1,000 with single forms against 3 per 1,000 (1 to 18) with combinations (seven events in total), withdrawals due to treatment more frequent with nasal spray than patch (3.0% against 0.9%) and with 42/44 mg than 21/22 mg patches (6.1% against 1.1%), all low or very low certainty.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions state high-certainty evidence that combination NRT beats single forms and that 4 mg beats 2 mg gum, and that fast-acting forms give similar quit rates to patches; the plain language summary says people have 'the same chance' with a patch or another type, that combination is '17% to 37% more likely' to work, that large studies in a separate review show NRT 'is safe to use', and that serious events were rare; the implications give 4 mg gum '12% to 83% higher'; the Discussion describes the review process as robust and says no biases were introduced. Gaps: (1) the high-certainty label for gum dose has no summary-of-findings table or GRADE rating behind it, the Discussion says only two comparisons reached high certainty (combination against single form; fast-acting form against patch), and the gum result has I2 63% and is confined to a post hoc higher-dependence subgroup; (2) '17% to 37%' and '12% to 83%' are the ends of the confidence intervals for relative risks, not a range of effects, and no absolute numbers are given in the abstract or plain language summary; (3) 'the same chance' is stronger than RR 0.90 (0.77 to 1.05), with a point estimate favouring the patch; (4) the safety statement rests on another review (Hartmann-Boyce 2018), which did not pool serious events and found chest pain or palpitations in 2.5% against 1.4% with NRT against control, while this review's own harm evidence is low or very low certainty; (5) industry funding was not assessed (judged less applicable to comparisons between ways of using NRT), yet 38 of 68 trials involved a manufacturer, including all 10 patch-dose trials; (6) the self-description of the process as robust, with no biases introduced, sits beside reference lists not screened uniformly, no selective-reporting domain, and a funnel plot for one comparison.

timeline.event: First version of the original Cochrane NRT review (Silagy et al.), from which the 2019 comparison-of-forms review was split.
Companion Cochrane review of NRT against placebo or no NRT (search 2017), covering the question of whether NRT works at all.
First publication of this review under its current title (Lindson et al.).
This update (search April 2022): conclusions unchanged after new studies were added.
Cochrane living review of electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation, which uses NRT as a comparator; read separately.

replication.where_it_stands: The main finding, that combination NRT beats a single form and that fast-acting forms and the patch give similar quit rates, comes from many trials with low heterogeneity and was stable across the 2019 and 2023 versions; the dose, duration and preloading results rest on few trials and range from moderate to very low certainty by the authors' own rating. Trials in this review also appear in the 2018 NRT-against-control review and in the comparator arms of vape trials, so those are not independent confirmations. The review is the standard comparison of ways of using NRT; most of its trials were funded or supplied by manufacturers, and it did not look for a funding effect.

funding.funder: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) infrastructure funding for the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group; internal support from the Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, University of Oxford (editorial base of the group). No industry funding of the review is declared.
funding.declared_conflicts: One author (CB) is a consultant for Johnson and Johnson, fiduciary officer of the Society for Research on Nicotine and Tobacco, and was involved in two included trials (Bullen 2010 and Walker 2011, funded by the NZ Health Research Council); another (NL) was involved in an included trial (Preloading Investigators 2018) and holds grants from Cancer Research UK and the NIHR; both state they did not extract data or assess bias for those trials. One author (SCC) is an NHS public-health consultant and Cochrane Clinical Answers associate editor. Three authors are members of the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group editorial team but took no part in the editorial process for this update; the others declare none known or no relevant interests. Funding of the included trials, from their Notes (editors' count; the review did not analyse by funder and says it judged industry funding less applicable to comparisons between ways of using NRT): of 68 trials, 38 name a manufacturer as funder, sponsor, supplier of product or employer of authors (20 as funder or sponsor, including Rose 2009 and Rose 2010 with Philip Morris USA money; 18 as supplier or through authors' affiliation), 23 name no manufacturer (22 public, charity or university funders; one reports no funding), and 7 report no source. All 10 patch-dose trials involve a manufacturer; of the 16 combination trials, 9 do (4 funded or sponsored by Pharmacia or employing its staff, 5 by product supply or affiliation) and 7 name none; of the 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials, 6 do, 1 names none and 1 reports no source; of the 9 preloading trials, 3 do and 6 name none; of the 5 gum-dose trials, 2 do (product supply), 1 names none and 2 report no source.
funding.affiliations_note: Author affiliations were not part of the page text read for this card.

what_would_settle_it: Adequately sized head-to-head trials, preferably not supplied or funded by manufacturers and with registered outcomes, for the comparisons the authors rate moderate to very low (patch dose, preloading, gum dose by dependence, durations); consistent reporting of cardiac events, serious events and withdrawals by arm so that harms can be pooled; and a funder-stratified analysis of the existing trials, which this review did not run.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People who smoked and were motivated to quit; any form, dose, duration or schedule of NRT; comparison with another variation of NRT use; abstinence at 6 months or more plus cardiac events, serious events and withdrawals; randomised trials.

A section compares protocol and review and lists one deviation (post hoc sensitivity analyses), and the fixed-effect model is described as chosen a priori; the protocol is not cited or numbered on the page, so registration cannot be confirmed.
Randomised, cluster-randomised and quasi-randomised trials; cross-over trials excluded with a reason (no assessment of longer-term effects).

Specialised Register built from CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and hand-searched conference abstracts, with ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO platform indexed in CENTRAL; no date or language limits; strategy in Appendix 1; searched April 2022, within 14 months of publication. Not done to the full standard: reference lists were not screened uniformly across versions (stated), and manufacturers were last contacted for the first version.
Two authors independently screened in the last three updates; earlier updates used one screener, so older selections were not duplicated.
Two authors independently extracted, with disagreements resolved by discussion or a third author; translators used for non-English reports.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Characteristics of excluded studies gives a reason for each of the 51 excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: A table for each trial gives design, country, recruitment, participants, interventions, outcomes, follow-up, validation, funding and conflicts, and risk-of-bias judgements with support.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, other) with two independent assessors for new trials; the Methods name no selective-reporting domain, so selection of the reported result was not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: The Notes field of each trial gives funders, product suppliers and conflicts, or says not reported (7 trials).

Fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios chosen a priori, with I2 reported, different comparators kept in separate subgroups, arms split to avoid double counting, and comparisons not pooled where durations differed. Judged met on balance, a close call: no random-effects check despite I2 of 63% for gum dose and 73% for withdrawals (the first explored with a post hoc dependence split).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analysis removing high-risk trials for the relevant comparisons; it changed only the preloading result.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE ratings and the Discussion state that preloading lost its clear effect without the five high-risk trials; the statement that the review process introduced no biases is a self-assessment.
I2 reported for each pool; subgroups by comparator and NRT type; a post hoc dependence split reduced heterogeneity in the gum-dose trials; high heterogeneity in withdrawals discussed.

A funnel plot (an image) for the one comparison with 10 or more trials (combination against single form, 16 studies) showed no sign of publication bias, interpreted with caution; the other comparisons had too few trials.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Sources of support and declarations of interest are given, including authors' roles in included trials.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical item is judged no. Three critical items are only partly met (2, 4 and 9), which AMSTAR 2 does not count as flaws, so the mechanical rating is high confidence. AMSTAR 2 rates how the review was done, not how good its trials are: 28 of 68 trials were at high risk of bias in at least one domain and 31 unclear; for most comparisons only one to three trials exist; the harm outcomes have low or very low certainty; industry funding was not assessed although 38 of 68 trials involved a manufacturer. May be cited for: the pooled difference between combination and single forms and between fast-acting forms and the patch, with the authors' high-certainty ratings; the patch-dose and preloading results as moderate-certainty findings; the list of comparisons with no clear difference. May not be cited for: the gum-dose result as high certainty (it has no GRADE table), safety or tolerability, or whether NRT works against no NRT.

key_findings.finding: Combination NRT (patch plus a fast-acting form) against single-form NRT, abstinence at 6 months or longer: RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.37), I2 12%, 16 studies, 12,169 participants. Absolute figures: 137 per 1,000 with a single form against 174 per 1,000 (160 to 187) with combination, about 4 more in 100 (editors' arithmetic). The authors rate this high certainty; the estimate was unchanged without the high-risk trials.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1; Analysis 4.1

key_findings.finding: Subgroups of the combination comparison: against patch alone RR 1.24 (1.13 to 1.37), I2 28%, 13 studies, 9,552 participants; against a fast-acting form alone RR 1.30 (1.09 to 1.54), I2 0%, 6 studies, 2,364; against a choice of a single form RR 5.16 (1.18 to 22.59), 1 study, 253 (Dignan 2019, rated high risk of bias because most participants were lost to follow-up). No clear subgroup difference (I2 45.8%, P = 0.16).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 1st paragraph; Analysis 4.1.1 to 4.1.3; Characteristics of included studies › Dignan 2019
key_findings.note: The review assumed that the patch was part of the combination in Dignan 2019 (a choice of one against a choice of two products).

key_findings.finding: The funnel plot for the combination comparison (16 studies, the only comparison with 10 or more) gave no evidence of publication bias, which the authors say should be read with caution because the number of studies is small. Of the 16 combination trials, 4 were funded or sponsored by Pharmacia or employed its staff, 5 had product supply or manufacturer-affiliated authors, and 7 name no manufacturer (editors' count).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3; Characteristics of included studies › Notes (editors' count)

key_findings.finding: Fast-acting NRT against the nicotine patch, abstinence at 6 months or longer: RR 0.90 (0.77 to 1.05), I2 0%, 8 studies, 3,319 participants; 164 per 1,000 with the patch against 148 per 1,000 (126 to 172) with a fast-acting form, about 2 fewer in 100 (editors' arithmetic; interval from 4 fewer to 1 more). By form: inhaler RR 0.59 (0.22 to 1.60; 1 study, 222), nasal spray 0.90 (0.64 to 1.27; 2 studies, 1,272), lozenge 0.94 (0.79 to 1.12; 3 studies, 1,707), gum 0.58 (0.26 to 1.31; 2 studies, 118). The authors rate this high certainty; no subgroup difference (P = 0.57).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Fast-acting NRT versus patch, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 5; Analysis 6.1

key_findings.finding: Patch dose (study conditions): 21 mg against 14 mg (24-hour patches) RR 1.48 (1.06 to 2.08), 1 study, 537 participants, 167 against 248 per 1,000; 25 mg against 15 mg (16-hour patches) RR 1.19 (1.00 to 1.41), I2 0%, 3 studies, 3,446, 123 against 146 per 1,000; 42/44 mg against 21/22 mg (24-hour) RR 1.09 (0.93 to 1.29), I2 38%, 5 studies, 1,655, 238 against 260 per 1,000. All three rated moderate certainty (imprecision). The lower and higher doses in the 21 against 14 mg and 25 against 15 mg comparisons are not the same dose per hour (about 0.9 against 0.6 mg an hour, and 1.6 against 0.9 mg an hour). All 10 patch-dose trials involve a manufacturer (editors' count).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Patch therapy › Dose, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary of findings, Table 3; Analysis 1.1

key_findings.finding: Gum dose: 4 mg against 2 mg gum RR 1.43 (1.12 to 1.83), I2 63%, 5 studies, 856 participants. In a post hoc split by dependence, higher-dependence people RR 1.85 (1.36 to 2.50), I2 13%, 4 studies, 618; lower-dependence RR 0.77 (0.49 to 1.21), I2 0%, 3 studies, 238; subgroup difference P = 0.002, with none of those trials at high risk of bias. The authors say the finding needs testing in adequately powered primary studies. The review has no summary-of-findings table or GRADE rating for this comparison, although the abstract's conclusions call it high certainty.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Fast-acting NRT › Gum dose, 1st paragraph; Analysis 8.1; Abstract › Authors' conclusions
key_findings.note: Of the five trials, two report no funder, one is publicly funded, and two were supplied with product by manufacturers.

key_findings.finding: Preloading (NRT started before the quit date while smoking) against use from the quit date only: RR 1.25 (1.08 to 1.44), I2 0%, 9 studies, 4,395 participants; 136 against 170 per 1,000 (147 to 196). Rated moderate certainty. Without the five studies at high risk of bias: RR 1.16 (0.93 to 1.46), 4 studies, 1,444. By product: patch alone RR 1.28 (1.09 to 1.49; 3,830 participants), gum alone 0.93 (0.58 to 1.49; 306), patch plus gum 1.35 (0.80 to 2.28; 259). Palpitations were more common with preloading in one study (RR 2.05, 1.15 to 3.62; 1,792 participants).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › NRT preloading versus standard post-quit use, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Summary of findings, Table 7; Analysis 10.1 to 10.2
key_findings.note: Of the 9 trials, 6 name no manufacturer, 2 had product supply, and Rose 2009 was funded through a grant from Philip Morris USA (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Patch duration: none of nine comparisons (from 4 weeks against 2 weeks to 52 weeks against 8 weeks; 7 studies) showed a statistically clear difference in quitting, for example 52 against 24 weeks RR 0.78 (0.53 to 1.15), 28 against 12 weeks 1.05 (0.88 to 1.26), 6 against 2 to 3 weeks 1.13 (0.91 to 1.40); not pooled because durations differ; rated low certainty. Combination duration: 16 against 8 weeks RR 0.96 (0.75 to 1.23; 637 participants) and 6 against 2 weeks 1.11 (0.94 to 1.31; 987), rated very low and low; a third trial (Schlam 2016, 26 against 8 weeks) was left out because of statistical interactions between its factors (odds ratio 1.40, 1.08 to 1.82, from the paper's model; 1.42, 0.98 to 2.05, from raw group data).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Patch therapy › Duration, 1st paragraph; Combination therapy › Duration of combination therapy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary of findings, Tables 2 and 4

key_findings.finding: No clear difference, each from one or two trials with wide intervals: tapering against abrupt stopping of the patch RR 0.99 (0.74 to 1.32; 2 studies, 264); fixed against as-needed dosing RR 1.12 (0.87 to 1.45; 4 studies, 828); 50 against 10 weeks of gum RR 1.04 (0.82 to 1.32; 402); 24-hour against 16-hour patch use RR 0.70 (0.36 to 1.34; 106); continuing against stopping the patch after a lapse RR 0.89 (0.77 to 1.02; 701); free against purchased NRT RR 1.38 (0.90 to 2.13; 2 studies, 740); 2 against 1 week of free NRT RR 1.63 (0.98 to 2.70; 562) and 8 against 4 weeks 0.97 (0.64 to 1.48; 1,495); a free one-week selection box and participant-chosen NRT against clinician-chosen NRT RR 1.28 (0.90 to 1.83; 1,410), 1.18 (0.96 to 1.45) and 1.07 (0.87 to 1.33) under three assumptions about unverified quits; type of fast-acting form in one trial of 100 people (all intervals include no difference).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Patch therapy › Effect of tapering, Other variations in patch use; Fast-acting NRT › Type, Gum duration, Fixed versus ad lib dosing schedule; Cost of NRT; Participant- versus clinician-selected NRT

key_findings.finding: Safety, combination against single form: any cardiac adverse event RR 0.66 (0.22 to 2.05; 2 studies, 656 participants); serious adverse events RR 4.44 (0.76 to 25.85; 5 studies, 2,888; seven events in total; 1 against 3 per 1,000, interval 1 to 18), rated low certainty; withdrawals due to treatment RR 1.12 (0.57 to 2.20; 5 studies, 3,070; I2 73%), rated very low. Only 3 of the 16 trials reported cardiac events at all; Piper 2009 (1,504 participants) reported 32 serious events not split by arm.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Summary of findings, Table 1; Appendix 2

key_findings.finding: Safety, fast-acting form against patch: withdrawals due to treatment RR 4.23 (1.54 to 11.63; 3 studies, 1,482 participants), 5 against 23 per 1,000, with nasal spray against patch RR 3.47 (1.15 to 10.46; 1 study, 922; 3.0% against 0.9%); serious events: three of four trials had none, one found RR 1.75 (0.52 to 5.92; 642 participants); cardiac events reported by arm in one small trial, none in either arm. Patch dose: serious events 42/44 mg against 21/22 mg RR 5.01 (0.87 to 28.82; 2 studies, 1,023 participants; 7 events in higher-dose arms and 1 in lower), withdrawals RR 4.99 (1.60 to 15.50; 2 studies, 554; 6.1% against 1.1%); fast or irregular heartbeat 25 mg against 15 mg RR 0.92 (0.64 to 1.33; 2 studies, 3,269). Preloading: serious events RR 1.11 (0.59 to 2.09; 4 studies, 3,908); cardiac serious events RR 1.94 (0.81 to 4.65; 3 studies, 3,529). All rated low or very low certainty.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Fast-acting NRT versus patch, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Patch therapy › Dose, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; NRT preloading versus standard post-quit use, 4th paragraph; Summary of findings, Tables 3, 5 and 7

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias across the 68 trials: 9 low in all domains, 28 high in at least one, 31 unclear. Sequence generation low in 30, unclear in 37, high in 1; allocation concealment low in 28, unclear in 40; blinding low in 21, unclear in 23, high in 24; incomplete outcome data low in 39, unclear in 22, high in 7. Removing high-risk trials changed the interpretation only for preloading.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Certainty of the evidence, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Funding of the 68 included trials (editors' count from the Notes field of Characteristics of included studies; the review did not analyse by funder): 38 name a manufacturer as funder, sponsor, supplier of product or employer of authors (20 as funder or sponsor, including Rose 2009 and Rose 2010 with Philip Morris USA money); 23 name no manufacturer; 7 report no source. The review states it did not assess bias from industry funding, judging it less applicable when comparing ways of using NRT rather than NRT against placebo.
key_findings.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Notes of each study (editors' count); Discussion › Certainty of the evidence, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Approximate: some entries mention a company only for product supply, and the Piper 2009 and Smith 2009 entries mention a research agreement for medication.

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: evidence for safety and tolerability of different ways of using NRT is limited; many comparisons rest on sparse studies and further research could strengthen or change findings; generalisation is restricted to adults motivated to quit who smoke about 20 or more cigarettes a day (highest mean 38); little evidence for under 15 a day; unpublished data may be missing; reference lists not screened uniformly across versions; e-cigarettes are not covered; one funnel plot only.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Potential biases in the review process; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice

key_findings.finding: Follow-up: all trials reported abstinence at 6 months or longer (6 or 12 months from baseline, with a 6-week window); the review does not analyse later relapse. Search ran to 29 April 2022; four ongoing trials (factorial designs of NRT combination and duration, one of a higher-dose patch) are listed.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures of treatment effect; Results › Ongoing studies; Characteristics of ongoing studies

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusions call 4 mg against 2 mg nicotine gum high-certainty evidence, but the review gives it no summary-of-findings table or GRADE rating (seven comparisons were rated, none of them gum dose), the Discussion says only two comparisons reached high certainty (combination against single form; fast-acting form against patch), and the gum result has I2 63% in a fixed-effect pool of five trials (856 participants) with the benefit confined to a post hoc higher-dependence subgroup.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Authors' conclusions; Methods › Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence; Discussion › Certainty of the evidence, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The gum-dose result is not cited as high certainty; the claim leaves it out and the card records the finding with the authors' own caution.

reporting_issues.issue: The plain language summary and the implications for practice express relative effects as '17% to 37% more likely' (combination) and '12% to 83% higher' (4 mg gum); these are the limits of the confidence intervals for RR 1.27 and RR 1.43, not a range of effects, and neither section gives absolute numbers (the summary-of-findings table does).
reporting_issues.locator: Plain language summary › Main results; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 1st and 2nd points
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim uses the summary-of-findings absolute figures (137 against 174 per 1,000) and the point estimate with its interval.

reporting_issues.issue: The plain language summary says people who smoke have 'the same chances' of quitting with a patch or another type of NRT; the pooled estimate is RR 0.90 (0.77 to 1.05), 148 against 164 per 1,000, with a point estimate favouring the patch and an interval that does not exclude a 23% lower rate with a fast-acting form.
reporting_issues.locator: Plain language summary › Main results, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 5
reporting_issues.consequence: Stated as no clear difference with the interval.

reporting_issues.issue: The plain language summary says large studies in a separate review show high-certainty evidence that NRT is safe to use for quitting smoking, and the conclusions say NRT is generally considered well tolerated. This review's own harm outcomes are low or very low certainty, and the separate review (Hartmann-Boyce 2018) did not pool serious adverse events and found chest pain or palpitations in 2.5% with NRT against 1.4% with control.
reporting_issues.locator: Plain language summary › How reliable are these results?; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 7th point
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim reports the harm findings with their certainty and does not repeat the safety statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives 9,522 participants for combination NRT against patch alone, and the Data and analyses table gives 9,552 (the table sums with the other two subgroups to the stated total of 12,169).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 1st paragraph; Analysis 4.1.1
reporting_issues.consequence: Table value used.

reporting_issues.issue: The withdrawals comparison of 42/44 mg against 21/22 mg patches is given as 544 participants in the abstract and Results text and as 554 in the summary-of-findings table and Analysis 1.5.1.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Main results; Results › Patch therapy › Dose, 5th paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 3; Analysis 1.5.1
reporting_issues.consequence: Table value (554) used; the estimate is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: For withdrawals, the text says the point estimate 'favoured' combination NRT against patch when RR 2.32 (0.99 to 5.40) means more withdrawals with combination, then says 'the same was observed' for combination against fast-acting forms, where RR 0.14 (0.02 to 1.08) points the other way (fewer withdrawals with combination).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 5th paragraph; Analysis 4.4.1 to 4.4.2
reporting_issues.consequence: Direction taken from the ratios; the two subgroups disagree and the pooled RR 1.12 (0.57 to 2.20) has I2 73%.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of new studies is five in the abstract and the Included studies section (Berlin 2011, Dignan 2019, Garvey 2006, LeBlanc 2017, Leung 2019) but four in the 'What's new' table; the Discussion also says the review includes 67 studies while elsewhere it is 68.

reporting_issues.consequence: 68 included studies and five new studies used, as in the abstract and Results.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of serious adverse events reported by Piper 2009 is 32 in the combination section and Appendix 2 and 36 in the fast-acting-against-patch section, neither split by arm.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Combination versus single form, 4th paragraph; Fast-acting NRT versus patch, 3rd paragraph; Appendix 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Not used in any claim; the trial's serious events could not be pooled either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Serious events in patch-dose trials are described as coming from three studies of which 'only two' contributed events, with three trials named, and given as 3 studies and 1,560 participants in the text against 2 studies and 1,023 in the summary-of-findings table; the figures reconcile only by adding the third trial (TNSG 1991, 537 participants), which had no events and sits in the 21 mg against 14 mg row.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Patch therapy › Dose, 4th paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 3; Analysis 1.4
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary-of-findings table value (2 studies, 1,023) is used for the 42/44 mg against 21/22 mg comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The risk-of-bias entry for Dignan 2019, whose combination-against-choice estimate (RR 5.16) is the largest in the combination pool, says the number followed up at 18 months was 16 participants and also less than half of the sample (of 254 randomised), so the figure is unclear; the trial's outcome was point prevalence at 18 months, later than the 6- or 12-month data the Methods say were mostly used.
reporting_issues.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Dignan 2019 (Outcomes; risk of bias, incomplete outcome data)
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimate is not used; the trial is flagged as high risk and the pooled combination result did not change without it.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to the withdrawals row in the combination summary-of-findings table calls I2 of 73% 'moderate' heterogeneity; the Methods define values above 50% as substantial.
reporting_issues.locator: Summary of findings, Table 1, footnote c; Methods › Assessment of heterogeneity
reporting_issues.consequence: Wording only; the one-level downgrade for inconsistency is consistent with substantial heterogeneity.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC10278922 (abstract, plain language summary, all seven Summary of findings tables, methods, results, discussion, authors' conclusions, what's new, history, acknowledgements, sources of support, declarations of interest, the Data and analyses tables, the start of the excluded-studies list and the start and Piper 2009 rows of Appendix 2 read; the Notes field of every one of the 68 included-study entries was extracted programmatically to count funders and read in a printed list, with the Dignan 2019, Piper 2016, Lerman 2004 and Baker 2016 entries read in full; the risk-of-bias tables of individual trials were not read trial by trial; Figures 1 to 3 (flow diagram, risk-of-bias summary, funnel plot) are images and were not extracted; Appendix 3 (BNF prescribing guidance) and the references were not read)

design_detail: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR; protocol preregistered on the Open Science Framework) of empirical studies of oral nicotine pouches, an update of the authors' 2024 review. MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO trial register were searched on 30 September 2025 (the first three from 2023 onward), English and German full texts. 481 titles and abstracts were screened by four reviewers independently and 181 full texts by two; 73 new studies were included (12 industry-funded), 135 across both reviews. Data were extracted in duplicate and reported in tables and narrative under five domains: use patterns, beliefs and perceptions, product characteristics, toxicity, and marketing and sales, with findings split by industry and non-industry funding. By the authors' own statement there was no risk-of-bias assessment and no statistical synthesis. The schema has no scoping-review design; 'systematic-review' is used because the search and selection are systematic.
can_establish: What surveys reported about how many people used pouches (US youth and adults to 2024, other countries to 2024) and who reported use; what laboratory analyses reported about pouch contents; what short trials reported about nicotine uptake, subjective ratings and cigarettes smoked; how few studies measure health outcomes; and how much of the literature is industry-funded.
cannot_establish: That pouches are less harmful than cigarettes or snus in the people who use them (there are no studies of disease or death, and the short measures of blood pressure and biomarkers are mixed); long-term effects (none measured); the certainty or quality of any finding (no appraisal); whether pouches help people stop smoking (trials of up to 6 months show fewer cigarettes and little quitting); how many people who never smoked take up pouches (prevalence among never-smokers is not given in the text); or comparability of prevalence between countries (sampling frames are not tabulated in the main text).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Six sources searched on 30 September 2025; MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science limited to 2023 onward (the first review's search ended January 2024), the three trial sources from inception; references of eligible papers searched by one reviewer; only the PubMed strategy is published (Supplementary File S1, not read) (Materials and methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed empirical studies of oral nicotine pouches within the five domains, English or German. Excluded: pouches without nicotine, studies of several oral nicotine products without pouch-specific results, literature reviews, editorials, case reports, commentaries, letters and conference papers. The criteria are given by reference to the first review (Materials and methods › Eligibility, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Mostly US studies; others from the UK, Germany, Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Poland, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Canada and Australia. Youth and adult surveys are reported separately (Results › Use patterns of ONPs, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Peer-reviewed papers in English or German only; no grey literature. The authors say the review's broad inclusion criteria allowed no appraisal and that associations with current use rest on generally small samples (Discussion, 9th paragraph). Prevalence figures mix national surveys with other samples (for example adult college students, online panels) without the main text saying which is which. The paper lists one pharmacokinetic and subjective-ratings crossover study (its reference 61) under non-industry-funded studies in one section and under industry-funded studies in another.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. Primary studies: self-reported lifetime use (ever) and current use (past 30 days, or every day or some days), measured product content, plasma nicotine in clinical crossover trials, urinary or blood biomarkers, and Nielsen retail sales (Materials and methods › Data synthesis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Measured product content cited from primary analyses: total nicotine 1.41 to 8.11 mg per pouch in 70 US tobacco-free products; 6.4 (SD 3.5) mg per pouch against 12.3 (SD 8.2) mg in tobacco-based pouches in a second analysis of 50 products; 2.20 to 56 mg per pouch in 31 products sold in Germany; freebase share 63.4% against 47.2% for tobacco-based pouches (Results › Product characteristics › Nicotine content and release from pouches). Trials used single uses of 20 to 60 minutes up to 6 months. Route: oral.
exposure.polysubstance: Dual use is a main result, not a nuisance: most US youth reporting current pouch use in the Monitoring the Future survey also reported vaping, and use is concentrated among people who currently or formerly smoked or vaped (Results › Use patterns › US prevalence estimates, 1st paragraph; Demographic characteristics, 3rd paragraph). Surveys therefore cannot attribute outcomes to pouches alone.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at review level; the pharmacokinetic trials enrolled people who smoke or use smokeless tobacco daily.

comparison.controls: Varies by primary study: continued smoking, nicotine gum, e-cigarettes, snus or moist snuff, cigarettes within the same session, or none in surveys.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not assessed at review level.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not assessed at review level; many trials enrolled people who smoked daily without intent to quit.

outcomes.instruments: Survey prevalence (PATH, National Youth Tobacco Survey, Monitoring the Future, TUS-CPS and others), measured content, pharmacokinetic maxima and areas under the curve, subjective ratings, cytotoxicity assays, biomarkers, cigarettes per day and quit rates in trials, and sales units and revenue.
outcomes.validity_norms: No risk-of-bias assessment. The review separates findings by industry and non-industry funding instead.
outcomes.operationalization: Prevalence is reported as lifetime (ever) and current use with each survey's own definition (Supplementary Table S2, not read). Harm is not operationalised; there are no disease outcomes.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening and extraction by two or four reviewers working independently.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled effect sizes. Reported ranges: US youth 2024, current use 1.8% (National Youth Tobacco Survey, middle and high school) and 2.6% (Monitoring the Future, grades 10 and 12), lifetime 3.5% and 5.4%; US adults 2022 to 2023, current use 0.4% (TUS-CPS) to 0.8% (PATH), lifetime 2.7% to 3.3%; other countries, lifetime use from 3.3% (British youth 2024) to 27% (Canadian college students 2024) and current use from 0.4% (adults in England 2023) to 19% (Australia 2023). Sales: 327 million units (July 2021) to 1,046 million (May 2024). Trials: cigarettes per day fell by nearly half among people assigned to pouches in an 8-week three-arm trial of 33 daily smokers on low incomes (one switched completely, three stopped using pouches), both strengths cut cigarettes in a 4-week trial of 30 (two quit, both on the stronger pouch), and by over 90% in a 6-month industry-funded trial of 100; nicotine uptake from pouches ranged from below to above that from a cigarette by strength and brand.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Preregistered protocol on the Open Science Framework (cited as reference 11); no deviation is described; the registration was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessed. The review does not appraise the primary studies and reports funders for them.
analysis.power: Not assessed; the authors say associations with current pouch use should be interpreted with caution because of generally small samples.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Surveys show low but rising use in the US (adult current use under 1% in 2022 to 2023; youth current use 1.8% to 2.6% in 2024, more than doubling in three years), higher use in men, young adults and people who smoke, vape or use smokeless tobacco, and much higher figures in some other countries and samples. Nicotine uptake varies widely by strength and brand and can exceed or fall short of a cigarette's. Trials last 4 weeks to 6 months and show fewer cigarettes smoked with little complete switching. Evidence on toxicity is laboratory content analysis, cell assays (several industry-funded) and a few biomarker studies with mixed results. No study follows disease.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract: nicotine uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more 'typically exceeds' that from cigarettes; pouches are 'considerably less toxic than cigarettes'; trials 'suggest' pouches can reduce smoking. Discussion: independent and industry-funded trials found that pouch use for up to 6 months 'significantly decreased' cigarette and smokeless tobacco consumption; the pouches 'may be a less hazardous alternative to traditional tobacco' but are 'not risk-free'. Gaps: (1) the Results show a 6 mg pouch with lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette in the independent German study, and 4 mg and 8 mg pouches below a cigarette in an industry series, while the Discussion moves the threshold to 8 mg and says 'often exceeds'; (2) 'considerably less toxic' rests on content and cell assays, a small biomarker comparison in which nicotine metabolites were comparable to those of people who smoke, and no reduction of tobacco-specific nitrosamines in the 4-week trial of dual use; (3) the Discussion says 'significantly decreased' for trials whose Results give no tests, the only 6-month trial being industry-funded.

timeline.event: The authors' first scoping review of oral nicotine pouches (search to January 2024; doi 10.1093/ntr/ntae131), which this review updates; it concluded that most evidence came from industry-funded studies.
Independent laboratory measurement of nicotine and tobacco-specific nitrosamines across pouch brands, one of the content analyses of the kind this review summarises.
Systematic review of the health effects of snus and tobacco-free pouches; it finds 15 human studies of pouches, none longer than 6 months.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent map of the pouch literature in this batch, and the main source for who uses pouches and how much. It is a summary of other studies, so none of its findings is an independent replication of another; its strength is the split by funder and the explicit statement that health effects are understudied.

funding.funder: Grant 2U54CA229974 from the US National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute, and the Food and Drug Administration; the paper says the funders had no input on the protocol, interpretation or publication, as printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: one author (Goniewicz) received a research grant from Pfizer, served on a scientific advisory board to Johnson & Johnson and consulted for Kenvue 'outside of this work', and has consulted for the US Food and Drug Administration, the World Health Organization, the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids and the Polish Medical Research Agency; another (Hartmann-Boyce) has consulted for Truth Initiative. The paper does not say whether the other five authors have none.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Georgetown University's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center, the University of Michigan, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, Rutgers Cancer Institute and the BC Cancer Research Institute. No tobacco-industry funding or tie is declared. Industry-funded primary studies (British American Tobacco, Altria, Japan Tobacco International) are identified in the text and set beside the others.

what_would_settle_it: Independent, registered cohorts and trials of people who use pouches alone, including people who never smoked, followed for years, with measured nicotine intake, biomarkers of exposure and harm and disease outcomes, reported beside people who smoke, people who use snus and people who use no nicotine; national surveys that record never-smoker status, product type (tobacco-free or tobacco-based) and sampling frame; and a quality appraisal of the laboratory and trial literature that is split by funder.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: A scoping review organised by five outcome domains, not by question components; population, comparator and outcomes are not set out in this paper, which defers to the first review's eligibility criteria.
A preregistered protocol on the Open Science Framework is cited; no deviations are described and the registration was not read. The widening of the search to three trial registers is stated.
All empirical designs were eligible ('broad inclusion criteria') with no reason given for each.

Six sources including three trial registers, a stated date and a flow chart, but peer-reviewed English or German papers only without a stated reason, the three main databases limited to 2023 onward (to avoid overlap with the first review), references checked by one reviewer, and no experts or grey literature. Judged 'no' on the project's reading of item 4 (decision p-amstar2-item4). Only the PubMed strategy is published, in a supplement not read.
Four reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently and two screened full texts independently; disagreements were settled by consensus.
Two reviewers extracted independently with a standardized tool and compared entries.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Counts only (181 read in full, 73 new studies kept); no list of the excluded studies is referenced in the page text; the flow chart (an image) was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The text gives design, size, duration, product and funder for many studies; characteristics of all 135 studies are in Supplementary Table S1, not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: None was done, by the authors' statement (Discussion, 9th paragraph).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Each section separates industry-funded studies from the rest and names the funders; 12 of the 73 new studies were industry-funded. One crossover study (reference 61) is placed in both groups.
No statistical synthesis.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: No assessment was made to account for; the Discussion weighs funder and sample size in passing ('mainly industry-funded', 'low sample sizes').

The Discussion attributes differences to survey definitions, populations and product features (nicotine content, release, freebase share) and says a conclusion for the whole product category cannot be made.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Grant and funder role stated; interests of two authors listed; the paper does not say whether the other authors have none.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 rates four critical items 'no' (search, list of excluded studies, risk-of-bias assessment, risk of bias in interpretation) and the protocol only partly, so the review is critically low confidence as an accurate and comprehensive summary of quality-appraised studies. AMSTAR 2 was written for reviews that appraise and combine evidence, which a scoping review does not set out to do, so the rating chiefly states what this review cannot supply (quality-graded conclusions). Its search and screening are otherwise careful (preregistered, duplicate screening and extraction, trial registers added, funders named and findings split by funding). It may be cited for the map it draws: survey prevalence and who reports use, the counts and designs of pouch studies, measured contents, the range of nicotine uptake, how long the trials ran, and which findings are industry-funded; each figure is second-hand from named primary studies. It may not be cited for a quality-weighted judgment, for harm or benefit of pouches, for a comparison with smoking or snus, or for the statement that nicotine uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more typically exceeds that from cigarettes.

key_findings.finding: Scope: 481 titles and abstracts screened, 181 full texts, 73 new studies (12 industry-funded), 135 across both reviews; six sources searched to 30 September 2025; English and German; no risk-of-bias assessment and no statistical synthesis; findings are split by industry and non-industry funding.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Materials and methods, 1st paragraph; Search strategy, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: US youth: in PATH (ages 12 to 17, 2022 to 2023) lifetime pouch use was 0.9% and current use 0.2%; in the National Youth Tobacco Survey (middle and high school) lifetime use rose from 1.9% to 3.5% and current use from 0.8% to 1.8% between 2021 and 2024; in Monitoring the Future (grades 10 and 12) lifetime use rose from 3% to 5.4% and current use from 1.3% to 2.6% between 2023 and 2024, with most reporting dual use with e-cigarettes. Among adolescents currently using pouches in 2024, 29% reported frequent use and 22% daily use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Use patterns of ONPs › US prevalence estimates, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: US adults 2022 to 2023: PATH lifetime pouch use 3.3% and current use 0.8%; TUS-CPS lifetime use 2.7% and current use 0.4%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Use patterns of ONPs › US prevalence estimates, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other countries, lifetime (current) use: British youth 2024 3.3% (1.2%); Quebec adolescents 2024 3.7% (2.6%); Australia 2023 26% (19%) among youth and adults; Pakistan 2022 17.2% (9.4%) among youth and adults; Finland 2022 14.4% (3.7%) among youth and adults and 2023 17.2% (7.2%) among youth; adults in the UK 2024 13%, Great Britain 5.4% (1%), Poland 2024 9.2% (4.3%), Canadian college students 2024 27% (12%); Saudi Arabia lifetime use 14.2% in the general population and 21.2% among people with a tobacco history; Sweden 1.4% and Denmark 0.8% current use in 2019.
key_findings.locator: Results › Use patterns of ONPs › Prevalence estimates in other countries, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Sampling frames are not given in the main text; the Swedish and Danish figures come from a British American Tobacco-funded survey (reference 15).

key_findings.finding: Who reports use: among adolescents and adults, higher odds of lifetime or current pouch use in males, younger ages, and people who currently or formerly smoked, vaped or used smokeless tobacco; in US surveys also non-Hispanic whites; education mixed; household income not associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Use patterns of ONPs › Demographic characteristics, 1st to 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Cross-sectional associations.

key_findings.finding: Pouches and other nicotine use: in an 8-week three-arm trial of 33 daily smokers on low incomes, those assigned to pouches cut cigarettes per day by nearly half, one person switched completely and three stopped using pouches; in a 4-week trial of 30, both 3 mg and 6 mg strengths cut cigarettes and two people on 6 mg stopped smoking; in a 6-month industry-funded trial of 100, cigarettes per day fell by over 90%; in a US cross-sectional study, quitting cigarettes was associated with daily pouch use; 73% of Pakistani adults currently using pouches also smoked; 41% of Saudi adults with a tobacco history who tried pouches reported quitting.
