key_findings.locator: Results › Impact on other tobacco/nicotine product use, 1st paragraph; Non-industry-funded studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nicotine uptake: in an independent German crossover study of adults who smoked daily, a 30 mg pouch gave the highest peak and total nicotine over 4 hours, then a cigarette, then 20 mg and 6 mg pouches (time to peak 5 minutes for the cigarette, 20 minutes for the 6 mg pouch); in adults who used smokeless tobacco daily, 8 mg pouches delivered comparable or more nicotine than smokeless tobacco after 30 minutes of use; in industry-funded series, 4 mg and 8 mg pouches gave lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette and 12 mg and 8 mg 'mini' pouches comparable or higher, with time to peak 35 to 40 minutes against 5 to 7 for a cigarette; in adults who used Swedish snus, peak and 60-minute nicotine from 6, 9 and 11.2 mg pouches were higher than from 11.2 mg snus (twice as high for the 11.2 mg pouch), and pouches delivered nicotine slightly faster than snus and nicotine gum. Four of eight new pharmacokinetic trials were industry-funded (British American Tobacco, Japan Tobacco International).
key_findings.locator: Results › Product characteristics › Pharmacokinetics; Non-industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph; Industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Measured content: a US analysis of 70 tobacco-free products found 1.41 to 8.11 mg total nicotine per pouch; a second analysis of 50 pouches found 6.4 (SD 3.5) mg against 12.3 (SD 8.2) mg in tobacco-based pouches with a higher freebase share (63.4% against 47.2%); 31 pouches sold in Germany held 2.20 to 56 mg; measured nicotine was generally equal to or below the label. Elemental analysis of six pouches found aluminium, barium, chromium, copper, iron, manganese, strontium, titanium and others (not quantified); artificial sweeteners were present at 0.3 to 1.2 mg per pouch, even in unflavoured products.
key_findings.locator: Results › Product characteristics › Nicotine content and release from pouches, 1st paragraph; Toxicity › Chemical content, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Toxicity in cells: an independent assay found more pro-inflammatory cytokines than a pure nicotine solution; a British American Tobacco-funded assay found seven of eight own-brand pouches non-cytotoxic, non-mutagenic and non-genotoxic and cigarettes positive in all three tests, with one 8 mg spice-flavoured pouch cytotoxic and genotoxic at high concentrations; an Altria-funded analysis found that two of seven nicotine degradants and impurities exceeded the toxicity of nicotine itself.
key_findings.locator: Results › Toxicity › In vitro toxicity › Non-industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph; Industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers and physiology in people: in PATH data (small sample), nicotine metabolites in people who used only pouches were higher than in people who used only e-cigarettes and comparable to people who smoked; minor tobacco alkaloids, cadmium and uranium were lower than in people who smoked and similar to vapers; lead was lower than in people who smoked or vaped; in the 4-week trial, dual use with pouches did not lower tobacco-specific nitrosamines; 20-minute use of 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette; an Altria-funded trial found less gingivitis and staining at 24 weeks after switching.
key_findings.locator: Results › Toxicity › Human studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sales and marketing: Nielsen data (excluding online and specialty shops) show US pouch sales rising from 327 million units in July 2021 to 1,046 million in May 2024 and revenue from US$61 million to US$232 million, with four brands holding 99.8%; exposure to marketing was associated with use and appeal in youth and adults.
key_findings.locator: Results › Marketing and sales › Market share and sales data, 1st paragraph; ONP advertising, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Authors' reading: health effects of pouches 'remain largely understudied'; the evidence of short-term benefit from switching is 'limited, mainly industry-funded'; co-use with other products is high and the effect on smoking cessation unclear; pouches 'may be a less hazardous alternative to traditional tobacco' but 'are not risk-free'.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Short quotations are the authors' wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says nicotine uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more typically exceeds that from cigarettes. In the Results, a 6 mg pouch gave lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette in the independent German study, and 4 mg and 8 mg pouches were below a cigarette in an industry series; the Discussion says 6 mg or more in the first review and 8 mg or more in the update 'often exceeds'.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › Product characteristics › Pharmacokinetics; Discussion, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Uptake relative to a cigarette depends on strength, brand and study; the abstract sentence cannot be cited as it stands.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says trials of up to 6 months, independent and industry-funded, 'significantly decreased' cigarette and smokeless tobacco use. The Results give no tests for the independent trials (n = 33, 8 weeks; n = 30, 4 weeks) and the only 6-month trial (n = 100) is industry-funded.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Results › Impact on other tobacco/nicotine product use
reporting_issues.consequence: The word 'significantly' is not supported by the Results text; use the Results figures.

reporting_issues.issue: One crossover study (reference 61, a 30-minute five-product study in people who use snus) is listed under non-industry-funded studies for subjective ratings and under industry-funded studies for pharmacokinetics; the funder is not named.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Product characteristics › Subjective ratings › Non-industry-funded studies, 2nd paragraph; Pharmacokinetics › Industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of 12 industry-funded studies cannot be reproduced from the text; the funder of this study is unresolved.

reporting_issues.issue: The 6-month 'parallel-group trial of 100' with over 90% fewer cigarettes and the 'Altria-funded' 24-week trial of gingivitis are both cited to reference 17 (an oral-health trial of switching to on! pouches); the snus-and-pouch review in this batch lists that trial with 155 participants and 44 men and 56 women.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Impact on other tobacco/nicotine product use › Industry-funded studies; Toxicity › Human studies; compare sc_kopa_stojak_2026
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the trial is printed as 100 here and 155 there; its funder is stated here (Altria) but not in the other review.

reporting_issues.issue: Prevalence figures come from national surveys and from other samples in one running list (for example Australia 26% lifetime, Canadian college students 27%, against 3.3% of US adults); the text does not say which are probability samples.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Use patterns › Prevalence estimates in other countries
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-country comparison of prevalence from this list is not safe.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 11, the protocol, carries the first review's journal volume and page numbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Clerical; the protocol could not be located from the printed reference.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC13660210 (author manuscript, published before final editing 2026-09-06; all sections of the main text, funding and interests statements, author affiliations and the reference list read as HTML; Figure 1 (image) and the Supplementary Material zip (Tables S1 to S4, File S1) not read)

design_detail: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021293500; Cochrane Handbook methods; GRADE certainty ratings) of human studies of cancer incidence, cancer-specific mortality and survival after a cancer diagnosis in people who use Swedish snus and no other tobacco, against people who never used tobacco. Search run in May 2022. 15 studies met the criteria (14 cohort studies, 1 case-control study), almost all in men and most drawing on the same Swedish construction-worker cohort. Results are given study by study; the only pooling is a two-study inverse-variance combination for rectal cancer. Studies by researchers linked to, or sponsored by, the tobacco industry were excluded by design.
can_establish: What the published cohort and case-control studies up to May 2022 found, cancer site by cancer site, about cancer and cancer death in men who use snus and nothing else against men who never used tobacco, and how confident the reviewers were in each graded estimate.
cannot_establish: Causation (all evidence is observational); anything about women (almost no data); how snus compares with smoking (a descriptive collation of separate studies, not a pooled comparison, and its figure was not read as numbers here); rare cancers (few events); risks at older ages (few snus-using men were followed past 70); other smokeless products or nicotine pouches; or independent replication (most estimates come from one cohort, the Construction Workers Cohort, or from pooled analyses that contain it).

sample.recruitment: Search of the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), PsycInfo, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and Web of Science in May 2022 by a head librarian, building on searches run in 2004, 2013 and 2018 at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health; geographic terms restricted the search to Swedish snus; reference lists of included studies were screened. English, Norwegian, Swedish and Danish only. Search strategy in Table S1 (supplement, not read) (Methods › 2.2 Search strategy).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human studies of any design reporting cancer risk, total mortality or cancer-specific mortality for people who use snus exclusively against people who never used tobacco; current use at baseline preferred where available. Excluded: estimates based only on combined snus and cigarette use, and studies by researchers with links to the tobacco industry or sponsored by it (Methods › 2.3 Study eligibility criteria). Exclusion reasons are in Table S4 (not read).
sample.demographics: Almost all men. Only one of the 15 studies gave any estimate for women (lymphoma, with no cases among women). More than 75% of the men using snus only in the construction-worker cohort were under 30 at entry, and few were followed beyond 70 (Discussion › 4.2, 3rd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Restricting to snus-only against never-tobacco removes confounding by smoking but also removes everyone who used both, so the review says nothing about dual use. Excluding industry-linked studies is a stated choice. One cohort dominates: in the pooled nine-cohort analysis, two thirds of participants and 72% of pancreatic cancer cases or deaths came from the Construction Workers Cohort (Results › 3.1.4, 2nd paragraph). When several studies drew on the same population, the one with most participants or longest follow-up was graded (Methods › 2.6).

exposure.measurement: Whatever the primary studies recorded: a single self-report of tobacco habits at baseline in the Swedish cohorts, with current use at baseline preferred. The authors note that the single recording, with young participants at baseline and cancer appearing mostly after 50, leaves the estimates open to later changes in habit; one Swedish study found that about 30% of men using snus only may later stop or switch to smoking (Discussion › 4.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesised. Some primary studies report amount or duration (for example colorectal cancer at seven cans or more a week, hazard ratio 1.36, 1.04 to 1.78; Hodgkin lymphoma after more than 30 years, incidence rate ratio 3.78, 1.23 to 11.60, 4 exposed cases) (Results › 3.1.5, 3.1.7). Route: oral.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled by design: only snus-only men against men who never used tobacco were graded, because adjusting for smoking in samples that included people who smoke and people who used both distorted snus estimates in one study (Discussion › 4.1, 1st paragraph). Residual smoking in the snus-only group is possible: in one study 13.2% of never-smoking men using snus had at least one repeat record showing smoking, against 6.7% of men who never used tobacco (Discussion › 4.2, 5th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Former use was not graded; the authors chose current use at baseline to avoid uncertainty about duration, dose and changes in snus constituents.

comparison.controls: People who never used tobacco, in each primary study.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Primary studies adjusted for different covariate sets (Table S2, not read).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Diet, alcohol, socio-economic position and occupational exposures differ between snus and no-tobacco groups in some cohorts; the authors judge occupational and socio-economic confounding in the construction-worker cohort to be small because workers are fairly uniform and two lung-cancer case-control studies there found little confounding by smoking (Discussion › 4.2, 6th paragraph); this is argument, not measurement.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Alcohol is not discussed as a confounder in the main text. Smoking is handled by restriction.

outcomes.instruments: Cancer incidence by site from cancer registers (oral cavity, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, colon, rectum, anus, lung, lymphoma, leukaemia and myeloma, melanoma, any cancer), total mortality, cancer-specific mortality, and mortality after a cancer diagnosis.
outcomes.validity_norms: Register-based outcomes. Risk of bias in the primary studies was rated moderate for all, mostly because of the validity of the exposure information (Results › 3.1, 3rd paragraph; Table S5, not read).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is cancer or death against never use of tobacco, as hazard, risk or incidence rate ratios. Confidence is graded by GRADE: observational evidence starts low, upgraded to moderate for estimates above 2.0 or below 0.5, and graded very low when the interval spans both harm and benefit.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable. About 15 cancer or mortality outcomes are graded or reported; no correction for multiple outcomes, and each rests on one study.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Study selection was done by two researchers independently at both stages; data extraction by one author and checked by another; risk of bias assessed and discussed by two researchers.

analysis.effect_sizes: GRADE table (Table 1), snus only against no tobacco, relative effect with absolute risk with and without snus per 100,000 over each study's follow-up: oral cancer HR 0.93 (0.59 to 1.44), 90 against 84, very low certainty; oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma HR 3.5 (1.6 to 7.6), 16 against 55, moderate; non-cardia stomach cancer HR 1.4 (1.1 to 1.9), 237 against 332, low; pancreatic cancer, 27 years of follow-up, RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.3 in the table, 1.2 to 3.6 in the text), 72 against 151, moderate; pancreatic cancer, 36 years, HR 1.07 (0.77 to 1.50), 225 against 241, very low; rectal cancer HR 1.38 (1.07 to 1.77), 339 against 468, low; rectal cancer pooled with a longer follow-up of the main cohort HR 1.10 (0.91 to 1.34), low; cancer-specific mortality HR 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26), 2,141 against 2,395, low. Not graded: lung cancer RR 0.8 (0.4 to 1.3, 15 exposed cases); colon cancer HR 1.08 (0.91 to 1.29); anal cancer HR 0.61 (0.07 to 5.07, 1 case); non-Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.77 (0.59 to 1.01); Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.88 (0.49 to 1.58); leukaemias and myeloma IRRs 0.81 to 1.24; all melanoma IRR 0.65 (0.52 to 0.82); any cancer in never-smoking men HR 1.1 (0.9 to 1.4); smoking-related cancers HR 1.6 (1.1 to 2.5). Mortality: all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20 to 1.35) from the pooled Swedish analysis, 1.23 (1.09 to 1.40) in a separate cohort; after any cancer diagnosis, total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05 to 1.20) and cancer death HR 1.15 (1.05 to 1.26); after prostate cancer, overall HR 1.19 (1.04 to 1.37) and prostate cancer death HR 1.24 (1.03 to 1.49); after colorectal cancer, overall HR 1.16 (0.89 to 1.50).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; studies of never-smoking men were chosen so that smoking would not need adjustment. Some primary studies adjusted for cancer site, age and other factors (Table S2, not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021293500 is cited; the article read gives no statement on deviations from the registered protocol, and the registration itself was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: GRADE rows were chosen for cancers with a graded estimate; ungraded outcomes (lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma, melanoma) are reported in text. Where several studies shared a population, the largest or longest was graded and, for pancreatic and rectal cancer, an earlier shorter-follow-up result was also shown. The abstract and conclusions foreground the increased estimates (oesophagus, pancreas, stomach, rectum) and give less weight to the null or lower estimates (oral cancer, lung cancer, lymphoma, melanoma, colon cancer).
analysis.power: Low for rare cancers, as the authors say. Examples: oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 10 exposed cases; oral cancer 25; anal cancer 1; pancreatic cancer 18 exposed cases at 27 years.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 15 mostly Swedish, mostly male, observational studies, men who used snus only did not clearly differ from men who never used tobacco in oral cancer (HR 0.93, 0.59 to 1.44), lung cancer (RR 0.8, 0.4 to 1.3) or colon cancer (HR 1.08, 0.91 to 1.29). Higher estimates were reported for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (HR 3.5, 1.6 to 7.6, 10 exposed cases), non-cardia stomach cancer (HR 1.4, 1.1 to 1.9), pancreatic cancer at 27 years (RR 2.1, 1.2 to 3.3) and rectal cancer (HR 1.38, 1.07 to 1.77), each from one study; at longer follow-up the pancreatic estimate fell to HR 1.07 (0.77 to 1.50) and the rectal estimate to 1.10 (0.91 to 1.34) when pooled with a longer follow-up of the main cohort. Cancer-specific death was slightly higher (HR 1.12, lower limit 1.00) and so was death after a cancer diagnosis (HR 1.13 to 1.19). Melanoma was lower (IRR 0.65). Certainty ranged from moderate (oesophagus, pancreas at 27 years) to very low.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says snus probably increases the risk of cancer of the oesophagus and pancreas, may increase the risk of stomach and rectal cancer, and that the evidence suggests more cancer-specific deaths; it concludes snus entails a cancer hazard whose size may depend on a person's history of use and susceptibility. Gaps: (1) causal verbs ('increases') rest on one observational study each, with 10 exposed cases for the oesophagus and 18 for the pancreas at 27 years; (2) the larger, longer pancreatic analysis (36 years) was rated very low and showed no clear difference, and the rectal estimate fell from 1.38 to 1.10 with 10 more years of follow-up, yet the abstract and conclusions list rectal and pancreatic cancer among the increased risks and the Discussion says there is reason to believe a causal link exists for rectal cancer; (3) all studies were rated at moderate risk of bias for exposure information, but this did not lead to any downgrade in the GRADE table, and the oesophagus is rated moderate although the footnote says it was downgraded for few events; (4) the conclusion is stated as 'hazard' (whether snus can cause cancer), not as the size of a person's risk, and no results are given for women; (5) the section comparing snus with smoking is descriptive, built from separate studies in one figure that was not read here.

timeline.event: Norwegian Knowledge Centre for the Health Services report, the first search (2004) on which this review's search builds.
Norwegian Institute of Public Health update (search 2013); a further update followed in 2019 (search 2018).
Pooled analysis of nine Swedish cohorts on oral cancer, the most recent study used for the oral cancer grade (as stated in the Results).
Pooled analysis of eight Swedish cohorts on mortality, whose cancer-specific death estimate (HR 1.12) is the review's mortality row.
This review (search May 2022); the authors say its findings agree with earlier evaluations by IARC and the US National Cancer Institute.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent systematic review of snus and cancer identified. Its findings overlap heavily with the pooled analysis of mortality (byhamre_2021) and with each other (the same construction-worker cohort contributes to most estimates), so the estimates are not independent replications. The oesophageal and pancreatic findings rest on one study each and have not been confirmed in a second independent cohort in this review; the pancreatic estimate shrank with longer follow-up.

funding.funder: Not stated in the page text read (the article has a conflict-of-interest statement and an acknowledgement for the librarian, but no funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: All the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health (Divisions of Climate and Environmental Health and for Health Services), the Nordic Institute of Dental Materials, the University of Oslo, the National Institute of Occupational Health and the Cancer Registry of Norway. The review excluded primary studies by researchers with a link to the tobacco industry or sponsored by it; the text read does not say which studies were excluded for that reason (Table S4 not read). The other review of snus and health in this batch (lee_2013), by a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry and supported by a snus manufacturer, reads an earlier body of evidence (to 2012) more reassuringly.

what_would_settle_it: Several independent, large cohorts of snus-only and never-tobacco men, women included, with tobacco use recorded repeatedly through follow-up (so quitting and switching to smoking are counted), and site-specific cancers followed beyond age 70, pooled with individual participant data so that each cancer site rests on more than one population; plus cancer-site studies of people who switched from smoking to snus, which were excluded here.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people using snus only), exposure, comparator (never use of tobacco), outcomes (cancer, mortality) and designs are specified.
PROSPERO CRD42021293500 is cited; the article does not describe deviations, and the registered protocol was not read.
Eligibility says there was no restriction on design; no reason is given for including cohort and case-control studies (only observational evidence exists for this question).

Six databases searched by a librarian, built on three earlier searches, with reference lists screened and the search within 24 months of publication; but language limited to English and three Scandinavian languages without a justification, no grey literature, no trial or study registries and no content experts mentioned. Judged 'no' because AMSTAR 2 item 4 is applied as written (unjustified publication restriction), as for every card of earlier batches (decision p-amstar2-item4). The search strategy itself is in a supplement not read.
Two researchers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently; disagreements were resolved by discussion.

One author extracted and another checked that the right information was extracted; authors of primary studies were contacted for missing data. Meets the item's first criterion as read in earlier cards of this project (two reviewers reaching consensus).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the text says excluded studies are listed with reasons in Table S4; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The main text gives, for each study, the outcome, comparison, number of exposed cases and often follow-up and cohort; effect estimates, characteristics of the snus groups and confounder adjustments are in Table S2 (not read); the text does not describe setting and follow-up for every study.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Joanna Briggs Institute checklists for cohort and case-control studies, assessed and discussed by two researchers, covering confounding, selection and exposure and outcome measurement; the checklists do not cover selection of the reported result, and the study-level ratings are in Table S5 (not read). All studies were rated moderate risk of bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the main text; Table S2, which lists other study details, was not read. The review did screen for industry links and sponsorship at eligibility.

The only pooling is a generic inverse-variance combination of two adjusted hazard ratios for rectal cancer from non-overlapping parts of the same collaboration (the non-construction cohorts and the longer follow-up of the construction cohort); it is appropriate for that purpose, though the model and heterogeneity are not stated.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meaningful quantitative synthesis: one two-study pooling, with all studies rated the same (moderate) risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion (4.2) analyses how single baseline recording of exposure, misclassification of smoking and cohort features could affect estimates and says why smoking was handled by restriction; but the moderate risk of bias did not lead to a GRADE downgrade.

Differences between estimates for the same cancer are examined (time-varying hazard ratios for pancreatic and rectal cancer across follow-up periods, with a shorter and a longer follow-up of the same cohort).
No meaningful quantitative synthesis, so no test is possible; the Discussion does not address publication bias or selective reporting qualitatively.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors declare no conflicts of interest; the funding of the review is not stated in the page text read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: AMSTAR 2 rates one critical item as 'no' (item 4: an unjustified language restriction and no other sources beyond databases and reference lists), and item 7 is provisional because Table S4 was not read; if that list does not give reasons, the rating becomes critically low. Items 2 and 9 are partly met. The review is registered, uses duplicate screening, a standard bias checklist and GRADE, and writes its uncertainty out, so its estimates are best cited as a transparent, graded summary of a small observational literature that is dominated by one cohort and one sex. It may be cited for the site-by-site estimates and their certainty, the absolute risks in its GRADE table, the shrinking of the pancreatic and rectal estimates with longer follow-up, and the absence of data on women; not for causal statements, for any comparison with smoking beyond what is stated, or for independent replication.

key_findings.finding: 2,450 records screened, 67 read in full, 15 studies included (14 cohort studies, 1 case-control study); all rated moderate risk of bias, mostly for the validity of exposure information. Only one study reported any estimate for women (lymphoma, no cases).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › 3.1 Cancer risk of snus use compared with no tobacco use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Graded estimates, snus only against no tobacco (Table 1): oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma HR 3.5 (1.6 to 7.6) from one cohort study of 142,891 men, 16 against 55 cases per 100,000, moderate certainty; non-cardia stomach cancer HR 1.4 (1.1 to 1.9), 237 against 332 per 100,000, low; rectal cancer HR 1.38 (1.07 to 1.77), 339 against 468 per 100,000, low; pancreatic cancer at 27 years RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.3 in the table), 72 against 151 per 100,000, moderate; oral cancer HR 0.93 (0.59 to 1.44), very low; cancer-specific mortality HR 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26), 2,141 against 2,395 per 100,000, low.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › 3.1.1 to 3.1.5, 3.1.11

key_findings.finding: Pancreatic cancer in the Construction Workers Cohort varied with the length of follow-up: HR 1.98 (0.97 to 4.03, 4 exposed cases) to 1994, 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6, 18 cases) to 2004, 1.34 (0.90 to 1.99, 31 cases) to 2013; the pooled nine-cohort analysis (36 years, 41 exposed cases) gave HR 1.07 (0.77 to 1.50), graded very low. In that pooled analysis two thirds of participants and 72% of cases or deaths came from the Construction Workers Cohort.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.4 Cancer of the pancreas, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure 2 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Rectal cancer: HR 1.38 (1.07 to 1.77, 73 exposed cases) at 27 years of follow-up in nine pooled cohorts; combining the non-construction cohorts with a 10-years-longer follow-up of the Construction Workers Cohort gave HR 1.10 (0.91 to 1.34), a drop of almost 20% in the point estimate. Colon cancer HR 1.02 to 1.08 and anal cancer 0.61 (0.07 to 5.07, 1 case) showed no clear difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.5 Cancer of the colon, rectum and anus, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Estimates close to no difference or lower: oral cancer (pooled 9 cohorts HR 0.93, 0.59 to 1.44, 25 exposed cases; a third study of oral and pharyngeal cancers combined HR 2.3, 0.7 to 8.3, 5 cases), lung cancer RR 0.8 (0.4 to 1.3, 15 cases), non-Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.77 (0.59 to 1.01), Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.88 (0.49 to 1.58), leukaemias and myeloma IRR 0.81 to 1.24, all melanoma IRR 0.65 (0.52 to 0.82); lymphoma, leukaemia and melanoma results were not graded because they were given as incidence rate ratios.

Mortality: pooled Swedish analysis all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20 to 1.35) and cancer-specific HR 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26); a separate cohort not in that analysis, HR 1.23 (1.09 to 1.40) for all-cause and 1.28 (0.96 to 1.69) for cancer death in never-smoking men who had ever used snus. After a cancer diagnosis in construction workers, total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05 to 1.20) and cancer death HR 1.15 (1.05 to 1.26); after prostate cancer, overall HR 1.19 (1.04 to 1.37) and prostate cancer death HR 1.24 (1.03 to 1.49); after colorectal cancer, overall HR 1.16 (0.89 to 1.50), and 1.89 (1.21 to 2.94, 22 deaths) when the construction cohort was left out.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.11 to 3.1.14

key_findings.finding: The authors' summary: snus probably increases the risk of cancer of the oesophagus and pancreas (moderate certainty), may increase the risk of stomach and rectal cancer (low), and the evidence suggests more cancer deaths and more deaths after a cancer diagnosis (low); they are very uncertain about the other cancers, and do not know the effect in women. They conclude snus entails a cancer hazard whose size may depend on a person's history of use and host susceptibility.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Summary of evidence for cancer risk

key_findings.finding: Smoking comparison: where smoking and snus were compared against the same never-tobacco group in the same studies, cancer risk estimates were higher for smoking than for snus at most sites, and all confidence intervals overlapped except for lung cancer; the figure with the estimates (Figure 4) was not read as numbers. The authors say it is not known how much switching from smoking to snus would reduce the benefit expected from quitting all tobacco.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.5 (snus compared with cigarettes), 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Figure 4 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Exposure caveats: a single baseline recording of tobacco habits; about 30% of men using snus only may later stop or switch to smoking (a Swedish study cited); more than 75% of men using snus only were under 30 at entry and few were followed beyond 70; seven of the included studies used construction-worker data from 1971 to 1975, when non-use could not be told from non-response; 13.2% of never-smoking men using snus, against 6.7% of men who never used tobacco, had a repeat record showing smoking, though the authors cite a sensitivity analysis in which 60% of the snus group would have to be smokers to shift one oesophageal result.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.2 Impact of exposure information, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Tobacco-industry studies were excluded by design; studies reporting only dual use of snus and cigarettes were also excluded; the review states that adjusting for smoking in samples that included smokers distorted snus estimates in one study.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.3 Study eligibility criteria; Discussion › 4.1 Grading the results, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the pancreatic cancer estimate at 27 years is printed as RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.3); the text prints the same estimate as 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6) twice. The table's absolute risk (151 per 100,000, upper limit 237) matches an upper limit of 3.3 (72 x 3.3 = 238).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1; Results › 3.1.4, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limit is uncertain by 0.3. IARC Monograph 100E (sc_iarc_2012) prints the Swedish construction-worker cohort's never-smoker pancreatic estimate as 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6; 18 cases), which agrees with the text of this review; the primary study has not been checked. The industry-linked review in this batch (Lee 2013) prints what appears to be the same study's never-smoker estimate as 2.00 (1.20 to 3.30), so the point estimate also differs (2.0 against 2.1).

reporting_issues.issue: The bracketed numbers in Table 1's absolute-risk column are the confidence limits of the risk with snus (for example oral cancer 53 to 130 per 100,000 around 84), but they are labelled 'fewer' and 'more' as if they were differences from the no-tobacco risk of 90.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader who takes '53 fewer to 130 more' as a difference would be misled; the claim should quote the risks with and without snus, not the bracketed words.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 attributes the oral cancer, 36-year pancreatic cancer and rectal cancer estimates all to 'Araghi et al' with the same reference number (18), while the text cites different reference numbers for these (25 for oral cancer, 23 for pancreatic cancer, 18 for colorectal cancer) and uses both 18 and 23 for the rectal cancer estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The three estimates come from different papers by the same group; the reference list must be checked before any is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The oesophageal estimate is rated moderate and footnote b says it was downgraded for very few events, while the review's own rule starts observational evidence at low and upgrades to moderate for an estimate above 2.0; a downgrade after an upgrade would give low.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 footnote b; Methods › 2.6, after Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The certainty for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma may be one level lower than printed; Table S3 (not read) holds the reasoning.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists stomach cancer as one study, the Results describe two (a case-control study and the cohort study), and the Discussion refers to 14 included studies where the Results count 15.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › 3.1.3; Discussion › 4.2, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor counting inconsistency; the case-control stomach result (OR 0.5, 0.2 to 1.2) is lower than the cohort result and is not part of the graded estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The cancer-specific mortality row cites 163,412 participants, whereas the source paper analysed 169,103 men; the difference of 5,691 equals the number of men who formerly used snus there.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (cancer-specific mortality row); compare sc_byhamre_2021
reporting_issues.consequence: Explained by counting only the two groups compared; the same estimate and its overlap with the mortality paper must not be counted twice in a claim.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ijc.34643 (all sections and Table 1 read as text, author affiliations, conflict-of-interest and author-contribution statements; Figures 1 to 4 are images and their values were not extracted; Supporting Information Tables S1 to S5 and the reference list were not read; the page has no funding statement)

design_detail: Single-session laboratory measurement followed by exposure modelling and toxicological risk assessment. 17 adult volunteers who vaped daily took 5 or 25 puffs on one of three device-and-liquid combinations and exhaled the first breath after each puff onto filters; nicotine, propylene glycol, glycerol, four tobacco-specific nitrosamines (TSNAs), three aldehydes and 13 metals were measured, with each person's own breath before vaping as the control. The amounts were scaled up with an assumed lung-retention fraction (a model first built for cigarette smoking) to air concentrations for two imagined scenarios, a one-hour trip in a small unventilated car with two people vaping and a child as the bystander, and a four-hour day in a ventilated office with one person vaping, and compared with air-quality limit values or margins of exposure. No bystander, room air or cigarette smoke was measured.
can_establish: What was in the first exhaled breath of 17 volunteers who vaped three products in a laboratory, compared with their own breath beforehand, and what air concentrations and margins of exposure follow if the stated scenario assumptions hold.
cannot_establish: What bystanders are actually exposed to or what happens to their health (no room, car or body was measured, and the scenarios are imagined and use worst-case assumptions); how exhaled vapour compares with second-hand tobacco smoke (not measured here); whether the findings hold for other devices, liquids or ways of vaping (three low-powered products with tobacco flavour were tested); or any long-term effect.

sample.recruitment: Online screening (computer-assisted web interviewing) of 44,439 members of a Dutch national panel database run by a market-research agency; volunteers were recruited from the people who met the criteria, with the sex ratio and dual-use status matched to those found in the screening. Ethics approval from the Medical Research Ethics Committee of Wageningen University.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: aged 18 or over; daily e-cigarette use with a nicotine-containing liquid (above 6 mg/mL); no diagnosis of diabetes or lung disease. No smoking or vaping for at least 30 minutes before the session. Age, vaping history and exact exclusions beyond these are not given in the main text.
sample.demographics: 10 men and 7 women; 9 also smoked cigarettes (dual use). Age is not reported in the main text.
sample.attrition: All 17 are listed in Table 2; no withdrawals are mentioned. Each person provided nicotine, propylene glycol and glycerol data (5 puffs) and only one 25-puff analysis (nitrosamines, aldehydes or metals), so the three 25-puff analyses rest on 9, 4 and 3 people.
sample.selection_effects: Small convenience group of volunteers who vape daily, from a national panel. The products were chosen by the researchers rather than the volunteers' own, all were tobacco-flavoured and relatively low-powered by the authors' account (a cig-a-like and a refillable device run at 7.6 W). The 113 potential subjects named in Methods and the 485 named in Results (see reporting issues) leave unclear how many people met the criteria.

exposure.measurement: Exhaled breath captured through a mouthpiece onto a quartz filter pad (and a carbon cartridge for aldehydes) immediately after each puff; filters and devices weighed before and after. Nicotine and TSNAs by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry; propylene glycol and glycerol by the WHO TobLabNet method; carbonyls by derivatisation and chromatography; metals by ICP-MS. Repeatability below 10% (below 5% for TSNAs) and recoveries 80 to 120% as stated. Only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled; the rest of what is exhaled is estimated by the model.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: 5 puffs for nicotine, propylene glycol and glycerol; 25 puffs for the other analytes; puff length, volume and interval were left to the volunteers (natural vaping). Liquid used per puff 5.6 ± 2.4 mg. Exhaled volume per exhalation 33 to 1528 mL. Products (Table 1): A, a non-refillable cig-a-like, tobacco flavour, 18 mg/mL nicotine, propylene glycol/glycerol 50/50; B, refillable dual-coil device (3.7 V battery), tobacco flavour, 18 mg/mL, 50/50; C, the same refillable device, tobacco flavour, 11 mg/mL, 80/20.
exposure.polysubstance: Nine of 17 volunteers also smoked. Breath collected before the first puff served as each person's control and was subtracted; the control breath contained small amounts of nicotine (up to 0.2 ng per puff) from earlier use or second-hand exposure. Total TSNAs did not differ between people who also smoked and people who only vaped (t-test, p = 0.79), tested in the 9 people analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 30 minutes without smoking or vaping before the session; not verified biologically.

comparison.controls: Each volunteer's own exhaled breath before the first puff. No comparison with cigarette smoke, with room air, or with people who do not vape.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person baseline).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to an exposure measurement; what was not measured: air in any room or car, particles, bystanders' blood, urine or saliva, second and later exhalations, changes in the vapour as it ages in air, and deposits on surfaces.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Mass gain of the trapping devices and the chemical analyses above. Risk assessment: modelled air concentrations compared with human limit values, WHO Air Quality Guidelines first, and otherwise a margin of exposure (the ratio between a dose that caused effects and the estimated exposure) against a point of departure; for cancer-causing substances a margin of at least 10,000 was taken as low concern. Limit values and the exhaled-fraction calculation are in two supplements that were not read.
outcomes.validity_norms: Analytical recoveries and repeatability are stated. For the model, 40% (local effects) and 33% (systemic effects) of the amount inhaled were assumed to appear in the first exhalation, using worst-case alveolar retention assumptions from a model developed for cigarette smoking. The four nitrosamines were all treated as equally potent as N-nitrosodimethylamine, which the authors say probably overestimates the risk.
outcomes.operationalization: Health risk to a bystander is the gap between a modelled concentration or dose and a limit value or point of departure, not an observed effect. Highest exhaled amounts among the volunteers were used for each chemical, and the final (highest) air concentration of each scenario was used rather than an average over the period.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: 23 analytes measured, descriptive; only two significance statements (mass gain, and the dual-versus-exclusive TSNA comparison, p = 0.79).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mass gain of the trapping device per exhalation: 4.24 ± 2.54 mg for exhaled vapour against 1.86 ± 1.28 mg for control breath (Table 2), strongly correlated with the water content of the extracts (R = 0.98), so mostly water. Editors' calculation from Table 2: mean paired difference 2.39 mg (95% CI 1.41 to 3.38), paired t = 5.15 with 16 degrees of freedom; 16 of 17 volunteers gained more mass with vapour than with control breath (subject 1 did not). Exhaled in the first breath after one puff (Table 3, range across volunteers and median): nicotine below the limit of quantification to 2140 ng, median 108 ng (detected in all samples but one); propylene glycol below the limit to 127 µg, median below the limit (seen in 4 of 17); glycerol below the limit in all 17; TSNAs in 9 people: NNN up to 111 pg (median 29), NNK up to 71 pg (15), NAT up to 40 pg (14), NAB up to 8 pg (2), total as N-nitrosodimethylamine equivalent up to 77 pg (median 28); formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein below the limit in all 4 people; 12 of 13 metals below the limit in 3 people, copper up to 2.92 ng (median below the limit). Modelled concentrations (Table 5; car / office): propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3; TSNAs as NDMA equivalent 5.8 / 1.31 ng/m3; copper 219 / 50 ng/m3. Editors' calculation: these Table 5 values are reproduced from the Table 3 maxima with the section 2.7 formula, the 40% exhaled fraction, the Table 4 scenario settings and, for the office, the 42.5% ventilation factor. Margins of exposure (Table 6; car / office): propylene glycol local 17 / 74 or 81; TSNAs local 521 / 2297; propylene glycol systemic 535 / 1475; nicotine systemic margin to the effect level 2.1 / 6; nicotine local 3 to 14 below the rat no-effect level and about 170 / 750 below a human airway effect level.
analysis.covariates: None. The model uses scenario parameters (people vaping, puffs per minute, minutes, room volume, ventilation) and assumed retention fractions.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All analytes measured are listed in Table 3. The limit values, points of departure and the exhaled-fraction calculation are in Supplementary Materials 1 and 2, which were not read. Which of the three products produced which result is not reported, and the nitrosamine content of the three liquids is not reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 17 volunteers overall and 9, 4 and 3 for the three 25-puff analyses; the authors point to large differences between people (editors' calculation: the highest nicotine value is about 20 times the median) and say that studies of second-hand vaping before theirs used three or fewer people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 17 volunteers vaping three low-powered products, the first breath after a puff held measurable nicotine (median 108 ng, up to 2140 ng), propylene glycol in 4 people, tobacco-specific nitrosamines in the 9 people tested (total up to 77 pg) and copper in one of three people tested; glycerol, three aldehydes and 12 other metals were below the detection limit in the few people tested for them. Scaling these up with worst-case assumptions gave modelled air concentrations; against limit values the margins were thin for propylene glycol irritation in the car scenario (17), for nicotine's effects on heart rate and blood pressure (2.1 in the car, 6 in the office) and for nitrosamine cancer risk (521 and 2297 against a threshold of 10,000). The authors themselves call the effects relatively mild even in the extreme scenario. Nothing was measured in a room, a car or a bystander, and no cigarette was measured.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions say bystanders may experience irritation of the respiratory tract from propylene glycol and glycerol, that systemic effects of nicotine should also be expected, with palpitations and a rise in systolic blood pressure, and that an increased risk of tumours cannot be excluded in the car scenario; the abstract also says e-cigarette use can clearly affect bystanders' health, while the discussion calls the effects relatively mild. Gaps: (1) the effects are model outputs from exhaled-breath measurements and worst-case assumptions, not observations in bystanders; (2) glycerol was below the detection limit in all 17 volunteers and the risk assessment itself says nothing is expected from amounts below that limit, yet glycerol is named as an irritant in the abstract and conclusions; (3) the expectation of nicotine effects rests on estimated exposure lying only 2.1 times below an effect level reported in one human study, with the authors adding variability between people; (4) the cancer statement rests on treating four nitrosamines as equal in potency to N-nitrosodimethylamine, on the highest exhaled amounts, and on nitrosamines whose source in the liquids was not measured; (5) 'increased levels of copper' rests on one of three people; (6) the claim that nitrosamines in exhaled vapour can be avoided is not tested in the paper. In the authors' favour, they state the worst-case assumptions and the opposite-direction limitations (low-powered products, few volunteers, only the first exhalation sampled).

timeline.event: Ballbe et al.: air and biomarker measurements in homes of people who vape, with difficulty excluding exposure to tobacco smoke elsewhere (as described in the introduction; not read).

Hess et al.: systematic review of passive exposure to e-cigarette vapour; the authors say it agrees with their main findings on upper-airway irritation and nicotine effects (as described in the discussion; not read).
National Academies review of the health consequences of e-cigarettes, cited as the first reference of this paper; read separately for the claims on this topic.
This study: the authors state it is the first toxicological risk assessment of e-cigarette vapour to bystanders and that earlier measurements of second-hand vaping used three or fewer volunteers.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small laboratory study with a modelled risk assessment. This card does not cover later measurements in rooms or in bystanders; the reviews read for the claim on vapour near others are named in that claim.

funding.funder: Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (research and article-processing charge).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors share affiliation number 1; the PMC text does not name the institution (the task brief names the Dutch national institute RIVM, and reference 9 is an earlier RIVM report with the same first author). A market-research agency helped with recruitment and the experiments, and two people named in the acknowledgments, who are not authors, carried out the risk assessment. No tobacco or vape industry funding is stated.

what_would_settle_it: Measurements in real rooms and cars of nicotine, particles, nitrosamines and other compounds during vaping and, in the same spaces, during smoking, across ventilation and room sizes, with a range of current devices, liquids and puffing patterns; plus nicotine and nitrosamine biomarkers (for example cotinine) in bystanders who are not exposed to tobacco smoke elsewhere, over days and weeks.

domains.note: 17 volunteers and three low-powered tobacco-flavoured products; the 25-puff analyses (nitrosamines, aldehydes, metals) rest on 9, 4 and 3 people; large differences between people.

Validated methods with stated recoveries and repeatability and a within-person baseline; only the first exhalation was sampled and many results were below the limit of quantification; glycerol was measured with lower sensitivity.

domains.domain: Measurement in air and in bystanders
domains.note: Nothing was measured in a room, a car or a bystander; the air concentrations are modelled from imagined scenarios.

Worst-case retention fractions from a cigarette model, highest exhaled amounts, final rather than average concentration, and equal potency of four nitrosamines; some assumptions run toward overestimation, others (low-powered products, few volunteers, no ageing of the aerosol) toward underestimation, as the authors state.
No comparison with second-hand tobacco smoke or with background air in the same rooms; the comparison is with limit values and points of departure from other studies, many in animals.

Glycerol named as an irritant though below the detection limit; 'increased' copper from one of three people; recruitment counts differ between Methods and Results; the three 25-puff analyses cover 16 of 17 people; no test named for the mass-gain difference.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a measurement-plus-modelling risk assessment (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains adapted to this design. The laboratory measurements are transparent and the authors state their assumptions, but the headline findings are model outputs about imagined scenarios resting on small numbers of people and no measurement in the places or people at issue. Citable for what was in the exhaled breath of 17 volunteers who vaped three products and for the authors' own risk estimates under stated assumptions; not citable for what bystanders are exposed to or for how this compares with second-hand smoke.

key_findings.finding: 17 volunteers took part (10 men, 7 women; 9 also smoked); 4 used product A, 6 used B and 7 used C. Product A was a non-refillable cig-a-like at 18 mg/mL, B and C a refillable dual-coil device at 18 and 11 mg/mL; all tobacco flavour. The volunteers' own breath before the first puff served as control.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.2 Collection and Analysis of Exhaled Vapor, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1; Results › 3.1 and 3.2

key_findings.finding: Mass gain of the trapping devices was higher with exhaled vapour (4.24 ± 2.54 mg per exhalation) than with control breath (1.86 ± 1.28 mg), strongly correlated with the water content of the extracts (R = 0.98); no test statistic is printed.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3 Analysis of Exhaled Vapor, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 2: mean paired difference 2.39 mg (95% CI 1.41 to 3.38), paired t = 5.15, 16 degrees of freedom; one volunteer (subject 1) had a lower value with vapour.

key_findings.finding: Nicotine was found in the first exhaled breath of all volunteers but one: range below the limit of quantification to 2140 ng per puff, median 108 ng; exhaled volume per exhalation ranged from 33 to 1528 mL; control breath held up to 0.2 ng and was subtracted.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 3rd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Propylene glycol was seen in 4 of 17 volunteers (maximum 127 µg per puff, median below the limit); glycerol was below the limit of quantification in all 17, and the method was less sensitive for glycerol.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 4th paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Tobacco-specific nitrosamines, measured in 9 volunteers: NNN up to 111 pg (median 29), NNK up to 71 pg (15), NAT up to 40 pg (14), NAB up to 8 pg (2); total as NDMA equivalent up to 77 pg (median 28) per puff. Total TSNAs did not differ between people who also smoked and people who only vaped (p = 0.79).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 5th paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein were below the limit of quantification in all 4 volunteers analysed (amounts of formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acetone found did not exceed control-breath levels); of 13 metals measured in 3 volunteers only copper was seen (maximum 2.92 ng, median below the limit).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 6th paragraph; Table 3; Results › 3.12 and 3.13

key_findings.finding: Scenarios modelled: car, 2 people vaping at 0.5 puffs a minute for 1 hour in a space of 2 m3 with no ventilation, the bystander a child; office, 1 person at 2 puffs a minute for 4 hours in 30 m3 with ventilation of 0.5 per hour (final concentration reduced to 42.5%). The authors say the car scenario approximates the highest levels expected in everyday situations and the office scenario a more typical level.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.4 Bystander Exposure, 1st paragraph; Table 4; Methods › 2.7, last paragraph; Conclusions, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Modelled air concentrations (car / office): propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3; TSNAs as NDMA equivalent 5.8 / 1.31 ng/m3; copper 219 / 50 ng/m3.
key_findings.locator: Table 5
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: reproduced from the Table 3 maxima, the 40% exhaled fraction and the Table 4 settings (for example nicotine 2.14 µg / 0.4 x 0.5 per min x 60 min x 2 people / 2 m3 = 0.16 mg/m3).

key_findings.finding: Propylene glycol: margin of exposure for upper-airway irritation 17 in the car and 74 or 81 in the office; local effects on the airways and eyes 'cannot be excluded' in the car and are expected to be mild if they occur; no local effects anticipated in the office; no systemic effects expected (margins 535 and 1475).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.7 Propylene Glycol; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Nicotine: local airway effects not expected in either scenario (exposure 3 to 14 times below the no-effect level in a two-year rat inhalation study and about 170 and 750 times below a human airway effect level); systemic effects (higher heart rate and systolic blood pressure) 'should be expected' in the car (margin to the human effect level 2.1) and cannot be excluded in the office (margin 6); the size is compared with the caffeine in 2 or 3 cups of coffee.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.9 and 3.10; Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Nitrosamines: margins of exposure 521 (car) and 2297 (office) against 10,000 taken as low concern; an increased risk of respiratory-tract tumours cannot be excluded in the car, and for the office a risk assessment cannot be made with sufficient certainty. All four nitrosamines were treated as equal in potency to N-nitrosodimethylamine, which the authors say probably overestimates the risk.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.11; Table 6; Methods › 2.8, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Copper stayed below a tolerable air concentration of 1 µg/m3 in both scenarios; the other metals were below the limit of quantification, with no conclusion possible for chromium (only total chromium, nickel and arsenic were measured).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.12 Copper; 3.13 Other Metals

key_findings.finding: The authors call the effects on bystanders relatively mild even in the extreme scenario, say the nitrosamine risk could be avoided if e-liquids had no detectable nitrosamines and that only a limited number of liquids on the market contain significant amounts, and say the study is the first toxicological risk assessment of e-cigarette vapour to bystanders.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusions › Regulatory Implications

key_findings.finding: Limitations the authors state: only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled and the rest estimated with an assumed retention; the model was originally developed for cigarette smoking; the final, highest concentration was used; the highest emissions seen probably do not represent the worst case with so few volunteers, and low-powered products probably lead to underestimation; changes of the vapour in air, nicotine reacting to form nitrosamines, and deposits on surfaces were not modelled; toxicity data are missing for most flavour compounds.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.7; Results › 3.5; Discussion, 3rd to 7th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Methods say the national panel screening of 44,439 respondents identified 113 potential test subjects; Results say 485 people who vaped matched the criteria. The screening method is written 'CAWI' in Methods and 'CIWA' in Results. Figure 1, which should explain the numbers, is an image and was not extracted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pool the 17 volunteers came from is unclear; no effect on the measurements.

reporting_issues.issue: The three 25-puff analyses cover 9 (nitrosamines), 4 (aldehydes) and 3 (metals) volunteers, which add to 16, although 17 volunteers are reported and the methods say each had one such analysis.
reporting_issues.consequence: One volunteer's 25-puff analysis is not accounted for; findings on aldehydes and metals rest on 4 and 3 people at most.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the conclusions name glycerol, with propylene glycol, as a cause of respiratory irritation for bystanders. Table 3 and section 3.6 report glycerol below the limit of quantification in all 17 volunteers (with a less sensitive method) and say amounts below the limit are not expected to cause effects; only propylene glycol carries a margin of exposure for irritation (Table 6).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract; Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Results › 3.3, 3.6; Table 6)
reporting_issues.consequence: Glycerol should not be cited as a finding of irritation from this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says increased levels of propylene glycol and copper were found in exhaled breath. Table 3 shows propylene glycol above the limit in 4 of 17 people (median below the limit) and copper above the limit in at most one of 3 people (median below the limit).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's list is stronger than the table; the scenario values use the single highest exhaled amount for each chemical.

reporting_issues.issue: The nitrosamine margin of exposure in the office scenario (2297) is below the 10,000 threshold the authors set for low concern, as in the car scenario (521); the abstract and conclusions state the cancer risk 'could not be excluded' only for the car, and the text says only that the office risk cannot be assessed with sufficient certainty.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two scenarios are not as different in this respect as the abstract suggests; neither meets the authors' own threshold.

reporting_issues.issue: The statements that the nitrosamines can be avoided and that only a limited number of liquids on the market contain significant amounts have no citation in the passage, and the nitrosamine content of the three liquids used, and which products produced the nitrosamines found, are not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 1st paragraph; Regulatory Implications; Table 3)
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of the nitrosamines in exhaled breath is not shown by this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The mass-gain difference between vapour and control breath is called significant without naming a test; the means and standard deviations in the text match Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on interpretation (editors' paired test confirms the difference); the gain is mostly water.

reporting_issues.issue: The car scenario names a child as the bystander, but the main text does not give the body weight, breathing rate or child-specific limit values used for the doses and margins; these are described as being in Supplementary Material 2, which was not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the margins apply to a child cannot be checked from the main text.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6539638 (all sections, Tables 1 to 6 as text, reference list, funding, conflicts and author contributions; Figure 1 is an image and was not extracted; Supplementary Materials 1 and 2 not read)

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis of published placebo-controlled randomized trials of oral nicotine products (gum, inhaler, sublingual tablet, 1 mg lozenge) on withdrawal symptoms and craving. Medline and Embase, the Cochrane NRT trials database, reference lists and colleagues were searched (no dates given); quality criteria served as inclusion criteria; results were tabulated as significant or not for each symptom in the first week of abstinence (vote counting). 27 studies reported effects on at least one symptom; 12 met the criteria (8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet, no lozenge).
can_establish: Whether placebo-controlled trials published to 2000 reported significant reductions in specific withdrawal symptoms with oral nicotine products in the first week of abstinence, symptom by symptom.
cannot_establish: How large any reduction is (no effect sizes), effects after the first week, effects of patches or nasal spray (outside its scope), or whether unreported non-significant results would change the counts (blanks in Table 3 mean not tested or not reported).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Included trials (Table 2) recruited people who smoked, mostly at least 10 cigarettes a day and wanting to stop; three included volunteers not necessarily wanting to stop (Schneider et al., 1984; Fagerstrom et al., 1993; Lunell et al., 1995) and one smokers waiting to join a clinic (West et al., 1984).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Published randomized trials with a placebo control; product started within 24 hours of the start of abstinence; symptoms assessed over at least 24 hours in the usual environment; a sample stated to be abstinent or nearly so; biochemical verification. All included trials excluded people with psychiatric or acute physical illness or on psychotropic medicines, and mostly included moderate to heavy smoking (p. 116).
sample.demographics: Not reported (Table 2 gives no age or sex).
sample.attrition: Per trial in Table 2, from 1 to 140 people dropped (for example 44 in Gross & Stitzer, 1989, with 40 analysed; 140 in Schneider et al., 1996, with 83 analysed); more dropouts on placebo in three trials (Gross & Stitzer, 1989; Hughes et al., 1991; Schneider et al., 1996).
sample.selection_effects: Published trials only. Lapsers were kept in the analyses in 5 of the 12 trials (Table 2), although the text says most trials included partially abstinent people (reporting issue 1).

exposure.measurement: Assigned product, nicotine against placebo; product use recorded in most trials (Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Table 2): 2 mg gum in the gum trials (Hughes et al., 1990, also tested 0.5 and 4 mg; West et al., 1984, compared 2 mg with 0.5 mg), about 6 to 12 pieces a day; inhaler about 6 to 11 a day; one sublingual tablet trial. The authors note that use was typically below the recommended level, except in the tablet trial (p. 120). Oral route; first week of abstinence.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: From the quit day; biochemical verification required, but lapsers were kept in five trials.

comparison.controls: Placebo gum, inhaler or tablet; in West et al. (1984) 0.5 mg gum served as the comparator for 2 mg gum (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Randomized; three crossover or within-person trials (Fagerstrom et al., 1993; Lunell et al., 1995; Molander et al., 2000).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (randomized).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: Symptom ratings of several kinds: 4-point severity ratings (Hughes et al.), the Smoker Complaint Scale, Profile of Mood States, visual analogue scales, 5-point mood and physical symptom ratings; craving as urges, desire or missing cigarettes (Table 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: No measure preferred; the authors note that craving ratings fell after quitting in some trials, which suggests measurement problems (p. 120).
outcomes.operationalization: A trial counts as positive for a symptom if it reported a significant difference from placebo in the first week (Table 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; nine symptom columns.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Placebo products; blinding integrity not assessed.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Fractions of trials with a significant effect in the first week (Table 3): irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2, hunger 2/5, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11 (gum 3/7; inhaler 3/3; tablet 1/1). No differences by date, size, inclusion of lapsers, use of baselines or product use (p. 117).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Blanks in Table 3 combine not tested and not reported, so trials may have measured symptoms without reporting null results.
analysis.power: Trials of 15 to 240 people; the authors say any pattern across trials would have to be very marked to show (p. 117).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 12 small placebo-controlled trials, all 9 that reported irritability found less with oral nicotine, 6 of 7 less total withdrawal and 3 of 4 less anxiety; other symptoms were mixed, and craving was lower in all inhaler and tablet trials but in fewer than half of the gum trials.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the strength of evidence for total withdrawal discomfort, irritability and anxiety is high, and the Discussion concludes that oral nicotine dosing forms all reduce the severity of withdrawal (p. 121). Gaps: (1) counts of significant results without effect sizes cannot support a high strength of evidence; (2) anxiety rests on 4 trials; (3) all forms includes the lozenge, for which no trial was found; (4) blanks may hide unreported null results; (5) industry funding is not discussed.

timeline.event: Silagy et al., Cochrane review of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking; in it only 14 of 49 gum trials found significant effects on quitting, but pooling showed a clear effect (as described, p. 120).
This review.

replication.where_it_stands: An early systematic tabulation of withdrawal outcomes in oral nicotine replacement trials, giving directions without sizes. Later Cochrane reviews concern quitting, not withdrawal symptoms; a claim about the size of the effect on withdrawal needs trials that report effects.

funding.funder: SmithKline Beecham (Acknowledgements, p. 121).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement is printed, and the funder's role is not described.
funding.affiliations_note: St George's Hospital Medical School, London, and University of Pittsburgh. The first author is an author of one included trial (West et al., 1984).

what_would_settle_it: A meta-analysis of all placebo-controlled oral nicotine replacement trials that measured withdrawal, including unpublished manufacturers' data, reporting standardized effects for each symptom by day over the first month.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People abstaining from smoking, oral nicotine products, placebo, withdrawal symptoms and craving.
None mentioned.
Each criterion (placebo control, start within 24 hours, usual environment, abstinence, biochemical verification) is justified (p. 116).

Two databases with keywords, a Cochrane trials database, reference lists and colleagues, but no search dates, published trials only without a stated reason and no grey literature (item 4 applied as written, decision p-amstar2-item4).
Not described.
Not described.

No pooling (effect sizes and exact p values were not reported by the trials).

domains.note: Strength of evidence is called high without weighing the inclusion of lapsers, dropouts or possible unreported results.
Variation is discussed (small samples, measurement, product use below recommended levels) and study features are examined (pp. 117, 120).
No pooling; the risk is not discussed.

domains.note: Funding by SmithKline Beecham is acknowledged, but no competing interests are declared and their management is not described.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Critical items 2, 4, 9 and 13 are not met (7 is met; 11 and 15 do not apply without pooling), so confidence is critically low. The review is transparent in listing excluded studies and tabulating every included trial, which lets readers see the vote counts, but counts of significant results from small trials, some keeping people who smoked again, with blanks that may hide null results, cannot give the size or the certainty of an effect.

key_findings.finding: Of 27 studies reporting effects of oral nicotine products on at least one withdrawal symptom, 12 met the quality criteria: 8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet and none of the 1 mg lozenge; meta-analysis was not possible and good data existed only for the first week of abstinence.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 1st paragraph (p. 116)

key_findings.finding: Fractions of trials finding a significant effect in the first week: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2, hunger 2/5, total withdrawal discomfort 6/7, craving 7/11; included trials had 15 to 240 participants.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, bottom row and n column (read on the rendered, rotated page)

key_findings.finding: Craving was reduced in all three inhaler trials and the tablet trial but in only 3 of 7 gum trials.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 117); Table 3, craving column

key_findings.finding: Lapsers were kept in the withdrawal analyses in 5 of the 12 trials (Hughes et al., 1984, 1989, 1990, 1991; Gross & Stitzer, 1989), and more people dropped out of the placebo group in three trials.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Comments rows
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 2; the text says most studies included partially abstinent people (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: No differences in findings by date, study size, inclusion of lapsers, use of baselines or product use, with the caveat that the number of studies was small.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Product use was typically below the recommended level, except in the tablet trial; a study of gum use (Gross et al., 1995, excluded for having no placebo) found that more use did not mean less withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 117); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 120)

key_findings.finding: Blanks in Table 3 mean that the product's effect on a symptom was not tested (sometimes because the placebo group showed no change) or not reported.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, footnote b

key_findings.finding: Funded by SmithKline Beecham.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgements

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that in most studies people were included in the withdrawal analyses even if only partially abstinent, but Table 2 records lapsers included in 5 of 12 trials and excluded, or assumed or presumed excluded, in the other 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: The extent of contamination by smoking is smaller than the text implies, but still affects five trials, all of them gum trials.

reporting_issues.issue: Criterion 1 requires a placebo control, yet West et al. (1984), the first author's own trial, compared 2 mg with 0.5 mg gum.
reporting_issues.consequence: One included trial's comparator contained nicotine, which would bias it towards no difference; it found effects on irritability and depression.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 'Schneider and Jarvik (1985), Schneider et al. (1984)' as one row, while Table 2 lists only Schneider et al. (1984).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two reports of one sample; counted once, as intended, but the source of the result is ambiguous.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion says oral nicotine dosing forms all reduce withdrawal severity, although no trial of the 1 mg lozenge was found.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion extends to a product with no trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The search dates are not given, and Table 3 prints 'P<01' for one irritability result.
reporting_issues.consequence: The search cannot be reproduced or dated; the typographical error is minor.
